paragraphs:
“Poirot,” I said, “a change of air would do you good.”

“You think so, _mon ami_?”

“I am sure of it.”

“Eh—eh?” said my friend, smiling. “It is all arranged, then?”

“You will come?”

“Where do you propose to take me?”

“Brighton. As a matter of fact, a friend of mine in the City put
me on to a very good thing, and—well, I have money to burn, as the
saying goes. I think a week-end at the _Grand Metropolitan_ would
do us all the good in the world.”

“Thank you, I accept most gratefully. You have the good heart to
think of an old man. And the good heart, it is in the end worth
all the little grey cells. Yes, yes, I who speak to you am in
danger of forgetting that sometimes.”

I did not quite relish the implication. I fancy that Poirot is
sometimes a little inclined to underestimate my mental capacities.
But his pleasure was so evident that I put my slight annoyance
aside.

“Then, that’s all right,” I said hastily.

Saturday evening saw us dining at the _Grand Metropolitan_ in the
midst of a gay throng. All the world and his wife seemed to be at
Brighton. The dresses were marvellous, and the jewels—worn sometimes
with more love of display than good taste—were something magnificent.

“_Hein_, it is a sight this!” murmured Poirot. “This is the home
of the Profiteer, is it not so, Hastings?”

“Supposed to be,” I replied. “But we’ll hope they aren’t all tarred
with the Profiteering brush.”

Poirot gazed round him placidly.

“The sight of so many jewels makes me wish I had turned my brains
to crime, instead of to its detection. What a magnificent
opportunity for some thief of distinction! Regard, Hastings, that
stout woman by the pillar. She is, as you would say, plastered with
gems.”

I followed his eyes.

“Why,” I exclaimed, “it’s Mrs. Opalsen.”

“You know her?”

“Slightly. Her husband is a rich stockbroker who made a fortune in
the recent Oil boom.”

After dinner we ran across the Opalsens in the lounge, and I
introduced Poirot to them. We chatted for a few minutes, and ended
by having our coffee together.

Poirot said a few words in praise of some of the costlier gems
displayed on the lady’s ample bosom, and she brightened up at once.

“It’s a perfect hobby of mine, Mr. Poirot. I just _love_ jewellery.
Ed knows my weakness, and every time things go well he brings me
something new. You are interested in precious stones?”

“I have had a good deal to do with them one time and another,
madame. My profession has brought me into contact with some of the
most famous jewels in the world.”

He went on to narrate, with discreet pseudonyms, the story of the
historic jewels of a reigning house, and Mrs. Opalsen listened with
bated breath.

“There now!” she exclaimed, as he ended. “If it isn’t just like a
play! You know, I’ve got some pearls of my own that have a history
attached to them. I believe it’s supposed to be one of the finest
necklaces in the world—the pearls are so beautifully matched and
so perfect in colour. I declare I really must run up and get it!”

“Oh, madame,” protested Poirot, “you are too amiable. Pray do not
derange yourself!”

“Oh, but I’d like to show it to you.”

The buxom dame waddled across to the lift briskly enough. Her
husband, who had been talking to me, looked at Poirot inquiringly.

“Madame your wife is so amiable as to insist on showing me her
pearl necklace,” explained the latter.

“Oh, the pearls!” Opalsen smiled in a satisfied fashion. “Well,
they _are_ worth seeing. Cost a pretty penny too! Still, the
money’s there all right; I could get what I paid for them any
day—perhaps more. May have to, too, if things go on as they are
now. Money’s confoundedly tight in the City. All this infernal
E.P.D.” He rambled on, launching into technicalities where I could
not follow him.

He was interrupted by a small page-boy who approached and murmured
something in his ear.

“Eh—what? I’ll come at once. Not taken ill, is she? Excuse me,
gentlemen.”

He left us abruptly. Poirot leaned back and lit one of his tiny
Russian cigarettes. Then, carefully and meticulously, he arranged
the empty coffee-cups in a neat row, and beamed happily on the
result.

The minutes passed. The Opalsens did not return.

“Curious,” I remarked, at length. “I wonder when they will come
back.”

Poirot watched the ascending spirals of smoke, and then said
thoughtfully:

“They will not come back.”

“Why?”

“Because, my friend, something has happened.”

“What sort of thing? How do you know?” I asked curiously.

Poirot smiled.

“A few moments ago the manager came hurriedly out of his office
and ran upstairs. He was much agitated. The lift-boy is deep in
talk with one of the pages. The lift-bell has rung three times,
but he heeds it not. Thirdly, even the waiters are _distrait_; and
to make a waiter _distrait_——” Poirot shook his head with an air
of finality. “The affair must indeed be of the first magnitude.
Ah, it is as I thought! Here come the police.”

Two men had just entered the hotel—one in uniform, the other in
plain clothes. They spoke to a page, and were immediately ushered
upstairs. A few minutes later, the same boy descended and came up
to where we were sitting.

“Mr. Opalsen’s compliments, and would you step upstairs.”

Poirot sprang nimbly to his feet. One would have said that he
awaited the summons. I followed with no less alacrity.

The Opalsens’ apartments were situated on the first floor. After
knocking on the door, the page-boy retired, and we answered the
summons, “Come in!” A strange scene met our eyes. The room was Mrs.
Opalsen’s bedroom, and in the centre of it, lying back in an
arm-chair, was the lady herself, weeping violently. She presented
an extraordinary spectacle, with the tears making great furrows in
the powder with which her complexion was liberally coated. Mr.
Opalsen was striding up and down angrily. The two police officials
stood in the middle of the room, one with a notebook in hand. An
hotel chambermaid, looking frightened to death, stood by the
fire-place; and on the other side of the room a Frenchwoman,
obviously Mrs. Opalsen’s maid, was weeping and wringing her hands,
with an intensity of grief that rivalled that of her mistress.

Into this pandemonium stepped Poirot, neat and smiling. Immediately,
with an energy surprising in one of her bulk, Mrs. Opalsen sprang
from her chair towards him.

“There now; Ed may say what he likes, but I believe in luck, I do.
It was fated I should meet you the way I did this evening, and I’ve
a feeling that if you can’t get my pearls back for me nobody can.”

“Calm yourself, I pray of you, madame.” Poirot patted her hand
soothingly. “Reassure yourself. All will be well. Hercule Poirot
will aid you!”

Mr. Opalsen turned to the police inspector.

“There will be no objection to my—er—calling in this gentleman, I
suppose?”

“None at all, sir,” replied the man civilly, but with complete
indifference. “Perhaps now your lady’s feeling better she’ll just
let us have the facts?”

Mrs. Opalsen looked helplessly at Poirot. He led her back to her
chair.

“Seat yourself, madame, and recount to us the whole history without
agitating yourself.”

Thus abjured, Mrs. Opalsen dried her eyes gingerly, and began.

“I came upstairs after dinner to fetch my pearls for Mr. Poirot
here to see. The chambermaid and Célestine were both in the room
as usual——”

“Excuse me, madame, but what do you mean by ‘as usual’?”

Mr. Opalsen explained.

“I make it a rule that no one is to come into this room unless
Célestine, the maid, is there also. The chambermaid does the room
in the morning while Célestine is present, and comes in after
dinner to turn down the beds under the same conditions; otherwise
she never enters the room.”

“Well, as I was saying,” continued Mrs. Opalsen, “I came up. I went
to the drawer here,”—she indicated the bottom right-hand drawer of
the knee-hole dressing-table—“took out my jewel-case and unlocked
it. It seemed quite as usual—but the pearls were not there!”

The inspector had been busy with his notebook. “When had you last
seen them?” he asked.

“They were there when I went down to dinner.”

“You are sure?”

“Quite sure. I was uncertain whether to wear them or not, but in
the end I decided on the emeralds, and put them back in the
jewel-case.”

“Who locked up the jewel-case?”

“I did. I wear the key on a chain round my neck.” She held it up
as she spoke.

The inspector examined it, and shrugged his shoulders.

“The thief must have had a duplicate key. No difficult matter. The
lock is quite a simple one. What did you do after you’d locked the
jewel-case?”

“I put it back in the bottom drawer where I always keep it.”

“You didn’t lock the drawer?”

“No, I never do. My maid remains in the room till I come up, so
there’s no need.”

The inspector’s face grew graver.

“Am I to understand that the jewels were there when you went down
to dinner, and that since then _the maid has not left the room_?”

Suddenly, as though the horror of her own situation for the first
time burst upon her, Célestine uttered a piercing shriek, and,
flinging herself upon Poirot, poured out a torrent of incoherent
French.

The suggestion was infamous! That she should be suspected of
robbing Madame! The police were well known to be of a stupidity
incredible! But Monsieur, who was a Frenchman—

“A Belgian,” interjected Poirot, but Célestine paid no attention
to the correction.

Monsieur would not stand by and see her falsely accused, while that
infamous chambermaid was allowed to go scot-free. She had never
liked her—a bold, red-faced thing—a born thief. She had said from
the first that she was not honest. And had kept a sharp watch over
her too, when she was doing Madame’s room! Let those idiots of
policemen search her, and if they did not find Madame’s pearls on
her it would be very surprising!

Although this harangue was uttered in rapid and virulent French,
Célestine had interlarded it with a wealth of gesture, and the
chambermaid realized at least a part of her meaning. She reddened
angrily.

“If that foreign woman’s saying I took the pearls, it’s a lie!”
she declared heatedly. “I never so much as saw them.”

“Search her!” screamed the other. “You will find it is as I say.”

“You’re a liar—do you hear?” said the chambermaid, advancing upon
her. “Stole ’em yourself, and want to put it on me. Why, I was only
in the room about three minutes before the lady come up, and then
you were sitting here the whole time, as you always do, like a cat
watching a mouse.”

The inspector looked across inquiringly at Célestine. “Is that
true? Didn’t you leave the room at all?”

“I did not actually leave her alone,” admitted Célestine reluctantly,
“but I went into my own room through the door here twice—once to
fetch a reel of cotton, and once for my scissors. She must have
done it then.”

“You wasn’t gone a minute,” retorted the chambermaid angrily. “Just
popped out and in again. I’d be glad if the police _would_ search
me. _I’ve nothing to be afraid of_.”

At this moment there was a tap at the door. The inspector went to
it. His face brightened when he saw who it was.

“Ah!” he said. “That’s rather fortunate. I sent for one of our
female searchers, and she’s just arrived. Perhaps if you wouldn’t
mind going into the room next door.”

He looked at the chambermaid, who stepped across the threshold with
a toss of her head, the searcher following her closely.

The French girl had sunk sobbing into a chair. Poirot was looking
round the room, the main features of which I have made clear by a
sketch.

[A sketch of the bedroom, adjoining maid's room, and corridor.]

“Where does that door lead?” he inquired, nodding his head towards
the one by the window.

“Into the next apartment, I believe,” said the inspector. “It’s
bolted, anyway, on this side.”

Poirot walked across to it, tried it, then drew back the bolt and
tried it again.

“And on the other side as well,” he remarked. “Well, that seems to
rule out that.”

He walked over to the windows, examining each of them in turn.

“And again—nothing. Not even a balcony outside.”

“Even if there were,” said the inspector impatiently, “I don’t see
how that would help us, if the maid never left the room.”

“_Évidemment_,” said Poirot, not disconcerted. “As Mademoiselle is
positive she did not leave the room——”

He was interrupted by the reappearance of the chambermaid and the
police searcher.

“Nothing,” said the latter laconically.

“I should hope not, indeed,” said the chambermaid virtuously. “And
that French hussy ought to be ashamed of herself taking away an
honest girl’s character!”

“There, there, my girl; that’s all right,” said the inspector,
opening the door. “Nobody suspects you. You go along and get on
with your work.”

The chambermaid went unwillingly.

“Going to search _her_?” she demanded, pointing at Célestine.

“Yes, yes!” He shut the door on her and turned the key.

Célestine accompanied the searcher into the small room in her turn.
A few minutes later she also returned. Nothing had been found on
her.

The inspector’s face grew graver.

“I’m afraid I’ll have to ask you to come along with me all the
same, miss.” He turned to Mrs. Opalsen. “I’m sorry, madam, but all
the evidence points that way. If she’s not got them on her, they’re
hidden somewhere about the room.”

Célestine uttered a piercing shriek, and clung to Poirot’s arm.
The latter bent and whispered something in the girl’s ear. She
looked up at him doubtfully.

“_Si, si, mon enfant_—I assure you it is better not to resist.”
Then he turned to the inspector. “You permit, monsieur? A little
experiment—purely for my own satisfaction.”

“Depends on what it is,” replied the police officer non-committally.

Poirot addressed Célestine once more.

“You have told us that you went into your room to fetch a reel of
cotton. Whereabouts was it?”

“On the top of the chest of drawers, monsieur.”

“And the scissors?”

“They also.”

“Would it be troubling you too much, mademoiselle, to ask you to
repeat those two actions? You were sitting here with your work,
you say?”

Célestine sat down, and then, at a sign from Poirot, rose, passed
into the adjoining room, took up an object from the chest of
drawers, and returned.

Poirot divided his attention between her movements and a large
turnip of a watch which he held in the palm of his hand.

“Again, if you please, mademoiselle.”

At the conclusion of the second performance, he made a note in his
pocket-book, and returned the watch to his pocket.

“Thank you, mademoiselle. And you, monsieur,”—he bowed to the
inspector—“for your courtesy.”

The inspector seemed somewhat entertained by this excessive
politeness. Célestine departed in a flood of tears, accompanied by
the woman and the plain-clothes official.

Then, with a brief apology to Mrs. Opalsen, the inspector set to
work to ransack the room. He pulled out drawers, opened cupboards,
completely unmade the bed, and tapped the floor. Mr. Opalsen looked
on sceptically.

“You really think you will find them?”

“Yes, sir. It stands to reason. She hadn’t time to take them out
of the room. The lady’s discovering the robbery so soon upset her
plans. No, they’re here right enough. One of the two must have
hidden them—and it’s very unlikely for the chambermaid to have done
so.”

“More than unlikely—impossible!” said Poirot quietly.

“Eh?” The inspector stared.

Poirot smiled modestly.

“I will demonstrate. Hastings, my good friend, take my watch in
your hand—with care. It is a family heirloom! Just now I timed
Mademoiselle’s movements—her first absence from the room was of
twelve seconds, her second of fifteen. Now observe my actions.
Madame will have the kindness to give me the key of the jewel-case.
I thank you. My friend Hastings will have the kindness to say
‘Go!’”

“Go!” I said.

With almost incredible swiftness, Poirot wrenched open the drawer
of the dressing-table, extracted the jewel-case, fitted the key in
the lock, opened the case, selected a piece of jewellery, shut and
locked the case, and returned it to the drawer, which he pushed to
again. His movements were like lightning.

“Well, _mon ami_?” he demanded of me breathlessly.

“Forty-six seconds,” I replied.

“You see?” He looked round. “There would not have been time for
the chambermaid even to take the necklace out, far less hide it.”

“Then that settles it on the maid,” said the inspector with
satisfaction, and returned to his search. He passed into the maid’s
bedroom next door.

Poirot was frowning thoughtfully. Suddenly he shot a question at
Mr. Opalsen.

“This necklace—it was, without doubt, insured?”

Mr. Opalsen looked a trifle surprised at the question.

“Yes,” he said hesitatingly, “that is so.”

“But what does that matter?” broke in Mrs. Opalsen tearfully. “It’s
my necklace I want. It was unique. No money could be the same.”

“I comprehend, madame,” said Poirot soothingly. “I comprehend
perfectly. To _la femme_ sentiment is everything—is it not so? But
monsieur, who has not the so fine susceptibility, will doubtless
find some slight consolation in the fact.”

“Of course, of course,” said Mr. Opalsen rather uncertainly.
“Still——”

He was interrupted by a shout of triumph from the inspector. He
came in dangling something from his fingers.

With a cry, Mrs. Opalsen heaved herself up from her chair. She was
a changed woman.

“Oh, oh, my necklace!”

She clasped it to her breast with both hands. We crowded round.

“Where was it?” demanded Opalsen.

“Maid’s bed. In among the springs of the wire mattress. She must
have stolen it and hidden it there before the chambermaid arrived
on the scene.”

“You permit, madame?” said Poirot gently. He took the necklace from
her and examined it closely; then handed it back with a bow.

“I’m afraid, madam, you’ll have to hand it over to us for the time
being,” said the inspector. “We shall want it for the charge. But
it shall be returned to you as soon as possible.”

Mr. Opalsen frowned.

“Is that necessary?”

“I’m afraid so, sir. Just a formality.”

“Oh, let him take it, Ed!” cried his wife. “I’d feel safer if he
did. I shouldn’t sleep a wink thinking some one else might try and
get hold of it. That wretched girl! And I would never have believed
it of her.”

“There, there, my dear, don’t take on so.”

I felt a gentle pressure on my arm. It was Poirot.

“Shall we slip away, my friend? I think our services are no longer
needed.”

Once outside, however, he hesitated, and then, much to my surprise,
he remarked:

“I should rather like to see the room next door.”

The door was not locked, and we entered. The room, which was a
large double one, was unoccupied. Dust lay about rather noticeably,
and my sensitive friend gave a characteristic grimace as he ran
his finger round a rectangular mark on a table near the window.

“The _service_ leaves to be desired,” he observed dryly.

He was staring thoughtfully out of the window, and seemed to have
fallen into a brown study.

“Well?” I demanded impatiently. “What did we come in here for?”

He started.

“_Je vous demande pardon, mon ami_. I wished to see if the door
was really bolted on this side also.”

“Well,” I said, glancing at the door which communicated with the
room we had just left, “it _is_ bolted.”

Poirot nodded. He still seemed to be thinking.

“And, anyway,” I continued, “what does it matter? The case is over.
I wish you’d had more chance of distinguishing yourself. But it
was the kind of case that even a stiff-backed idiot like that
inspector couldn’t go wrong over.”

Poirot shook his head.

“The case is not over, my friend. It will not be over until we find
out who stole the pearls.”

“But the maid did!”

“Why do you say that?”

“Why,” I stammered, “they were found—actually in her mattress.”

“Ta, ta, ta!” said Poirot impatiently. “Those were not the pearls.”

“What?”

“Imitation, _mon ami_.”

The statement took my breath away. Poirot was smiling placidly.

“The good inspector obviously knows nothing of jewels. But presently
there will be a fine hullabaloo!”

“Come!” I cried, dragging at his arm.

“Where?”

“We must tell the Opalsens at once.”

“I think not.”

“But that poor woman——”

“_Eh bien_; that poor woman, as you call her, will have a much
better night believing the jewels to be safe.”

“But the thief may escape with them!”

“As usual, my friend, you speak without reflection. How do you know
that the pearls Mrs. Opalsen locked up so carefully to-night were
not the false ones, and that the real robbery did not take place
at a much earlier date?”

“Oh!” I said, bewildered.

“Exactly,” said Poirot, beaming. “We start again.”

He led the way out of the room, paused a moment as though
considering, and then walked down to the end of the corridor,
stopping outside the small den where the chambermaids and valets
of the respective floors congregated. Our particular chambermaid
appeared to be holding a small court there, and to be retailing
her late experiences to an appreciative audience. She stopped in
the middle of a sentence. Poirot bowed with his usual politeness.

“Excuse that I derange you, but I shall be obliged if you will
unlock for me the door of Mr. Opalsen’s room.”

The woman rose willingly, and we accompanied her down the passage
again. Mr. Opalsen’s room was on the other side of the corridor,
its door facing that of his wife’s room. The chambermaid unlocked
it with her pass-key, and we entered.

As she was about to depart Poirot detained her.

“One moment; have you ever seen among the effects of Mr. Opalsen
a card like this?”

He held out a plain white card, rather highly glazed and uncommon
in appearance. The maid took it and scrutinized it carefully.

“No, sir, I can’t say I have. But, anyway, the valet has most to
do with the gentlemen’s rooms.”

“I see. Thank you.”

Poirot took back the card. The woman departed. Poirot appeared to
reflect a little. Then he gave a short, sharp nod of the head.

“Ring the bell, I pray of you, Hastings. Three times, for the
valet.”

I obeyed, devoured with curiosity. Meanwhile Poirot had emptied
the waste-paper-basket on the floor, and was swiftly going through
its contents.

In a few moments the valet answered the bell. To him Poirot put
the same question, and handed him the card to examine. But the
response was the same. The valet had never seen a card of that
particular quality among Mr. Opalsen’s belongings. Poirot thanked
him, and he withdrew, somewhat unwillingly, with an inquisitive
glance at the overturned waste-paper-basket and the litter on the
floor. He could hardly have helped overhearing Poirot’s thoughtful
remark as he bundled the torn papers back again:

“And the necklace was heavily insured. . . .”

“Poirot,” I cried,  “I see——”

“You see nothing, my friend,” he replied quickly. “As usual,
nothing at all! It is incredible—but there it is. Let us return to
our own apartments.”

We did so in silence. Once there, to my intense surprise, Poirot
effected a rapid change of clothing.

“I go to London to-night,” he explained. “It is imperative.”

“What?”

“Absolutely. The real work, that of the brain (ah, those brave
little grey cells), it is done. I go to seek the confirmation. I
shall find it! Impossible to deceive Hercule Poirot!”

“You’ll come a cropper one of these days,” I observed, rather
disgusted by his vanity.

“Do not be enraged, I beg of you, _mon ami_. I count on you to do
me a service—of your friendship.”

“Of course,” I said eagerly, rather ashamed of my moroseness. “What
is it?”

“The sleeve of my coat that I have taken off—will you brush it?
See you, a little white powder has clung to it. You without doubt
observed me run my finger round the drawer of the dressing-table?”

“No, I didn’t.”

“You should observe my actions, my friend. Thus I obtained the
powder on my finger, and, being a little over-excited, I rubbed it
on my sleeve; an action without method which I deplore—false to
all my principles.”

“But what was the powder?” I asked, not particularly interested in
Poirot’s principles.

“Not the poison of the Borgias,” replied Poirot, with a twinkle.
“I see your imagination mounting. I should say it was French
chalk.”

“French chalk?”

“Yes, cabinet-makers use it to make drawers run smoothly.”

I laughed.

“You old sinner! I thought you were working up to something
exciting.”

“Au revoir, my friend. I save myself. I fly!”

The door shut behind him. With a smile, half of derision, half of
affection, I picked up the coat, and stretched out my hand for the
clothes-brush.


  •   •   •   •   •   •   •

The next morning, hearing nothing from Poirot, I went out for a
stroll, met some old friends, and lunched with them at their hotel.
In the afternoon we went for a spin. A punctured tyre delayed us,
and it was past eight when I got back to the _Grand Metropolitan_.

The first sight that met my eyes was Poirot, looking even more
diminutive than usual, sandwiched between the Opalsens, beaming in
a state of placid satisfaction.

“_Mon ami_ Hastings!” he cried, and sprang to meet me. “Embrace
me, my friend; all has marched to a marvel!”

Luckily, the embrace was merely figurative—not a thing one is
always sure of with Poirot.

“Do you mean——” I began.

“Just wonderful, I call it!” said Mrs. Opalsen, smiling all over
her fat face. “Didn’t I tell you, Ed, that if he couldn’t get back
my pearls nobody would?”

“You did, my dear, you did. And you were right.”

I looked helplessly at Poirot, and he answered the glance.

“My friend Hastings is, as you say in England, all at the seaside.
Seat yourself, and I will recount to you all the affair that has
so happily ended.”

“Ended?”

“But yes. They are arrested.”

“Who are arrested?”

“The chambermaid and the valet, _parbleu_! You did not suspect?
Not with my parting hint about the French chalk?”

“You said cabinet-makers used it.”

“Certainly they do—to make drawers slide easily. Somebody wanted
that drawer to slide in and out without any noise. Who could that
be? Obviously, only the chambermaid. The plan was so ingenious that
it did not at once leap to the eye—not even to the eye of Hercule
Poirot.

“Listen, this was how it was done. The valet was in the empty room
next door, waiting. The French maid leaves the room. Quick as a
flash the chambermaid whips open the drawer, takes out the
jewel-case, and, slipping back the bolt, passes it through the
door. The valet opens it at his leisure with the duplicate key with
which he has provided himself, extracts the necklace, and waits
his time. Célestine leaves the room again, and—pst!—in a flash the
case is passed back again and replaced in the drawer.

“Madame arrives, the theft is discovered. The chambermaid demands
to be searched, with a good deal of righteous indignation, and
leaves the room without a stain on her character. The imitation
necklace with which they have provided themselves has been concealed
in the French girl’s bed that morning by the chambermaid—a master
stroke, _ça!_”

“But what did you go to London for?”

“You remember the card?”

“Certainly. It puzzled me—and puzzles me still. I thought——”

I hesitated delicately, glancing at Mr. Opalsen.

Poirot laughed heartily.

“_Une blague!_ For the benefit of the valet. The card was one with
a specially prepared surface—for finger-prints. I went straight
to Scotland Yard, asked for our old friend Inspector Japp, and laid
the facts before him. As I had suspected, the finger-prints proved
to be those of two well-known jewel thieves who have been ‘wanted’
for some time. Japp came down with me, the thieves were arrested,
and the necklace was discovered in the valet’s possession. A clever
pair, but they failed in _method_. Have I not told you, Hastings,
at least thirty-six times, that without method——”

“At least thirty-six thousand times!” I interrupted. “But where
did their ‘method’ break down?”

“_Mon ami_, it is a good plan to take a place as chambermaid or
valet—but you must not shirk your work. They left an empty room
undusted; and therefore, when the man put down the jewel-case on
the little table near the communicating door, it left a square
mark——”

“I remember,” I cried.

“Before, I was undecided. Then—I _knew_!” There was a moment’s
silence.

“And I’ve got my pearls,” said Mrs. Opalsen as a sort of Greek
chorus.

“Well,” I said, “I’d better have some dinner.” Poirot accompanied
me.

“This ought to mean kudos for you,” I observed.

“_Pas du tout_,” replied Poirot tranquilly. “Japp and the local
inspector will divide the credit between them. But”—he tapped his
pocket—“I have a cheque here, from Mr. Opalsen, and, how say you,
my friend? This week-end has not gone according to plan. Shall we
return here next week-end—at my expense this time?”

first_paras:
“Brighton. As a matter of fact, a friend of mine in the City put
me on to a very good thing, and—well, I have money to burn, as the
saying goes. I think a week-end at the _Grand Metropolitan_ would
do us all the good in the world.”

We arrived at the *Grand Metropolitan* on a Saturday afternoon. The hotel was crowded, and the air was thick with the scent of expensive perfume and the hum of polite conversation. It was during dinner that our attention was first drawn to a couple at an adjacent table. The man was large and florid, with a heavy gold watch chain across his waistcoat; the woman, stout and somewhat overdressed, was literally ablaze with jewels. Poirot, his head slightly to one side, watched them with the peculiar intensity that always marked his interest in human nature. "Observe, Hastings," he whispered, "the good lady carries a small fortune upon her person. It is not prudent, perhaps, but it is certainly magnificent."

The Grand Metropolitan was crowded, as it always is in the height of the season. We were sitting in the lounge after dinner, sipping our coffee, when Poirot's eyes were suddenly caught by a couple at a nearby table. The man was large and florid, wearing a dinner jacket that seemed a trifle too tight, while his companion—a woman of generous proportions—was literally ablaze with diamonds. It was Mr. and Mrs. Opalsen, whom I had met once or twice in the City, and it was not long before they noticed us and came over to join us.

We arrived at the *Grand Metropolitan* on Friday evening in time for dinner. The hotel was crowded, mostly with a flamboyant, moneyed set that seemed to fascinate and slightly repel Poirot at the same time. As we sat in the opulent lounge afterward, sipping our coffee, my friend’s eyes traveled continually from the over-gilded ceiling to the extravagant displays of jewelry worn by the ladies seated around us. He seemed particularly interested in a stout, florid woman a few tables away, whose neck and bosom were literally ablaze with diamonds.

The Grand Metropolitan was crowded, as it usually is on a Saturday. We had a table in a corner of the dining-room, and we were able to observe our fellow-guests at leisure. To my left sat a middle-aged man of somewhat florid appearance, accompanied by a woman who, though clearly past her first youth, was still handsome in a bold, over-dressed fashion. She was literally encrusted with jewels—diamonds, rubies, and emeralds sparkled upon her fingers and bosom. Poirot’s eyes returned to them again and again with a look of intense interest that I found rather singular.

Saturday evening found us comfortably installed at the Grand Metropolitan. The dining room was crowded, but Poirot’s keen eyes were already busy surveying the assembly. My friend has a penchant for people-watching that borders on the professional. “Observe, Hastings,” he murmured, indicating a table nearby. “The stout gentleman with the very red face and the lady who is, as you say, ‘bejewelled.’ One does not often see such magnificent pearls outside of a museum. It is Mr. and Mrs. Opalsen. He is a man of the stocks and shares, very rich, and very proud of his acquisitions.”

Saturday evening saw us dining at the _Grand Metropolitan_ in the
midst of a gay throng. All the world and his wife seemed to be at
Brighton. The dresses were marvellous, and the jewels—worn sometimes
with more love of display than good taste—were something magnificent.

“_Hein_, it is a sight this!” murmured Poirot. “This is the home
of the Profiteer, is it not so, Hastings?”

“Supposed to be,” I replied. “But we’ll hope they aren’t all tarred
with the Profiteering brush.”

Poirot gazed round him placidly.

“There are pearls,” said Mrs. Opalsen, nodding her head with a satisfied air. “I suppose you have seen many of the finest in the world, Mr. Poirot? But I have some myself that are not to be despised. They are upstairs now—I do not like to wear them in the dining-room for fear of some accident—but I would be delighted to show them to you. My maid, Célestine, is looking after them at this moment. She is very devoted to me, and I never leave my jewels without her or my husband being in the room.”

“There’s one thing I must show you,” she cried. “The most beautiful pearls you ever saw! I’ve got them with me here. I don’t believe in leaving them at the bank, though Ed says it’s risky. I keep them in a little jewel-case, and I always take them about with me. I’ll go and get them now, and you shall see them.”

“Oh, Ed, isn’t he a dear?” she added, as she rose, addressing her husband.

Mr. Opalsen beamed on us both.

“My wife is a regular child about her toys,” he said. “But they are good pearls. I gave five hundred for them only last week. A bargain, too!”

“There’s one thing I must show you,” she said, leaning forward. “My pearls. They really are quite exceptional. Ed bought them for me last year—it was the time of the North-East Petroleum merger—and I don’t believe there’s a finer string in the country.” She glanced at her husband. “Isn't that so, Ed?” Mr. Opalsen nodded with a satisfied air, puffing at his cigar. “They cost a pretty penny, I can tell you that. I believe in buying the best. If you're going to have pearls, have 'em big and have 'em matched.”

“There is one piece in particular,” Mr. Opalsen remarked, leaning back and puffing contentedly at his cigar, “that I am rather proud of. A necklace of pearls, Mr. Poirot. I don’t suppose you’ve seen many to beat it. I gave a cool five-and-twenty thousand for it only last month.” His wife nodded her agreement with enthusiasm. “It is a truly beautiful thing, is it not, Ed? I must show it to you, Mr. Poirot. It is upstairs in my jewel-case. Célestine, my maid, is looking after it at this very moment. She is a most devoted creature, a French girl, and I never let the case out of her sight when we are traveling.”

“There’s one thing I must show you,” cried Mrs. Opalsen, her face beaming with pride. “Ed gave it to me only last month for our wedding anniversary. It’s a string of pearls—quite unique. Even the experts say they’ve never seen such a lustre.” She leaned forward confidentially. “I have them with me here. I don’t believe in leaving my best things at home in a safe; I like to wear them. Would you like to see them, Mr. Poirot?”

“There now!” she exclaimed, as he ended. “If it isn’t just like a
play! You know, I’ve got some pearls of my own that have a history
attached to them. I believe it’s supposed to be one of the finest
necklaces in the world—the pearls are so beautifully matched and
so perfect in colour. I declare I really must run up and get it!”

“Oh, madame,” protested Poirot, “you are too amiable. Pray do not
derange yourself!”

“Oh, but I’d like to show it to you.”

The buxom dame waddled across to the lift briskly enough. Her
husband, who had been talking to me, looked at Poirot inquiringly.

“Madame your wife is so amiable as to insist on showing me her
pearl necklace,” explained the latter.

He had been gone but a few minutes when he reappeared, his face a mask of agitation. He beckoned to us urgently, and we rose and joined him. “The pearls!” he gasped. “They have been stolen!” Poirot’s eyes gave a sudden flash, the only sign of the keen interest that possessed him. Without a word, we followed the distracted man to the lift. On the second floor, he led the way to their suite. In the doorway stood a dark-haired girl, her face blanched with terror, sobbing into a handkerchief. This, I gathered, was Célestine, the lady’s maid. Inside the room, Mrs. Opalsen was collapsed in an armchair, while a frightened-looking chambermaid stood by the window, nervously twisting the ends of her white apron.

He hurried away in the direction of the lift. Poirot’s eyes followed him, a curious expression on his face. “One senses a drama, Hastings,” he remarked, lighting one of his tiny cigarettes. We waited for several minutes, Poirot appearing perfectly composed, while I, I must admit, felt a growing sense of unease. It was not long before Mr. Opalsen reappeared, but his previous air of self-satisfaction had vanished completely. He stumbled toward us, his face a pasty white. “The pearls!” he gasped, clutching at Poirot’s sleeve. “They’re gone! My wife is nearly out of her mind!”

He followed the boy, his face betraying a sudden anxiety. Poirot and I looked at each other. Scarcely two minutes had elapsed before the page reappeared, breathless, and beckoned to us. 

“Mr. Opalsen’s compliments, sir, and would you and the other gentleman come upstairs at once? Room 417.”

We followed him without a word. In the corridor on the fourth floor, we found Mr. Opalsen pacing up and down. His face was no longer satisfied; it was a mottled purple. Inside the room, through the open door, I could hear the sound of violent sobbing.

He strode away, leaving Poirot and me to exchange a glance of surprise. My friend sat back, delicately adjusting the symmetry of a matchbox on the table, his eyes narrowed as he watched the lift. “An interruption, Hastings,” he murmured. “I wonder if the jewels of madame have a more exciting history than we anticipated?” We were not left long in suspense. Scarcely three minutes had passed before Mr. Opalsen reappeared, his face a pale, sickly colour and his hands twitching with suppressed excitement. He beckoned to us urgently. “Come upstairs at once!” he cried in a choked voice. “A terrible thing has happened. The pearls—the pearls are gone!”

He had been gone no more than a few minutes when he reappeared, his face a curious shade of grey and his hands shaking with agitation. “The pearls!” he gasped, clutching Poirot by the arm. “They’re gone! My wife is nearly frantic. They’ve been stolen from right under our very noses in the middle of this crowded hotel! Come up, I beg of you—the police must be sent for, but I want you there first!”

He left us abruptly. Poirot leaned back and lit one of his tiny
Russian cigarettes. Then, carefully and meticulously, he arranged
the empty coffee-cups in a neat row, and beamed happily on the
result.

The minutes passed. The Opalsens did not return.

“Curious,” I remarked, at length. “I wonder when they will come
back.”

Poirot watched the ascending spirals of smoke, and then said
thoughtfully:

“They will not come back.”

“Why?”

“Because, my friend, something has happened.”

“What sort of thing? How do you know?” I asked curiously.

Poirot smiled.

Two men in plain clothes entered and were at once conducted upstairs by the perturbed manager. A few minutes later, Mr. Opalsen reappeared. He was gasping for breath and his face was a bright beet-red. He looked about him, spotted us, and waddled in our direction as fast as his short legs would carry him. “Monsieur Poirot!” he wheezed. “A most terrible thing! The pearls—my wife’s pearls! They have been stolen!”

Two men in plain clothes, accompanied by a uniformed inspector, passed rapidly through the lounge and headed for the stairs, their presence casting a sudden, chilling shadow over the festive atmosphere. A moment later, Mr. Opalsen reappeared; his face was a mottled purple, and he stumbled toward us, his breath coming in short, ragged gasps. “It’s gone!” he cried out, oblivious to the curious stares of the surrounding diners. “The necklace—the pearls! Stolen right from the jewel-case! My wife is in a state of collapse, and her maid, Célestine, is doing nothing but shriek in French. The police are up there now, but what can they do? It is a disaster—a total disaster!”

Two men in plain clothes entered and were at once conducted upstairs by the manager, followed shortly by a visibly distraught Mr. Opalsen who hurried toward us, his usual composure shattered. "It’s gone!" he gasped, leaning heavily on our table; "the pearls—the necklace I was just telling you about—it’s been stolen! My wife went up to the room, and the jewel case was empty; she is in a state of complete collapse." Poirot rose with his accustomed deliberation, his eyes shining with that peculiar green light that signified his interest was fully aroused. "This is most distressing, Mr. Opalsen," he said smoothly, "and if it would not be considered an intrusion, I should like to offer my humble services in this matter." Opalsen seized his arm with relief, and together we hurried toward the lift, Poirot’s face a mask of placid contemplation as we ascended to the scene of the crime.

Two men in plain clothes, followed by the manager, disappeared into the lift. Poirot rose with alacrity. I followed him. We were just in time to be hemmed into the lift by a party of gay evening-dress folk. We stepped out on the third floor, and made our way along the corridor towards the Opalsens’ suite. A little knot of people were gathered outside the door. Mr. Opalsen was there, looking much distressed. A maid in a black dress was weeping copiously, and a younger woman, who appeared to be a hotel chambermaid, stood by, looking scared and white-faced.

Two men in plain clothes were indeed crossing the lounge toward the stairs. A moment later, Mr. Opalsen reappeared. He was no longer the smug, successful stockbroker of a few minutes ago. His face was ashen, and he walked with the uncertain gait of a man who has received a physical blow. He made straight for us, his breath coming in short, jagged gasps. “Poirot!” he cried. “It’s gone! The necklace! The whole case has been rifled!”

Two men had just entered the hotel—one in uniform, the other in
plain clothes. They spoke to a page, and were immediately ushered
upstairs. A few minutes later, the same boy descended and came up
to where we were sitting.

“Mr. Opalsen’s compliments, and would you step upstairs.”

Poirot sprang nimbly to his feet. One would have said that he
awaited the summons. I followed with no less alacrity.

“Oh, Mr. Poirot! It is too awful! They are gone! My beautiful pearls! Stolen! Right out of my jewel case while I was downstairs at dinner! You must find them for me—you must, you must! I will pay any reward you care to name!” She clutched at his arm, her eyes wide with desperation. Her husband came forward to support her, adding in a gruff voice, “It is quite true, Mr. Poirot. The pearls have vanished. The case was locked, and the key was in my wife’s handbag. When she came up just now to fetch them, the case was empty.”

“Oh, Mr. Poirot!” she cried. “They are gone! My beautiful pearls! Stolen! Right from my very dressing-table! You must find them for me—you must! I’ve told the police, but they don’t seem to know a thing. It’s a perfect scandal!” Poirot took her hand and patted it soothingly. “Calm yourself, I pray of you, madame. Reassure yourself. All that can be done, shall be done. And now, let us have the facts of the case, as quickly and as simply as possible.”

“They’re gone, Mr. Poirot! My pearls! My beautiful, beautiful pearls! Stolen! Right out of my jewel case!” Mr. Opalsen intervened, placing a steadying hand on her shoulder. “Calm yourself, Nellie, calm yourself. Mr. Poirot, the fact of the matter is that my wife’s pearls have disappeared. She came up to fetch them to show you, as she had promised, and found the case empty. The lock has not been tampered with, but the jewels have vanished into thin air.”

“They’re gone, Mr. Poirot! They’re gone! My beautiful pearls! Stolen! Right from under my very nose!” Poirot gently extricated himself from the lady’s grasp. “Calm yourself, I pray of you, madame. Let us see. It is the pearls that are missing?” “The necklace, the most beautiful in the world!” sobbed Mrs. Opalsen. “The drawer was forced, Mr. Poirot,” explained her husband, pointing to the dressing-table. “The jewel-case was inside, but when my wife opened it, she found it empty. The Inspector here is already making his inquiries.”

“Oh, M. Poirot!” she wailed, clutching at his arm. “They are gone! My beautiful, beautiful pearls! Stolen! Right from under my very nose!” Poirot took her hand and patted it soothingly, his eyes already darting about the room with a sharp, bird-like intensity. “Calm yourself, I pray of you, madame. Rest assured that we shall find them if it is humanly possible. Now, tell me exactly what has occurred.” Mr. Opalsen broke in, his face a mottled purple. “It’s an outrage, Poirot! My wife came up to get the necklace for you, and the jewel-case was empty—clean as a whistle! And the door was bolted from the inside, mind you, so how the devil anyone got in is beyond me!”

“There now; Ed may say what he likes, but I believe in luck, I do.
It was fated I should meet you the way I did this evening, and I’ve
a feeling that if you can’t get my pearls back for me nobody can.”

“Calm yourself, I pray of you, madame.” Poirot patted her hand
soothingly. “Reassure yourself. All will be well. Hercule Poirot
will aid you!”

Mr. Opalsen turned to the police inspector.

“There will be no objection to my—er—calling in this gentleman, I
suppose?”

“None at all, sir,” replied the man civilly, but with complete
indifference. “Perhaps now your lady’s feeling better she’ll just
let us have the facts?”

Mrs. Opalsen looked helplessly at Poirot. He led her back to her
chair.

“Seat yourself, madame, and recount to us the whole history without
agitating yourself.”

Thus abjured, Mrs. Opalsen dried her eyes gingerly, and began.

“I came upstairs after dinner to fetch my pearls for Mr. Poirot
here to see. The chambermaid and Célestine were both in the room
as usual——”

“Excuse me, madame, but what do you mean by ‘as usual’?”

Mr. Opalsen explained.

“I came in,” continued Mrs. Opalsen, “and, as I said, the two maids were both here. I went straight to the dressing-table, took my key—which I always carry in my evening bag—and unlocked the jewel-case. To my horror, it was empty! The pearls were gone—every single one of them! I screamed, and Ed came running, and then the manager, and then the police. Oh, my beautiful pearls! They were worth twenty thousand pounds if they were worth a penny!”

"I went straight to the dressing-table," Mrs. Opalsen continued, her voice trembling again. "The jewel-case was there, exactly as I had left it. I took my key from my bag, unlocked it, and—oh, it was horrible! The velvet lining was there, but the pearls, my beautiful pearls, were gone! I screamed, and Célestine here came running from the small room adjoining, and then Ed came in, and we found the chambermaid just about to leave. It's a miracle I didn't faint dead away!"

Mrs. Opalsen picked up her story. “I came in,” she said, “and there were Célestine and the chambermaid, just as Ed says. I went straight to the dressing-table, took my keys from my bag, and unlocked the middle drawer. I keep the jewel-case there. I pulled it out, but the moment I handled it, I knew something was wrong. It felt too light. I snapped it open—and it was empty! The pearls were gone! I think I must have shrieked, for Ed came running in almost at once, and then we sent for the manager and the police.”

“I came in,” Mrs. Opalsen continued, her voice trembling. “Célestine was folding away my evening wrap, and the chambermaid was just finishing the beds. I went straight to the dressing-table and unlocked the middle drawer with the key I keep in my silk bag. I took out the morocco case, but the moment I touched it, I knew something was wrong. It felt—how shall I say it?—too light! I snapped it open, and—oh, Mr. Poirot!—the pearls were gone! Nothing was left but the velvet lining!” She dissolved into a fresh paroxysm of grief.

"I came in," Mrs. Opalsen continued, her voice trembling, "and Célestine was at the wardrobe, while the chambermaid was just finishing the beds. I went straight to the dressing-table, unlocked the middle drawer with the key from my bag, and took out the jewel-case. It was light—too light! I snapped it open, and the pearls were gone! I tell you, I nearly fainted. I screamed for Célestine, and then Ed came running in from the sitting-room next door. It’s a nightmare, a positive nightmare!"

“Well, as I was saying,” continued Mrs. Opalsen, “I came up. I went
to the drawer here,”—she indicated the bottom right-hand drawer of
the knee-hole dressing-table—“took out my jewel-case and unlocked
it. It seemed quite as usual—but the pearls were not there!”

The inspector had been busy with his notebook. “When had you last
seen them?” he asked.

“They were there when I went down to dinner.”

“You are sure?”

“Quite sure. I was uncertain whether to wear them or not, but in
the end I decided on the emeralds, and put them back in the
jewel-case.”

“Who locked up the jewel-case?”

“I did. I wear the key on a chain round my neck.” She held it up
as she spoke.

The inspector examined it, and shrugged his shoulders.

“The thief must have had a duplicate key. No difficult matter. The
lock is quite a simple one. What did you do after you’d locked the
jewel-case?”

“I put it back in the bottom drawer where I always keep it.”

“You didn’t lock the drawer?”

“No, I never do. My maid remains in the room till I come up, so
there’s no need.”

The inspector’s face grew graver.

“Am I to understand that the jewels were there when you went down
to dinner, and that since then _the maid has not left the room_?”

“Monsieur, you see my position? I, who have been with Madame for
six years? You will clear my reputation? You will not allow them
to arrest me? Oh, Mon Dieu, that it should ever come to this!”

Poirot succeeded at last in calming the poor girl.

“There, there, my child. Tranquillise yourself. No one has yet
accused you of anything. The police, they are but looking into
the facts. Now, let us see. You were in this room when Madame
went down to dinner?”

“_Mais oui_, Monsieur. I was here with the chambermaid.”

“And you did not leave the room?”

“Not for one single moment.”

“And the chambermaid?”

“She was here also. We were occupied together with the beds of
Madame and Monsieur.”

“Did either of you go near the dressing-table?”

“_Mais non_, Monsieur. I was at the wardrobe, and she—she was
by the washstand.”

The chambermaid, a girl with a scared face and light-coloured
eyes, stepped forward.

“I never went near the table, sir—indeed I didn’t. I don’t know
nothing about it. I’m a respectable girl, I am.”

Poirot looked from one to the other of them.

“You both remained here until Madame returned?”

“Yes, Monsieur.”

“And no one else entered the room?”

“No one, Monsieur.”

Poirot turned to the inspector.

“It is a problem of the most interesting!” he murmured. “The pearls
were in the drawer when Madame went down to dinner. The drawer was
never left. Yet the pearls have vanished!”

The inspector looked at him with some suspicion.

“You’re sure they were there, ma’am?” he asked, turning to Mrs.
Opalsen.

“I’ve already said so. I saw them when I put my emeralds away.”

“And you locked the case?”

“Yes.”

“And kept the key?”

“Yes.”

The inspector sighed.

“It seems a bit of a puzzle. If these two didn’t take them, who
did? Are there any other doors?”

“Only the one into the corridor,” replied Mr. Opalsen. “And that’s
bolted on the inside.”

“What about the window?”

The inspector went across and examined it.

“First floor—too high for any one to get in that way. Besides, the
sash is down. No, it looks as though it must be one of these two.”

He looked significantly at Célestine and the chambermaid.

“I’d like to have a word with the manager,” he added.

“I’ll come with you,” said Mr. Opalsen.

The three men left the room. Mrs. Opalsen followed them, still
sobbing. Célestine and the chambermaid remained, looking at each
other with mutual distrust.

Poirot was left alone with me.

“What do you think of it, Poirot?” I asked.

He did not answer. He was down on his knees by the dressing-table,
examining the drawer from which the jewel-case had been taken.

“Hastings,” he said, looking up, “this is very curious. Look at
this drawer.”

I looked. To all appearances it was an ordinary drawer.

“Do you see anything?”

“Nothing.”

“Exactly. There is nothing to see. And yet—it is very curious!”

He got up and began to wander round the room.

“The pearls are not here,” he said, half to himself. “They have
gone. But where have they gone? And how? Ah, that is the question!”

He went over to the washstand and examined it. Then he went to the
wardrobe. Finally he went back to the dressing-table.

“Nothing!” he murmured. “Nothing! And yet——”

He stopped and looked at the two women.

“You,” he said to Célestine, “how long have you been with Madame?”

“Six years, Monsieur.”

“And you?” he asked the chambermaid.

“Three months, sir.”

“You like your place?”

“Yes, sir.”

“Have you ever been in any trouble before?”

“Never, sir.”

Poirot looked at her for a moment. Then he turned to Célestine.

“Madame was in the habit of keeping her jewels in that drawer?”

“Yes, Monsieur. Always.”

“And she always kept the case locked?”

“Yes, Monsieur.”

“And the key on her person?”

“Yes, Monsieur.”

“But she did not lock the drawer?”

“No, Monsieur.”

“And you were in the room the whole time?”

“Yes, Monsieur.”

“You did not leave it for a single second?”

“Not for one second, Monsieur.”

“Neither of you?”

“Neither of us.”

Poirot sighed.

“It is very strange,” he said. “Very strange indeed.”

He went to the door and looked out into the corridor. Then he came
back into the room and shut the door.

“Hastings,” he said, “there is something here that I do not
understand. Something very simple, and yet I cannot see it.”

He sat down on a chair and closed his eyes. I knew that he was
thinking, and I did not disturb him.

Suddenly he opened his eyes and stood up.

“I have it!” he cried. “I have it! But it is incredible!
Incredible!”

“What is it?” I asked.

“Wait!” he said. “Wait!”

He went to the washstand and picked up a piece of soap. Then he
went to the dressing-table and began to rub the soap on the runners
of the drawer.

“What on earth are you doing?” I asked.

“I am making the drawer slide easily, Hastings. Very easily.”

He pushed the drawer in and out several times.

“Yes,” he said, “that is much better. Much better.”

He turned to the two women.

“Now,” he said, “I want you to tell me exactly what you did while
Madame was at dinner.”

Célestine spoke first.

“I was busy with the wardrobe, Monsieur. I was folding Madame’s
dresses and putting them away.”

“And you?” he asked the chambermaid.

“I was making the beds, sir. And then I went to the washstand to
tidy it up.”

“I see,” said Poirot. “And did you hear anything?”

“Hear anything, sir?”

“Yes. Any noise? A click? A rustle?”

“No, sir. I didn’t hear nothing.”

“And you?” he asked Célestine.

“Nothing, Monsieur.”

Poirot looked at them both.

“You are sure?”

“Quite sure, Monsieur.”

“Very well,” said Poirot. “You may go.”

The two women left the room.

“Poirot,” I said, “what is it? What have you discovered?”

“I have discovered that the drawer was very stiff, Hastings. Very
stiff indeed.”

“But what has that to do with the pearls?”

“A great deal, my friend. A great deal.”

He went to the door and called the manager.

“Monsieur,” he said, when the latter appeared, “I have a request
to make. I want you to find out for me if any of the guests in the
hotel have lost anything lately.”

“Lost anything?” said the manager. “Why, yes. There was a lady on
the third floor who lost a gold watch last week. And a gentleman on
the second floor who lost a tie-pin the day before yesterday.”

“Aha!” said Poirot. “I thought so! And have you any idea who
could have taken them?”

“None at all, Monsieur. We have made every inquiry, but without
result.”

“I see,” said Poirot. “And now, Monsieur, I want you to do one
more thing for me. I want you to give me a list of all the people
who have been in this room during the last twenty-four hours.”

“That will be easy, Monsieur. There is only the chambermaid and
the maid.”

“No one else?”

“No one else.”

“Are you sure?”

“Quite sure.”

“What about the valet?”

“The valet does not come into this room. He only attends to the
gentlemen’s clothes in their own rooms.”

“I see,” said Poirot. “Well, Monsieur, I think that is all for
the present.”

The manager bowed and withdrew.

“Poirot,” I said, “I don’t understand. What has the stiff drawer
and the lost watch to do with the pearls?”

“Everything, Hastings. Everything. But we must be patient. We
must wait.”

The door opened and Mr. Opalsen entered. He looked more cheerful
than he had done a few minutes before.

“Well,” he said, “the police have been at work. They’ve searched
the two girls, but they haven’t found anything. They’re going to
search their rooms now.”

“I do not think they will find anything,” said Poirot quietly.

“Why not?”

“Because the person who took the pearls was not so foolish as to
keep them on her person.”

“Then you think it was one of the girls?”

“I did not say so.”

“But who else could it have been?”

“That is what I am going to find out,” said Poirot.

He went to the window and looked out.

“It is a fine night,” he said. “A very fine night. Shall we take
a little stroll, Hastings?”

I was surprised, but I followed him. We went down the stairs and
out into the night air.

Poirot walked along the front for some time in silence. Then he
turned to me.

“Hastings,” he said, “what do you think of Mr. Opalsen?”

“Mr. Opalsen? I think he’s a very pleasant man.”

“And Mrs. Opalsen?”

“She’s a bit loud, perhaps, but she seems kind-hearted.”

“And their pearls? What do you think of them?”

“They’re magnificent. Must be worth a fortune.”

“They are,” said Poirot. “They are worth at least twenty thousand
pounds.”

“Good heavens!” I exclaimed. “No wonder she’s upset!”

“Yes,” said Poirot. “It is a large sum of money. A very large sum
of money.”

He was silent for a moment. Then he said:

“Hastings, do you remember what Mr. Opalsen said about money being
tight in the City?”

“Yes. He said something about the Oil boom and E.P.D.”

“Exactly,” said Poirot. “Money is very tight in the City just
now. Many people are in difficulties.”

“But you don’t mean——”

“I mean nothing, Hastings. I am only thinking.”

We walked on in silence.

“Poirot,” I said at last, “you don’t really think Mr. Opalsen took
his own wife’s pearls?”

“It has been done before, Hastings. Many times.”

“But why should he?”

“To get the insurance money, perhaps. Or to pay his debts. Who
knows?”

“But how could he have done it? He was downstairs with us the whole
time.”

“Was he? Are you sure?”

“Of course. We were talking to him.”

“Not the whole time, Hastings. Not the whole time. He went away
for a few minutes when the page-boy called him.”

“But that was after the pearls were missed!”

“Was it? Are you sure?”

“Of course. Mrs. Opalsen came down and told us.”

“No, Hastings. She did not come down. She sent for him.”

“It’s the same thing.”

“Is it? Think, Hastings. Think.”

I thought.

“You’re right,” I said. “The boy came and told him his wife
wanted him. But the pearls must have been taken before that.”

“Why?”

“Because she went up to get them.”

“Exactly. She went up to get them. And when she got there, they
were gone.”

“But then how could he have taken them?”

“He couldn’t—unless he had taken them before.”

“But she said they were there when she went down to dinner!”

“She said so—yes.”

“And you think she was lying?”

“I do not say so. I only say it is possible.”

“But why should she lie?”

“Perhaps she and her husband are in it together.”

“I can’t believe it!” I cried. “They seemed so genuine.”

“Appearances are often deceptive, Hastings. It is one of the
first things a detective learns.”

We had reached the hotel again. Poirot stopped and looked up at
the first-floor windows.

“A very interesting case,” he murmured. “A very interesting case
indeed.”

We went inside. The lounge was almost empty now. We sat down in a
corner.

“And now, Hastings,” said Poirot, “I will tell you what I am going
to do. I am going to have a little talk with Célestine.”

“But you’ve already talked to her!”

“I want to talk to her again. Alone.”

He sent a page-boy to fetch her. In a few minutes she appeared,
looking very pale and anxious.

“Sit down, Mademoiselle,” said Poirot kindly. “I want to ask you
a few more questions.”

“Yes, Monsieur?”

“When you were in the room with the chambermaid, did either of you
leave it for any reason? Even for a moment?”

“No, Monsieur. I have already told you.”

“I know. But think again. Was there no time when one of you went
out—perhaps to fetch something?”

Célestine hesitated.

“Well,” she said at last, “now I come to think of it, the
chambermaid did go out for a moment.”

“Aha!” said Poirot. “And why did she go out?”

“To fetch some fresh water for the washstand, Monsieur.”

“I see. And how long was she gone?”

“Only a minute or two, Monsieur.”

“And were you alone in the room all that time?”

“Yes, Monsieur.”

“And you did not leave it?”

“No, Monsieur.”

“I see,” said Poirot. “Thank you, Mademoiselle. That is all.”

Célestine rose and left us.

“Well,” I said, “that seems to settle it. It must have been the
chambermaid.”

“Why, Hastings?”

“Because she was out of the room. She could have taken the pearls
then.”

“But the pearls were in the drawer, Hastings. And Célestine was
in the room. How could the chambermaid have taken them without
Célestine seeing her?”

“She could have taken them before she went out!”

“But Célestine was there then too!”

“Then they must have been in it together!”

“Perhaps,” said Poirot. “Perhaps.”

He rose and began to pace up and down.

“But there is still the stiff drawer, Hastings. Do not forget the
stiff drawer.”

“What has that to do with it?”

“A great deal. A great deal.”

He stopped and looked at me.

“Hastings, I have a plan. It is a very simple plan, but I think
it will work.”

“What is it?”

“I am going to catch the thief, Hastings. I am going to catch
the thief red-handed!”

“How?”

“You will see, my friend. You will see.”

He went to the manager’s office and spoke to him for a few minutes.
Then he came back to me.

“Everything is arranged,” he said. “And now, Hastings, I think
we will go to bed. We have a busy day before us tomorrow.”

I was dying with curiosity, but I knew it was no use asking him
any more questions. I went to my room and was soon fast asleep.

The next morning Poirot was up early. He seemed in high spirits.

“Come, Hastings!” he cried. “The sun is shining! The birds are
singing! It is a beautiful day for catching a thief!”

We went down to breakfast. The Opalsens were already there. They
looked very gloomy.

“Any news?” asked Mr. Opalsen, as we sat down.

“Not yet,” said Poirot. “But I have hopes. Great hopes.”

“The police haven’t found anything,” said Mrs. Opalsen
tearfully. “They’ve searched everything—the girls’ rooms, their
trunks—everything! But there’s no sign of the pearls.”

“I did not think they would find them there,” said Poirot.

“Then where do you think they are?”

“I have a theory,” said Poirot. “A very interesting theory.”

He would say no more. After breakfast he asked me to come with him
to the Opalsens’ room.

When we got there, we found the inspector and the manager.

“Well, Monsieur Poirot,” said the inspector, “have you any more
ideas?”

“I have a very good idea,” said Poirot. “But first, I want to
ask the chambermaid a few questions.”

The manager sent for her. She came in looking more frightened than
ever.

“Now, my girl,” said Poirot, “I want you to tell me the truth.
When you went out of this room to fetch the water, did you see
anybody in the corridor?”

“No, sir. No one at all.”

“Are you sure?”

“Quite sure, sir.”

“And you didn’t go anywhere else? You only went to the
housemaid’s cupboard?”

“Yes, sir. That’s all.”

“I see,” said Poirot. “And now, I want you to show me exactly
what you did when you came back.”

The girl went to the washstand and began to arrange the jugs and
basins.

“I see,” said Poirot. “And then what did you do?”

“I went to the beds, sir, to help the other young woman.”

“I see,” said Poirot. “Thank you. That will do.”

The girl left the room.

“And now,” said Poirot, “I want to see the housemaid’s cupboard.”

The manager led the way. The cupboard was a small one, situated
at the end of the corridor. It contained various cleaning
materials, a sink, and a few shelves.

Poirot examined it carefully. Then he turned to the manager.

“Who has the key of this cupboard?”

“The chambermaid on this floor, Monsieur.”

“No one else?”

“The head housemaid has a master key, of course.”

“I see,” said Poirot. “And was the cupboard locked last night?”

“It should have been, Monsieur.”

“But was it?”

“I—I cannot say for certain, Monsieur.”

“I see,” said Poirot. “Well, I think that is all.”

We went back to the Opalsens’ room.

“Well?” said the inspector. “What have you found out?”

“I have found out,” said Poirot, “that the pearls are not in this
room. And they are not in the girls’ rooms. And they are not in
the housemaid’s cupboard.”

“Then where are they?”

“They are in a very safe place,” said Poirot. “A very safe place
indeed.”

He turned to Mr. Opalsen.

“Monsieur,” he said, “I want you to do me a favour. I want you
to give me your jewel-case.”

“My jewel-case? But it’s empty!”

“I know. But I want it all the same.”

Mr. Opalsen went to the drawer and took out the case. He handed
it to Poirot.

Poirot took it and examined it carefully. Then he opened it and
looked inside.

“Empty!” he murmured. “Quite empty!”

He closed the case and put it on the table.

“And now,” he said, “I want everyone to leave the room. Everyone
except Hastings and myself.”

The others looked surprised, but they did as they were told.

When they had gone, Poirot turned to me.

“Hastings,” he said, “I want you to help me. I am going to perform
a little experiment.”

“What is it?” I asked.

“I am going to show you how the pearls were stolen.”

He went to the dressing-table and opened the drawer.

“You see this drawer, Hastings? It is very stiff. Very stiff
indeed.”

“Yes,” I said. “You told me that before.”

“Now,” said Poirot, “watch!”

He took the jewel-case and put it in the drawer. Then he tried
to close the drawer. It would not go in. He pushed and pulled,
but it remained stuck.

“You see, Hastings? It is very difficult to close. One has to
use a great deal of force.”

“Yes,” I said. “I see that.”

“Now,” said Poirot, “suppose someone wanted to take something
out of this drawer without being heard. What would they do?”

“I don’t know.”

“They would make the drawer slide easily, Hastings. Very easily.
They would rub soap on the runners, as I did last night.”

“I see!” I cried. “So that’s why you did it!”

“Exactly. But there is more, Hastings. Much more.”

He took the jewel-case out of the drawer and opened it.

“You see this case? It is a very fine case. Very well made.”

He began to feel the lining with his fingers.

“Aha!” he cried. “What have we here?”

He pulled at a piece of the velvet lining. It came away, revealing
a small compartment underneath.

“A secret compartment!” I exclaimed.

“Exactly. And look, Hastings! Look!”

He reached into the compartment and pulled out a string of
magnificent pearls.

“The pearls!” I cried. “You’ve found them!”

“Yes,” said Poirot. “I have found them.”

“But how did they get there?”

“That,” said Poirot, “is what I am going to show you.”

He put the pearls back in the secret compartment and replaced the
lining. Then he put the case back in the drawer and closed it.

“And now, Hastings,” he said, “we will call the others back.”

He went to the door and opened it.

“Come in!” he cried. “Come in, everyone!”

They all filed into the room, looking very expectant.

“Well?” said Mr. Opalsen. “Have you found them?”

“I have,” said Poirot.

“Where were they?”

“They were in this room,” said Poirot. “In this very room.”

“But where?”

“They were in the jewel-case,” said Poirot.

“In the jewel-case? But I looked there myself!”

“You looked in the main part of the case, Monsieur. You did not
look in the secret compartment.”

“Secret compartment? I didn’t know there was one!”

“Neither did the thief, apparently,” said Poirot.

He went to the table and picked up the jewel-case. He opened it
and showed them the secret compartment.

“There!” he said. “The pearls!”

Mrs. Opalsen gave a cry of joy.

“Oh, my pearls! My beautiful pearls!”

She snatched them from the case and began to kiss them.

“But who put them there?” asked the inspector. “And why?”

“That,” said Poirot, “is the most interesting part of the whole
affair.”

He turned to the chambermaid.

“My girl,” he said, “I think you have something to tell us.”

The girl began to tremble.

“I—I don’t know what you mean, sir.”

“I think you do,” said Poirot. “I think you know very well.”

He turned to the others.

“Yesterday evening, when this young woman went out to fetch the
water, she did not go to the housemaid’s cupboard. She went to
another room on this floor. A room occupied by a certain gentleman.”

“What gentleman?” asked the inspector.

“A gentleman who is very clever at his business,” said Poirot.
“A gentleman who specializes in stealing jewels from hotels.”

“You mean a professional thief?”

“Exactly. He has been in this hotel for some time. He is the
one who stole the watch and the tie-pin.”

“But how did he get the pearls?”

“It was very simple. He and this young woman were in league
together. She was to take the pearls and hand them to him in the
corridor. But there was a difficulty. Célestine was in the room.”

“So how did they do it?”

“They waited until Célestine was occupied with the wardrobe.
Then the chambermaid opened the drawer. But the drawer was stiff,
and it made a noise. Célestine heard it and looked round. The
chambermaid had only just time to close the drawer and pretend
to be busy at the washstand.”

“I see,” said Mr. Opalsen. “And then?”

“Then,” said Poirot, “the chambermaid realized that she could not
take the pearls while Célestine was in the room. So she hit upon
a very clever plan. She went out to fetch the water, and while
she was gone, she spoke to her confederate in the corridor. He
gave her a piece of soap.”

“Soap?”

“Yes. She came back into the room and, while Célestine was still
busy, she rubbed the soap on the runners of the drawer. Then,
later on, when Célestine was again occupied, she opened the drawer
silently, took the pearls, and replaced them with a string of
imitation ones that her confederate had given her.”

“Imitation pearls?”

“Yes. She put them in the jewel-case and locked it with a duplicate
key. Then she went out again and gave the real pearls to her
confederate.”

“But then,” I said, “where did the real pearls come from just now?
You found them in the secret compartment!”

“Ah!” said Poirot. “That is where the thief made a mistake. A
very big mistake.”

He looked at the chambermaid, who was now weeping bitterly.

“You see,” he continued, “the thief did not know about the secret
compartment. He thought he had the real pearls. But he didn’t.
He had the imitation ones!”

“What?” cried Mr. Opalsen. “You mean my wife was wearing imitation
pearls all the time?”

“No, Monsieur. She was wearing the real ones. But when she put
them away, she put them in the secret compartment for safety.
She had forgotten all about it!”

“Is that true, ma’am?” asked the inspector.

Mrs. Opalsen looked confused.

“Why—why, yes. I believe I did. I remember now—I was so worried
about them that I thought I’d better hide them somewhere safe.
And then I forgot where I’d put them!”

There was a moment of stunned silence. Then the inspector turned
to the chambermaid.

“Well, my girl,” he said, “I think you’d better come with me.”

He led her away, still weeping.

“Well, Poirot,” I said, when they had gone, “that was certainly
a very clever piece of work.”

“It was simple, Hastings. Very simple. But it just shows you—the
little grey cells, they never fail!”

He smiled and lit another cigarette.

“And now,” he said, “I think we will go and have some lunch.
Catching thieves always gives me an appetite!”

Poirot gently detached her clinging hands.

“Be calm, my child. If you are innocent you have nothing to fear.
Mr. Opalsen, you have a high opinion of this woman?”

“I have always found her most honest and reliable,” replied that
gentleman.

“She has been with us some time?”

“Ever since we were married, twelve years ago.”

“And you, madame?”

“Oh, I’m sure Célestine is as honest as the day. I’d trust her
with anything. It’s some common thief who’s got in.”

“How?” asked the inspector. “The window is on the first floor, but
it’s quite inaccessible. The door was locked.”

“No,” said Mrs. Opalsen. “Célestine was in the room.”

“And then?”

“The chambermaid came in to turn down the beds. Célestine tells
me she didn’t leave her for a moment.”

“The chambermaid,” repeated the inspector, turning to the girl.
“What’s your name?”

“Elizabeth Jane Cole, sir.”

“How long have you been in this hotel?”

“Four months, sir.”

“Have you ever been in trouble before?”

“No, sir, indeed I haven’t.” The girl began to cry.

“Now then, no crying. Was the maid in the room all the time you
were there?”

“Yes, sir.”

“And she didn’t leave it?”

“No, sir.”

“And you? Did you leave it?”

“No, sir.”

“How long were you in the room?”

“About ten minutes, sir.”

“And you were both there the whole time?”

“Yes, sir.”

The inspector looked at Poirot.

“It seems to me, sir, that this is a very simple case. If the
jewels were there when Mrs. Opalsen went down to dinner, and the
two maids were in the room the whole time, then one of them must
have taken them. Which of them it was I’m not prepared to say at
present, but I’ve a pretty good idea. We’ll have them both
searched.”

Mrs. Opalsen looked at him in dismay.

“Oh, inspector, I’m sure neither of them would do such a thing!
They’ve both been with us—I mean, Célestine has been with us for
years, and Elizabeth Jane—well, she looks a very nice, honest
girl.”

“Appearances are often deceptive, ma’am,” said the inspector
sententiously. “Now, if you’ll just step into the next room with
the two maids, I’ll have them searched at once.”

Mrs. Opalsen and the two girls withdrew, followed by the inspector’s
assistant.

“Now, Mr. Opalsen,” said the inspector, “I’ll just have a look
round the room. You don’t mind, I suppose?”

“Not at all. Do anything you think necessary.”

The inspector began his search. He looked under the bed, in the
wardrobe, and even in the chimney. Then he turned his attention
to the dressing-table. He examined the drawer where the jewel-case
had been kept, and then the jewel-case itself. It was a handsome
affair of green morocco, with Mrs. Opalsen’s initials in gold on
the lid.

“Nothing here,” he said, as he replaced it in the drawer. “Now
let’s have a look at the other drawers.”

He went through them one by one, but without result.

“Well,” he said, as he finished, “there’s nothing in the room.
That’s certain. Now we’ll see what the search has brought to
light.”

He went to the door and called his assistant. In a few minutes the
man appeared, followed by Mrs. Opalsen and the two maids.

“Well?” asked the inspector.

“Nothing, sir.”

The inspector’s face fell.

“You’re sure?”

“Quite sure, sir.”

“And the room’s been thoroughly searched?”

“Every inch of it, sir.”

The inspector looked baffled.

“It’s very strange,” he said. “If the jewels were there when Mrs.
Opalsen went down to dinner, and the two maids were in the room the
whole time, they must be somewhere. They can’t have vanished into
thin air.”

“Perhaps,” suggested Poirot, “they were not there when Mrs. Opalsen
went down to dinner.”

“But I tell you I saw them!” cried Mrs. Opalsen.

“You are sure, madame? You did not merely _think_ you saw them?”

“I am quite sure. I took the necklace out of the case, and then
I decided not to wear it, and put it back again.”

“And you locked the case?”

“Yes.”

“And the key?”

“Is here, as I told you.” She held it up again.

Poirot took it from her and examined it closely.

“A very ordinary key,” he remarked. “As the inspector says, any
duplicate would open the lock. Now, madame, will you tell me
exactly what you did when you came into the room after dinner?”

“I went straight to the dressing-table, took the jewel-case out
of the drawer, and unlocked it. And the pearls were gone!”

“You are sure the case was locked?”

“Quite sure.”

“And you had the key all the time?”

“Yes, round my neck.”

“Did you leave the room at all after you had put the pearls away
before dinner?”

“No, I went straight down to the lounge.”

“And Célestine was in the room all the time?”

“Yes.”

“And you, Célestine, you did not leave the room?”

“No, Monsieur, not for a single moment.”

“And the chambermaid?”

“She came in just as Madame was leaving.”

“And she stayed until Madame returned?”

“Yes, Monsieur.”

“And you were both in the room the whole time?”

“Yes, Monsieur.”

Poirot turned to the chambermaid.

“Is that so?”

“Yes, sir,” said the girl, who was still crying.

“You did not leave the room at any time?”

“No, sir.”

“Not even for a moment?”

“No, sir.”

Poirot looked at her thoughtfully for a moment, and then turned
to the inspector.

“It is a very pretty little problem,” he said. “A very pretty
little problem indeed. With your permission, I will just have a
look round the room myself.”

“Certainly, sir,” said the inspector. “But I don’t think you’ll
find anything we’ve missed.”

Poirot began his search. It was a very different affair from the
inspector’s. He did not look under the bed or in the wardrobe.
Instead, he spent a long time examining the dressing-table and the
jewel-case. Then he went to the window and looked out. Finally,
he went to the door and examined the lock.

“Well?” asked the inspector, as Poirot finished. “Have you found
anything?”

“I have found several things,” replied Poirot. “But whether they
are of any importance remains to be seen. For instance, I have
found this.”

He held up a small piece of white thread.

“What of it?” asked the inspector.

“It was caught in the hinge of the jewel-case,” explained Poirot.

“Well, what does that prove?”

“Perhaps nothing—perhaps a great deal. Then I have found this.”

He held up a small piece of black silk.

“And where did you find that?”

“It was caught in the bolt of the door.”

The inspector shrugged his shoulders.

“It doesn’t seem to me to amount to much,” he said.

“Perhaps not,” agreed Poirot. “But there is one other thing.
Madame, when you went down to dinner, did you lock the door of
your room?”

“No, I never do. Célestine is always here.”

“I see. And when you came up after dinner, was the door locked?”

“No, it was open. Célestine was just coming out.”

“I see,” said Poirot again. He turned to the maid. “Célestine,
why were you coming out of the room?”

“I was going to fetch some water for Madame, Monsieur.”

“And the chambermaid?”

“She had already left, Monsieur.”

“I see,” said Poirot for the third time. He remained silent for
a moment, lost in thought. Then he turned to Mr. Opalsen.

“Mr. Opalsen, I should like to have a few words with you in private,
if I may.”

“Certainly,” said Mr. Opalsen. “We’ll go into the sitting-room.”

He led the way into the adjoining room, followed by Poirot and
myself. When the door was closed, Poirot turned to him.
