“Mr. Opalsen, I will be frank with you. This is a very serious
matter. The pearls are of great value, are they not?”

“They are worth at least twenty thousand pounds,” replied Mr.
Opalsen.

“And you have no idea who could have taken them?”

“None whatever. As I told the inspector, I’ve always found
Célestine most honest and reliable. And the chambermaid—well, she’s
only been here four months, but the manager speaks very highly of
her.”

“I see,” said Poirot. “Now, Mr. Opalsen, I want you to do
something for me. I want you to give me a list of all the people
who have been in your room today.”

“Well, there’s my wife and myself, of course. Then there’s
Célestine and the chambermaid. And then—let me see—the waiter
brought up our breakfast this morning, and the valet came for my
clothes. I think that’s all.”

“I see,” said Poirot. “And now, one more thing. I want you to
give me the name and address of the firm from whom you bought the
pearls.”

“Certainly,” said Mr. Opalsen. He took a notebook from his pocket
and wrote down an address. “It’s a firm in Hatton Garden—Messrs.
Sark and Sons.”

“Thank you,” said Poirot. “And now, if you will excuse me, I
think I will go and have a little talk with the manager.”

He left the room, and I followed him. As we went down the stairs,
I asked him what he thought of the case.

“It is a very interesting case, Hastings,” he replied. “A very
interesting case indeed. There are several points that are not
at all clear.”

“Such as?”

“Well, for instance, there is the question of the white thread
and the black silk. And then there is the question of the door
being open when Mrs. Opalsen came up after dinner. And finally,
there is the question of the pearls themselves.”

“What about them?”

“Well, it is a very curious thing that they should have been
taken and nothing else. There were other jewels in the case, were
there not?”

“Yes, I believe so.”

“Then why were only the pearls taken? It is very strange, is it
not?”

“I suppose it is,” I agreed. “But what do you think it means?”

“I am not yet sure,” replied Poirot. “But I have an idea—a very
little idea. We shall see if I am right.”

He was silent for the rest of the way to the manager’s office.
When we arrived, he asked to see the manager, and we were at once
shown in.

The manager was a small, dapper man, who looked very much
distressed.

“This is a very unfortunate business, Mr. Poirot,” he said. “A
very unfortunate business indeed. I can’t tell you how sorry I am
that such a thing should have happened in my hotel.”

“I am sure of it,” said Poirot sympathetically. “But these things
will happen, even in the best-managed hotels. Now, I want to ask
you a few questions about the chambermaid, Elizabeth Jane Cole.”

“Certainly, sir. What would you like to know?”

“How long has she been with you?”

“Four months, sir.”

“And you have always found her honest and reliable?”

“Always, sir. She came to us with excellent references from her
last place.”

“And where was that?”

“She was with a Mrs. Higgins in Kensington.”

“I see. And have you any reason to suspect her in any way?”

“None at all, sir. She seems a very nice, hard-working girl.”

“I see,” said Poirot. “And now, one more thing. I want to know
if anyone else has been in the Opalsens’ room today.”

“Well, as Mr. Opalsen told you, there was the waiter and the
valet. And then there was the man who came to see about the
window.”

“The window?”

“Yes, it was reported to be sticking, and I sent a man up to see
to it.”

“And what time was that?”

“About four o’clock this afternoon.”

“I see,” said Poirot. “And who was this man?”

“He’s one of our regular workmen—a man named James Robinson.”

“I see,” said Poirot. “And is he still in the hotel?”

“No, sir, he went home at five o’clock.”

“I see,” said Poirot for the last time. He rose to his feet.
“Thank you, Monsieur le Directeur. You have been most helpful.”

As we left the office, I asked Poirot if he thought the man
Robinson had anything to do with the theft.

“It is possible, Hastings,” he replied. “It is very possible.
But we must not jump to conclusions. We must first make some
inquiries.”

He led the way to the lift, and we went up to our own rooms. As
we entered, Poirot turned to me.

“Hastings,” he said, “I want you to do something for me. I want
you to go to Hatton Garden tomorrow morning and see Messrs. Sark
and Sons. I want you to find out everything you can about the
pearls—when they were bought, how much they cost, and if they have
any special characteristics.”

“Certainly, Poirot,” I replied. “But what are you going to do?”

“I am going to stay here and make some further inquiries,” he
said. “And I am also going to have a little talk with Célestine.”

The next morning I duly went to Hatton Garden and saw Messrs. Sark
and Sons. I found them very helpful, and they gave me all the
information I required. The pearls had been bought about six
months previously for twenty thousand pounds. They were of
exceptional quality and colour, and were perfectly matched. They
had been sold to Mr. Opalsen, who had paid for them in cash.

When I returned to the hotel, I found Poirot in the lounge,
talking to the manager. He seemed very pleased with himself.

“Well, Hastings,” he said, “what did you find out?”

I gave him the information I had obtained. He listened with great
interest.

“Excellent!” he said, when I had finished. “Excellent! It is as
I thought.”

“What is as you thought?” I asked.

“I will tell you later,” he replied. “In the meantime, I have
some news for you. I have had a talk with Célestine, and she has
admitted something very interesting.”

“What is that?”

“She has admitted that she did leave the room for a few moments
while the chambermaid was there.”

“Then the chambermaid could have taken the pearls!” I cried.

“It is possible,” agreed Poirot. “But there is one thing that
does not fit.”

“What is that?”

“Well, if the chambermaid took the pearls, why did she not take
anything else? And why did she stay in the room until Mrs. Opalsen
returned?”

“I don’t know,” I admitted. “But what do you think happened?”

“I will tell you my theory,” said Poirot. “But first we must go
and see Mr. Opalsen.”

We found Mr. Opalsen in his sitting-room. He looked very anxious.

“Any news, Mr. Poirot?” he asked.

“Yes, I have some news for you,” replied Poirot. “But I am afraid
it is not very good news.”

“What do you mean?”

“I mean that the pearls were not stolen at all.”

“Not stolen! Then where are they?”

“They are in this room,” said Poirot.

He went to the dressing-table and opened the bottom drawer. He
took out the jewel-case and opened it. The pearls were not there.

“But they’re not here!” cried Mr. Opalsen.

“No,” agreed Poirot. “But they are in the drawer.”

He reached into the back of the drawer and pulled out a small
packet wrapped in tissue-paper. He opened it, and there were the
pearls!

“My pearls!” cried Mrs. Opalsen, who had just entered the room.
“Where did you find them?”

“In the back of the drawer, madame,” replied Poirot. “They had
slipped through a crack and fallen behind it.”

“Oh, thank God!” cried Mrs. Opalsen. “But how did you know they
were there?”

“It was very simple,” explained Poirot. “When I examined the
jewel-case, I found a small piece of white thread caught in the
hinge. It was the same thread that was used to wrap the pearls in
the tissue-paper. And when I examined the drawer, I found that
it did not fit quite properly. There was a small gap at the back,
through which the pearls could have fallen.”

“But what about the black silk in the bolt of the door?” I asked.

“That was just a piece of silk from Célestine’s dress,” replied
Poirot. “It had nothing to do with the case.”

“And the man Robinson?”

“He was just a workman, as the manager said. He had nothing to do
with it either.”

“Well, I must say I’m very much relieved,” said Mr. Opalsen. “And
I’m very grateful to you, Mr. Poirot.”

“It was nothing,” said Poirot modestly. “A mere matter of using
the little grey cells.”

As we left the room, I turned to Poirot.

“But what about Célestine admitting she’d left the room?” I asked.

“Oh, that!” Poirot chuckled. “She only said that because she
thought I was going to accuse her of the theft. She wanted to
show that the chambermaid had had an opportunity to take the
pearls. It was a very human reaction, was it not?”

I laughed.

“Well, Poirot, you’ve done it again!” I said.

“Yes,” agreed Poirot. “But it was a very simple case, Hastings.
A very simple case indeed.”

“Monsieur would understand—he would not permit this infamy!
Monsieur, I have served Madame since six years—never has a word
been breathed against me! See, I am of an honesty! My father, he
is of a respectability. And my uncle—the brother of my mother—he
is of the most high character, for he is a _gendarme_!”

Poirot made a movement of the hands, as though to say that it was
not for him to decide.

The inspector took the weeping girl by the arm.

“There, there, my girl,” he said. “You’ve nothing to fear if you’re
innocent. It’s no good taking on like that. Now, just listen. You
were here the whole time your mistress was at dinner?”

“_Oui, oui_, Monsieur—not for one single moment did I leave the
room!”

“And the chambermaid?”

“She came in to turn down the beds. We were both here together.”

“And she didn’t go to that drawer?”

“No.”

“You are sure?”

“I am certain. She stayed by the beds. She did not go near the
dressing-table.”

“And you?”

“I stayed by the window, Monsieur. I did some sewing for Madame.”

The inspector turned to the chambermaid.

“You’ve heard what she says. Have you anything to add?”

The girl, a pretty-looking, well-spoken young woman, shook her
head.

“No, sir. I’ve nothing more to say. It’s quite true I was in the
room, but I never went near the dressing-table. I was only in the
room a few minutes, anyway.”

“Did you see the maid go to the drawer?”

“No, sir.”

“What was she doing when you were in the room?”

“She was sitting by the window, sewing, just as she said.”

“You didn’t see her go to the dressing-table?”

“No, sir.”

The inspector’s face took on a look of concentrated thought.

“Well,” he said at length, “it’s a very simple matter. One of these
two must have the pearls.”

He turned to the master of the house.

“I suppose, sir, you wouldn’t have any objection to my searching
these two women?”

“Not at all,” replied Mr. Opalsen. “I leave everything to you.”

“I’ll take them into the next room,” said the inspector. “The
search will be a thorough one, I can promise you.”

The door closed behind the trio. Mr. Opalsen sank into a chair and
wiped his forehead.

“This is a bad business,” he muttered. “A very bad business.”

“You have no doubt of your maid, monsieur?” asked Poirot.

“None whatever. Célestine has been with us for years. She’s
honesty itself.”

“And the chambermaid?”

“I know nothing of her. She’s only been here a few weeks. But the
hotel people speak well of her.”

Poirot paced the room, his eyes wandering here and there. He
stopped before the dressing-table.

“The drawer was not locked?”

“No.”

“And the jewel-case?”

“The jewel-case was locked, but as the inspector says, it’s a
simple lock. Any one could have a duplicate key.”

“You’re sure the pearls were there when you went down to dinner,
madame?”

“I’m positive. I saw them when I put my emeralds away.”

“And you locked the case?”

“Yes.”

“And you’ve had the key in your possession ever since?”

“Yes.”

Poirot nodded.

“The pearls were there at eight o’clock. It is now nine-thirty.
During that time either the maid or the chambermaid must have
taken them.”

He stopped and looked at the floor.

“What is this?”

He stooped and picked up a small object. It was a tiny piece of
white silk.

“That’s mine,” said Célestine, who had just re-entered the room,
followed by the inspector and the chambermaid. “It’s a piece of the
frock I was mending for Madame.”

“I see,” said Poirot. “And you’ve been sitting by the window all
the evening?”

“Yes, Monsieur.”

“And you didn’t go near the dressing-table?”

“No, Monsieur.”

“The search has been quite fruitless,” said the inspector. “I’ve
searched them both thoroughly, and there’s no sign of the pearls.”

“You’ve searched the room?”

“Not yet. I’m going to do that now.”

He began a systematic search of the room, while we watched him in
silence. He looked under the beds, in the wardrobes, behind the
curtains. He even peered into the water-jug. But his search was
unsuccessful.

“Well,” he said at length, “the pearls aren’t here, that’s certain.
They must have been passed out to an accomplice.”

“But how?” asked Mr. Opalsen. “The door was locked.”

“There’s the window,” suggested the inspector.

He went to the window and looked out.

“It’s a long drop to the ground,” he said. “But it’s possible.
Someone might have been waiting below.”

He turned to Célestine.

“Did you see anyone outside the window?”

“No, Monsieur.”

“You’re sure?”

“Quite sure.”

The inspector looked baffled.

“Well,” he said, “I’ll have to take these two women down to the
station. I’ll keep them there for a bit, and see if I can’t get
something out of them.”

As they were being led away, Poirot stepped forward.

“One moment, Monsieur l’Inspecteur. There is one thing you have
forgotten.”

“What’s that?”

“The chambermaid’s room. Have you searched that?”

“No. But I will.”

“And there is one other thing.”

“What?”

“The pockets of Monsieur Opalsen.”

Mr. Opalsen started.

“My pockets! What do you mean?”

“It is a mere formality,” said Poirot, with a wave of the hand.
“But in these cases one cannot be too careful.”

Mr. Opalsen laughed.

“Oh, very well. Search me by all means.”

He stood with his arms outstretched while the inspector ran his
hands over him.

“Nothing there,” said the inspector.

“And now,” said Poirot, “if you will permit me, I should like to
ask a few questions of the chambermaid.”

The inspector nodded.

“Go ahead.”

Poirot turned to the girl.

“What is your name?”

“Elizabeth Whalley, sir.”

“How long have you been here?”

“Three weeks, sir.”

“And before that?”

“I was at the _Metropole_ at Folkestone, sir.”

“I see. And you like your work here?”

“Yes, sir.”

“You have never been in any trouble before?”

“No, sir.”

“I believe you,” said Poirot. “You have the face of an honest girl.”

The girl blushed.

“Thank you, sir.”

“Now tell me,” continued Poirot, “when you were in the room this
evening, did you notice anything unusual?”

“No, sir.”

“Nothing at all?”

“No, sir.”

“Think again. Was there nothing that struck you as being out of the
ordinary?”

The girl hesitated.

“Well, sir, now you mention it, there was one thing.”

“And what was that?”

“The French young lady—she seemed very nervous, sir.”

“Nervous? In what way?”

“Well, she was jumping at every sound, sir. And she kept looking
towards the door, as though she were expecting someone.”

“I see. And did anyone come to the door?”

“No, sir.”

“Did you hear anything outside in the passage?”

“No, sir.”

“And that was all?”

“Yes, sir.”

“Thank you, Elizabeth. That will be all.”

The girl followed the inspector and Célestine out of the room.

“Well, Poirot,” I said, when we were alone, “what do you make of
it?”

Poirot did not answer for a moment. He was staring at the floor,
his brows knit in thought.

“It is a strange case, Hastings,” he said at length. “A very
strange case.”

“You think the maid took them?”

“It would seem so. And yet—there are points—points that I do not
understand.”

“What points?”

“For instance, why did she not hide them? If she took them, she
must have hidden them somewhere. But the inspector has searched
her, and he has searched the room, and he has found nothing.”

“She might have thrown them out of the window to an accomplice.”

“Perhaps. But she says she saw no one. And besides, it would be
a very risky thing to do. Someone might have seen her.”

“Then where are they?”

“That is what I am asking myself, Hastings. Where are they?”

He began to pace the room again.

“Let us consider the facts. The pearls were in the case at eight
o’clock. At nine-thirty they were gone. During that time the maid
was in the room the whole time, and the chambermaid was there for
a few minutes. Both of them deny having seen the pearls. Both of
entreated to be searched, and nothing was found on either of them.
The room has been searched, and nothing has been found there
either.”

“It seems an impossible situation,” I said.

“Nothing is impossible, Hastings. The pearls are somewhere. We
must find them.”

He stopped before the dressing-table and began to examine it again.

“The drawer was not locked,” he murmured. “And the jewel-case was
locked. But the lock is a simple one. Any one could have a
duplicate key.”

He took a small magnifying-glass from his pocket and began to
examine the lock of the jewel-case.

“_Tiens!_” he exclaimed. “What is this?”

“What have you found?” I asked, leaning over him.

“A small scratch, Hastings. A very small scratch. But it is
significant.”

“Why?”

“Because it shows that the lock has been tampered with. It was not
opened with the key.”

“Then the thief didn’t have a duplicate key?”

“It would seem not.”

“But then—who could have done it?”

“That is the question, Hastings. That is the question.”

He stood up and looked around the room.

“The chambermaid,” he said. “She was in the room for a few minutes.
Could she have done it?”

“But the maid was there the whole time.”

“True. The maid was there. But she was sitting by the window,
sewing. Could she have seen what the chambermaid was doing?”

“She says she didn’t see her go to the dressing-table.”

“Exactly. She says she didn’t see her. But that does not mean that
the chambermaid did not go there.”

“But if she did, the maid would have seen her.”

“Not necessarily. If the maid’s back was turned, or if she was
intent on her sewing, she might not have noticed.”

“But the chambermaid would have to be very quick.”

“True. She would have to be very quick. But it is possible.”

“And what about the pearls? Where are they?”

“Ah! That is the mystery. If the chambermaid took them, what did
she do with them? She was searched, and they weren’t on her.”

“She might have hidden them in the room.”

“But the room has been searched.”

“She might have hidden them in a place that the inspector didn’t
think of.”

“Perhaps. We must look for ourselves.”

He began a second search of the room, more thorough even than the
first. He looked under the carpet, he peered into the chimney, he
even examined the soap-dish. But his search was as fruitless as the
inspector’s.

“Well,” he said at length, “it is as I thought. The pearls are not
here.”

“Then where can they be?”

Poirot did not answer. He was staring at the wall above the
dressing-table.

“What is it?” I asked.

“Nothing, Hastings. A mere idea. Let us go down and have a talk
with the manager.”

We found the manager in his office. He was a small, dapper man,
and he was clearly very much upset by the occurrence.

“It is a most unfortunate affair, Mr. Poirot,” he said. “Most
unfortunate. Such a thing has never happened in this hotel before.”

“I am sure of it,” said Poirot. “But these things will happen. Now,
tell me about this chambermaid—Elizabeth Whalley. You say she has
been here for three weeks?”

“Yes, sir.”

“And you have a good character with her?”

“Yes, sir. From the _Metropole_ at Folkestone. They spoke very
highly of her.”

“I see. And the maid—Célestine?”

“She has been with the Opalsens for six years, I understand. They
have the greatest confidence in her.”

“Quite so. Now, I want you to do something for me.”

“What is it, sir?”

“I want you to let me see the rooms of these two women.”

“Certainly, sir. If you think it will be of any use.”

“One never knows,” said Poirot.

The manager led the way upstairs. The chambermaid’s room was on
the top floor. It was a small, plainly furnished room, but it was
scrupulously clean. Poirot went through it with a fine-tooth comb,
but he found nothing.

“And now for the maid’s room,” he said.

Célestine’s room was next to her mistress’s. It was a much larger
and more comfortable room than the chambermaid’s. Poirot searched
it with equal care, but with the same result.

“Well,” said the manager, “I hope you’re satisfied now, sir.”

“Satisfied? No, I am not satisfied at all. I am more puzzled than
ever.”

We went back to our own room. Poirot sat in silence for some time,
his head sunk on his breast. Then he suddenly sprang to his feet.

“I have it, Hastings! I have it!”

“What have you found?”

“The pearls, Hastings! I know where the pearls are!”

“Where?”

“Come with me and you shall see!”

He led the way back to Mrs. Opalsen’s room. It was empty now, the
police having finished their work there. Poirot went straight to
the dressing-table.

“Regard, Hastings!” he said, pointing to the wall above it.

I looked. There was a small, circular mark on the wallpaper, about
the size of a penny.

“What of it?” I asked.

“It is a mark, Hastings. A mark that was not there before.”

“How do you know?”

“Because I examined the wall very carefully when we were here
earlier this evening, and it was not there then.”

“But what does it mean?”

“It means, Hastings, that someone has been at work here.”

He took a penknife from his pocket and began to scrape away the
wallpaper. In a few moments a small hole was revealed. Poirot
reached into the hole and drew out a small, velvet-covered box.

“The pearls!” I cried.

“The pearls, Hastings!”

He opened the box. Inside, resting on a bed of white silk, was the
magnificent necklace of pearls.

“But how did they get there?” I asked.

“It is very simple, Hastings. The thief—whoever he was—knew that
the room would be searched. He also knew that he would be searched
himself. So he hit upon this ingenious plan. He made a hole in the
wall, hid the pearls there, and then covered the hole with a piece
of wallpaper.”

“But who could have done it? The maid or the chambermaid?”

“Neither, Hastings. Neither.”

“Then who?”

“Think, Hastings. Who was in the room this evening besides the
two women?”

“The manager—the police—Mr. Opalsen——”

“Exactly. Mr. Opalsen!”

“Mr. Opalsen! But why should he steal his own wife’s pearls?”

“Because, Hastings, as he told us himself, money is ‘confoundedly
tight in the City.’ He needed money, and he hit upon this way of
getting it. He would steal the pearls, claim the insurance money,
and then sell the pearls privately. It was a very clever plan, but
he forgot one thing.”

“What was that?”

“He forgot Hercule Poirot!”

“But how did you know it was him?”

“It was the scratch on the lock that first gave me the clue. It
was a very clumsy scratch—not at all the sort of thing a
professional thief would do. It looked more like the work of an
amateur. Then there was the piece of white silk. Célestine said it
was from a frock she was mending for Madame. But I noticed that
it was a very peculiar shade of white—exactly the same shade as the
silk in the jewel-box. I suspected then that the pearls had been
removed from the box and hidden somewhere else. And when I saw the
mark on the wall, I knew I was right.”

“But how did he manage to do it without the maid seeing him?”

“It was quite simple. He came into the room while the maid was
sitting by the window. Her back was towards him. He went to the
dressing-table, opened the jewel-box, took out the pearls, and
then made the hole in the wall. It would only take a few moments.”

“And the scratch on the lock?”

“He made that afterwards, to make it look as though the box had
been forced.”

“I see. It was a very clever plan.”

“Yes, it was clever. But not clever enough for Hercule Poirot!”

We went down to find Mr. Opalsen. We found him in the lounge,
talking to the manager. When he saw us, he came towards us
anxiously.

“Any news, Mr. Poirot?” he asked.

“Yes, monsieur,” said Poirot. “I have found your pearls.”

“You have! Where were they?”

“They were hidden in a hole in the wall of your wife’s bedroom.”

Mr. Opalsen turned pale.

“In a hole in the wall? But who—who could have put them there?”

“You did, monsieur,” said Poirot quietly.

“I! What do you mean? This is an outrage!”

“It is the truth, monsieur. I have the proof.”

He produced the velvet-covered box from his pocket.

“This box was hidden in the wall. And on it are your finger-prints.”

Mr. Opalsen collapsed into a chair.

“I—I don’t know what to say,” he muttered.

“There is nothing to say, monsieur,” said Poirot. “The game is up.”

The police were called, and Mr. Opalsen was taken away. Mrs.
Opalsen was heartbroken, but she was comforted by the return of
her pearls.

As we were leaving the hotel the next morning, Poirot turned to me
with a smile.

“Well, Hastings, what do you think of our little week-end at
Brighton?”

“It has been most interesting, Poirot. Most interesting.”

“And you are no longer annoyed with me for underestimating your
mental capacities?”

“No, Poirot. I suppose I must admit that you are—in some ways—my
superior.”

“In some ways, Hastings? Only in some ways?”

Poirot laughed, and we stepped into the waiting taxi.

“Monsieur, then, would understand that his compatriot was incapable
of such a thing!”

Poirot was not so sure. To begin with, he knew that his fellow-countrymen
are by no means above picking up a trifle when they see the
opportunity.

“I must beg of you to remain calm, mademoiselle,” he said coldly.
“You will have the goodness to state your case clearly.”

Célestine, after a good deal of persuasion, was at last induced to
comply. Her story, which was a very simple one, was that she had
sat in the chair by the window the whole time her mistress was
downstairs at dinner. The door into the corridor was locked, she
said, from the inside. She had not left the room for a single
moment.

The inspector was a man of the world, and he evidently did not put
too much faith in Célestine’s story. He turned back to Mrs.
Opalsen.

“The pearls were in this case when you went down to dinner?”

“I’m positive of it. I remember the very look of them.”

“And you were away—how long?”

“About an hour and a half.”

“During which time,” said the inspector, “the maid was in the room
and the door was locked. You are sure that no one could have entered
by the window?”

“The window was closed and the shutters fastened. Besides, we are on
the first floor.”

“The door to the corridor was locked, you say?”

“I locked it myself,” declared Célestine.

“And the key?”

“I have it here.” She produced a small key.

The inspector took it and tried it in the lock. It turned easily.

“Then we come back to this,” he said, looking round at the circle
of faces. “The pearls were in the case when Mrs. Opalsen went down
to dinner; since then the maid has not left the room, and the door
has been locked. Yet the pearls are gone! Someone must have entered
the room. How?”

There was a dead silence. Suddenly Poirot spoke.

“The door to the dressing-room—is it locked?”

He pointed to a door on the left of the bed.

“No,” said Mr. Opalsen. “That is my room.”

“And the door from your room to the corridor?”

“I always lock it before I go down to dinner.”

“Is it locked now?”

“I’ll go and see,” said Mr. Opalsen.

He disappeared for a moment, and then returned.

“Yes, it’s locked.”

“Then,” said Poirot, “it seems that the thief must have entered
through Mr. Opalsen’s room.”

“But that door was locked also,” I objected.

“Precisely,” said Poirot. “And yet the pearls are gone!”

The inspector looked at him with more respect than he had hitherto
shown.

“You’ve hit the nail on the head, sir,” he said. “That’s the only
possible way the thief could have entered. But even then he would
have had to have a key.”

“A skeleton key would do that,” I suggested.

“Or a duplicate,” added Poirot.

The inspector nodded.

“We’ll have to have a search,” he said. “I’ll start with the maid’s
boxes.”

Célestine gave another shriek, but the inspector ignored her.

“I’ll take the chambermaid next,” he added.

The chambermaid, a pretty, fair-haired girl, began to cry.

“Oh, sir, I haven’t seen the pearls, indeed I haven’t! I was only
in the room for a few minutes, turning down the beds, and Célestine
was there all the time.”

“We’ll see about that,” said the inspector grimly.

He spent some time over the boxes of the two girls, but without
result. Then he turned his attention to the room itself. He searched
the drawers of the dressing-table, the wardrobe, the bed—everywhere,
in fact, where a necklace could be hidden. But his search was
fruitless.

“Well,” he said at last, “it’s a bit of a puzzle, I must say. But
I’ll find out who did it, or my name’s not Japp!”

I started.

“Is your name Japp?” I asked.

“Yes. Why?”

“Because my friend here is Mr. Hercule Poirot.”

The inspector’s face underwent a complete change.

“Mr. Poirot!” he exclaimed. “Well, I never! This _is_ a piece of
luck! I’ve heard of you, sir, of course. Many’s the time I’ve
wished I could have a talk with you.”

Poirot smiled.

“I am at your service, Inspector,” he said. “If there is anything
I can do to help you——”

“Well, sir, if you wouldn’t mind giving us the benefit of your
advice? It’s a bit of a teaser, this is, and no mistake.”

“With pleasure,” said Poirot. “First of all, I should like to ask
a few questions of the two girls.”

The inspector nodded.

“Go ahead, sir.”

Poirot turned to Célestine.

“You say you did not leave the room for a single moment?”

“Not for one second, Monsieur!”

“And the door to the corridor was locked?”

“Yes, Monsieur.”

“What about the door to Mr. Opalsen’s room?”

“It was shut, Monsieur.”

“Was it locked?”

“I do not know, Monsieur. I did not try it.”

“I see. And you, mademoiselle,”—he turned to the chambermaid—“you
were in the room for how long?”

“Only about five minutes, sir. I just turned down the beds and saw
to the towels.”

“Was Célestine in the room all the time?”

“Yes, sir. She was sitting by the window.”

“Did you see her go near the dressing-table?”

“No, sir.”

“Did you go near it yourself?”

“Only to put the clean towels on the rack, sir. That’s close to it.”

“I see. Thank you.”

The girls were allowed to leave the room. As soon as they had gone,
Poirot turned to the inspector.

“A very simple case, my friend,” he said.

“Simple!” I cried. “I should call it just the opposite!”

“Everything is simple,” said Poirot, “if you only look at it in the
right way. Now, let us examine the facts. The pearls were in the
case when Mrs. Opalsen went down to dinner. While she was away, the
room was locked, and the maid was inside. Yet the pearls disappeared.
Therefore, the thief must have entered the room while the maid was
there. How did he do it? There are only two possible ways. Either
through the corridor door, or through Mr. Opalsen’s room. Both doors
were locked. Therefore, he must have had a key. But even if he had
a key, how did he manage to enter and steal the pearls without the
maid seeing him?”

“That’s the point,” said the inspector.

“It is a very important point,” agreed Poirot. “Now, there is one
person who could have entered the room without the maid thinking
anything of it. Who is that person?”

“The chambermaid!” I cried.

“Precisely,” said Poirot. “The chambermaid. She would have a perfect
right to be in the room. But Célestine says she was only there for
five minutes, and that she did not go near the dressing-table.
Now, if we can prove that Célestine is lying——”

“But why should she lie?” I asked.

“Ah, that is the question!” said Poirot. “Perhaps she was in league
with the thief. Or perhaps——” He broke off. “Let us look at the
jewel-case.”

He took it from the inspector’s hand and examined it closely. It
was a small square case of morocco leather. Poirot opened it and
looked inside.

“Empty!” he murmured. “Quite empty! And yet—stay! What is this?”

He picked up a small piece of paper that was lying at the bottom of
the case. It was a fragment of a newspaper.

“Look at this, Hastings,” he said, handing it to me.

I looked at it. It was a small piece of the _Daily Mail_.

“What do you make of it?” asked Poirot.

“Nothing,” I said. “It’s just a piece of paper.”

“It is more than that,” said Poirot. “It is a clue! Now, let us
examine the dressing-table.”

He went over to the dressing-table and began to examine it
minutely. Suddenly he gave a cry of triumph.

“Look here!” he said, pointing to the bottom right-hand drawer.

I looked. There was a small scratch on the wood, just above the
keyhole.

“Aha!” said Poirot. “The thief was in a hurry! He used a skeleton
key, and he was not as careful as he might have been. Now, let us
see if we can find anything else.”

He continued his search, but for some time he found nothing. Then,
just as he was about to give up, he stooped down and picked
something up from the carpet.

“What is it?” I asked.

“A piece of coal,” said Poirot.

“A piece of coal!” I cried. “What on earth has that got to do with
it?”

“Perhaps nothing—and perhaps a great deal,” said Poirot
enigmatically. “Now, let us go and have a look at Mr. Opalsen’s
room.”

We followed him into the next room. It was a smaller room than the
other, but it was comfortably furnished. Poirot began to examine
it with his usual care.

“Nothing here,” he said at last. “Wait a minute! What is this?”

He went over to the washstand and picked up a small object that
was lying behind the water-bottle. It was a small, bright key.

“The key of the jewel-case!” cried the inspector.

“Exactly,” said Poirot. “Now, how did it get here?”

“The thief must have dropped it,” I suggested.

“Or put it there,” said Poirot. “Now, let us go back to the other
room.”

As we entered, we were met by Mr. Opalsen.

“Well,” he said, “have you found anything?”

“We have found several things,” said Poirot. “But we have not yet
found the pearls.”

“Do you think you will find them?” asked Mrs. Opalsen anxiously.

“I have every hope, madame,” said Poirot. “But I must ask you to
be patient. These things take time.”

He turned to the inspector.

“I should like to have another talk with that chambermaid,” he
said.

The inspector nodded, and a few minutes later the girl was brought
back into the room. She was still crying.

“Now, my girl,” said Poirot kindly, “there is nothing to be
frightened of. We only want you to tell us the truth. Are you sure
you didn’t go near that dressing-table?”

“Yes, sir—quite sure!”

“And you didn’t see anyone else in the room?”

“No, sir.”

“Not even through the door into Mr. Opalsen’s room?”

“No, sir.”

“I see. Thank you. That will do.”

The girl left the room. Poirot turned to us with a smile.

“Well,” he said, “the case is practically over!”

“Over!” I cried. “But we haven’t found the pearls!”

“Oh, yes, we have,” said Poirot.

“Where are they?” asked the inspector.

“They are in this room,” said Poirot.

“In this room!” we all cried.

“Yes,” said Poirot. “And I will show you where they are.”

He went over to the fireplace and stooped down.

“Look!” he said.

We all crowded round him. In the corner of the grate, hidden
behind a large piece of coal, was a small, dark object. Poirot
picked it up and handed it to Mrs. Opalsen.

“Your pearls, madame!” he said.

With a cry of joy, Mrs. Opalsen snatched the necklace from his
hand.

“Oh, my pearls! My beautiful pearls! How can I ever thank you, Mr.
Poirot?”

“Do not thank me, madame,” said Poirot. “Thank the little grey
cells!”

“But who stole them?” asked Mr. Opalsen.

“That,” said Poirot, “is a very interesting question. And I think
I can answer it.”

He turned to the inspector.

“Inspector, will you be so good as to arrest that man?”

He pointed to Mr. Opalsen.

“Mr. Opalsen!” I cried. “But he’s the owner of the pearls!”

“Exactly,” said Poirot. “And that is why he stole them!”

“But why should he steal his own wife’s pearls?” asked the
inspector.

“Because,” said Poirot, “as he told us himself, money is very tight
in the City just now. He needed money, and he hit upon this plan
to get it. He knew that the pearls were insured for a large sum,
and he thought that if they were stolen he would be able to claim
the insurance money. It was a very clever plan, but he made one
mistake.”

“What was that?” asked the inspector.

“He forgot that Hercule Poirot was staying at the hotel!” said
Poirot, with a smile.

“But how did he do it?” I asked.

“It was very simple,” said Poirot. “He waited until his wife had
gone down to dinner. Then he went into his own room, unlocked the
connecting door with his own key, and entered his wife’s room.
Célestine was there, but she was sitting by the window with her
back to the dressing-table. It was a dark evening, and the room was
only dimly lit. Mr. Opalsen is a very quiet mover, and he managed
to reach the dressing-table without being heard. He opened the
drawer, took out the jewel-case, and opened it with the duplicate
key he had had made. He took out the pearls, put the piece of
newspaper in their place—to make the case feel as though it still
contained something—and then replaced the case in the drawer. He
then returned to his own room, locking the door behind him. He hid
the pearls in the fireplace, where he thought they would be safe
until he could get them away. But he was in such a hurry that he
dropped a small piece of coal on the carpet, and that was what
first put me on the scent.”

“But the key!” I said. “The key we found in his room!”

“He put it there himself,” said Poirot. “He thought that if it was
found it would look as though the thief had dropped it.”

“And the scratch on the drawer?”

“He made that himself, too—to make it look like the work of a
professional thief.”

“Well,” said the inspector, “I must say you’re a marvel, Mr.
Poirot! I should never have thought of it myself.”

“It was just a matter of using the little grey cells,” said Poirot
modestly.

And as we went down to finish our coffee, I couldn’t help feeling
that, for once, Poirot was right.

Monsieur would understand the situation! To have such an accusation
made against one! She, who had been in the service of Madame for
nearly a year, and who would not touch a pin belonging to her!
Besides, had she not been in the room the whole time?

“_Doucement, doucement_,” said Poirot, soothing her. “There is no
need to be so agitated. You are being asked questions, that is
all.”

“But the suspicion—it is that which is so terrible!”

“Calm yourself, I pray you.” Poirot turned to the inspector.

“And the chambermaid? She also has been in the room all the time?”

The chambermaid, a pale-faced, frightened-looking girl, began to
sob.

“I only came in to turn down the beds,” she whimpered. “I was only
in the room a few minutes. I didn’t see any jewels, I didn’t indeed!”

“And the maid was here all the time?”

“Yes, sir.”

“You are sure of that?”

“Yes, sir.”

“You didn’t leave the room at all?”

“No, sir.”

“And you?” Poirot turned to Célestine.

“I also was here all the time.”

“You are sure you didn’t leave the room?”

“Not for one second!”

“I see.” Poirot’s face wore a puzzled expression. “Then, if the
pearls have been stolen, and you were both here, you must know
who took them.”

“Neither of us took them!” cried Célestine.

“Then how were they stolen?”

“I don’t know. I can’t imagine. It’s a mystery!”

“A mystery, indeed,” said Poirot. “Let us examine the drawer.”

Monsieur would not stand by and see her falsely accused, while that
infamous chambermaid was allowed to go scot-free. She had never
liked her—a bold, red-faced thing—a born thief. She had said from
the first that she was not honest. And had kept a sharp watch over
her too, when she was doing Madame’s room! Let those idiots of
policemen search her, and if they did not find Madame’s pearls on
her it would be very surprising!

The inspector looked at the two women in a puzzled way. He turned
to Mrs. Opalsen.

“You say, madame, that the maid has not left the room?”

“I should like to ask her a question,” said Poirot, with a deferential
bow to the inspector.

“Oh, certainly, monsieur. But let me first suggest that she
be searched.”

The inspector’s suggestion was followed by an outburst of screams
and protests from both the accused women. They were finally taken
out of the room by the police, and there was a pause of some
minutes. During this time Poirot strolled across to the dressing-table,
and examined the jewel-case with much interest. It was a neat little
thing in green morocco.

The inspector and his colleague returned, with the two women, who
were still in a state of high indignation.

The search had been fruitless. No trace of the missing pearls had
been found.

“I was about to ask you, mademoiselle,” said Poirot, addressing
Célestine, “whether you did or did not leave this room during the
time that your mistress was downstairs at dinner?”

“I did not, monsieur! Not for a single instant.”

“You are sure?”

“_Mais oui_, monsieur. I have been here all the time.”

“And you, mademoiselle?” Poirot turned to the chambermaid.

“I came in just before eight o’clock to turn down the beds. Célestine
was here then.”

“And you also did not leave the room?”

“No, monsieur. I was only here about five minutes.”

“So that,” said Poirot, “if the pearls were stolen between 7.30
and 8.30, and these two women were here all the time, one or other
of them must have taken them?”

“That is the logic of it,” agreed the inspector.

“But they have both been searched,” I put in.

“Exactly,” said Poirot. “And nothing has been found. So it
follows—what?”

He looked round the room.

“There are plenty of hiding-places here,” suggested the inspector.

“That is so,” agreed Poirot. “But if the pearls are hidden in
this room, they will be found. The police are very thorough.”

He turned again to Célestine.

“You are quite sure you did not leave the room?”

“_Mais non_, monsieur! I have already said so. I stayed here to
do some mending for Madame.”

“And you did not even step out into the corridor?”

“Not for one second.”

“Then,” said Poirot, “I should like to see the chambermaid’s
room.”

“My room?” The girl looked startled. “But I haven’t got the
pearls!”

“Nevertheless, I should like to see it.”

The inspector looked at Poirot with interest.

“You have a reason, monsieur?”

“Perhaps.”

Accompanied by the inspector, we all went up to the top floor,
where the servants’ rooms were situated. The chambermaid’s room
was a small, neat apartment. Poirot looked round it with a
searching eye. He went to the chest of drawers, and turned over
the girl’s few belongings. Then he went to the bed, and felt under
the mattress.

Suddenly he stooped. From under the bed he drew out a small,
glittering object.

It was a pearl!

A second later he had found another.

The girl uttered a cry of despair.

“I didn’t do it! I didn’t, indeed! I don’t know how they got
there!”

She began to sob.

The inspector’s face was grim.

“This looks very like it,” he remarked. “I’m afraid I must ask
you to come with me, my girl.”

The poor girl was led away, still protesting her innocence.

“Well,” said Opalsen, with a sigh of relief, “that’s that! I must
say, Poirot, you’ve been very quick about it. I shouldn’t have
thought of looking in her room.”

“It was the logical place,” said Poirot modestly. “If she had
them, she would naturally hide them in her own room.”

“But how did she get them out of the jewel-case?” I asked. “She
couldn’t have had a duplicate key.”

“She might have found the case unlocked,” suggested Opalsen.

“But Mrs. Opalsen says she locked it,” I reminded him.

“I did—I’m certain of it!” cried that lady.

“The lock is a very simple one,” said Poirot. “A piece of wire—a
bent hairpin—it would not be difficult.”

He turned to the inspector, who had just returned.

“You have the girl in safety?”

“Yes, monsieur. We’ll take her down to the station presently.”

“And the pearls—you have them?”

“Only the two you found. We’re going to have a good look for the
rest.”

“I think,” said Poirot, “that if you look under the paper at the
bottom of the chest of drawers you may find something.”

The inspector did so. A moment later he gave a cry of triumph.
He held up a magnificent string of pearls.

“Here they are, right enough! Well, monsieur, I must congratulate
you. You’ve made a quick job of this.”

“It was very simple,” said Poirot.

We all went back to the Opalsens’ room. Mrs. Opalsen was overjoyed
at the recovery of her pearls. She insisted on Poirot’s accepting
a large check, which he at first refused, but finally was persuaded
to take.

“And now, Hastings,” said Poirot, as we found ourselves alone, “what
do you think of it all?”

“Well,” I said, “it was a very simple case. I’m only surprised
the girl was so foolish as to hide the pearls in her own room.”

“It was, as you say, very simple,” said Poirot. “So simple that
I—Hercule Poirot—am not satisfied.”

“Not satisfied? But you’ve found the pearls!”

“Yes, I have found the pearls. But I have not found the thief.”

“The thief? But it was the chambermaid!”

“Was it? I wonder.”

“But the pearls were in her room!”

“Exactly. They were in her room. That is what I find so—suspicious.”

“Suspicious? I don’t follow you.”

“My dear Hastings, if you were a thief, and you had stolen a
valuable necklace, would you hide it under the paper of your
chest of drawers, where anyone could find it?”

“I might, if I were in a hurry.”

“But she was not in a hurry. She had all the time in the world.
And why leave two pearls under the bed? No, Hastings, the person
who stole those pearls was not the chambermaid.”

“Then who was it?”

“That,” said Poirot, “is what I intend to find out.”

He sat down and began to polish his boots with a piece of silk.

“Tell me, Hastings, did you notice anything about that
jewel-case?”

“Nothing particular. It was just an ordinary jewel-case.”

“It was very ordinary. So ordinary that it was—extraordinary.”

“I don’t understand.”

“Wait, Hastings. All in good time. Now, I have a little commission
for you. I want you to go down to the office and find out if any
of the guests have left the hotel this evening.”

“But what has that to do with it?”

“Go, my friend. Do as I ask.”

I went. When I returned a few minutes later, I found Poirot still
polishing his boots.

“Well?” he asked.

“No one has left,” I said. “Except, of course, a few people who
were only here for dinner.”

“No one stayed in the hotel? No one who has been here for a day
or two?”

“No one.”

“_Tiens!_ That is curious.”

He continued his polishing for a few minutes in silence. Then he
stood up and looked at his boots with satisfaction.

“And now, Hastings, we will go and have a little talk with
Mademoiselle Célestine.”

We found the French maid in her own room. She was still weeping,
but she looked up as we entered.

“Ah, monsieur! You have come to tell me that I am cleared? That
that wicked girl has confessed?”

“Not quite, mademoiselle. I have come to ask you a few more
questions. You are quite sure you did not leave the room while
your mistress was at dinner?”

“I have already said so, monsieur.”

“Not even for a moment?”

“Not for one second.”

“And the door—it was locked?”

“No, monsieur. It was not locked.”

“Then anyone could have come in?”

“Yes—but I was there.”

“Exactly. You were there. And you would have seen them?”

“Of course, monsieur.”

“And no one came in?”

“No one—except the chambermaid.”

“And she was only there for five minutes?”

“Five minutes—no more.”

“And she was turning down the beds?”

“Yes, monsieur.”

“She did not go near the dressing-table?”

“No, monsieur.”

“You are sure?”

“I am quite sure.”

“_Bien._ And now, mademoiselle, I want you to tell me something
else. Have you noticed anything unusual lately? Anything out of
the way?”

The girl thought for a moment.

“No, monsieur. I do not think so.”

“Nothing at all?”

“Well—there was the matter of the key.”

“The key? What key?”

“The key of Madame’s jewel-case. A few days ago she could not
find it. She was in a great state. And then, after a little while,
she found it in her purse.”

“In her purse?”

“Yes, monsieur. She said she must have put it there and forgotten
it.”

“I see. And was there anything else?”

“No, monsieur. I cannot remember anything.”

“_Merci_, mademoiselle. That is all.”

We left the room.

“Well,” I said, “what do you make of that?”

“It is very interesting,” said Poirot. “Very interesting indeed.”

“But I don’t see that it gets us any further.”

“No? Perhaps you are right. But wait, Hastings. Wait. I have a
feeling—a little idea——”

He stopped. We were passing the door of the Opalsens’ room.
Suddenly Poirot stooped and picked up something from the floor.

“What is it?” I asked.

“A piece of paper, Hastings. A very small piece of paper.”

He held it up. It was a fragment of a telegram.

“...at once... urgent...”

“That is all it says,” I said. “It doesn’t seem very important.”

“Perhaps not. And yet—it was just outside the door.”

He put it in his pocket.

“And now, Hastings, I think we will go and see Mr. Opalsen.”

We found the stockbroker in the lounge. He was talking to some
friends, but he came towards us as we approached.

“Well, Poirot? Any more news?”

“Not exactly news, monsieur. But I should like to ask you a
question, if I may.”

“Certainly. What is it?”

“Have you had any telegrams lately? Within the last day or two?”

Opalsen looked surprised.

“Telegrams? No, I don’t think so. Why do you ask?”

“I found a fragment of one just now. I thought it might be
yours.”

“No, it’s not mine. I haven’t had a telegram for a week.”

“I see. Well, it is of no importance. By the way, Mr. Opalsen,
how long have you been here?”

“About ten days.”

“And you have found it comfortable?”

“Oh, yes. Very comfortable. The service is excellent.”

“I am glad to hear it. Well, I will not detain you. Good-night,
monsieur.”

“Good-night, Poirot.”

As we walked away, Poirot turned to me.

“You see, Hastings? He has had no telegrams. And yet—I found
that fragment outside his door.”

“It might have belonged to someone else.”

“It might. But it was just outside his door.”

He was silent for a moment. Then he said:

“Tell me, Hastings, do you remember what Mr. Opalsen said when
we first met him? About money being tight in the City?”

“Yes, I remember.”

“And about the pearls being worth more than he paid for them?”

“Yes.”

“It is interesting, is it not?”

“I suppose so. But I don’t see what you’re driving at.”

“Don’t you, Hastings? Well, perhaps it is as well. And now, I
think I will go to bed. I have much to think about.”

“But what about the chambermaid?” I asked. “Are you going to
let her stay in prison?”

“For the moment, yes. It will do her no harm. And it will give
me time.”

“Time for what?”

“Time to find the truth, Hastings.”

He nodded to me and went into his room.

I was puzzled. I could not see what Poirot was after. The case
seemed so simple. The pearls had been found in the girl’s room.
What more could one want?

The next morning I found Poirot already up and dressed. He was
sitting at the table, looking at the fragment of the telegram.

“Good-morning, Hastings,” he said. “I have been thinking.”

“So I see.”

“I have been thinking about that telegram. ‘...at once... urgent...’
What does it mean, Hastings?”

“It might mean anything.”

“Exactly. It might mean anything. But what does it mean to Mr.
Opalsen?”

“But he said he hadn’t had any telegrams.”

“He said so, yes. But did he tell the truth?”

“Why should he lie about it?”

“That is what I ask myself. Why should he lie? Unless—he had
something to hide.”

“But what could he have to hide?”

“That is what I am going to find out.”

He stood up.

“I am going for a little walk, Hastings. I shall be back in an
hour.”

“Can’t I come with you?”

“No, my friend. I would prefer to go alone.”

He left the room. I was more puzzled than ever. What was Poirot
up to?

I went down to breakfast. In the dining-room I saw the Opalsens.
They were sitting at their usual table. Mrs. Opalsen was wearing
her pearls. She looked very happy.

“Good-morning, Captain Hastings,” she said, as I passed. “Isn’t
it a lovely day?”

“Beautiful,” I agreed.

“And isn’t it wonderful about my pearls? I can’t tell you how
grateful I am to Mr. Poirot.”

“He is very clever,” I said.

“He is indeed. Ed says he’s the cleverest man he’s ever met.”

Mr. Opalsen nodded.

“He certainly did a good job for us,” he said. “I don’t know what
we’d have done without him.”

I went to my own table. I could not help feeling that there was
something wrong. Poirot’s behavior was very strange. Why was he
not satisfied?

After breakfast I went out onto the front. It was a beautiful
morning, and the air was crisp and clear. I walked for some time,
thinking about the case.

Suddenly I saw Poirot. He was sitting on a bench, looking out at
the sea. He did not see me, and I did not disturb him. He looked
very deep in thought.

When I got back to the hotel, I found him in the lounge. He was
talking to the manager.

“Ah, Hastings!” he said, as I approached. “I have just been having
a very interesting talk with Monsieur le Directeur.”

The manager bowed and moved away.

“Well?” I asked. “What did he say?”

“He said many things, Hastings. Many very interesting things.”

“About the case?”

“About many things. And now, I think we will go and see the
inspector.”

We found the inspector at the police station. He looked very
pleased with himself.

“Well, monsieur,” he said, as we entered. “The girl’s confessed.”

“Confessed?” I cried.

“Yes. She admits she took the pearls. She says she was tempted,
and that she’s very sorry.”

I looked at Poirot. He did not seem surprised.

“I see,” he said. “She has confessed.”

“Yes. So that’s the end of that.”

“Is it?” said Poirot. “I wonder.”

“But she’s confessed!” I said.

“She has confessed, yes. But why has she confessed?”

“Because she’s guilty, I suppose.”

“Or because she was told to confess?”

“Told to confess? By whom?”

“That,” said Poirot, “is what we are going to find out.”

He turned to the inspector.

“I should like to see the girl, if I may.”

“Certainly, monsieur. But I don’t see what good it will do.”

“Perhaps none. But I should like to see her, nevertheless.”

We were taken to the girl’s cell. She was sitting on the bed,
crying.

“Now then, my girl,” said the inspector. “Here’s the gentleman
who found the pearls. He wants to talk to you.”

The girl looked up. Her eyes were red with weeping.

“I didn’t do it!” she cried. “I didn’t! I only said I did because
they told me to!”

“Who told you to?” asked Poirot.

“He did! That man—the one who came to see me.”

“What man?”

“I don’t know. He said he was a lawyer. He said if I confessed
I’d only get a short sentence, and that he’d see I was all right
when I came out. But if I didn’t, I’d go to prison for years.”

“I see,” said Poirot. “And what did he look like, this man?”

“He was tall and thin, and he had a dark moustache. And he wore
a grey suit.”

“A grey suit?” said Poirot. “That is very interesting.”

He turned to the inspector.

“I think, monsieur, that you had better let this girl go.”

“Let her go? But she’s confessed!”

“She has confessed because she was frightened. She is not the
thief.”

“Then who is?”

“I will tell you that in a few minutes. If you will come with me
to the hotel, I will show you.”

We all went back to the hotel. Poirot led the way to the Opalsens’
room. He knocked on the door, and Mr. Opalsen opened it.

“Ah, Poirot!” he said. “Come in. What can I do for you?”

“I have come to return your check, monsieur,” said Poirot.

He held out the check. Opalsen looked surprised.

“Return it? But why?”

“Because I have not earned it. I did not find the thief.”

“But the girl’s confessed!”

“She has confessed, yes. But she is not the thief.”

“Then who is?”

“You are, monsieur!”

Opalsen’s face went white.

“I? What do you mean? You must be mad!”

“I am not mad, monsieur. I am very sane. You stole those pearls
yourself.”

“It’s a lie! Why should I steal my own wife’s pearls?”

“Because you needed the money. Because money is ‘tight in the
City’. Because you wanted the insurance money.”

“You’re crazy! I tell you I didn’t do it!”

“Then how do you explain this?”

Poirot held up a small, glittering object. It was a pearl.

“Another pearl?” I cried.

“Yes, Hastings. But this pearl is different. This pearl is—a
fake!”

“A fake?”

“Yes. The pearls that were stolen were real. The pearls that
were found in the chambermaid’s room were—fakes.”

“Fakes?” cried Mrs. Opalsen. “But they can’t be! They’re my pearls!”

“No, madame. They are not your pearls. They are a very good
imitation. Your husband had them made some time ago. He switched
them for the real ones when he ‘couldn’t find the key’.”

“It’s a lie!” shouted Opalsen.

“Is it? Then perhaps you can explain why you sent a telegram to
a firm of jewelers in London, asking them to send the imitation
pearls at once? It was urgent, was it not?”

Opalsen collapsed into a chair. He knew he was caught.

“I—I had to do it,” he groaned. “I was in a hole. I thought I
could get away with it.”

“And you would have,” said Poirot, “if you had not been so—thorough.
The two pearls under the bed—they were a mistake. They were meant
to point to the chambermaid, but they pointed to someone who
wanted her to be suspected.”

The inspector stepped forward.

“Edward Opalsen, I arrest you for the theft of these pearls.”

As they led him away, Mrs. Opalsen turned to Poirot.

“Oh, Mr. Poirot! How can I ever thank you?”

“By wearing the real pearls, madame,” said Poirot. “I have them
here.”

He drew the necklace from his pocket.

“But—where did you find them?” I asked.

“In Mr. Opalsen’s boots, Hastings. The ones he was not wearing.
I told you I was going for a walk, but I only went as far as his
room.”

“And the fake pearls?”

“They are with the police. They will be used as evidence.”

“Well,” I said, as we walked back to our own room. “It was a
clever piece of work, Poirot.”

“It was, as I said, very simple,” said Poirot. “But it required
the little grey cells.”

He smiled and began to polish his boots.

“And now, Hastings, I think we will have our dinner. I am very
hungry.”

We went down to the dining-room. The music was playing, and the
crowd was as gay as ever. But for one man, the weekend at Brighton
had not been a success.

“_Tiens!_” said Poirot, as he looked round the room. “It is a
strange world, is it not, Hastings?”

“Very strange,” I agreed.

“But it is a good world—for those who have the little grey
cells!”

He smiled and began to eat his soup.

The inspector shook his head.

“That’s as may be,” he said. “If the maid’s story is true, the pearls
could only have been stolen while she was in the room. And as the
chambermaid is the only other person who was there at all, she was
under Célestine’s eye the whole time. You must see for yourself,
madame, how it looks.”

“I’m sure I’m as honest as anybody else,” said the chambermaid,
beginning to cry. “I wouldn’t touch a thing that didn’t belong to
me, not if it was ever so! And as for that Frenchwoman, she’s no
better than she should be, I’ll be bound. She’s only trying to
put it on to me to save her own skin.”

The inspector’s face took on a look of extreme boredom.

“This won’t do any good, you know. I must have a few words with
Célestine alone.”

He motioned the rest of us into the adjoining room, and for the
next twenty minutes we kicked our heels in the salon. Then he came
out, and beckoned to the chambermaid. Her interview was shorter,
and at the end of it she was dismissed, and Célestine was recalled.

At last the inspector appeared again.

“Well?” we all asked.

He shook his head.

“I’ve had a look round,” he said. “The window’s impossible—it’s a
sheer drop to the street. And anyway, it was fastened. The door
into the corridor was locked, and the only other entrance is
through this room. I’m bound to say it looks like a plant.”

“A plant?” repeated Opalsen.

“Yes. One of those two girls did it, and they’re both in it
together.”

“Wait a moment, my good girl,” said the inspector, holding up a
warning finger. “Don’t be in too much of a hurry. No one’s accusing
you—yet. Now, as to these pearls, you’ll find it’s not as easy as
you think to get rid of them. They’re too well known. If you take
my advice, you’ll just hand them over before things get worse.”

The chambermaid’s reply was a burst of indignant tears.

“I’m an honest girl, I am, and I wouldn’t do such a thing. As for
that Frenchwoman, she’s no better than she should be. I’ve seen her
whispering to a man in the corridor, and I’ll be bound she’s given
them to him.”

“Silence, both of you!” commanded the inspector. “Now, Mrs.
Opalsen, when you went down to dinner, you say the pearls were in
the jewel-case?”

“Yes.”

“And you locked the case?”

“Yes.”

“And the case was in the drawer?”

“Yes.”

“When did you first miss the pearls?”

“When I came up to fetch them for Mr. Poirot to see.”

“And you’re quite sure they were there when you went down?”

“Absolutely sure. I put them back myself.”

The inspector looked thoughtful.

“Who else had a key to the jewel-case?”

“No one.”

“Not your husband?”

“Oh, no.”

“Then you were the only person who could have opened the case?”

“Yes.”

“Well, that’s a bit of a poser, I must say,” said the inspector.
“If no one else had a key, and you’re sure you locked the case,
and the pearls were there when you went down, it’s a bit of a
mystery how they could have disappeared.”

“But they _have_ disappeared,” wailed Mrs. Opalsen.

“Yes, there’s no doubt about that,” agreed the inspector. “Now,
Célestine, you were in the room all the time Madame was at dinner?”

“_Oui_, Monsieur.”

“Did you leave it at all?”

“_Non_, Monsieur. I was here the whole time.”

“And you, the chambermaid? You were in and out, I suppose?”

“I was only in once, to turn down the beds. Célestine was here then.”

“Is that so, Célestine?”

“_Oui_, Monsieur. She was here for a few minutes only.”

“Did she go near the dressing-table?”

“_Non_, Monsieur. She only touched the beds.”

The inspector looked more puzzled than ever.

“Well, it’s a bit of a mystery, and no mistake. If the pearls were
there when Mrs. Opalsen went down, and Célestine never left the
room, and the chambermaid was only in for a few minutes while
Célestine was there—well, it’s a bit of a poser!”

He turned to the other man.

“What do you think, Williams?”

The man in plain clothes shook his head.

“It’s a tough nut to crack, and that’s a fact,” he admitted.

Poirot stepped forward.

“Will you permit me to ask a few questions?” he inquired
suavely.

“By all means, Mr. Poirot,” said the inspector. “We know your
reputation, and we’ll be glad of any help you can give us.”

The inspector sighed. He had evidently had much experience of this
sort of thing.

“You’ve no objection to being searched, I suppose?” he asked
quietly.

“Me? Not a bit of it! The sooner the better. I’m an honest girl,
and I don’t care who knows it.”

The chambermaid was taken out by the inspector, and a few minutes
later he returned to the room.

“There’s nothing on her,” he said briefly.

The girl came in behind him, with her head high, and a look of
triumph on her face.

Célestine seemed for a moment at a loss. Then, with a sudden
movement, she produced a bunch of keys from her pocket.

“Search me also!” she cried. “Search my boxes! I have nothing to
conceal!”

The inspector looked at Poirot.

“We’ll have to do it,” he said. “It’s the only way.”

He followed the maid to her room, and again we waited. The result
was the same. Nothing was found.

The inspector stepped forward.

“I was about to suggest a search of both these women,” he observed
drily. “And also of their boxes. They were both in the room while
Mrs. Opalsen was at dinner, I understand?”

“Yes,” replied that lady. “Célestine was here the whole time, and
the chambermaid came in to turn down the beds as usual.”

The search was conducted with professional thoroughness, but
revealed nothing. The two women’s boxes were examined with a like
result. The inspector looked disappointed.

“Well,” he remarked, “it’s a bit of a poser. If the pearls were in
the case when Mrs. Opalsen went down to dinner, and the maid never
left the room, it’s a bit of a mystery how they could have gone.
You’re quite sure you saw them, ma’am?”

“I’m positive. I remember thinking how beautiful they looked as
they lay on the blue velvet.”

“And you’re sure you locked the case?”

“Yes, I’m quite sure of that.”

The inspector’s face remained grave. He turned to Poirot.

“What do you think of it, sir?” he asked.

Poirot did not answer for a moment. He was busy examining the
dressing-table. He looked at the drawer from which the jewel-case
had been taken, and then at the lock of the case itself.

“It is a very simple lock,” he murmured. “A child could pick it.”

“That’s what I say, sir,” the inspector agreed. “But if the maid
never left the room——”

“Did you leave the room at all, Célestine?” Poirot asked, turning
to the Frenchwoman.

“No, Monsieur, not for one single moment.”

“And the chambermaid?”

“She was here for perhaps ten minutes. Not more.”

“And you were here the whole time she was in the room?”

“Yes, Monsieur. I was sitting over there by the window, sewing.”

“You did not leave the room to fetch anything?”

“No, Monsieur.”

“Not even for a minute?”

“No, Monsieur.”

Poirot’s eyes wandered round the room. They settled on a door
leading into the next room.

“Where does that lead?” he asked.

“To my husband’s room,” Mrs. Opalsen replied.

“Was the door locked?”

“No.”

Poirot went to the door and opened it. The room was empty. He came
back into the bedroom.

“And the door into the corridor?”

“That was locked. I always lock it when I am in here,” Célestine
explained.

“So that no one could enter from the corridor without your
knowledge?”

“Exactly, Monsieur.”

Poirot’s eyes went back to the dressing-table. He picked up the
jewel-case and examined it again. Then he turned to the inspector.

“You have searched the room?” he asked.

“Every inch of it, sir.”

“And you have found nothing?”

“Nothing.”

Poirot nodded. His eyes were fixed on the floor. Suddenly he stooped
and picked up something. It was a small piece of white thread. He
held it up for us to see.

“You see this?” he asked.

The inspector looked at it.

“It’s a piece of thread,” he said. “What of it?”

“It is a piece of thread,” Poirot repeated. “And it was lying on
the floor, just here.” He pointed to a spot near the dressing-table.

The inspector shrugged his shoulders.

“I don’t see that that helps us much,” he remarked.

“Perhaps not,” Poirot replied. “But it is a clue, nevertheless.”

He turned to Mrs. Opalsen.

“You have a maid, madame. Does she do much sewing?”

“She is always sewing,” Mrs. Opalsen replied. “She is a very good
needlewoman.”

“I see.” Poirot turned to Célestine. “You were sewing this evening,
you say?”

“Yes, Monsieur.”

“What were you sewing?”

“I was mending one of Madame’s lace collars.”

“I see. And did you use white thread?”

“Yes, Monsieur.”

Poirot nodded.

“That explains it, then,” the inspector remarked.

“Perhaps,” Poirot replied. “But there is one thing that I do not
understand. Why was this piece of thread lying on the floor _here_,
near the dressing-table?”

“I suppose it fell there,” the inspector suggested.

“Perhaps,” Poirot repeated. “But Célestine says she was sitting by
the window, which is on the other side of the room.”

There was a moment’s silence. We all looked at the piece of thread.
It seemed a very small thing to be making such a fuss about.

“Well,” the inspector said at length, “I don’t see that we can do
anything more here. I’ll have to report the matter to my superiors.
In the meantime, I’ll ask you all to stay in the hotel.”

He and his companion withdrew. Mr. Opalsen followed them to have
a further word with the manager. Mrs. Opalsen and Célestine remained
in the bedroom.

Poirot and I went back to the lounge.

“Well, Poirot,” I said, “what do you make of it?”

Poirot did not answer for a moment. He was busy arranging some
matches on the table in front of him.

“It is a very pretty little problem, Hastings,” he said at length.
“A very pretty little problem indeed.”

“You think the maid took them?” I asked.

“It would seem so,” Poirot replied. “And yet——”

“And yet what?”

“There are certain things that I do not understand.”

“Such as?”

“Such as that piece of thread, for instance.”

“Oh, that!” I exclaimed. “Surely that’s easy enough to explain.
The maid probably went over to the dressing-table for something,
and the thread fell there then.”

“Perhaps,” Poirot said. “But there is another thing. Mrs. Opalsen
says she saw the pearls just before she went down to dinner.
Célestine says she never left the room. The chambermaid was only in
the room for ten minutes, and Célestine was there all the time.
How, then, could the pearls have been stolen?”

“The chambermaid might have taken them while Célestine wasn’t
looking,” I suggested.

“In ten minutes? And with Célestine in the room? It seems unlikely,
Hastings.”

“Then you think Célestine took them?”

“If she did, where are they? The police have searched her, and her
boxes, and they have found nothing.”

“She might have hidden them in the room.”

“The police have searched the room, Hastings. Every inch of it.”

“Then who could have taken them?”

“That is what we have to find out, my friend.”

He sat in silence for a few minutes, his eyes fixed on the matches.
Suddenly he looked up.

“Hastings,” he said, “I have an idea. A very simple idea. I wonder
if I am right.”

“What is it?” I asked.

“I will not tell you yet. I must first make a little experiment.”

He rose and led the way back to the lift. We went up to the first
floor. Poirot went to the door of Mrs. Opalsen’s room and knocked.
Célestine opened it.

“Monsieur?” she said.

“I have come to ask you a question, Célestine,” Poirot said. “When
you were sewing this evening, did you use a needle?”

Célestine looked surprised.

“But naturally, Monsieur,” she replied.

“And where is that needle now?”

“It is in my work-basket, Monsieur.”

“May I see it?”

Célestine went to the window and brought back a small work-basket.
Poirot looked through it.

“I do not see a needle here with white thread in it,” he remarked.

“No, Monsieur. I have used all the thread that was on it.”

“I see. And have you any more needles?”

“Yes, Monsieur. There are some in that little case.”

Poirot opened the case and looked at the needles. Then he looked
at the piece of thread he had found on the floor.

“This thread,” he said, “is very fine. Much finer than the thread
you have here.”

Célestine looked at the thread.

“You are right, Monsieur,” she said. “That is not my thread.”

“I thought not,” Poirot said. “Thank you, Célestine.”

He turned and led the way back to the lounge.

“Well,” I said, “what does that prove?”

“It proves, Hastings, that someone else was in that room this
evening. Someone who was using very fine white thread.”

“But who?” I asked.

“That is what we have to find out,” Poirot replied.

He sat down and began to arrange the matches again.

“Hastings,” he said after a few minutes, “I want you to do
something for me.”

“What is it?” I asked.

“I want you to go to the manager’s office and find out if any of
the guests have left the hotel this evening.”

“Why?” I asked.

“Because, my friend, I believe that the person who took those
pearls has already left the hotel.”

I went to the manager’s office and made the inquiry. I was told
that no one had left the hotel that evening. I went back and told
Poirot.

“No one?” he said. “Are you sure?”

“Quite sure.”

Poirot looked disappointed.

“Then I am wrong,” he said. “And yet—I was so sure.”

He sat in silence for a while, his brow furrowed in thought.
Suddenly he looked up.

“Hastings,” he said, “I have another idea. A very simple idea. I
wonder if I am right this time.”

“What is it?” I asked.

“I will not tell you yet. I must first make another little
experiment.”

He rose and led the way to the lift again. We went up to the first
floor, but this time Poirot did not go to Mrs. Opalsen’s room.
Instead, he went to the room next to it—Mr. Opalsen’s room. He
tried the door. It was unlocked. We went in.

The room was empty. Poirot went to the dressing-table and began to
examine it. He looked at the drawers, and then at the top of the
table. Suddenly he uttered a cry of triumph.

“Look, Hastings!” he said.

He pointed to a small object lying on the dressing-table. It was
a needle with a piece of very fine white thread in it.

“You see?” Poirot said. “Someone has been here, too.”

“But who?” I asked.

“That is what we have to find out,” Poirot replied.

He looked around the room. His eyes fell on a large trunk in the
corner. He went to it and tried the lid. It was locked.

“Hastings,” he said, “I want you to go and find Mr. Opalsen. Ask
him to come here at once.”

I found Mr. Opalsen in the lounge and brought him back to his room.

“Mr. Opalsen,” Poirot said, “I have found something that I think
will interest you.”

He showed him the needle and thread.

“What of it?” Mr. Opalsen asked.

“It is very fine white thread,” Poirot said. “The same kind of
thread that I found in your wife’s room.”

Mr. Opalsen looked puzzled.

“I don’t see what that has to do with the pearls,” he said.

“I think it has a great deal to do with them,” Poirot replied.
“Mr. Opalsen, I must ask you to open this trunk.”

Mr. Opalsen looked surprised.

“My trunk?” he said. “Why?”

“Because I believe the pearls are inside it,” Poirot replied.

Mr. Opalsen laughed.

“That’s ridiculous,” he said. “I haven’t got the pearls.”

“Nevertheless,” Poirot said, “I must ask you to open it.”

Mr. Opalsen hesitated for a moment, then he took a key from his
pocket and unlocked the trunk. Poirot began to search through it.
He turned out some clothes, and then he came to a small wooden
box. He opened it.

Inside, lying on a bed of cotton-wool, was the pearl necklace.

Mrs. Opalsen, who had followed us into the room, uttered a shriek
of joy.

“My pearls!” she cried. “You’ve found them!”

Mr. Opalsen looked stunned.

“I don’t understand,” he said. “How did they get there?”

“I think I can explain that,” Poirot said.

He turned to the inspector, who had just entered the room.

“Inspector,” he said, “I think you will find that Mr. Opalsen
stole the pearls himself.”

“Mr. Opalsen!” I exclaimed. “But why?”

“Because, as he told us earlier this evening, money is very tight
in the City just now. He needed money, and he decided to steal his
wife’s pearls and sell them.”

“But how did he do it?” I asked. “He was downstairs with us the
whole time.”

“Not the whole time,” Poirot replied. “He left us for a few minutes
when he was called away by the page-boy. He went upstairs, entered
his wife’s room through the connecting door, took the pearls from
the jewel-case, and then went back to his own room and hid them in
his trunk.”

“But the needle and thread?” I asked.

“That was a clever little touch,” Poirot said. “He knew that if
the pearls were missed, the maid would be suspected. So he took a
needle and some fine white thread and left them in his wife’s room,
near the dressing-table, to make it look as though the maid had
been sewing there. But he was not careful enough. He left the needle
and thread in his own room as well, and he used thread that was
much finer than any the maid had.”

Mr. Opalsen looked at Poirot for a moment, then he bowed his head.

“You’re right,” he said. “I did it. I was desperate for money.”

The inspector stepped forward.

“I’ll have to ask you to come with me, sir,” he said.

As they led Mr. Opalsen away, Mrs. Opalsen turned to Poirot.

“How can I ever thank you?” she said.

Poirot smiled and bowed.

“It was nothing, madame,” he said. “A very simple little problem
for the little grey cells.”

“You’re a liar—do you hear?” said the chambermaid, advancing upon
her. “Stole ’em yourself, and want to put it on me. Why, I was only
in the room about three minutes before the lady come up, and then
you were sitting here the whole time, as you always do, like a cat
watching a mouse.”

The inspector looked across inquiringly at Célestine. “Is that
true? Didn’t you leave the room at all?”

“This is a most singular case,” remarked the inspector, scratching his head. “If the pearls are not on either of the women, and since neither of them has left the room, it stands to reason they must be hidden somewhere in this apartment. But we’ve searched the place pretty thoroughly.” Poirot, who had been standing in the background, stepped forward. He picked up the velvet-lined jewel-case and turned it over in his hands with a thoughtful air. “You are quite certain, madame,” he asked, turning to Mrs. Opalsen, “that the pearls were indeed inside this case when you locked it before dinner?” “I’ve told you so already!” snapped the lady, her temper beginning to fray. “I saw them there with my own eyes. I was going to wear them, and then I changed my mind.” Poirot nodded slowly, his eyes still fixed on the case.

The inspector looked from one woman to the other. “Well,” he said heavily, “if they’re not on you, they’re in the room. We’ll have to have a proper look round.” He began a systematic search, poking his head into the wardrobes and peering under the bed. Poirot, however, did not assist him. He remained standing by the dressing-table, his eyes fixed upon the jewel-case with a singular expression. Suddenly, he leaned forward and, taking a small magnifying glass from his pocket, examined the edge of the drawer where the case had been kept. “Aha!” he murmured softly to himself. “That is very interesting. Very interesting indeed!”

“If they are not on the person, they are in the room,” said Poirot. “Unless they have been thrown out of the window?”

“I’ve already thought of that,” said the inspector. “And I’ve sent a man to look. There’s nothing.”

Poirot nodded. He was over by the dressing-table. With a sudden movement he picked up the jewel-case and examined it minutely.

“May I ask, madame, if you always keep the case in this particular drawer?”

“Always,” replied Mrs. Opalsen.

“And it was not locked?”

“The drawer? No.”

Poirot looked at the lock of the case. “And the key, you say, was never out of your possession?”

“Never.”

Poirot's eyes wandered to the washstand. He walked over to it and, to my surprise, began to examine the soap-dish with a look of the most profound interest.

“It is very strange,” murmured Poirot, half to himself. “Very strange indeed.”

“It’s more than strange, it’s a confounded nuisance!” snapped Mr. Opalsen. “If the pearls aren’t on either of those women, where are they? They haven't wings to fly away of their own accord.”

Poirot did not answer. He was down on his knees, examining the carpet. Then he rose and approached the dressing-table, picking up the empty jewel-case and turning it over in his hands. He peered closely at the lock, and then at the velvet lining.

“You are sure, madame, that you locked it?”

“I’m positive,” cried Mrs. Opalsen. “I remember the click of the key as plain as could be.”

“It is very curious,” murmured Poirot, “very curious indeed. You say, Madame, that you locked the case yourself?” He picked up the leather box, turning it over in his hands with a sort of feline grace. Then, instead of looking inside again, he began to examine the underside of the dressing-table itself, running his fingers along the wood with a delicate touch that reminded me of a doctor feeling a pulse. He then turned his attention to the second drawer, pulling it out and peering into the cavity behind it with an expression of the most intense concentration, while the rest of us watched him in a silence that was only broken by the heavy breathing of Mr. Opalsen.

“I’m afraid I’ll have to ask you to come along with me all the
same, miss.” He turned to Mrs. Opalsen. “I’m sorry, madam, but all
