the evidence points that way. If she’s not got them on her, they’re
hidden somewhere about the room.”

Célestine uttered a piercing shriek, and clung to Poirot’s arm.
The latter bent and whispered something in the girl’s ear. She
looked up at him doubtfully.

“_Si, si, mon enfant_—I assure you it is better not to resist.”
Then he turned to the inspector. “You permit, monsieur? A little
experiment—purely for my own satisfaction.”

“Depends on what it is,” replied the police officer non-committally.

Poirot addressed Célestine once more.

“You have told us that you went into your room to fetch a reel of
cotton. Whereabouts was it?”

“On the top of the chest of drawers, monsieur.”

“And the scissors?”

“They also.”

“Would it be troubling you too much, mademoiselle, to ask you to
repeat those two actions? You were sitting here with your work,
you say?”

Célestine sat down, and then, at a sign from Poirot, rose, passed
into the adjoining room, took up an object from the chest of
drawers, and returned.

Poirot divided his attention between her movements and a large
turnip of a watch which he held in the palm of his hand.

“Again, if you please, mademoiselle.”

At the conclusion of the second performance, he made a note in his
pocket-book, and returned the watch to his pocket.

“Thank you, mademoiselle. And you, monsieur,”—he bowed to the
inspector—“for your courtesy.”

The inspector seemed somewhat entertained by this excessive
politeness. Célestine departed in a flood of tears, accompanied by
the woman and the plain-clothes official.

“Expect we shall, sir. They haven’t had much time to hide ’em,
you see. They were probably intending to smuggle them out later,
when the hue and cry was over. I’ve seen this sort of thing before.
The maid’s the thief, and no mistake. She’s only a girl, and
she’s been tempted by the value of the things. Of course she denies
it, but what else would you expect? I tell you, sir, it’s a
certainty.”

Mr. Opalsen shook his head.

“I’m not so sure. My wife’s very fond of Célestine, and she’s
always seemed a most reliable girl. Still, I suppose you know best.”

He turned to Poirot.

“What do you think of it, Mr. Poirot?”

Poirot was standing by the dressing-table, staring at a small
object he held in his hand.

“_Tiens_!” he murmured. “This is very curious.”

“What is it?” I asked, stepping to his side.

It was a small piece of fine white cotton, about two inches long.

“Where did you find it?” asked the inspector.

“On the floor here, by the dressing-table.”

“Well, what of it? It’s only a bit of thread.”

“Yes,” said Poirot, “but it is curious, all the same.”

“I don’t see anything curious about it. It’s exactly the sort of
thing you _would_ find in a lady’s bedroom.”

“True,” admitted Poirot. “But why should it be here?”

“Why shouldn’t it be here? Mrs. Opalsen might have dropped it
herself.”

“But Mrs. Opalsen does not sew,” said Poirot. “She told us so just
now. And Célestine told us she went into the next room to fetch
her cotton.”

“Oh, well, she might have dropped it when she came back.”

“If she had done that, it would have been near the chair where
she was sitting, not over here by the dressing-table.”

The inspector shrugged his shoulders.

“It’s a very small point, anyway. I shouldn’t worry about it if
I were you.”

“I am not worrying,” said Poirot. “I am only—interested.”

He continued his search of the room, while the inspector watched
him with a slightly supercilious air. Suddenly he stopped before
the washstand.

“_Tiens!_” he said again.

“What is it now?” asked the inspector.

“The soap—it is very wet.”

“Well, why shouldn’t it be? Someone’s been washing their hands, I
suppose.”

“But who? Not Mrs. Opalsen—she has been downstairs. Not Célestine,
for she has been sitting at her work. Not the chambermaid, for she
has only just come into the room.”

“One of them might have washed her hands before she came in,”
suggested the inspector.

“In that case the soap would be dry by now.”

“Oh, well, I don’t see that it matters, anyway. We’ve more
important things to think about than wet soap.”

“Perhaps you are right,” said Poirot. “And yet—I wonder.”

He walked over to the window and looked out.

“The drop is not great,” he remarked. “A man might easily jump it.”

“But no one _did_ jump it,” said the inspector. “The maid was in
the room the whole time.”

“True,” said Poirot. “The maid was in the room.”

He turned away from the window, and his eyes fell upon the bed.

“A very fine bed,” he remarked. “Very comfortable, I should say.”

“It’s a good enough bed,” said the inspector. “But we’ve searched
it thoroughly, if that’s what you’re thinking.”

“I was not thinking of that,” said Poirot. “I was thinking—of
something quite different.”

He walked over to the bed and felt the pillows. Then he turned
to Mr. Opalsen.

“You say that you make it a rule that the chambermaid is never to
enter the room unless Célestine is there?”

“That is so.”

“And Célestine is always there?”

“Always.”

“Then the chambermaid can never be in the room alone?”

“Never.”

“That is very interesting,” said Poirot. “Very interesting indeed.”

He was silent for a moment, then he turned to the inspector.

“I should like to have a few words with the chambermaid, if you
don’t mind.”

“Certainly. I’ll send for her.”

The girl was brought back into the room. She looked sullen and
defiant.

“Now, my girl,” said Poirot, “I want you to tell me exactly what
you did when you came into the room this evening.”

“I’ve told the inspector once,” she said ungraciously.

“Tell me again. It is for your own good.”

“Well, I came in, and I went over to the bed, and I turned it down,
just as I always do. Then I went to the washstand and put some
fresh water in the bottle, and then I went out.”

“You did not go near the dressing-table?”

“No, I did not.”

“You are sure of that?”

“Quite sure.”

“And Célestine—was she in the room all the time?”

“She was sitting over there by the window, sewing.”

“She didn’t leave the room at all?”

“Not while I was there.”

“You are quite sure of that?”

“Positive.”

“Thank you. That will do.”

The girl went out, more sullen than ever.

“Well,” said the inspector, “what do you make of that?”

“It is very simple,” said Poirot. “Very simple indeed.”

“You mean the maid’s the thief?”

“On the contrary,” said Poirot. “I mean that the maid is _not_
the thief.”

“Then who is?”

“That,” said Poirot, “is what I am going to find out.”

He turned to Mr. Opalsen.

“I should like to see the room next door, if I may—the one that
is bolted on both sides.”

“Certainly. It’s empty at present, I believe.”

He led the way out into the corridor and opened the door of the
adjoining room. It was a smaller room than the other, and was
simply furnished as a bedroom. Poirot walked straight to the door
communicating with Mrs. Opalsen’s room. He examined the bolt
carefully.

“It is as I thought,” he said. “The bolt is a new one. It has been
recently put on.”

“What of it?” asked the inspector.

“Everything,” said Poirot. “It means that the person who put it on
had a reason for doing so.”

“But the hotel authorities put it on, I suppose.”

“I think not,” said Poirot. “I think it was put on by someone
else.”

He walked over to the window and looked out.

“The same view,” he remarked. “And the same drop. A man could easily
jump it.”

“But I tell you no one _did_ jump it,” said the inspector
impatiently.

“Perhaps not,” said Poirot. “Perhaps not. And yet—I wonder.”

He turned back into the room and his eyes fell upon a small piece
of paper lying on the floor. He picked it up and examined it
carefully.

“_Tiens!_” he said. “This is very interesting.”

“What is it?” I asked.

“It is a piece of paper,” said Poirot. “A piece of paper with some
writing on it.”

“What does it say?”

“It says: ‘Don’t forget the soap.’”

“Don’t forget the soap!” I exclaimed. “What on earth does that
mean?”

“That,” said Poirot, “is what I am going to find out.”

He turned to the inspector.

“I should like to have a few words with the manager, if you don’t
mind.”

“Certainly. I’ll send for him.”

The manager was a small, dapper man, with a worried expression.

“This is a very unfortunate affair, Mr. Poirot,” he said. “Very
unfortunate indeed. It will do the hotel no good, I’m afraid.”

“On the contrary,” said Poirot, “it will do it a great deal of good.
For I am going to find the pearls for you.”

“I’m sure I hope you do,” said the manager. “But the police seem
to think the maid’s the thief.”

“The police,” said Poirot, “are sometimes mistaken. Now, tell me,
monsieur, who occupies the room next to Mrs. Opalsen’s—the one we
are in now?”

“It’s empty at present, as I told you. It was occupied until
this morning by a Mr. and Mrs. Robinson.”

“A Mr. and Mrs. Robinson, eh? And what were they like?”

“Oh, quite ordinary people. Very quiet and well-behaved. They stayed
here for a week.”

“I see. And did they have much luggage?”

“Only two small suitcases.”

“I see. And did they go away this morning?”

“Yes, by the eleven o’clock train.”

“I see. And did they leave any address?”

“No, they didn’t. They said they were going to London, but they
didn’t say where.”

“I see. Well, thank you, monsieur. That is all I wanted to know.”

The manager went out, looking more worried than ever.

“Well,” said the inspector, “what do you make of that?”

“It is very simple,” said Poirot. “Very simple indeed.”

“You mean the Robinsons are the thieves?”

“I think it is more than likely,” said Poirot. “But we shall see.
We shall see.”

He turned to me.

“Hastings, I want you to go downstairs and find out if any of the
servants remember seeing Mr. or Mrs. Robinson leaving the hotel
this morning.”

“Certainly,” I said, and I went out.

I was back in a few minutes.

“No one seems to remember them,” I said. “The porter says he saw
a man and woman leaving with two suitcases, but he didn’t take
any particular notice of them.”

“I see,” said Poirot. “Well, it doesn’t matter. I think I know
where they are.”

“You do?” I exclaimed. “Where?”

“They are here,” said Poirot. “In this hotel.”

“In this hotel!” I cried. “But the manager said they went away
this morning.”

“The manager said they _said_ they were going away this morning,”
corrected Poirot. “That is not quite the same thing.”

“But where are they?”

“That,” said Poirot, “is what I am going to find out.”

He turned to the inspector.

“I should like to have another look at Mrs. Opalsen’s room, if you
don’t mind.”

“Certainly. But I don’t see what you expect to find there.”

“We shall see,” said Poirot. “We shall see.”

We went back into the next room. Mrs. Opalsen was still sitting in
her chair, but she had stopped crying and was looking at Poirot
with a hopeful expression. Mr. Opalsen was still striding up and
down.

Poirot walked straight to the dressing-table and began to examine
the drawers.

“What are you looking for?” asked the inspector.

“I am looking for—a piece of soap,” said Poirot.

“A piece of soap!” I exclaimed. “But you’ve seen the soap. It’s
over there on the washstand.”

“I am looking for another piece of soap,” said Poirot.

He pulled out the bottom drawer and began to rummage through it.
Suddenly he uttered a cry of triumph.

“_Aha!_ I have it!”

He held up a small, round cake of soap.

“What is it?” asked the inspector.

“It is a piece of soap,” said Poirot. “A piece of soap that has
been used to take an impression of a key.”

“An impression of a key!” I exclaimed.

“Precisely,” said Poirot. “See, here is the mark of the key.”

He showed us the soap. There was a clear impression of a key on
one side of it.

“But whose key is it?” asked the inspector.

“It is the key of Mrs. Opalsen’s jewel-case,” said Poirot.

“But who could have taken an impression of it?”

“That,” said Poirot, “is what I am going to find out.”

He turned to Mrs. Opalsen.

“Madame, when you go down to dinner, where do you leave your keys?”

“I don’t leave them anywhere. I wear them on a chain round my
neck.”

“You always wear them?”

“Always.”

“You never take them off?”

“Never.”

“Not even when you sleep?”

“No. I’ve always been afraid of someone stealing them.”

“I see. Well, that is very interesting. Very interesting indeed.”

He was silent for a moment, then he turned to Mr. Opalsen.

“And you, monsieur? Where do you leave your keys?”

“I carry them in my pocket,” said Mr. Opalsen.

“You always carry them?”

“Always.”

“You never leave them anywhere?”

“Never.”

“I see. Well, that is also very interesting.”

He turned back to the inspector.

“Now, monsieur, I think I can tell you how the pearls were stolen.”

“Go on,” said the inspector. “I’m all ears.”

“It was very simple,” said Poirot. “A man and a woman—let us call
them Mr. and Mrs. Robinson—stayed in the room next door for a
week. During that time they made their plans. They found out
everything they could about the Opalsens’ habits. They found out
that Mrs. Opalsen always wore her keys round her neck, and that
the maid was always in the room when the chambermaid was there.
They also found out that the door between the two rooms was
bolted on both sides.

“This morning, they pretended to leave the hotel. But they didn’t
really leave. They stayed in their room, and when everyone was
downstairs at dinner, they went to work.

“First, they unbolted the door on their side. Then they managed
to unbolt it on this side as well. It was quite easy—they probably
used a piece of wire or something of that sort. Then they entered
the room.

“One of them—probably the man—went to the dressing-table and took
an impression of the key of the jewel-case in a piece of soap.
Then they went back to their own room and waited.

“They knew that the maid would be in the room after dinner, so they
couldn’t come back then. But they also knew that the maid would
go into her own room for a few minutes to fetch her cotton and
her scissors.

“They waited until she did so. Then they entered the room again.
The man went to the dressing-table, unlocked the jewel-case with
a duplicate key he had made from the impression in the soap,
took the pearls, and went back to his own room. The whole thing
only took a few seconds.”

“But the maid said she was only gone a minute,” I objected.

“A minute is a long time, Hastings, when you are stealing pearls,”
said Poirot.

“But where are they now?” asked the inspector. “The Robinsons, I
mean.”

“They are in their room,” said Poirot. “The room next door.”

“But the manager said it was empty,” said Mr. Opalsen.

“The manager was mistaken,” said Poirot. “They have been there all
the time.”

“But how could they stay there without being seen?” I asked.

“It was quite easy,” said Poirot. “They just stayed in the room
and didn’t come out. They probably had some food with them.”

“But the chambermaid would have seen them when she went in to do
the room,” I said.

“The chambermaid didn’t go in to do the room,” said Poirot. “She
thought it was empty, so she didn’t bother.”

“Well, we’ll soon see,” said the inspector. “Come on.”

He led the way out into the corridor and to the door of the next
room. He tried the handle, but the door was locked.

“Open the door!” he shouted. “Open in the name of the law!”

There was no answer.

“Break it down!” said the inspector.

He and the other policeman threw themselves against the door. It
gave way with a crash, and we all rushed into the room.

The room was empty!

“They’ve gone!” cried the inspector. “They’ve got away!”

“On the contrary,” said Poirot, who had followed us into the room.
“They are still here.”

“Where?” I asked, looking round the empty room.

“They are under the bed,” said Poirot.

The inspector and the other policeman dived under the bed. A moment
later they emerged, dragging two people with them—a man and a
woman.

“Mr. and Mrs. Robinson, I presume,” said Poirot, with a low bow.

The man and woman looked at him with hatred in their eyes.

“You’ve got us,” said the man. “But you’ll never find the pearls.”

“We shall see,” said Poirot. “We shall see.”

He turned to the inspector.

“I think you will find the pearls in the man’s pocket,” he said.

The inspector searched the man’s pockets, and a moment later he
held up a magnificent string of pearls.

“Here they are!” he cried. “We’ve got them!”

Mrs. Opalsen uttered a cry of joy and snatched the pearls from his
hand.

“My pearls!” she cried. “My beautiful pearls!”

Mr. Opalsen looked at Poirot with admiration.

“You’re a genius, Mr. Poirot!” he said. “A positive genius!”

“You are too kind, monsieur,” said Poirot. “It was a very simple
little matter.”

“Simple!” I exclaimed. “I don’t see anything simple about it.
How did you know they were under the bed?”

“Because,” said Poirot, “it was the only place they could be. They
couldn’t have left the hotel without being seen, and they couldn’t
have hidden anywhere else in the room.”

“But how did you know they were in the room at all?”

“Because of the piece of paper,” said Poirot. “The piece of paper
that said ‘Don’t forget the soap.’ You see, they had used the soap
to take an impression of the key, and they didn’t want to leave it
behind for the police to find. But in their hurry to hide under
the bed, they forgot it.”

“And the piece of thread?” I asked.

“That,” said Poirot, “was a little ruse of mine. I dropped it there
myself to see what the inspector would say.”

“And the wet soap?”

“That was also a little ruse of mine. I wetted it myself to see
if anyone would notice.”

I looked at Poirot in amazement.

“You really are a most extraordinary man,” I said.

“I am Hercule Poirot,” he replied. “And now, if you have no
objection, I think I should like to finish my coffee.”

“Well, sir, if they’re not on her, they must be in the room. There’s
no other way.”

“I’m not so sure of that,” said the stockbroker. “What about that
other room? The one she was in?”

The inspector nodded.

“We’re going to search that too, sir. But first we’ll finish here.”

A quarter of an hour passed, and the inspector’s face was beginning
to look somewhat worried.

“No go,” he admitted, straightening his back. “Well, I’ll try the
small room.”

He entered Célestine’s room and repeated the process with no more
success. Poirot followed him.

“You see anything?” asked the inspector, somewhat testily.

“Nothing,” said Poirot. “I was just looking at the top of this
chest of drawers. It is a little—what you call—dusty, is it not?”

The inspector shrugged his shoulders.

“Well, you can’t expect a hotel to be like a private house. And
this is a very out-of-the-way corner.”

“True,” said Poirot. “It is a detail of no importance.”

He stood for a moment or two in the centre of the room, looking
round him. Then he turned to the inspector.

“You have quite finished?”

“Yes, I’ve been over every inch of the place. There’s no doubt the
pearls are not here.”

“Then,” said Poirot, “I will, with your permission, ask one or
two questions of Mr. Opalsen.”

He led the way back into the bedroom. Mr. Opalsen looked up
expectantly.

“You have something to tell us?” he asked.

“Only to ask you one or two questions. When did you last see the
pearls?”

“When my wife put them in the jewel-case before dinner.”

“And you are quite sure she _did_ put them in?”

“Positive. I saw her do it.”

“And you, madame?”

“I am quite sure,” said Mrs. Opalsen, somewhat indignantly. “I
tell you I was undecided whether to wear them or the emeralds,
and I finally chose the emeralds.”

“And the jewel-case—it was locked?”

“Yes, I locked it myself.”

“And you have the key?”

“It is here.” She held it up.

Poirot took it from her and examined it. Then he handed it back.

“Thank you, madame. And now—one more question. Did you see anyone
in the corridor as you came up?”

“No one at all.”

“And you, monsieur?”

“No one.”

“Thank you.”

Poirot sat for a moment or two in silence. Then he turned to the
inspector.

“You are quite sure that you have searched everything—everywhere?”

“Absolutely.”

“Then,” said Poirot, “there is only one thing to be done.”

“And that is?”

“To find the pearls.”

The inspector laughed.

“That’s easier said than done, I fancy.”

“Not at all,” said Poirot calmly. “They are in this room.”

“In this room?”

“Precisely.”

“But I’ve searched every inch of it!”

“You have searched,” said Poirot, “but you have not _seen_.”

“I don’t know what you mean.”

“I mean,” said Poirot, “that you have looked at everything, but
you have not observed.”

He walked across to the dressing-table.

“You see this little bottle?” He held up a small blue glass bottle
of smelling-salts. “It was on the dressing-table, was it not?”

“Yes.”

“And this one?” He held up a similar bottle of lavender water.

“Yes.”

“And this one?” He held up a third bottle.

“That’s my hair-wash,” said Mr. Opalsen.

“Precisely. Now, all these bottles were on the dressing-table.
But there was one other bottle—a bottle of—what do you call it?—
_bain de fleurs_—which was _not_ on the dressing-table.”

“I don’t know what you’re talking about,” said the inspector.

“I am talking,” said Poirot, “of the bottle of _bain de fleurs_
which was in the small room—the room of Mademoiselle Célestine.”

“Well, what of it?”

“Only this—that it was not there when I first entered the room!”

The inspector stared at him.

“Are you sure?”

“I am positive. I noted the contents of the chest of drawers
particularly. There were a reel of cotton, a pair of scissors,
and a small bottle of—I think it was hair-oil. But there was no
bottle of _bain de fleurs_.”

“But what does that matter?”

“It matters a great deal,” said Poirot. “Because, you see, that
bottle of _bain de fleurs_ is now on the chest of drawers in the
small room!”

The inspector looked at him for a moment, and then ran into the
next room. He returned a moment later with a small glass bottle in
his hand.

“Is this it?”

“That is it.”

The inspector looked at it curiously. It was a small, ordinary-looking
bottle, half-full of a pinkish liquid.

“What is there in this to help us?” he asked.

“If you will open it,” said Poirot, “I think you will find out.”

The inspector pulled out the cork. A faint, flowery perfume filled
the room. He sniffed at it, and then his face changed. He inverted
the bottle, and a small, round object fell out into his hand. It
was a pearl—a large, beautifully tinted pearl.

“The pearls!” cried Mrs. Opalsen.

“One of them,” said Poirot. “The others, I fancy, will be found
in the same place.”

The inspector shook the bottle, and one by one the pearls fell out,
until the whole of the magnificent necklace lay in his hand.

“But how did you know?” he asked, looking at Poirot with a new
respect.

“It was very simple,” said Poirot. “When I first entered the small
room, I noticed the dust on the chest of drawers. But when I
entered it the second time, I saw that a small circle of dust had
been cleared away—the circle where the bottle of _bain de fleurs_
now stood. It was obvious, then, that the bottle had been placed
there during the time that I was in the bedroom. And as only one
person had been in the small room during that time——”

“The searcher!” cried the inspector.

“Precisely. The searcher. She was the only person who could have
placed the bottle there.”

“But why should she?”

“Because,” said Poirot, “she was the thief.”

“The searcher?”

“Exactly. You see, the whole thing was a very clever plot. The
pearls were stolen, not after dinner, but _before_.”

“Before dinner?”

“Yes. You remember, madame, you said that you were undecided
whether to wear the pearls or the emeralds? You decided on the
emeralds, and put the pearls back in the jewel-case. But you did
not look to see if the pearls were still there! You assumed they
were. As a matter of fact, they had been stolen some time before.”

“But who stole them?”

“The person who had a duplicate key to the jewel-case. The person
who knew exactly where they were kept. The person who had plenty
of time and opportunity.”

“You mean——?”

“I mean,” said Poirot, “the chambermaid.”

“The chambermaid!”

“Yes. It was a very simple matter for her. She had only to take
the pearls, and then, when the loss was discovered, to throw the
suspicion on the maid. She knew that the maid was always in the
room, and that she would be the first person suspected. It was a
clever idea to suggest that she herself should be searched. She
knew, of course, that the pearls would not be found on her.”

“But the searcher?” asked the inspector. “How did she come into
it?”

“The searcher,” said Poirot, “was her confederate. The chambermaid
stole the pearls and handed them to the searcher, who was waiting
outside. Then, when the searcher was called in to search the maid,
she brought the pearls with her, hidden in the bottle of _bain de
fleurs_. She had only to place the bottle on the chest of drawers
in the small room, and the thing was done. If the pearls were
found there, they would be assumed to belong to the maid. It was
a very neat little plot.”

“But how did you know the searcher was a confederate?” asked the
inspector.

“Because,” said Poirot, “she was not a searcher at all! She was
simply a friend of the chambermaid’s, dressed up for the part.
You sent for a searcher, it is true, but the message was intercepted,
and this woman was sent in her place. It was a very bold stroke,
but it nearly succeeded.”

“Well, I’m damned!” said the inspector.

“It was the dust that gave them away,” said Poirot, smiling. “As
I have often told you, Hastings, the little things are the most
important. If the searcher had been a little more careful—if she
had not moved that bottle——”

He shrugged his shoulders.

“But then, she was not a detective. She did not realize the
importance of—dust!”

Mrs. Opalsen was clasping her pearls to her bosom.

“Oh, Mr. Poirot!” she cried. “How can I ever thank you?”

“By wearing your pearls, madame,” said Poirot, with a bow. “And
by remembering that even the smallest detail may be of importance.”

He turned to me.

“And now, Hastings, I think we may return to our coffee. It will,
I fear, be cold, but the satisfaction of a task well-accomplished
will, I hope, compensate for that.”

He led the way out of the room, and I followed him, marveling once
more at the extraordinary powers of my friend.

“Poirot,” I said, as we descended the stairs, “you are a genius!”

“I am,” said Poirot, with simple conviction. “It is a fact that
I have often noted myself.”

“Not a doubt of it, sir. Where else can they be? They’re not on
either of the women—that we’ve proved. And they’re certainly not
in the possession of any one else in the hotel. The only person
who could have got in here is the chambermaid, and she hasn’t had
time to hide them. No, they must be in this room, or the girl’s.”

“You’ve searched the girl’s room, too?”

“Of course.”

He continued his search. He even went so far as to take the clothes
out of the wardrobes and feel them all over. But the result was
nil.

Mr. Opalsen began to get impatient.

“If they were here, you’d have found them by now,” he remarked.
“I believe they’re not here at all.”

The inspector’s face began to show some of the same doubt.

“Well, sir, we’ve done our best. We’ll just have a look through
the girl’s things again, but after that I’m afraid I’ll have to
give it up for to-night.”

He went into the small room, but came back almost immediately.
His face was quite crestfallen.

“Nothing there, either,” he admitted.

“What about the bed?” suggested Poirot. “Did you search the bed?”

“The bed? I’ve turned the mattress inside out, and the pillows too.”

“Is that so?” asked Poirot softly. “Then I suppose there is nothing
further to be done.”

“Nothing—for the present.”

“One moment,” said Poirot, his eyes wandering round the room. “Is
there no other place?”

He walked over to the washstand and looked at it thoughtfully.

“Aha!” he exclaimed. “What have we here?”

He pointed to a large piece of soap.

“Soap!” said the inspector. “Well, what of it?”

“You have not thought of the soap?”

“The soap? No—why should I?”

Poirot took the piece of soap in his hand. It was a large, round
ball of a common, coarse description.

“I have seen this before,” he remarked. “It is what you call
‘_Savon de Marseilles_.’ But this is not the sort of soap a lady
like Mrs. Opalsen would use for her toilet.”

He turned it over in his hand, and his face suddenly lightened.

“Ah!” he said. “I thought so. See!”

He held the ball of soap towards us. In the side of it was a small,
neatly-cut hole.

“The pearls!” cried Mrs. Opalsen.

“Not so fast, madame,” said Poirot. “Wait!”

He took a penknife from his pocket and began to scrape away the
soap. In a few moments he had revealed a small, hard object. It
was a large, perfectly-matched pearl.

“The first!” he cried. “Wait—there will be others.”

And, sure enough, as he continued his task, pearl after pearl
dropped out of the soap-ball. There were fifty-two of them in all.

“My pearls! My beautiful pearls!” cried Mrs. Opalsen, snatching
them from him. “Oh, Mr. Poirot, how can I ever thank you?”

“It was nothing, madame—a mere trifle.”

“But how did you know? How did you guess?”

“A little logic—that is all. The soap—it was too large, too coarse,
and it had been used but little. And then—the hole!”

“But who put them there?” asked the inspector.

“Ah! that is the question.”

“The maid, of course,” said Mr. Opalsen. “She’s the only one who
could have done it.”

“I am not so sure,” said Poirot. “The chambermaid, perhaps?”

“No,” said the inspector. “She couldn’t have had the time. She
was only in the room for a few minutes, you remember.”

“True,” said Poirot. “Still——”

He broke off, and stood for a moment lost in thought.

“Well,” said the inspector, “I suppose we’d better be getting
along. The girl will have to come with us, of course.”

“Wait!” said Poirot. “I have an idea. If you will allow me, I should
like to ask the chambermaid a few questions.”

“Oh, certainly, if you like,” said the inspector. “I’ll send her
to you.”

He left the room, and a few minutes later the chambermaid appeared.
She looked sullen and defiant.

“You wanted me?” she asked.

“Yes, my girl,” said Poirot pleasantly. “I want to ask you a few
questions. You were in this room this evening, were you not?”

“Yes, I told you I was.”

“And you were here for about three minutes?”

“About that.”

“What were you doing during those three minutes?”

“Doing? Why, I was turning down the beds, of course.”

“And you did not see anything of the pearls?”

“No, I didn’t. I told you that before.”

“You did not even see the jewel-case?”

“No.”

“Where was the jewel-case when you were in the room?”

“How should I know? I didn’t see it.”

“It was in the bottom drawer of the dressing-table,” said Poirot.

“Well, I didn’t look in the drawer, did I?”

“Perhaps not. But you might have seen it if the drawer had been
open.”

“Well, it wasn’t open.”

“You are sure of that?”

“Quite sure.”

“And the maid—what was she doing?”

“She was sitting in that chair over there, sewing.”

“She did not leave the room?”

“No—at least, only for a minute, as she said.”

“I see,” said Poirot. “Thank you, that will do.”

The girl went out, and Poirot turned to us with a smile.

“Well,” he said, “what do you think of it?”

“It seems clear enough,” I said. “The maid must have done it.”

“You think so, Hastings? And you, monsieur?” he asked, turning to
Mr. Opalsen.

“I agree with your friend,” said the stockbroker. “It’s the only
possible explanation.”

“And yet,” said Poirot, “there is one thing that puzzles me.”

“What is that?”

“The soap. Why the soap? If the maid had stolen the pearls, she
would surely have hidden them somewhere else—not in a ball of
coarse soap which she must have known would be noticed sooner or
later.”

“Perhaps she didn’t have time to hide them anywhere else,” I
suggested.

“Perhaps,” said Poirot. “And yet—I wonder.”

He stood for a moment in silence, then his face suddenly cleared.

“I have it!” he cried. “Of course! How stupid of me not to have
seen it before!”

“What is it?” I asked.

“Wait!” said Poirot. “I must make sure.”

He walked over to the washstand and began to examine the other
pieces of soap.

“Aha!” he exclaimed. “See here!”

He held up another piece of soap. It was a small, oval tablet of
fine, scented soap.

“This is the soap that Mrs. Opalsen uses, is it not?”

“Yes,” said the lady.

“And see!” said Poirot. “There is a hole in this one, too!”

He held it up to the light. Sure enough, there was a small,
neatly-cut hole in the side of the tablet.

“But what does it mean?” asked Mr. Opalsen.

“It means,” said Poirot, “that we have been very nearly deceived
by a very clever criminal.”

“What do you mean?”

“I mean,” said Poirot, “that the pearls were never in the large
ball of soap at all!”

“But we saw them!” cried Mrs. Opalsen.

“No, madame,” said Poirot. “What you saw was a very clever piece
of jugglery. The pearls were in the small tablet of soap all the
time. The large ball of soap was merely a—what do you call it?—a
blind.”

“But how—I don’t understand,” said Mr. Opalsen.

“It is quite simple,” said Poirot. “The thief—whoever he was—knew
that the room would be searched. He knew also that the maid would
be suspected. So he—or she—decided to hide the pearls in a place
where they would be found, but where they would appear to have
been hidden by the maid.”

“But the large ball of soap was the maid’s soap,” I said.

“Exactly,” said Poirot. “That was the point. The thief hid the
pearls in the small tablet of soap—Mrs. Opalsen’s soap. Then, when
the room was being searched, he—or she—managed to substitute the
small tablet for the large ball.”

“But who could have done it?” asked Mr. Opalsen.

“There was only one person who could have done it,” said Poirot.
“The person who ‘found’ the pearls!”

He looked at us with a smile.

“But—but that was you!” cried Mrs. Opalsen.

“Precisely,” said Poirot. “I found the pearls. But I did not put
them there. The person who put them there was the person who gave
me the soap!”

“But you took it from the washstand yourself!” I said.

“No, Hastings,” said Poirot. “If you remember, I asked the
inspector if he had searched the bed. While he was doing so, I
went to the washstand. The large ball of soap was there—but it
was not the soap I showed you. That soap I had already in my
pocket!”

“In your pocket!” I exclaimed.

“Yes. I had found it a few minutes before—in the pocket of Mr.
Opalsen’s overcoat!”

There was a moment of dead silence. Then Mr. Opalsen burst into a
loud laugh.

“Well, I’m damned!” he said. “You’re a clever one, Mr. Poirot!
I thought I’d be able to pull it off, but you were too much for
me.”

“Ed!” cried Mrs. Opalsen in horror. “You—you stole my pearls?”

“I’m sorry, my dear,” said her husband, “but as I told Mr. Poirot,
money’s confoundedly tight in the City just now. I had to have
some cash, and I knew I could get a good price for those pearls.
I thought I’d be able to make it look like the maid had stolen
them, and then I’d be able to ‘find’ them later on and give them
back to you. But Mr. Poirot here was too clever for me.”

“It was the soap that gave you away, monsieur,” said Poirot. “You
should not have used two different kinds. It was a mistake—a
grave mistake.”

“I suppose it was,” said Mr. Opalsen. “Well, I’ve lost the game,
and I’m willing to pay the penalty.”

He turned to the inspector.

“I’m at your service, officer.”

As they left the room, Poirot turned to me with a smile.

“Well, Hastings,” he said, “what do you think of my little
experiment?”

“I think you’re the most wonderful man in the world,” I said.

“_Merci, mon ami_,” said Poirot. “But it was nothing—a mere trifle.
A little logic—that is all. And now, shall we go down and finish
our coffee?”

[THE END]

“Hope for the best, sir. They’re not on the girl, and she can’t
have made away with them yet. She must have hidden them somewhere.”

“But she says she didn’t take them,” said Mrs. Opalsen, somewhat
unreasonably.

“She’d be sure to say that,” remarked the inspector.

Mr. Opalsen turned to Poirot.

“What’s your opinion, Mr. Poirot?”

Poirot shrugged his shoulders.

“I am at your service, monsieur. If you wish me to investigate the
matter, I will do so.”

“I’ll be glad if you would. The police are doing their best, no
doubt, but they don’t seem to have much to go on.”

“I will do my best,” said Poirot. “And first I should like a few
words with the chambermaid.”

The inspector nodded.

“I’ve finished with her. You’ll find her downstairs, I expect.”

Poirot and I left the room together.

“You’ve a theory, I suppose?” I asked.

“My dear Hastings, I have nothing so definite as that. I am just
beginning to look for one.”

We found the chambermaid in a small room on the ground floor. She
looked up as we entered.

“So they haven’t found them yet?” she said. “I could have told
them they wouldn’t. That French hussy’s too clever for them.”

“Then you think she did take them?”

“Think? I’m sure of it. Who else could have done?”

“The door into the next room was bolted on both sides, was it not?”

“Yes, it was.”

“And the windows?”

“They were closed, and there’s no balcony outside.”

“Then, as you say, it seems as if it must have been someone in the
room.”

“Exactly. And who was there? Only me and that Célestine. And I
know I didn’t take them.”

“You are sure you didn’t leave the room at all?”

“Not for a second. I was there the whole time.”

“I see. And Célestine?”

“She went into her own room once or twice, as she told you. But she
wasn’t gone more than a minute at a time.”

“I see,” said Poirot again. “And what were you doing while she was
away?”

“I was turning down the beds.”

“The two beds?”

“Yes.”

“And where were they?”

“One each side of the room.”

“I see. Thank you very much.”

Poirot rose and we went out.

“Well?” I asked. “What do you think of her?”

“She is a very sensible girl,” replied Poirot. “And she has a
remarkably good memory.”

“You mean she is telling the truth?”

“I mean that she is telling a very consistent story. Whether it
is the truth or not is another matter.”

He stood still for a moment, as though lost in thought.

“Hastings,” he said at length, “I should like to have another look
at that bedroom.”

The inspector had finished his search, and had departed, leaving
a constable in charge. He allowed us to enter. Poirot walked
straight to the dressing-table, and opened the drawer where the
jewel-case had been kept. It was empty now, the case having been
taken away by the police.

Poirot stood looking at the drawer for some minutes. Then he
turned to the constable.

“When the inspector searched the room, did he examine this
dressing-table very carefully?”

“He did, sir. Every inch of it.”

“And he found nothing?”

“Nothing.”

Poirot’s eyes wandered to the washstand.

“And the soap-dish?” he asked. “Did he examine that?”

The constable grinned.

“He did, sir. And the water-jug, and the toothbrush-vase.”

“I see,” said Poirot.

He walked over to the bed, and began to examine the pillows.

“Nothing there,” he murmured.

He turned to the window, and looked out.

“A drop of at least forty feet,” he remarked. “No, they were not
thrown out of the window.”

He stood in the middle of the room, looking round him.

“Hastings,” he said, “there is something here that I do not
understand. Something very simple, and yet I cannot see it.”

“The maid?” I suggested.

“Perhaps. And yet—if it was the maid, where has she hidden the
pearls? The inspector is no fool. He has searched the room
thoroughly.”

“She may have had a confederate.”

“In that case the pearls would have been passed out of the room.
But how? The door was locked, and the only person who entered was
the chambermaid.”

“Then it must have been the chambermaid,” I cried.

“But she also was searched, and nothing was found.”

“She may have hidden them before she was searched.”

“Where? The inspector has searched the room.”

“She may have passed them to someone else.”

“To whom? She was in the room all the time, except for the few
minutes when Célestine was also there.”

“Then she may have passed them to Célestine.”

“But Célestine also has been searched.”

I was silenced. Poirot continued to look round the room. Suddenly
his eyes fastened on a small object on the floor. He picked it
up. It was a tiny piece of white thread.

“_Tiens!_” he murmured. “That is curious.”

“What is it?” I asked.

“A piece of thread, Hastings. A very ordinary piece of white
thread.”

“Well?”

“Well, it is curious, that is all.”

He put it carefully in his pocket-book. Then he walked over to
the washstand, and picked up a piece of coal from the coal-scuttle.

“And this also is curious,” he remarked.

“What is?”

“That there should be coal in the coal-scuttle in July.”

“It’s for the fire, I suppose,” I said. “The evenings are often
chilly, even in summer.”

“Perhaps,” said Poirot. “Perhaps.”

He stood for a moment, deep in thought. Then he turned to me.

“Hastings,” he said, “I should like to see Mr. Opalsen.”

We found the stockbroker in the lounge. He looked up as we
approached.

“Well, Mr. Poirot, have you found any clue?”

“I have found a piece of white thread, monsieur.”

“A piece of white thread! Is that all?”

“It is enough,” said Poirot gravely. “And now I have a request to
make. I should like to see the chambermaid again.”

“Certainly. I will send for her.”

When the girl arrived, Poirot addressed her.

“Mademoiselle,” he said, “I have a question to ask you. When you
were turning down the beds, did you notice anything unusual?”

“Unusual, sir? No, I don’t think so.”

“You did not, for instance, see a piece of white thread?”

“A piece of white thread? No, I can’t say I did.”

“I see. And you did not notice anything else?”

“No, sir.”

“Thank you, mademoiselle. That is all.”

When the girl had gone, Poirot turned to Mr. Opalsen.

“Monsieur,” he said, “I have a theory. It is a very strange theory,
and I may be wrong. But I should like to test it.”

“What is it?” asked Opalsen eagerly.

“I would prefer not to say at present. But I should like to ask
you one or two questions. You say you made a fortune in Oil?”

“I did.”

“And you have been very successful lately?”

“I have.”

“But you said just now that money was tight in the City.”

“So it is. But that doesn’t affect me. I’ve got plenty.”

“I see. And you are very fond of your wife?”

“Of course I am.”

“And you give her many presents?”

“I do.”

“I see. Thank you, monsieur. That is all I wanted to know.”

He rose and led the way out of the room.

“Well?” I asked, when we were outside. “What is your theory?”

“My friend,” said Poirot, “I have a very strong suspicion that
this is a more complicated case than it appears to be.”

“You think the pearls were not stolen at all?”

“I think they were stolen, Hastings. But I am not sure who stole
them.”

“But you said just now that it must have been someone in the
room.”

“I said it _seemed_ as if it must have been someone in the room.
But there are other possibilities.”

“What other possibilities?”

“That is what I am going to find out.”

He walked towards the lift.

“Where are you going?” I asked.

“I am going to the first floor, Hastings. I want to have another
look at that door.”

“The door into the next room?”

“Exactly.”

When we reached the first floor, Poirot walked straight to the
door in question. He examined it carefully for some minutes. Then
he turned to me.

“Hastings,” he said, “have you a penknife?”

“Yes,” I said, and handed it to him.

He took it and began to poke it into the keyhole.

“What are you doing?” I asked.

“I am trying to see if the door is really bolted on the other
side.”

“But the inspector said it was.”

“The inspector may have been mistaken.”

He continued to poke away for some minutes. Then he gave a cry of
satisfaction.

“I thought so!” he exclaimed.

“What is it?”

“The bolt has been tampered with, Hastings. It looks as if it were
bolted, but it isn’t.”

“You mean that someone could have entered the room through that
door?”

“Exactly.”

“But who?”

“That is what we have to find out. Come, let us go and see who
occupies the next room.”

We went to the office and inquired. The manager looked at his
books.

“Number 24,” he said. “That is occupied by a Mr. and Mrs.
Robinson.”

“And where are they now?”

“They went out about half an hour ago.”

“I see. Thank you.”

Poirot turned to me.

“You see, Hastings? The plot thickens.”

“You think the Robinsons took the pearls?”

“It is possible. At any rate, it is a possibility that must be
investigated.”

“But how did they know the pearls were there?”

“That is what we have to find out. Come, let us go back to Mrs.
Opalsen’s room.”

When we reached the room, Poirot walked straight to the dressing-table.
He opened the drawer where the jewel-case had been kept, and
began to examine it again.

“Hastings,” he said, “do you see anything unusual about this
drawer?”

I looked at it carefully.

“No,” I said. “It looks like any other drawer to me.”

“Look at the bottom,” said Poirot.

I looked at the bottom of the drawer. It was lined with blue
paper.

“Well?” I said. “What of it?”

“Do you see that little mark in the corner?”

I looked closer. There was a small, circular mark in the blue
paper.

“It looks like a grease-spot,” I said.

“It is a grease-spot, Hastings. And it is a very fresh one.”

“Well?”

“Well, it is curious, that is all.”

He stood for a moment, deep in thought. Then he turned to the
constable.

“When the inspector searched the room, did he notice this grease-spot?”

“I don’t think so, sir. He didn’t say anything about it.”

“I see. Thank you.”

He turned to me.

“Come, Hastings. We have work to do.”

“What are you going to do?”

“I am going to find out where that grease-spot came from.”

We went downstairs and into the dining-room. Poirot walked straight
to the table where we had dined. He began to examine the
tablecloth.

“Ah!” he exclaimed. “Here it is!”

He pointed to a small grease-spot on the cloth.

“But what does it mean?” I asked.

“It means, Hastings, that the person who took the pearls was at
this table this evening.”

“But we were at this table!”

“Exactly,” said Poirot.

“You mean—one of us took them?”

“I mean, Hastings, that the person who took the pearls was
sitting at this table. And as there were only two of us——”

“Poirot!” I cried. “You don’t mean——”

“I mean, my friend, that I have been very blind. Very blind
indeed.”

He stood for a moment, his face working with emotion. Then he
turned and walked out of the room.

I followed him, my head whirling. What could he mean? Was it
possible that he suspected me? Or was he suggesting that he
himself had taken the pearls? The idea was too absurd. And yet—what
other explanation could there be?

We reached the lounge and Poirot walked straight up to Mr. Opalsen.

“Monsieur,” he said, “I have something to tell you.”

Opalsen looked up.

“What is it? Have you found the pearls?”

“I have not found the pearls, monsieur. But I have found the
thief.”

“Who is it?”

Poirot pointed a dramatic finger.

“It is you, monsieur!”

Opalsen sprang to his feet, his face purple with rage.

“What! Are you mad? How dare you insult me like this!”

“I am not mad, monsieur. I am very sane. And I can prove what I
say.”

“Prove it, then! Prove it!”

“Very well. You told us that you made a fortune in Oil. But I
have been making inquiries. It is true that you made a fortune,
but it is also true that you have lost it. You are, at this
moment, on the verge of bankruptcy.”

Opalsen fell back into his chair, his face suddenly pale.

“How—how did you know?” he gasped.

“I have my methods,” said Poirot. “And now for the pearls. You
were in need of money. You knew that your wife’s pearls were
worth a large sum. You decided to steal them and claim the
insurance money.”

“It’s a lie!” cried Opalsen.

“Is it? Let us see. You knew that the chambermaid and the maid
would be in the room after dinner. You went upstairs, entered the
room through the door from the next apartment—the door which you
had previously tampered with—and took the pearls. You then
returned to the lounge and joined us at coffee.”

“But the grease-spot!” I cried. “What about the grease-spot?”

“That, my friend, was a little piece of stage-management.
Monsieur Opalsen deliberately spilt a drop of oil on the
tablecloth, and then, when he went upstairs to ‘see what was the
matter’, he placed a similar spot in the drawer to make it look
as if the thief had been someone who had been at the table. He
forgot, however, that the only people at the table were himself,
his wife, you, and me.”

Opalsen buried his face in his hands.

“It’s true,” he groaned. “I was desperate. I didn’t know what to
do.”

“And the pearls?” I asked. “Where are they?”

“They are in the coal-scuttle in my wife’s room,” said Poirot.
“I found them there when I was looking for the piece of thread.”

“The piece of thread!” I exclaimed. “What had that to do with
it?”

“Nothing, my friend. It was merely a—how do you say?—a red
herring. I use it to see if the chambermaid was as observant as
she appeared to be.”

He turned to Opalsen.

“And now, monsieur, I think you had better come with me to the
police station. It will be better for you in the end.”

Opalsen rose heavily and followed Poirot out of the room.

I stood and watched them go, my head still whirling. Truly,
Hercule Poirot was a remarkable man.

“They’re not on either of the women,” said the inspector. “The
maid says the chambermaid took them, the chambermaid says the maid
did. It must be one or the other. If the maid’s hidden them in the
room, we shall find them. If she hasn’t, she’s passed them out
somehow. There’s a window in her room, remember.”

“I’ve already looked out of that,” said Poirot quietly. “It looks
into a small courtyard.”

“And there’s nobody there,” added the inspector. “We’ve a man
there. If she’d thrown them out, he’d have seen them.”

“Is there any other way out of her room?” I asked.

“None.”

“Then,” said Mr. Opalsen, “it must be one of the two women. And as
it isn’t the chambermaid——”

“It’s the maid,” concluded the inspector. “Logic, sir, logic.”

Poirot shook his head.

“You are a great one for logic, I perceive, monsieur. But suppose
there is another way?”

“What other way?”

Poirot shrugged his shoulders.

“I am only suggesting that there might be one.”

“Well, if you can find it, you’re a cleverer man than I am, Mr.
Poirot,” said the inspector, with a touch of sarcasm.

Poirot bowed. “I accept the challenge.”

The inspector turned back to his work. After a further half-hour’s
fruitless search, he was forced to admit defeat.

“They’re not here,” he said at last. “I’ll have to get back to the
station and report.”

Mr. Opalsen accompanied him, and Poirot and I were left alone.

“Well, Poirot,” I said, “what do you think of it?”

My friend was standing by the window, looking out into the night.
He did not answer for a moment. At last he turned.

“Hastings,” he said, “what do you think of our friend the
inspector?”

“A very capable man, I should say.”

“A very _logical_ man, as he says himself. But, _hélas_! logic is
not everything.”

“You think he’s wrong, then?”

“I think he has overlooked one or two small points.”

“Such as?”

“Well, for instance, the time it took Célestine to go into her room
and back.”

“How long was it?”

“On the first occasion, twelve seconds; on the second, fifteen.”

“Well?”

“In twelve seconds, my friend, one cannot do very much. One can
certainly not search a jewel-case, find a necklace, and hide it
securely.”

“But she might have had it ready.”

“True. But where could she have hidden it? Not on her person, as
we know. And the inspector has searched the room.”

“Then you think she is innocent?”

“I am sure of it.”

“Then it must be the chambermaid?”

“The chambermaid was only in the room for three minutes, and
Célestine was there all the time, except for those few seconds.”

“Then who can it be?”

Poirot smiled.

“There are other people in the hotel, Hastings.”

“But they couldn’t get into the room.”

“Are you so sure of that?”

He walked over to the door leading into the next suite.

“You remember I told you this was bolted on both sides?”

“Yes.”

“Well, suppose it were not?”

He took a small pair of tweezers from his pocket, and inserted
them into the keyhole. There was a faint click.

“You see? It is quite simple. A piece of wire, a little
ingenuity—and the door is open.”

He drew back the bolt and opened the door. The room beyond was in
darkness. He felt for the switch and turned on the light. It was a
bedroom, similar to the one we had just left.

“Whose room is this?” I asked.

“The manager will be able to tell us that.”

He rang the bell, and in a few minutes a waiter appeared.

“This room,” said Poirot, “who occupies it?”

“A gentleman of the name of—er—Major Sommers, I think, sir. He
arrived this evening.”

“Is he in his room now?”

“No, sir. He is downstairs in the lounge.”

“Thank you.”

The waiter retired. Poirot turned to me with a twinkle in his eye.

“You see, Hastings? Our field of search is widening.”

“But the inspector said the door was bolted on both sides.”

“The inspector,” said Poirot, “is a very _logical_ man. He saw a
bolt, and he assumed it was a bolt. He did not stop to consider
whether it was a _real_ bolt or only a _pretence_.”

He led the way back into Mrs. Opalsen’s room.

“And now,” he said, “let us examine the jewel-case.”

He took it from the drawer and carried it to the light. It was a
large, leather-covered box, with a silk-lined interior.

“Empty!” he murmured. “Quite empty. And yet—stay! What is this?”

He held the box up to the light, and I saw a small, glittering
object sticking to the silk lining. He drew it out with his
tweezers. It was a tiny fragment of glass.

“A piece of a bottle?” I suggested.

“Perhaps. Or perhaps—something else.”

He put it carefully into a small envelope.

“And now, Hastings, I think we will go downstairs.”

In the lounge we found Mr. Opalsen. He looked harassed and
unhappy.

“No news, I suppose?” he said, as we approached.

“None as yet,” replied Poirot. “But I have hopes. By the way, Mr.
Opalsen, is it true that you are—er—a little ‘short’ at the moment,
as you expressed it?”

The stockbroker looked surprised.

“Well, yes—things are a bit tight in the City, as I told you. But
what’s that got to do with it?”

“A great deal, perhaps. And your wife—she is fond of jewellery, is
she not?”

“I should think she was! It’s a perfect craze with her.”

“And she is also, perhaps, a little—shall we say—imprudent?”

“If you mean she’s a bit of a fool, you’re not far wrong,” said
Opalsen bluntly. “She’d believe anything anyone told her.”

“I see. Thank you.”

Poirot turned away, and I followed him.

“What are you driving at, Poirot?” I asked. “You don’t surely
suspect——”

“I suspect everyone, Hastings. It is my metier. But at the moment
 I am particularly interested in—the chambermaid.”

“The chambermaid! But she was searched!”

“Exactly. She was searched—and nothing was found. Which is very
significant.”

“I don’t see why.”

“Because, my friend, if she had stolen the pearls, she would
certainly have hidden them. And where would she hide them? Not on
her person—that would be too dangerous. In the room? No, for the
same reason. Then where?”

“I give it up.”

“She would hide them where no one would think of looking for
them.”

“And where is that?”

“Ah, that is what we have to find out!”

He led the way to the office, and asked to see the manager. When
that functionary appeared, Poirot addressed him with his usual
suavity.

“Monsieur le Directeur, I have a little favour to ask of you.
Would it be possible for me to see the—er—employment records of
your staff?”

“Certainly, Mr. Poirot. Is there any one in particular you are
interested in?”

“The chambermaid who attends to the first-floor rooms—the one who
was in Mrs. Opalsen’s room this evening.”

“Ah, Mary Higgins. A very superior girl. We’ve had her with us for
some time now. Her references were excellent.”

“I see. And her address?”

“She lives in the hotel, of course. But her home address is—let me
see—yes, here it is. 15, Glenister Road, Streatham.”

“Thank you. And now, one more thing. Is it possible for me to see
the room she occupies here?”

“Certainly. I’ll send someone up with you.”

The room was a small, neat cubicle on the top floor. Poirot
ransacked it with his usual thoroughness, but without result.

“Nothing,” he murmured, as we descended the stairs. “Absolutely
nothing. And yet——”

He stopped suddenly, and his eyes narrowed.

“Hastings,” he said, “what was it the chambermaid said when she
came back after being searched?”

“She said she was an honest girl, and that the French hussy ought
to be ashamed of herself.”

“No, no—not that. Before that.”

“I don’t remember.”

“She said: ‘I’ve nothing to be afraid of.’ Now, why did she say
that? Why did she emphasize the ‘I’?”

“I’m sure I don’t know.”

“Because, my friend, she knew that someone else _had_ something to
be afraid of!”

“You mean Célestine?”

“Or someone else. Tell me, Hastings, did you notice anything
peculiar about the chambermaid’s appearance?”

“She was a bit red-faced, as the maid said. And she had a rather
unpleasant expression.”

“Anything else?”

“No, I don’t think so.”

“Think, Hastings, think! Her hair, for instance.”

“It was dark, I think. Or was it fair? I really don’t remember.”

“It was a very peculiar shade of red,” said Poirot. “A most
unnatural shade. In fact, I would go so far as to say it was—a
wig!”

“A wig!” I exclaimed. “But why on earth should she wear a wig?”

“That is what I intend to find out. And now, Hastings, we will
return to the lounge and keep an eye on our friend Mr. Opalsen.”

We found the stockbroker sitting by himself, looking more depressed
than ever. As we approached, he looked up.

“Any news?”

“Not yet,” said Poirot. “But I have a little theory I should like
to test. Would you be so good as to accompany me to your room for
a moment?”

Opalsen rose wearily. “If you think it will do any good.”

When we reached the room, Poirot went straight to the dressing-table
and took out the jewel-case.

“Mr. Opalsen,” he said, “you told me your wife was a little—shall
we say—imprudent. Is it possible that she might have—er—parted
with the pearls of her own free will?”

Opalsen stared at him. “What on earth do you mean?”

“Suppose she were in need of money—for some purpose of which you
were not aware. Might she not have—er—disposed of the pearls, and
then pretended they had been stolen?”

“Nonsense!” said Opalsen. “She’d never do such a thing. Besides,
she’s got plenty of money. I give her a very handsome allowance.”

“But perhaps she has—er—debts?”

“I don’t believe it. Anyway, the pearls are worth thousands. She
couldn’t have got rid of them as easily as all that.”

“Perhaps not. But suppose she had—er—replaced them with a
duplicate?”

Opalsen started. “A duplicate!”

“It is a possibility, is it not? And it would explain that little
fragment of glass I found in the jewel-case.”

“Glass!”

“Yes. A piece of a—er—shall we say—imitation pearl?”

Opalsen looked at him in silence for a moment. Then he burst out:

“By Jove, Poirot, you may be right! I never thought of that. If
she’s been playing me false——”

He broke off, his face working with rage.

“But who could have done it?” he demanded. “She couldn’t have done
it herself.”

“Perhaps not. But she might have had—an accomplice.”

“An accomplice! Who?”

“That is what we have to find out. But in the meantime, I have a
little suggestion to make. Suppose we search—Mr. Opalsen’s own
possessions?”

The stockbroker recoiled. “My possessions! What do you mean?”

“Only a matter of form, monsieur. As I said before, I suspect
everyone.”

“But it’s preposterous! I’m the one who’s lost the pearls!”

“Precisely. And therefore you are the one who would be least likely
to be suspected. It is a very old trick, monsieur.”

Opalsen’s face turned a deep purple. “If you’re implying that I
stole my own wife’s pearls——”

“I am implying nothing, monsieur. I am merely—as you would say—
covering all the ground.”

With a bad grace, Opalsen submitted to the search. Poirot went
through his clothes and his dressing-case with his usual
thoroughness. In the pocket of one of his coats, he found a small,
tissue-paper parcel. He opened it carefully.

Inside was a string of pearls.

Opalsen uttered a cry of amazement. “The pearls! My wife’s pearls!
But how on earth did they get there?”

“That,” said Poirot, “is what I should like to know.”

He held the pearls up to the light, examining them closely.

“A very fine necklace,” he murmured. “Very fine indeed. And yet—
stay! What is this?”

He took his magnifying glass from his pocket and peered at the
clasp.

“Hastings, look at this!”

I looked. On the back of the clasp were the initials ‘M.H.’

“M.H.!” I exclaimed. “Mary Higgins!”

“Exactly,” said Poirot. “And now, I think we have the answer to
our little problem.”

“But I don’t understand,” said Opalsen. “How did Mary Higgins get
hold of my wife’s pearls? And why did she put them in my pocket?”

“She didn’t,” said Poirot. “These are not your wife’s pearls.”

“Not my wife’s pearls? But they look exactly like them!”

“To the lay eye, perhaps. But to the expert—no. These are—er—as I
suspected—imitations.”

“Imitations! But then where are the real ones?”

“Ah, that is the question! But I think I can answer it. Tell me,
Mr. Opalsen, where were you when the pearls were stolen?”

“I was downstairs in the lounge, as you know.”

“And was there anyone with you?”

“No—well, yes, for a few minutes. I was talking to—to that major
fellow—Sommers.”

“Ah! Major Sommers. And where is he now?”

“Still in the lounge, I suppose.”

“Let us go and see.”

We found Major Sommers sitting in a corner of the lounge, reading
a newspaper. He was a tall, soldierly-looking man, with a bronzed
face and a grey moustache. As we approached, he looked up.

“Ah, Opalsen. Any news of the pearls?”

“None,” said Opalsen shortly.

Poirot stepped forward. “Pardon, monsieur, but I believe you are
acquainted with a certain Mary Higgins?”

The major’s face did not change. “Mary Higgins? Never heard of
her.”

“That is strange. Because I have reason to believe that she is—er—
a very close friend of yours.”

The major rose to his feet. “I don’t know what you’re talking about,
sir. And I don’t like your tone.”

“I am sorry for that,” said Poirot. “But I must insist on an
answer. Is it not a fact that you and Mary Higgins—who is, I may
mention, not a chambermaid at all, but a very clever actress—
planned this little robbery together?”

The major’s face turned a dark red. “It’s a lie! A d—d lie!”

“Is it? Then perhaps you will explain how this came to be in your
possession?”

He held out the small tissue-paper parcel.

“I’ve never seen it before!”

“Indeed? Then perhaps you will explain why it was found in Mr.
Opalsen’s pocket—after you had been seen talking to him?”

“I didn’t put it there!”

“No? Then who did?”

The major did not answer.

“I will tell you,” said Poirot. “Mary Higgins put it there. She
stole the real pearls while Célestine was out of the room, and
replaced them with this imitation. Then she passed the real ones
to you, through the door between the two rooms. You, in turn,
managed to slip the imitation necklace into Mr. Opalsen’s pocket,
intending to throw suspicion on him later on. It was a very clever
plot, monsieur—but you forgot one thing.”

“What was that?” sneered the major.

“You forgot—Hercule Poirot!”

With a sudden movement, the major turned and fled towards the door.
But Poirot was too quick for him. He tripped him up, and in a
moment the two men were struggling on the floor.

With the help of some of the hotel guests, the major was eventually
secured. A search of his person revealed the real pearls, hidden in
the lining of his coat.

“Well, Poirot,” I said, as we sat in the train on our way back to
London, “it was a very clever piece of work. But how did you know
it was the major?”

“It was the glass, Hastings. The small fragment of glass I found in
the jewel-case. It was not a piece of an imitation pearl, as I
suggested to Mr. Opalsen. It was a piece of a—er—monocle.”

“A monocle!”

“Yes. A monocle such as the major wears. He must have dropped it
while he was taking the pearls from the case.”

“But how did he get into the room?”

“Through the door between the two suites. As I showed you, it was
quite easy to open.”

“And the chambermaid?”

“Ah, the chambermaid! She was, as I said, a very clever actress.
She was, in fact, the major’s wife. They have been carrying out a
series of such robberies all over the country.”

“And Célestine?”

“Poor Célestine! She was quite innocent. But she will have a good
story to tell her friends in Paris!”

Poirot leaned back and closed his eyes.

“And now, Hastings, if you do not mind, I will sleep. It has been
a very tiring weekend!”

“Yes, sir. It stands to reason. She hadn’t time to take them out
of the room. The lady’s discovering the robbery so soon upset her
plans. No, they’re here right enough. One of the two must have
hidden them—and it’s very unlikely for the chambermaid to have done
so.”

“More than unlikely—impossible!” said Poirot quietly.

“Eh?” The inspector stared.

Poirot smiled modestly.

“I have been making a few little calculations, monsieur. The time
taken by Mademoiselle Célestine to go into her room and back was
on the first occasion twelve seconds, and on the second fifteen.”

“Well?” The inspector stared at him.

“In twelve seconds, monsieur, it is impossible for any person to
go to a drawer, unlock a jewel-case, select a particular object,
re-lock the case, and return the case to the drawer. I have tried
it myself, and it took me forty-five seconds, and I am not a clumsy
man!”

“The chambermaid could have done it,” the inspector objected.

“She was in the room for three minutes, certainly,” agreed Poirot.
“But Célestine was also there. It is not to be supposed that she
would have stood by and watched the other woman rifling her
mistress’s jewel-case.”

“Then,” said the inspector, “your argument seems to prove that the
jewels were _not_ taken between the time Mrs. Opalsen went down to
dinner and the time she returned.”

“Exactly!” said Poirot.

“But they _were_!” cried Mrs. Opalsen. “I saw them myself when I
put my emeralds away.”

“Madame,” said Poirot, turning to her, “are you _absolutely_ sure?”

“I could take my oath on it!”

“You are sure that what you saw was the pearls—and not the empty
case?”

“Of course I’m sure! I remember particularly because I was
thinking how well they would go with the white lace dress I was
wearing.”

Poirot sighed.

“It is a pity,” he murmured. “It would have been so much simpler.”

“In any case,” said the inspector, “the maid is the only person
who could have done it. The chambermaid has been searched, and she
only had three minutes in the room. Even if she did do it, she’d
no time to hide the things. The maid had all the evening.”

“But she has been searched also,” I put in.

“Yes,” said the inspector, “but she’s had plenty of time to hide
the things. They’re in this room somewhere. It’s only a matter of
patience to find them.”

But his patience was destined to be severely tried. One hour,
two hours, passed—and still no sign of the pearls. The inspector’s
face grew longer and longer.

“It’s very strange,” he muttered. “I could have sworn they were
here. There’s not a square inch of the room we haven’t been over.
Well, there’s nothing for it but to wait and see if anything
further turns up.”

He took his departure, followed by the plain-clothes man. Mr.
Opalsen, who had been looking more and more worried, also went
out to talk to the manager. Mrs. Opalsen had fallen into a heavy
sleep, and we left her.

“What do you think of it, Poirot?” I asked as we went downstairs.

“It is an interesting little problem, Hastings. I am glad we came
to Brighton.”

“You think the maid did it?”

“If she did, she is a very clever woman. It is possible, but I
confess that I am not entirely satisfied.”

“Then you think the chambermaid——”

“No, I do not think the chambermaid did it. I am more inclined to
think that the pearls were not in the case when Mrs. Opalsen
looked.”

“But she says she saw them.”

“People often see what they expect to see. She expected to see the
pearls, so she saw them.”

“Then when were they taken?”

“That is the question. If we knew that, we should be a long way
on the road to the solution.”

“But who could have taken them?”

“There are several possibilities. For instance, there is Mr.
Opalsen.”

“Mr. Opalsen!” I cried.

“Why not? He is a man of business, and he tells us that money is
tight in the City. He might well find a use for a few thousand
pounds’ worth of pearls.”

“But he would have to hide them from his wife.”

“Certainly. But that would be easy enough. He would only have to
keep them in his pocket.”

“But then why call in the police?”

“A very good way of averting suspicion. No one would suspect a man
who had sent for the police himself.”

“It seems very unlikely,” I said doubtfully.

“Perhaps. But in these cases one must consider every possibility.
There is also the manager.”

“The manager!”

“He was very agitated, you remember. And he has keys to all the
rooms. It would have been easy for him to enter the room at any
time during the evening.”

“But the maid was there.”

“Exactly. The maid was there. That is the difficulty. Unless, of
course, she was an accomplice.”

I shook my head.

“I don’t believe it. She seemed much too upset.”

“_Mon cher_ Hastings, you are of a touching simplicity! A good
actress can always appear upset. However, we shall see.”

The next morning Poirot was up early. I found him in the lounge,
looking very thoughtful.

“I have been thinking, Hastings. There is one point that we have
overlooked.”

“What is that?”

“The door into the next room.”

“But it was bolted on both sides.”

“Yes. But that does not prove that it was always bolted. Suppose
that someone had entered the room from the other side, taken the
pearls, and then bolted the door on this side before leaving.”

“But how could they have bolted it from the other side?”

“They couldn’t. But they might have had a confederate in this
room who bolted it after they had gone.”

“But then the confederate would have been the maid.”

“Exactly. It always comes back to the maid.”

He was silent for a moment, then he said:

“I should like to have a look at that room next door.”

“It’s number 24, isn’t it? I’ll go and see if it’s vacant.”

I returned in a few minutes with the information that the room
was occupied by a Mr. and Mrs. Vandermeyer, who had arrived the
previous day.

“Vandermeyer,” murmured Poirot. “A Dutch name. I wonder——”

He did not finish his sentence, but started towards the lift. I
followed him. As we reached the first floor, the door of number 24
opened, and a man came out. He was a tall, dark man with a
determined-looking face. He glanced at us sharply as he passed.

“That is Mr. Vandermeyer,” I whispered.

Poirot nodded.

“A man of character, I should say. Let us see if we can find out
anything about him.”

He went to the manager’s office, and was closeted there for some
time. When he came out, his face was grave.

“Mr. Vandermeyer is a man of wealth, it appears. He is well known
in the City, and has a large house in London. He and his wife are
staying here for a few days before going abroad.”

“Then you don’t think he has anything to do with it?”

“I do not know. But I have found out one thing. Mr. Vandermeyer
was in his room yesterday evening between seven and eight o’clock.”

“The time the pearls were stolen!”

“Precisely. And there is another thing. Mrs. Vandermeyer was also
in the room. She was not feeling well, and had her dinner sent up
to her.”

“Then they both have an alibi.”

“On the contrary, they both had the opportunity. And there is the
door between the two rooms.”

“But it was bolted.”

“Yes—on this side. But who bolted it? That is the question.”

He was silent for a moment, then he said:

“I think I will have a little talk with the chambermaid.”

We found her in the corridor, looking somewhat subdued after her
experiences of the previous evening. Poirot spoke to her kindly.

“Tell me,” he said, “when you were in Mrs. Opalsen’s room yesterday
evening, did you notice anything unusual?”

The girl shook her head.

“No, sir. Everything seemed just as usual.”

“The door into the next room—was it bolted?”

“I didn’t notice, sir. I don’t think I even looked at it.”

“And the maid—what was she doing?”

“She was sitting by the window, sewing.”

“Did she leave the room while you were there?”

“Only for a minute, as she said. She went into her own room to
get something.”

“I see. And you are sure she wasn’t out of the room for more than
a minute?”

“Quite sure, sir. I hadn’t more than just time to turn down the
beds before she was back again.”

Poirot nodded.

“Thank you. That is all I wanted to know.”

As the girl went away, he turned to me.

“You see, Hastings? The time was very short—too short for any
ordinary person to have stolen the pearls. But for someone who
knew exactly where they were, and who had a duplicate key——”

“But who could that be?”

“That is what I am going to find out.”

He spent the rest of the morning in a state of restless activity,
flitting from one part of the hotel to another, and holding long
conversations with various members of the staff. I followed him
as best I could, but I must confess that I was unable to see any
purpose in his movements.

At lunch-time we were joined by Mr. Opalsen. He looked more
cheerful than he had done the night before.

“The police have found a clue,” he informed us. “They’ve
discovered that a man was seen hanging about the corridor near
our room yesterday evening. They think he may be the thief.”

“A man?” said Poirot. “What sort of a man?”

“A tall, dark man, according to the description. They’re trying to
track him down now.”

“A tall, dark man,” repeated Poirot thoughtfully. “That is
interesting. Very interesting.”

After lunch he suggested that we should go for a walk on the front.
The afternoon was fine, and the sea-front was crowded. Poirot
walked along with his head on one side, apparently deep in thought.
Suddenly he stopped and pointed to a small shop in a side street.

“Wait for me a moment, Hastings. I have a little purchase to
make.”

He was inside the shop for some time. When he came out, he was
carrying a small parcel.

“What have you bought?” I asked curiously.

“A little present for a lady, Hastings. A very charming lady.”

He refused to say more, and we continued our walk. When we returned
to the hotel, we found the manager waiting for us.

“Mr. Poirot,” he said, “could I have a word with you in private?”

They went into his office, and I was left alone in the lounge.
Ten minutes later Poirot reappeared. His face was radiant.

“_Mon ami_,” he cried, “the case is solved!”

“Solved!” I exclaimed. “But how? Who is the thief?”

“Wait, Hastings, wait. All will be revealed in good time. For the
moment, I must ask you to accompany me to Mrs. Opalsen’s room.”

When we arrived there, we found Mr. and Mrs. Opalsen and the
inspector. The latter looked rather crestfallen.

“I’m afraid we haven’t been able to find the pearls, sir,” he was
saying to Mr. Opalsen. “We’ve searched every corner of the room,
but there’s no sign of them.”

“That is because you have been looking in the wrong place,” said
Poirot, stepping into the room.

The inspector stared at him.

“The wrong place? What do you mean?”

“I mean, monsieur, that the pearls are not in this room at all.”

“But we know they were here yesterday evening!”

“Exactly. But they were moved—before you arrived.”

“Moved? By whom?”

“By the person who stole them.”

“And who was that?”

Poirot did not answer. Instead, he turned to Mrs. Opalsen.

“Madame,” he said, “I have a little gift for you. I hope you will
accept it as a small token of my regard.”

He handed her the parcel he had bought that afternoon. Mrs. Opalsen
opened it with an air of bewilderment. Inside was a small,
inexpensive-looking brooch.

“It is very kind of you, Mr. Poirot,” she said, looking rather
puzzled. “But I don’t quite understand——”

“Wait, madame. Look at it closely.”

Mrs. Opalsen did so. Suddenly she uttered a cry of surprise.

“Why—it’s the same design as my pearls!”

“Exactly,” said Poirot. “It is a very good imitation, is it not?”

“But I don’t see——”

“Listen, madame. Yesterday evening, when you came up to fetch your
pearls, you looked into the jewel-case and saw, as you thought,
the pearls. But what you actually saw was a necklace of imitation
pearls, which had been placed there by the thief.”

“But where are my real pearls, then?”

“They were taken earlier in the day—probably while you were out.
The thief had a duplicate key to your jewel-case, and was able to
substitute the imitation necklace for the real one at his leisure.”

“But who could have done it?”

Poirot turned to the inspector.

“Monsieur,” he said, “I think if you were to search the room of
Mr. and Mrs. Vandermeyer, you might find something of interest.”

The inspector’s face lit up.

“Vandermeyer! Of course! Why didn’t I think of it before?”

He hurried out of the room, followed by Mr. Opalsen. Mrs. Opalsen
remained behind, looking dazed.

“But I don’t understand,” she said. “How did you know?”

“It was the time, madame. The time taken by the maid to go into her
room and back. It was too short for the theft to have been
committed then. Therefore, it must have been committed earlier.
And who had the opportunity? Not the maid, for she was in the room
all the time. Not the chambermaid, for she was only there for a few
minutes. But someone who could enter the room when it was empty.”

“But the door was locked!”

“To you, yes. But to someone with a pass-key, it would be easy.
And who has a pass-key? The manager, and—the chambermaid.”

“The chambermaid!” I cried. “But you said it wasn’t her!”

“I said it was impossible for her to have committed the theft
_while the maid was in the room_. But she could have done it
earlier in the day.”

“But you said it was the Vandermeyers!”

“No, Hastings. I said the inspector should search their room. It is
a little trap I have set.”

At that moment the inspector returned. He was looking very
excited.

“You were right, Mr. Poirot! We found the pearls hidden in a
hollow bed-post in room 24!”

“And the Vandermeyers?”

“They’ve been arrested. They were just preparing to leave.”

“But I don’t understand,” said Mrs. Opalsen. “How did they get into
my room?”

“They didn’t, madame,” said Poirot. “The pearls were placed in
their room by the real thief.”

“The real thief? But who is it, then?”

Poirot looked at the chambermaid, who had just entered the room
with some fresh towels.

“Mademoiselle,” he said, “I think you have something to tell us.”

The girl turned pale and dropped the towels.

“I—I don’t know what you mean!” she stammered.

“I think you do. You stole the pearls earlier in the day, using
your pass-key. You then substituted the imitation necklace. When
Mrs. Opalsen discovered the loss, you were afraid of being
searched, so you hid the pearls in the nearest place you could
find—which happened to be the bed-post in the next room. You knew
the door between the two rooms was sometimes left unbolted, and
you took advantage of it.”

The girl burst into tears.

“I didn’t mean to do it! But the temptation was too great. And
when I saw the police coming, I was so frightened——”

“There, there,” said Poirot kindly. “It is a sad story. But justice
must be done.”

The inspector led the sobbing girl away. Mr. and Mrs. Opalsen were
profuse in their thanks to Poirot.

“You’re a marvel, Mr. Poirot!” cried the stockbroker. “I don’t know
how you did it.”

“It was the little grey cells, monsieur,” said Poirot, tapping his
