forehead. “The little grey cells.”

As we went down to dinner, I turned to my friend.

“But Poirot, how did you know about the imitation necklace?”

“I didn't, Hastings. It was a little bluff. I bought the brooch
this afternoon, and used it to test my theory. If Mrs. Opalsen
hadn't recognized the design, I should have known I was wrong.
But as it was——”

He shrugged his shoulders and smiled.

“_C’est magnifique!_” I cried.

“_C’est assez bien_,” said Poirot modestly. “But come, let us eat.
The dinner, it will be getting cold.”

“Because she was never alone in the room, monsieur.”

“Oh, that’s what she says,” retorted the inspector with a wink.
“You must take those stories for what they’re worth. Naturally
she wouldn’t admit to leaving her alone—it would make her
responsible.”

“No,” said Poirot, shaking his head. “I think that part of her
story was true. It is of a different kind from the rest. It has
the ring of truth.”

“Well, we’ll see,” said the inspector. “But we’re searching the
room—and if they’re here we’ll find them. They aren’t anywhere
else.”

He continued his work with a will, but the search was unsuccessful.
He was evidently much disconcerted.

“Never mind,” he said, more to himself than to anyone else. “We’ve
got the girl anyway, and if we keep her a bit—ten to one she’ll
give herself away.”

He gathered up his hat and prepared to depart.

“Good-night, sir. Good-night, madam.”

“Good-night, Inspector.”

He turned towards the door. Poirot followed him.

“A word with you, monsieur, if you please.”

They spoke together in low tones for a few moments, then the
inspector nodded and went out.

Mr. Opalsen had sunk into a chair.

“Well, they’ve gone,” he said gloomily. “And the pearls have
gone too! A nice business, I must say. What do you think of it,
Mr. Poirot?”

Poirot was standing by the window, his head slightly on one side.
He did not answer.

“I was asking you what you thought of it,” repeated Mr. Opalsen
irritably.

“I was thinking of a certain problem, monsieur.”

“The pearls?”

“No—the chambermaid.”

“What about her?”

“She is a very pretty girl, is she not?”

“Is she? I hadn’t noticed. What on earth has that got to do with
the case?”

“A great deal, I assure you. But I must be going. Hastings, are
you ready? Good-night, monsieur. Good-night, madame.”

We went out. Poirot walked down the corridor, humming a little
tune to himself. He seemed in the best of spirits.

“Well,” I said, as we reached our own rooms, “what do you make
of it? It’s a very simple case, isn’t it?”

“Simple? On the contrary, it is most interesting.”

“Why? It’s obvious the maid took them.”

“Is it?”

“Of course. She’s the only one who could have. The chambermaid
was only in the room a few minutes.”

“True. But during those few minutes the maid was in her own room.
She might have slipped out for a moment then.”

“She says she didn’t.”

“Naturally. But she might have.”

“And then?”

“And then what?”

“What did she do with the pearls?”

“That is the question, Hastings. If she took them, she must have
hidden them. But where? The inspector has searched the room
thoroughly.”

“She may have hidden them on herself.”

“The searcher found nothing.”

“She might have managed to pass them to someone else.”

“To whom?”

“The chambermaid.”

“Ah! Now we are getting to it. But the chambermaid was also
searched.”

“Well, then,” I said, “it must be Célestine after all.”

“Wait a bit, Hastings. Let us look at it from another point of
view. Suppose someone else took them.”

“Who?”

“The husband?”

“Mr. Opalsen? My dear Poirot! He’s a most respectable man. Besides,
he’s a rich man—why should he want his wife’s pearls?”

“Money is sometimes tight in the City, as he said himself. But
I agree it is unlikely. Then there is the chambermaid.”

“But you said yourself it was impossible!”

“I said it was impossible for her to have hidden them in the room
because she was never alone there. But suppose she took them _out_
of the room with her?”

“How? She was searched.”

“Ah!” Poirot’s eyes twinkled. “Exactly. How?”

“Well, then,” I said, “it must be Célestine.”

“Maybe. But I should like to know more about that chambermaid.
I think I will have a little talk with her.”

“You won’t get anything out of her.”

“We shall see.”

He went towards the door.

“Where are you going?”

“To the kitchen, Hastings. I have a great weakness for kitchens.”

He disappeared. I sat down and waited. It was nearly an hour before
he returned. He was looking very thoughtful.

“Well?” I asked. “Did you see her?”

“Yes.”

“And what did she say?”

“Nothing very much. But I have found out one thing.”

“What’s that?”

“She has a young man.”

“I don’t see how that helps.”

“He is a very superior young man—a valet to one of the visitors.
A very handsome young man, I am told.”

“Really, Poirot! What has that to do with the case?”

“A great deal, Hastings. A great deal.”

He sat down and began to polish his nails.

“I have also,” he said, after a minute or two, “sent a telegram.”

“A telegram? To whom?”

“To a friend of mine. A very useful friend. He is in the—er—pearl
business.”

“I don’t see how that’s going to help you find the thief.”

“Perhaps not. But it may help me to find the pearls.”

“The pearls? But you think they’re still in the hotel?”

“I am sure of it.”

“Then why did you send a telegram?”

“Because, Hastings, I am a very prudent man. I like to be prepared.”

He would say no more, and I was forced to go to bed with my
curiosity unsatisfied.

The next morning Poirot was up early. He seemed to be in a very
restless mood. He wandered in and out of the rooms, and finally
announced his intention of going for a walk.

“Will you come, Hastings?”

“With pleasure.”

We walked along the front for some time in silence. Then Poirot
suddenly turned to me.

“Hastings,” he said, “do you remember the sketch I made of the
rooms?”

“Yes.”

“And the door between the two rooms?”

“Yes.”

“The inspector said it was bolted on both sides.”

“Yes.”

“I examined it myself. It was bolted on the bedroom side. I drew
back the bolt and tried it. It would not open.”

“No, because it was bolted on the other side.”

“Exactly. But I did not see it bolted on the other side.”

“No, but you could feel it was.”

“Could I? I am not so sure. I should like to be sure.”

“Well, you can’t be now. Célestine’s in prison.”

“Is she? I wonder.”

“Of course she is. The inspector took her away.”

“He took her away, certainly. But whether he took her to prison
is another matter. I gave him a little piece of advice, you see.”

“What was it?”

“I suggested that he should take her to a—er—more comfortable
place, and keep a very sharp watch on her.”

“I see. You think she will try to get rid of the pearls?”

“It is possible.”

“But if she hasn’t got them?”

“Then someone else may try to get rid of them. And that is why
I want to be sure about that door.”

“But you said it was bolted.”

“On the bedroom side—yes. But was it bolted on the other side?
I have a little idea, Hastings. Let us go back to the hotel.”

When we arrived there, Poirot went straight to the manager’s
office. He was there for some time, and when he came out he was
smiling.

“It is all right, Hastings. I have got the key.”

“The key of what?”

“Of the room next to Mrs. Opalsen’s. It is vacant at present.”

He led the way upstairs. We entered the room, which was a small
single one. Poirot went straight to the door communicating with
the bedroom. He examined it closely.

“_Tiens!_” he said. “It is as I thought.”

“What?”

“The bolt is a very old-fashioned one. It is quite easy to move
it from the other side.”

“How?”

“With a piece of wire. See!”

He produced a piece of wire from his pocket and inserted it in
the crack of the door. After a moment’s fumbling, there was a
sharp click.

“There!” he said. “The door is now unbolted.”

He opened it. We were looking into Mrs. Opalsen’s bedroom.

“But what does this prove?” I asked.

“It proves, Hastings, that it was possible for someone to enter
the room from this side, even if the door was bolted.”

“But who could have done it?”

“Ah! That is the question. Not the chambermaid, at any rate. She
was in the room the whole time.”

“Then it must have been someone else.”

“Exactly.”

“But who?”

“Let us think. Who had access to this room?”

“Anyone, I suppose, when it was vacant.”

“True. But someone must have known that the pearls were in the
other room.”

“Mr. Opalsen knew. And Célestine.”

“And the chambermaid.”

“Yes, but you said it wasn’t her.”

“I said it wasn’t her who hid them in the room. But she might have
had an accomplice.”

“The valet?”

“The handsome young man? It is possible. But let us look a little
further. Suppose someone had been in this room while the pearls
were being stolen.”

“But they couldn’t have been. The door was bolted.”

“On the other side—yes. But as I have shown you, that is easily
remedied. Now, Hastings, I want you to do something for me.”

“What is it?”

“I want you to go down to the lounge and keep a sharp watch on
Mr. Opalsen. If he comes upstairs, let me know at once.”

“Mr. Opalsen? You suspect him?”

“I suspect everyone, Hastings. It is my rule. Now go.”

I went down to the lounge and took up a position where I could
see the lift and the stairs. Mr. Opalsen was sitting in a corner,
reading a newspaper. He seemed quite absorbed in it.

I waited for about half an hour. Then I saw him get up and go
towards the lift. I followed him at a discreet distance.

He got out at the first floor and went along the corridor. I saw
him enter his wife’s room.

I ran back to the room where I had left Poirot. He was not there.

I looked into the bedroom. He was not there either.

I was beginning to feel rather uneasy. Where could he have gone?

Suddenly I heard a sound from the maid’s room. I went to the door
and looked in.

Poirot was there, sitting on the floor, and he was busily engaged
in—of all things—polishing a pair of shoes!

“Poirot!” I exclaimed. “What on earth are you doing?”

He looked up and winked at me.

“I am being a valet, Hastings. It is a very interesting profession.”

“But what are you doing with those shoes?”

“They belong to the handsome young man, Hastings. I took the
liberty of borrowing them.”

“But why?”

“Because, my friend, they are very interesting shoes. Very
interesting indeed.”

He got up and handed them to me.

“What do you see, Hastings?”

I looked at them. They were a pair of very ordinary black patent-leather
shoes.

“I don’t see anything unusual about them,” I said.

“Look at the heels, Hastings. The heels!”

I looked at the heels. They were slightly worn on one side, but
otherwise there was nothing remarkable about them.

“I don’t see anything,” I repeated.

Poirot sighed.

“You have no eyes, Hastings. No eyes at all. Look here!”

He pointed to a small, almost invisible crack in one of the heels.

“What of it?”

“It is not a crack, Hastings. It is a lid!”

He inserted his fingernail into the crack and pulled. To my intense
surprise, the bottom of the heel came away, revealing a small
hollow space inside.

And in that space, gleaming with a soft, iridescent light, were
the pearls!

“Poirot!” I cried. “You’ve found them!”

“_Mais oui_, Hastings. I told you I should.”

“But how did you know they were there?”

“It was simple, my friend. Very simple. I knew they must be hidden
somewhere. I knew they could not have been taken out of the room.
I knew the chambermaid could not have hidden them. Therefore,
someone else must have done it. Who? The only person who had the
opportunity was the person in the next room. And who was that?
The handsome young man—the valet!”

“But you said the room was vacant!”

“It was—until yesterday afternoon. Then it was taken by a young
man—a very handsome young man. He was the valet of one of the
other visitors. He had plenty of opportunity to unbolt the door
and slip into the next room while Célestine was in her own room.”

“I see! And he hid the pearls in his shoes!”

“Exactly. It was a very clever hiding-place. No one would think
of looking there.”

“But how did you know it was him?”

“I didn't. But I suspected him. And then I remembered his shoes.
I noticed them last night when I saw him in the corridor. They
were very new—and they had very thick heels. It was a little
unusual, you see.”

“Poirot, you are wonderful!”

“I am—er—not without a certain amount of intelligence,” he said
modestly. “But now, Hastings, we must return the shoes—and the
pearls.”

“Return them? But shouldn’t we call the police?”

“Not yet, Hastings. Not yet. I have a little plan.”

He replaced the pearls in the heel and closed the lid. Then he
carefully polished the shoe again.

“There!” he said. “Now no one would know it had been opened.
Now, Hastings, you must take these back to the young man’s room.
Be very careful that no one sees you.”

“But what about the pearls? We can’t just leave them there!”

“Do as I tell you, Hastings. Trust me.”

I went back to the young man’s room and replaced the shoes. Then
I returned to Poirot.

“What now?” I asked.

“Now, Hastings, we will go and see Mr. Opalsen.”

We found him still in his wife’s room. He looked up as we entered.

“Well?” he asked. “Any news?”

“Yes, monsieur,” said Poirot. “I have found the pearls.”

“What!” Mr. Opalsen sprang to his feet. “Where are they?”

“They are in a very safe place, monsieur. But before I tell you
where they are, I must ask you a question.”

“Well, what is it?”

“Is it true that you are in need of money, monsieur?”

Mr. Opalsen’s face turned a deep red.

“What do you mean?” he demanded.

“I mean, monsieur, that it is sometimes very tempting for a man
who is in financial difficulties to—shall we say—borrow his wife’s
jewels?”

“Are you accusing me of stealing my wife’s pearls?”

“I am merely asking a question, monsieur.”

“It’s a lie! I never touched them!”

“Then how do you explain this?”

Poirot held out a small piece of paper. It was the telegram he
had received that morning.

Mr. Opalsen took it and read it. His face went white.

“Where did you get this?” he whispered.

“It was delivered to me by mistake, monsieur. It is from a firm
of jewellers in London. It says: ‘Pearls received. Will send
valuation tomorrow.’”

Mr. Opalsen sank back into his chair.

“I—I can explain,” he stammered.

“I am sure you can, monsieur. But I think it would be better if
you explained it to your wife.”

At that moment the door opened and Mrs. Opalsen entered. She
looked from one to the other of us in surprise.

“What is it?” she asked. “What’s happened?”

“Your husband has something to tell you, madame,” said Poirot
gravely.

Mr. Opalsen looked at his wife for a moment, then he bowed his
head.

“I’m sorry, Mary,” he said. “I—I took the pearls.”

“You!” Mrs. Opalsen stared at him in horror. “But why?”

“I needed the money. Things haven’t been going well lately. I
thought I could—borrow them for a while and then put them back.”

“But how did you do it? The door was bolted!”

“I—I had a duplicate key. I went in while you were at dinner.”

“But what about the valet? And the shoes?” I asked.

Poirot smiled.

“Ah, the valet! He was a very useful person, Hastings. He was
my accomplice.”

“Your accomplice!”

“Yes. I suspected Mr. Opalsen from the first. But I had no proof.
So I arranged with the valet—who is an old friend of mine—to
pretend to have stolen the pearls and hidden them in his shoes.
I knew that if Mr. Opalsen thought he was going to be found out,
he would confess.”

“But the telegram?”

“That was also part of the plan, Hastings. I sent it to myself,
knowing that the waiter would deliver it to Mr. Opalsen by
mistake.”

“Poirot, you are a devil!” I exclaimed.

“No, Hastings. I am only a man who uses his little grey cells.”

He turned to Mr. Opalsen.

“And now, monsieur, I think you have some explaining to do.”

As we left the room, I heard Mrs. Opalsen’s voice raised in
indignation.

“Well, Poirot,” I said, as we walked down the corridor, “you’ve
done it again. But I must say, I’m a bit disappointed. I thought
it was going to be a real mystery.”

Poirot smiled.

“It was a real mystery, Hastings. The mystery of the human heart.
And that is the most interesting mystery of all.”

He paused for a moment, then added:

“And besides, I have a very good friend in the pearl business. He
will be very pleased to hear that I have found the pearls.”

“But you haven’t found them!” I reminded him. “They’re still in
London!”

“Ah, yes. I forgot. But no matter. They will be returned tomorrow.
And in the meantime, we have had a very pleasant week-end at
Brighton.”

He hummed a little tune to himself as we went down to lunch.

THE END

“Wait, wait,” he said, as if to himself. “There is something here
that—that—does not fit. How if the chambermaid _had_ taken them?”

The inspector shrugged his shoulders. “I’ve just told you why she
couldn’t have done it. She wasn’t in the room alone for a minute.
The maid was there the whole time.”

“True, true. But how if the maid took them?”

The inspector smiled. “Well, then, we’ll find them. They must be
somewhere about the room.”

“And if you don’t find them?”

The inspector’s face fell.

“In that case I shall be very much surprised. But we _must_ find
them.”

He continued his search. He even went so far as to examine the
curtain-rods. Mr. Opalsen’s face grew more and more gloomily
sceptical. Finally the inspector gave it up.

“It beats me,” he admitted. “But we’ll have another look in the
morning. I’m not beaten yet.”

The Opalsens went to another room, and Poirot and I were left
alone. He walked over to the bed, and looked at it thoughtfully.
Then he looked at the dressing-table. Finally he turned to me.

“What do you think of it, Hastings?”

“Well, it’s a difficult case. It looks as if one of the two women
must have taken them. And yet, if they did, where did they hide
them?”

“Precisely. That is the point. Where did they hide them? Because,
you see, they _must_ be in the room.”

“Unless they were thrown out of the window.”

“I have already looked. There is nothing on the ground below.”

“Then they must be in the room.”

“They are not in the room,” said Poirot.

“But they must be!”

“My dear Hastings, when I tell you a thing is not, it is because
it is _not_! If the pearls were in the room, the inspector would
have found them. He is a very thorough man, though he lacks
imagination.”

“Then who took them?”

“Ah!” Poirot’s eyes sparkled. “That is the question! Let us
consider the facts. The pearls were in the case when Mrs. Opalsen
went down to dinner at eight o’clock. At nine o’clock they had
vanished. During that time the maid, Célestine, was in the room
the whole time, with the exception of two very brief absences into
the adjoining room. During one of these absences the chambermaid
was in the room. Now, if the chambermaid took them, she must have
done so in about thirty seconds. Is that possible?”

“Hardly.”

“If Célestine took them, she had all the time in the world. But
then she had no opportunity of hiding them, or of passing them to
an accomplice.”

“She might have had an accomplice in the next room.”

“The door was bolted, Hastings.”

“She might have handed them through the door.”

“It was bolted on this side, remember.”

“Yes, but she could have unbolted it, handed them through, and
bolted it again.”

“A very good suggestion, Hastings. But, unfortunately, the door
was also bolted on the other side.”

“How do you know?”

“Because I tried it!”

I felt a little crestfallen. Poirot, however, did not seem to
notice it. He was pacing the room with rapid steps. Suddenly he
stopped.

“Hastings, I have an idea! A very simple idea! So simple that I
wonder I did not think of it before. Come with me.”

He led the way out of the room. We went down the corridor to the
end, where there was a small door. Poirot opened it. It led into
a sort of housemaid’s cupboard, containing brooms, pails, and
cleaning materials.

“What are we looking for?” I asked.

“Wait!”

He was rummaging among some old rags in a corner. Finally he
produced a small object. It was a piece of white wax.

“What is that for?” I asked.

“It is a clue, Hastings! A very important clue! And now, if you
please, we will go back to our own rooms. I have much to think
over.”

He would say no more, and we retired to bed. I must confess that I
did not sleep very well. The mystery of the stolen pearls haunted
me. Who could have taken them? And where could they be? And what
was the meaning of that piece of white wax?

The next morning Poirot was up early. He seemed to be in a very
good humour.

“Well, Hastings,” he said, as we sat at breakfast. “I think I have
the hang of the affair now.”

“You have? Who is the thief?”

“A very clever person, Hastings! A very clever person indeed! But
not quite clever enough for Hercule Poirot!”

“Is it Célestine?”

“No, it is not Célestine.”

“The chambermaid?”

“No, it is not the chambermaid.”

“Then who is it?”

“Wait, wait, my friend! All in good time. First of all, I must
make a few inquiries.”

He rose from the table and left the room. I followed him. We went
to the manager’s office. Poirot asked to see the plan of the
hotel. The manager produced it. Poirot studied it for a few
minutes.

“Thank you,” he said. “That is all I want to know.”

We went back to the Opalsens’ room. The inspector was there,
looking very disgruntled.

“No luck, I suppose?” said Poirot.

“None at all. We’ve searched the room again, but there’s not a
sign of them. I’m beginning to think the French girl’s got away
with them after all.”

“I don’t think so,” said Poirot. “In fact, I’m sure she hasn’t.”

“Then who has?”

“If you will come with me, I think I can show you.”

He led the way out of the room and down the corridor. He stopped
in front of the door of the room next to the Opalsens’.

“Who occupies this room?” he asked.

“An American gentleman, I believe,” said the inspector. “A Mr.
Lowen. But what has that got to do with it? The door’s bolted on
both sides.”

“Precisely,” said Poirot. “That is what makes it so interesting.”

He knocked on the door. There was no answer. He turned the handle,
but the door was locked.

“He is out,” said Poirot. “But no matter. I have seen what I
wanted to see.”

He walked back to the Opalsens’ room.

“And now,” he said, “I will tell you what happened. The pearls
were not taken by the maid, nor by the chambermaid. They were taken
by—Mr. Opalsen!”

“What!” we all cried in chorus.

“Yes,” said Poirot. “It is very simple. Mr. Opalsen was in need of
money. He told us himself that money was ‘confoundedly tight in the
City.’ He decided to steal his wife’s pearls and claim the
insurance money. He had a duplicate key made for the jewel-case—that
is what the white wax was for; I found it in the housemaid’s
cupboard where he had hidden it. He waited until his wife had gone
down to dinner, then he went up to the room—he could easily have
done so without being seen—unlocked the jewel-case, took the
pearls, and locked it again. Then he went back to the lounge and
waited for his wife to discover the loss.”

“But the maid!” I cried. “She was in the room the whole time!”

“She was not in the room the whole time,” said Poirot. “She went
into her own room twice. It was during one of those absences that
Mr. Opalsen entered the room.”

“But the door was locked!”

“No, it was not. Mrs. Opalsen told us she never locked the drawer,
and she didn’t say anything about the door. It was only later,
when the police arrived, that the door was found to be locked.
Mr. Opalsen had locked it himself, to make it appear as though the
theft had been committed by someone inside the room.”

“But the chambermaid?”

“She was merely a pawn in the game. Mr. Opalsen knew that she would
be in the room at that time, and he timed his visit accordingly.
He wanted to throw suspicion on her, or on the maid.”

“But how did he get the pearls out of the room?”

“He didn’t. He hid them in a very clever place. A place where no
one would think of looking for them.”

“Where?”

“In the piece of white wax!”

“What!”

“Yes. He had hollowed out the wax and placed the pearls inside.
Then he had hidden the wax in the housemaid’s cupboard, intending
to retrieve it later.”

“But—but—” Mr. Opalsen was white with rage. “This is monstrous!
It’s a lie! I never did such a thing!”

“Then how do you account for this?” asked Poirot.

He held up a small object. It was a pearl—a large, beautifully
matched pearl.

“I found it in your pocket, monsieur, when I ‘accidentally’ bumped
into you in the lounge this morning.”

Mr. Opalsen collapsed into a chair. The inspector stepped forward.

“I think you’d better come with me, sir,” he said.

As they left the room, Mrs. Opalsen burst into tears once more.

“Oh, Ed!” she wailed. “How could you? And those were my best
pearls, too!”

Poirot patted her hand.

“Be comforted, madame. You will get your pearls back. And as for
your husband—well, perhaps it will be a lesson to him.”

He turned to me.

“Well, Hastings, what do you think of my ‘little grey cells’ now?”

“I think they’re marvellous, Poirot! Simply marvellous!”

“_Évidemment_!” said Poirot, with a twinkle in his eye. “But it was
a very simple case, Hastings. Very simple indeed!”

“I’ve made a little experiment, you see. I timed the movements of
Mademoiselle. She was away on each occasion exactly twelve seconds.
During that time, Hastings, could you have unlocked a jewel-case,
taken out a necklace, relocked the case, and hidden the necklace
in some secure place?”

“I should think it most unlikely,” I said.

“Twelve seconds!” Poirot laughed. “I should think so indeed! It is
impossible.”

“But the chambermaid——” began the inspector.

“The chambermaid was only in the room for a few minutes,”
interrupted Poirot. “And she was being watched the whole time by
Mademoiselle.”

“That’s true,” said Mr. Opalsen.

The inspector looked from one to the other of us.

“Then what do you propose, monsieur?” he asked of Poirot.

Poirot turned to Mrs. Opalsen.

“Would you mind, madame, if I looked through your jewel-case? It’s
of no consequence, but I have a whim.”

“By all means, Mr. Poirot. There it is—in the drawer.”

Poirot lifted it out and placed it on the table. It was a large
leather case, with a tray in it. Underneath the tray were various
trinkets and a few pieces of more expensive jewellery.

Poirot took them out one by one, examined them, and laid them aside.
When he had finished, he took up the case and looked at it
carefully, tapping it with his fingers.

“A very good case,” he remarked. “Very solid. No false bottoms, I
think.”

He shook it, then held it up to his ear.

“No—there is nothing. But what is this?”

He had discovered a small piece of paper which had been wedged
into the hinge of the lid. He held it up.

“It is a piece of newspaper. It has been used to wrap something in.”

He unfolded it. Inside was a tiny, brilliant speck.

“A diamond!” cried Mrs. Opalsen. “One of the small diamonds out of
my ring!”

“Wait!” Poirot held up his hand. “There is something else.”

He picked up a small, dark object from the floor.

“A piece of black thread,” he said. “Most interesting.”

He turned to the inspector.

“I should be very much obliged if you would let me see the two
girls again—one at a time, if you please.”

The inspector nodded.

“The chambermaid first,” suggested Poirot.

The girl was brought back. She was still looking very angry.

“I want to ask you one or two questions,” said Poirot. “When you
were in this room after dinner, did you see anyone else besides
the maid?”

“No, sir.”

“Did you notice anything unusual?”

“Nothing at all.”

“Think again. Did you not see something that struck you as being
out of the common?”

The girl thought for a moment.

“Well, now you mention it, sir, I _did_ notice a piece of black
thread hanging from the bottom drawer—the one the jewel-case was in.”

“Ah!” Poirot’s eyes sparkled. “And did you do anything?”

“No, sir. I just wondered what it was doing there, and then I
forgot all about it.”

“Thank you. That will do.”

The chambermaid was dismissed, and Célestine was brought in. She
had recovered her composure somewhat, but was still very pale.

“Mademoiselle,” said Poirot, “I want you to tell me exactly what
you did when you went into your own room.”

“I have told you, monsieur. I went to fetch a reel of cotton and
some scissors.”

“Where were they?”

“On the chest of drawers.”

“Both of them?”

“Yes, monsieur.”

“And you are quite sure you did not go anywhere else?”

“Quite sure.”

“You did not, for instance, go to the window?”

“The window? No, monsieur. Why should I?”

“I only wondered. Thank you, mademoiselle.”

When she had gone, Poirot turned to us with a look of triumph.

“The case is clear,” he said. “The necklace is not in this room.”

“Not in this room?” cried the inspector. “But it must be!”

“On the contrary,” said Poirot, “it is at this moment being carried
away from the hotel.”

“But how? Who by?”

“By the person who stole it.”

“But who was that?”

“The person,” said Poirot, “who was in this room after dinner.”

“But that was only the maid and the chambermaid!”

“Exactly. And as we have seen, neither of them could have done it.”

“Then who did?”

“There was someone else,” said Poirot.

“Someone else? Who?”

“The person who was behind that door!” Poirot pointed to the door
leading into the next apartment.

“But it was bolted on both sides!”

“Precisely,” said Poirot. “And that is how it was done.”

He walked over to the door and examined the bolt.

“See,” he said. “The bolt is a very simple one. A piece of black
thread, a little ingenuity—and the thing is done.”

He explained his theory. The thief, who was in the next room, had
waited until the maid’s back was turned. Then, by means of the
thread, he had drawn back the bolt, entered the room, stolen the
pearls, and retreated, bolting the door behind him in the same
way.

“But the thread would be left hanging!” I objected.

“Precisely. That is what the chambermaid saw.”

“But the other door? The one from the corridor?”

“It was locked, of course. But a duplicate key is easily obtained.”

The inspector looked impressed.

“It’s a clever theory,” he admitted. “But who is the thief? The
next room is occupied by a Mr. and Mrs. Vandermeyer. They’ve been
here for some time, and are people of the highest respectability.”

“Are they?” said Poirot. “I should like to see them.”

The inspector hesitated.

“I don’t know that I can allow that. Still, I might make a few
inquiries.”

He left the room. Mr. Opalsen turned to Poirot.

“You really think it’s these Vandermeyers?”

“I am almost sure of it,” said Poirot.

In a few minutes the inspector returned. His face was rather red.

“They’ve gone,” he said.

“Gone?”

“Yes. They left about half an hour ago. Said they’d had a telegram
calling them away.”

“Aha!” said Poirot. “The telegram! The classic excuse! And did
they take much luggage?”

“Only two suitcases. They left the rest to be forwarded.”

“I thought so,” said Poirot. “And the suitcases—did you see them?”

“No. But the hall porter did. He says they were quite light.”

“Light!” Poirot laughed. “Of course they were light! The pearls
were in one of them.”

“But how did they get away? The police were at the door.”

“There are other ways of leaving an hotel,” said Poirot. “The
service stairs, for instance.”

The inspector looked chagrined.

“I’ll get on to the station at once. They may not have started
yet.”

He hurried from the room. Mr. Opalsen followed him.

“Well, Poirot,” I said, “you’ve done it again.”

“It was simple, my friend, very simple. The black thread, you see—it
was the clue.”

“But how did you know about the bolt?”

“I did not know. I only suspected. But when I saw the thread, I
knew I was right.”

“And the diamond?”

“Ah, the diamond! That was a little piece of bluff. I found it in
the jewel-case, it is true, but it had nothing to do with the
robbery. It was just a small stone that had fallen out of its
setting.”

“And the piece of newspaper?”

“That also was bluff. I had to have something to wrap the diamond
in, you see.”

I laughed.

“You are a wonderful man, Poirot.”

“I am a very simple one, Hastings. But I have the eyes that see,
and the brain that thinks. And now, I think we might go down to
the lounge and wait for the news.”

We found Mrs. Opalsen in the lounge, surrounded by a sympathetic
crowd. She was still weeping, but was also enjoying the notoriety
of her position.

“Oh, Mr. Poirot!” she cried, as she saw us. “Have you any news?”

“The police are doing their best, madame. I have great hopes.”

We sat down and waited. It was nearly an hour before the inspector
returned. He looked very dejected.

“No luck,” he said. “They’d started ten minutes before I got to
the station. We’ve wired to London, of course, but I’m afraid it’s
too late.”

“And the luggage?” asked Poirot.

“We’ve got that. But it’s only clothes. No sign of the pearls.”

“That is bad,” said Poirot. “Very bad.”

He looked thoughtful for a moment. Then he turned to Mr. Opalsen.

“I should like to see that luggage, if I may.”

“Certainly, if you think it will help.”

We went up to the room where the suitcases had been taken. They
were two ordinary-looking suitcases, filled with clothes. Poirot
turned them out on the floor and examined them carefully.

“Nothing,” he said, at last. “Nothing at all.”

He looked round the room.

“And the other luggage? The pieces that were to be forwarded?”

“They’re downstairs in the hall.”

“Let us see them.”

We went down to the hall. There were three large trunks, heavily
laden. Poirot looked at them with interest.

“You have the keys?” he asked the inspector.

“Yes.”

The inspector unlocked the trunks, and Poirot began to rummage
through them. He seemed to be looking for something in particular.

“Aha!” he said, at last. “What have we here?”

He had found a small, heavy box, carefully wrapped in brown paper.
He tore off the paper and opened the box. Inside was a set of
heavy iron weights.

“Weights!” said the inspector. “What on earth would they want with
weights?”

“To make the trunks heavy, of course,” said Poirot. “It is an old
trick. The trunks are filled with rubbish, and the weights are
added to give them the appearance of being full of valuable
property.”

“But the pearls?” I asked. “Where are the pearls?”

“That,” said Poirot, “is what we have to find out.”

He turned to the inspector.

“I should like to see the chambermaid once more.”

“The chambermaid? But we’ve seen her already.”

“I know. But I have a question to ask her.”

The girl was sent for. She looked more angry than ever.

“Look here,” she said, as she entered the room. “I’ve had about
enough of this. I’ve been searched once, and I’m not going to be
searched again.”

“Calm yourself, my girl,” said Poirot. “I only want to ask you a
very simple question. When you were in Mrs. Opalsen’s room, did
you see a piece of soap?”

“Soap?” The girl stared at him. “Of course I saw a piece of soap.
There’s always soap in the rooms.”

“What kind of soap was it?”

“Just ordinary soap. The kind the hotel provides.”

“And where was it?”

“In the soap-dish, of course. Where else would it be?”

“Was it a new piece?”

“No. It had been used.”

“Thank you. That will do.”

The girl went out, muttering to herself.

“Soap!” said the inspector. “What on earth has soap got to do with
it?”

“A great deal,” said Poirot. “Hastings, my friend, have you a
knife?”

“Yes.” I handed it to him.

Poirot took a piece of soap from a nearby washstand and began to
whittle it away.

“See,” he said. “It is very easy. One makes a small hole, so. Then
one puts the pearls inside, and covers the hole with a little more
soap. Then one puts the soap back in the soap-dish, and it is ready.”

“But the pearls would be ruined!” I cried.

“Not if they are wrapped in a piece of oiled silk. It is a very
safe hiding-place. No one would think of looking in a piece of
used soap.”

“But the soap wasn’t in the room!” said the inspector. “We looked.”

“Exactly,” said Poirot. “The thief took it with him.”

“But who was the thief?”

“The person,” said Poirot, “who had the best opportunity of
taking the soap.”

“But who was that?”

“The chambermaid!” I cried.

“No, no, my friend. Not the chambermaid. She would have no reason
to take the soap. She could have hidden the pearls in a dozen
better places.”

“Then who?”

“Think, Hastings. Who was it who was so anxious to have the
chambermaid searched?”

“Célestine!”

“Exactly. Célestine. She knew the pearls were not on the
chambermaid, because she had them herself. She had hidden them in
the soap, and she was waiting for an opportunity to get them out
of the hotel.”

“But the Vandermeyers?”

“The Vandermeyers were a plant. Célestine knew they were leaving,
and she used them as a blind. She made up the story of the black
thread and the door, and the inspector fell into the trap.”

The inspector’s face was a study.

“But the bolt?” I asked. “How do you explain the bolt?”

“It was never moved,” said Poirot. “Célestine just said it was.
She knew no one would think of questioning her word.”

“And the soap?”

“She must have it on her now. She was searched, it is true, but
the searcher would never think of looking for a piece of soap.”

The inspector did not wait to hear any more. He rushed out of the
room. In a few minutes he returned, looking triumphant.

“We’ve got her!” he said. “She had the soap in her pocket. And the
pearls are inside it, just as you said.”

Mrs. Opalsen was overjoyed. She insisted on kissing Poirot, much to
his embarrassment.

“Oh, Mr. Poirot!” she cried. “How can I ever thank you?”

“It is nothing, madame, nothing. A little matter of the grey
cells, that is all.”

Later, when we were alone, I asked Poirot how he had first
suspected Célestine.

“It was the time, Hastings. The twelve seconds. It was too short
for the door-and-thread trick, but it was just right for the soap.
And then, she was so very anxious to have the chambermaid searched.
That is always a suspicious sign.”

“You are a wonderful man, Poirot,” I said.

“I am a very simple one, Hastings. But I have the eyes that see,
and the brain that thinks.”

He looked at his watch.

“And now, I think we might go and have some dinner. I am very
hungry.”

“Simply that she was not in the room more than three minutes.
I have timed her, monsieur. No one could have committed such a
robbery, and concealed the jewels in the room, in so short a
space of time. No, the chambermaid did not take the pearls.”

“If she didn’t, who did?”

“The other woman—Célestine.”

The inspector looked at him sharply. “You’re so sure of that?
If she’s not got them on her, where are they? It wouldn’t take
a minute to slip them into one of these drawers, or up a chimney,
or—well, in twenty other places.”

“But it would take a great deal more than a minute to find a
hiding-place where it would be impossible for _you_ to find them,
monsieur,” said Poirot, with a slight bow.

The inspector looked somewhat taken aback. Mr. Opalsen intervened.

“What do you mean, Mr. Poirot?”

“Just this: if the pearls are in this room, they are in a place
where no one would ever think of looking for them.”

The inspector laughed.

“I’ll find them, if they’re here, don’t you fear!”

He resumed his search with renewed energy. At the end of half an
hour, however, he was forced to admit defeat.

“They’re not here!”

“They must be!” cried Mrs. Opalsen. “Where else could they be?”

The inspector looked at Poirot.

“What was it you were saying just now?”

Poirot smiled.

“I said that if the pearls were in this room, they were in a place
where no one would ever think of looking for them. But as they are
_not_ in this room——”

“You think they’ve been taken out, after all?”

“I am sure of it.”

“But how? No one’s left the room but the two maids.”

“Exactly.”

“And you say the chambermaid didn’t do it?”

“I am sure of it.”

“Then it must have been Célestine.”

“If you will be so good as to come with me,” said Poirot, rising,
“I think I can show you how it was done.”

We followed him into the small room occupied by Célestine. It was
little more than a slip of a room, and very simply furnished.
A bed, a chest of drawers, and a chair. On the chest of drawers
stood a few toilet requisites and a large pincushion.

Poirot walked up to the latter.

“A very useful article, a pincushion,” he remarked.

The inspector looked at him.

“I don’t follow you.”

Poirot did not answer. He was busy examining the pincushion.
Suddenly he uttered an exclamation of satisfaction, and held it
up.

“Regard, messieurs!”

He pointed to a small hole in the side of the cushion.

“And see here!”

He drew out a long hat-pin, and inserted it into the hole.

“There is something here—something hard. Let us see.”

With a small pair of scissors he slit the silk of the cushion.
A moment later, he held up a string of shimmering, milky-white
pearls.

Mrs. Opalsen gave a cry of joy, and snatched them from him.

“My pearls! Oh, Mr. Poirot, how can I ever thank you?”

The inspector was looking at Poirot with a new respect.

“You’ve a head on you, sir, and no mistake! I should never have
thought of looking there. But how did she manage it? She must
have been pretty quick.”

“She was,” said Poirot. “I timed her, you remember? It took her
exactly two minutes to go into her room, hide the pearls, and
return. Quite long enough for anyone who had already prepared the
hiding-place. The hole was there ready, you see.”

“But she was searched!”

“The pearls were not on her then. She had already hidden them.”

“I see. Well, I’d better be getting along. I’ll have to report
this. I suppose you’ll be staying on here for a bit, Mr. Poirot?”

“For a few days, yes.”

“Well, if I want you, I’ll know where to find you. Good-night,
sir—and thank you.”

He hurried away, followed by the plain-clothes man. Mr. Opalsen was
profuse in his thanks.

“I don’t know how to thank you, Mr. Poirot. You’ve been a real
friend to us. If there’s anything I can do——”

“There is one thing, monsieur.”

“And that is?”

“I should like to have a few minutes’ talk with you—alone.”

“Certainly. Come into the sitting-room.”

He led the way into the adjoining room, and Poirot followed him,
motioning to me to stay behind.

I was a little disappointed, I must confess. I should have liked
to hear what Poirot had to say. However, I consoled myself with
the thought that I should hear all about it later.

In about ten minutes Poirot reappeared. He looked thoughtful.

“Well?” I asked, as we went downstairs. “What did you say to him?”

“I asked him a few questions, Hastings—that is all.”

“What sort of questions?”

“About his business—and other things.”

“And what did he say?”

“He was very communicative. He told me a great deal.”

“But what has that got to do with the pearls?”

“Perhaps nothing—and perhaps a great deal. We shall see.”

“You don’t think Célestine did it, after all?”

“I am sure she did not.”

“But you’ve just proved she did!”

“I have proved that the pearls were in her pincushion—that is all.”

“But who else could have put them there?”

“That is what we have to find out, Hastings.”

I stared at him in amazement.

“You mean—you don’t think she’s the thief?”

“I am certain of it.”

“Then why on earth did you let the inspector take her away?”

“Because, my friend, it was necessary. If the real thief is to
be caught, he must think himself safe. And what better way than
to have someone else arrested for the crime?”

“I see. But who is the real thief?”

“That, Hastings, is what I hope to find out before the night is
over.”

“You have a suspicion?”

“I have more than a suspicion—I have a certainty.”

“Who is it?”

“Wait, my friend—wait. All will be revealed in good time. For the
moment, let us go and have a little quiet talk with the manager.”

We found the manager in his office. He was a small, dapper man,
very much upset by the events of the evening.

“A most regrettable occurrence, Mr. Poirot! Most regrettable!
Nothing of the kind has ever happened at the _Grand Metropolitan_
before. I am sure I don’t know what to say to Mr. Opalsen.”

“Reassure yourself, monsieur,” said Poirot. “The pearls have been
recovered.”

“Recovered! You don’t say so! This is indeed good news! Where
were they?”

“In the maid’s pincushion.”

“The maid! I should never have thought it. She seemed such a
respectable girl.”

“She is a very respectable girl,” said Poirot. “That is why I am
so sure she did not steal the pearls.”

The manager looked puzzled.

“But if they were in her pincushion——”

“Exactly. If they were in her pincushion, someone must have put
them there. And that someone was not Célestine.”

“Then who was it?”

“That is what I want you to help me find out. You have a list of
all the guests in the hotel?”

“Certainly.” He handed a ledger to Poirot.

The latter turned the pages rapidly.

“Ah! Here we are. Mr. and Mrs. Opalsen—Room 28. And who is in
Room 27—the room on the other side of the maid’s?”

“A Mr. and Mrs. Vanderberg. They have been here for some weeks.”

“And in Room 29—on the other side of the bedroom?”

“The room is at present empty.”

“I see. And who was in it last?”

“A gentleman of the name of—let me see—ah, yes, Mr. Samuel Lowen.
He left this morning.”

“I see.” Poirot handed back the ledger. “Thank you, monsieur.
That is all I wanted to know.”

As we went out into the hall, I turned to Poirot.

“You think this Mr. Lowen had something to do with it?”

“It is possible, Hastings—it is possible. But for the moment, I am
more interested in Room 27.”

“The Vanderbergs?”

“Exactly. Let us go and see if they are in the lounge.”

We found the lounge crowded, but there was no sign of the
Vanderbergs.

“Perhaps they are in their room,” I suggested.

“We will go and see.”

We went upstairs again. As we reached the first floor, we saw a
man coming out of Room 27. He was a tall, dark man, with a
somewhat sinister expression.

“Mr. Vanderberg?” inquired Poirot, stepping forward.

The man started.

“Yes. What do you want?”

“I should like a few words with you, if I may.”

“I’m busy just now. Some other time——”

“I am afraid it must be now, monsieur.”

Vanderberg looked at him for a moment, then shrugged his shoulders.

“Oh, very well. Come in.”

He led the way into the room. It was a large, luxuriously
furnished apartment, similar to the one occupied by the Opalsens.

“Well?” he asked, as he closed the door. “What is it?”

“It is about the pearls of Mrs. Opalsen,” said Poirot quietly.

Vanderberg’s face changed.

“The pearls! What have I to do with them?”

“That is what I want you to tell me, monsieur.”

“Are you suggesting——”

“I am suggesting nothing—as yet. I am merely asking for
information.”

“I know nothing about the pearls—nothing at all. I heard they’d
been stolen, of course, but that’s all.”

“I see. And your wife—does she know nothing either?”

“My wife is not here. She went to London this afternoon.”

“Indeed? That is—unfortunate.”

“Why?”

“Because I should have liked to ask her a few questions.”

“What sort of questions?”

“About the door between her room and the maid’s.”

Vanderberg laughed.

“The door’s bolted—on both sides. I’ve tried it myself.”

“I know,” said Poirot. “I have tried it too. But bolts, monsieur,
can sometimes be drawn—from the other side.”

“What do you mean?”

“I mean that if one has a thin piece of wire, and a certain amount
of—er—dexterity, it is not difficult to draw a bolt from the other
side of a door.”

Vanderberg’s face went white.

“You—you are accusing me——”

“I am accusing no one—yet. I am merely stating a fact.”

“It’s a lie! I haven’t been near the room.”

“And yet, monsieur, there are certain—shall we say, traces?”

“Traces? What traces?”

“A few grains of powder—of a very particular kind. The kind used
by Mrs. Opalsen.”

Vanderberg laughed again, but his voice was a little shaky.

“That proves nothing. Mrs. Opalsen may have been in here.”

“She has not been in here, monsieur. I have her word for it.”

“Then the maid——”

“The maid has not been in here either.”

“Then how did the powder get there?”

“That, monsieur, is what I am asking you.”

Vanderberg did not answer. He was looking at Poirot with a
mixture of fear and defiance.

“I think, monsieur,” said Poirot, “that it would be better if you
told me the truth.”

Vanderberg hesitated for a moment, then he broke down.

“All right! I’ll tell you. I did take the pearls.”

“I thought so,” said Poirot quietly.

“But I didn’t do it for myself—I swear I didn’t! I’m in a
desperate state—financially, I mean. I owe money everywhere.
And then I saw the pearls—and I thought—well, I thought they’d
solve all my difficulties.”

“I see. And how did you do it?”

“It was easy enough. I’d seen the maid go into her room, and I
knew she always left the door between the two rooms unbolted on
her side. So I waited till she went into the bedroom to help Mrs.
Opalsen, and then I slipped in, took the pearls from the
jewel-case, and went back to my own room.”

“And the pincushion?”

“I put them there later—after the alarm had been raised. I thought
it was the safest place. No one would ever think of looking there.”

“I see. And what did you do with the powder?”

“The powder? Oh, I see. I must have spilt some when I was taking
the pearls. Mrs. Opalsen had been using it just before she went
down to dinner.”

“I see.” Poirot nodded. “Thank you, monsieur. You have been very
frank.”

“What are you going to do?” asked Vanderberg hoarsely.

“I am going to ask you to come with me to the manager’s office.”

“You’re going to give me up?”

“I have no choice, monsieur.”

Vanderberg bowed his head.

“I suppose not. Well, I’m ready.”

We went down to the manager’s office, and Poirot explained the
situation. The manager was horrified.

“Mr. Vanderberg! I should never have thought it! A guest of the
hotel too!”

“I am sorry, monsieur,” said Vanderberg. “I can only say that I
was desperate.”

“That is no excuse for theft, sir,” said the manager severely.
“I shall have to send for the police.”

“Wait!” said Poirot. “Before you do that, there is one thing I
should like to say.”

“What is it?”

“I should like to ask Mr. Vanderberg one more question.”

He turned to the unfortunate man.

“Mr. Vanderberg, you said just now that you took the pearls from
the jewel-case. Is that right?”

“Yes.”

“And they were in a string?”

“Yes.”

“And you put them in the pincushion?”

“Yes.”

“And you did not take anything else?”

“No.”

“I see. Thank you.” Poirot turned to the manager. “You can send
for the police now, monsieur.”

As we went out into the hall, I turned to Poirot.

“Well, you were right, after all. But I don’t understand about
the pincushion. How did you know the pearls were there?”

“I didn’t, Hastings. I only guessed.”

“Guessed? But you seemed so sure!”

“I was sure—of one thing.”

“And what was that?”

“That Célestine did not steal the pearls.”

“But why?”

“Because, my friend, she is a Frenchwoman. And no Frenchwoman
would ever hide pearls in a pincushion.”

“Why not?”

“Because it is too—how shall I say?—too simple. A Frenchwoman
would have hidden them in her hair, or in her shoe—or in a dozen
other places. But a pincushion—no!”

“I see. But then—who did put them there?”

“Mr. Vanderberg, as he has just confessed.”

“But you said just now that you were sure Célestine didn’t do it
because she was French. But Mr. Vanderberg is not French.”

“Exactly, Hastings—exactly! That is why he hid them in the
pincushion. It was the sort of thing an Englishman would do.”

“But he’s not an Englishman—he’s an American!”

“It is the same thing, Hastings—the same thing. They both have
the same—er—lack of imagination.”

I laughed.

“Well, you’ve certainly done it this time, Poirot. But what about
the powder? How did you know about that?”

“I didn’t, Hastings. I invented it.”

“Invented it!”

“Certainly. It was a—what you call—a bluff. And it worked, as
you saw.”

“But what if he hadn’t confessed?”

“Then I should have had to think of something else. But I was
fairly sure he would. He is not a professional criminal, you see.”

“I see. Well, it’s been a most interesting case.”

“It has, Hastings—it has. And now, let us go and have our dinner.
I feel that I have earned it.”

And so, once more, the little grey cells of Hercule Poirot had
triumphed. The mystery of the missing pearls was solved, and
justice had been done. Or had it? For even as we sat down to
dinner, I could not help wondering—was Mr. Vanderberg really the
thief? Or was there someone else—someone we had overlooked?
But Poirot only smiled, and tucked his napkin into his collar.

“Eat your soup, Hastings,” he said. “It is excellent.”

“I will demonstrate. Hastings, my good friend, take my watch in
your hand—with care. It is a family heirloom! Just now I timed
Mademoiselle’s movements—her first absence from the room was of
twelve seconds, her second of fifteen. Now observe my actions.
Madame will have the kindness to give me the key of the jewel-case.
I thank you. My friend Hastings will have the kindness to say
‘Go!’”

“Go!” I said.

Poirot crossed to the dressing-table, took out the jewel-case,
unlocked it, removed a small object, relocked it, and returned it
to the drawer.

“Now, my friend—how long?”

“Twenty-eight seconds.”

“And I have not hidden the object!” Poirot’s eyes were shining with
triumph. “What do you say to that, monsieur?”

“A very pretty little experiment,” admitted the inspector,
“and—granted—the maid could not have stolen the jewels _and_ hidden
them. But what’s to prevent her from having just _stolen_ them,
and having them on her all the time? A necklace like that doesn’t
take up much room.”

“_Pardon_,” said Poirot, “I think you forget that Mademoiselle has
already been searched by your woman searcher—and she found nothing.”

The inspector’s face fell.

“That’s true,” he admitted. “But then—who _did_ take them? If it
wasn’t the maid, and it wasn’t the chambermaid——”

He stopped, his eyes fixed on Mr. Opalsen.

“I hope you’re not suggesting _I_ took my wife’s pearls?” said the
latter, with a short, uneasy laugh.

“No, no, sir! But you were in the room, weren’t you, while your
wife was dressing?”

“I was. But I left it before she did. I went down to the lounge
to wait for her.”

“And you, madam?”

“I? I was only here for a few minutes. I came up, as I said, to
get my pearls, and found they were gone.”

“Yes, yes. But _before_ dinner?”

“Oh, I was here then, of course. Célestine was with me all the
time.”

The inspector looked more and more puzzled.

“It seems a very difficult case,” he said. “If the maid didn’t
take them, and the chambermaid didn’t take them, and—er—nobody
else was in the room——”

He broke off, his eyes wandering round the room once more.

“There’s that door,” he said, pointing to the one by the window.
“You say it’s bolted on both sides?”

“I will show you,” said Poirot.

He led the way to the door, and drew back the bolt.

“Now, monsieur.”

The inspector turned the handle. The door remained fast.

“You see?” said Poirot.

The inspector nodded.

“Yes, it’s bolted on the other side all right. Who’s in the next
room?”

“A Mr. and Mrs. Saunders, I believe,” said Mr. Opalsen. “I don’t
know them, but the manager told me they’d been here for some time.”

The inspector looked thoughtful.

“I’d like to have a word with them,” he said. “If you’ll excuse me,
sir.”

He left the room, followed by the plain-clothes man. Mr. Opalsen
sank into a chair.

“Well,” he said, “this is a nice business! My wife’s pearls gone,
and the police don’t seem to have a clue.”

“Don’t say that, Ed!” cried Mrs. Opalsen. “Mr. Poirot will find
them for us—I know he will.”

Poirot bowed.

“I will do my best, madame. But I must have time—time to think.”

He sat down and closed his eyes. For some minutes no one spoke.
Then he opened them and turned to Mr. Opalsen.

“Tell me, monsieur—this Mr. Saunders—what is he like?”

“Oh, a quiet, middle-aged sort of man. I’ve only seen him once or
twice in the lift.”

“And his wife?”

“I’ve never seen her. She’s an invalid, I believe—never leaves her
room.”

“I see.” Poirot relapsed into silence again.

Presently the inspector returned. His face was gloomy.

“Nothing there,” he said. “The door’s bolted on this side, too,
and Mr. Saunders was in the room all the evening with his wife.
They didn’t hear anything, and they didn’t see anything.”

“_Tiens_!” murmured Poirot. “That is very interesting.”

“What do you mean?” asked the inspector.

“I was thinking,” said Poirot, “of the chambermaid.”

“But you said just now——”

“I said it was impossible for her to have hidden the jewels in the
time at her disposal. I did not say it was impossible for her to
have _taken_ them.”

“But she was searched!”

“Precisely. And nothing was found. Therefore, if she took them,
she must have disposed of them at once. But how? She did not leave
the room.”

“The window?” suggested the inspector.

“I have already told you there is no balcony.”

“Then—how?”

Poirot smiled.

“That is what we have to find out.”

He turned to Mrs. Opalsen.

“Madame, would you have the kindness to show me your jewel-case
once more?”

Mrs. Opalsen handed it to him. It was a small, leather-covered box,
with a good lock. Poirot examined it carefully.

“_Un moment_,” he said.

He took a small magnifying-glass from his pocket and studied the
lock. Then he handed the case back to Mrs. Opalsen.

“Thank you, madame. And now—the key.”

He examined the key in the same way.

“Nothing there,” he murmured. “A very ordinary key.”

He stood for a moment, lost in thought. Then he turned to the
inspector.

“Monsieur, I have an idea. It is, perhaps, a little fantastic,
but—one never knows. Would it be possible for me to see the room
next door—the one occupied by Mr. and Mrs. Saunders?”

“I don’t see why not,” said the inspector. “But as I’ve already
told you, the door is bolted on this side.”

“I know, I know. But if I might just see the room for a moment.”

The inspector shrugged his shoulders.

“Well, if you like. But I don’t see what you expect to find there.”

He led the way out of the room and along the corridor. He knocked
at the door of the next suite, and it was opened by a small,
anxious-looking man.

“Oh, it’s you again, inspector,” he said. “Is there anything more
I can do for you?”

“This gentleman would like to see your room for a moment, Mr.
Saunders—if you’ve no objection.”

“None at all—none at all. Come in, gentlemen.”

The room was similar in size and arrangement to the one we had just
left. A lady was lying on a sofa by the window, her face turned
away from us.

“My wife is a great sufferer, as I told you,” said Mr. Saunders
apologetically.

Poirot walked across the room to the door communicating with the
Opalsens’ suite. He examined the bolt, then turned the handle.
The door remained fast.

“You see?” said Mr. Saunders. “It’s bolted on your side.”

“Yes, yes,” said Poirot. “I see.”

He walked over to the window and looked out. Then he turned back to
the room. His eyes fell on a small table by the sofa, on which
stood a glass of water and a bottle of medicine.

“Your wife is not well, monsieur?” he said, with an air of
sympathy.

“No, she has been a great invalid for many years. It is a sad
trial to us both.”

“I am sure of it,” said Poirot. “Well, monsieur, I will not
disturb you any longer. I thank you for your kindness.”

We returned to the Opalsens’ room. The inspector looked at Poirot
with a touch of sarcasm.

“Well,” he said, “did you find what you were looking for?”

“I found,” said Poirot, “what I expected to find.”

“And what was that?”

“Nothing,” said Poirot.

The inspector laughed.

“I thought as much! Well, Mr. Opalsen, I’m afraid I must be going.
I’ll let you know if anything turns up, but I’m bound to tell you
it doesn’t look very promising.”

He left the room, followed by the plain-clothes man. Mr. Opalsen
turned to Poirot.

“Well, Mr. Poirot, what do you think? Is there any hope?”

“There is always hope, monsieur. But I must ask you to leave me
now. I wish to think.”

“Of course, of course. Come along, Ed. We’ll go down to the lounge.”

Mrs. Opalsen followed her husband out of the room. I was about to
follow them when Poirot called me back.

“Hastings, stay with me a moment. I have need of you.”

I turned back. Poirot was standing in the middle of the room, his
eyes fixed on the dressing-table.

“Hastings,” he said, “what do you think of it all?”

“I don’t know what to think,” I confessed. “It seems a most
extraordinary case. If the maid didn’t take the pearls, and the
chambermaid didn’t take them——”

“But one of them _must_ have taken them!”

“But they were both searched!”

“Precisely. And nothing was found. Therefore, the pearls were not
on them. But they were in the room—they must have been in the
room—until the alarm was given. And then—what happened to them?”

“I don’t know,” I said. “Unless——”

“Unless what?”

“Unless they were thrown out of the window!”

“I have already told you there is no balcony. And the pearls were
not found on the ground below.”

“Then—I give it up!”

Poirot smiled.

“Do not despair, my friend. All will yet be revealed. But for the
moment, I have a little task for you.”

“What is it?”

“I want you to go down to the office and find out all you can about
Mr. and Mrs. Saunders. How long they have been here, where they
came from—everything you can discover.”

“But the inspector has already——”

“Never mind the inspector! I wish to know for myself. Go, my
friend, and return as soon as you have the information.”

I went. It was not difficult to find out what I wanted. Mr. and
Mrs. Saunders had been at the hotel for about a fortnight. They
had come from London, but beyond that the manager knew nothing.
Mr. Saunders was a very quiet, unassuming man, and his wife, as
he had said, was a great invalid. They rarely went out, and spent
most of their time in their own rooms.

I returned to Poirot and gave him the information I had obtained.
He listened in silence, then nodded his head.

“It is as I thought,” he said.

“What do you mean?”

“Nothing—nothing. And now, Hastings, we will go down to the lounge
and join the Opalsens. I think we have done all we can here for the
present.”

We found the Opalsens in the lounge, looking very depressed. Poirot
did his best to cheer them up, but with little success. Mrs.
Opalsen was still in tears, and her husband was in a state of
smouldering indignation.

“It’s a disgrace!” he said. “A hotel like this, and people’s
property isn’t safe! I shall certainly report the matter to the
management.”

“I have already done so, monsieur,” said Poirot. “And I have also
taken the liberty of asking the manager to have a search made of
the hotel.”

“A search? What’s the use of that?”

“One never knows, monsieur. The pearls may have been hidden in some
unlikely place.”

“Well, I hope you’re right, but I don’t believe it myself.”

The evening wore on, but no news came of the missing pearls. At
last we all retired to bed, Poirot promising to see us again in
the morning.

When I went to his room the next morning, I found him already up and
dressed. He was sitting at the table, with a number of small
objects spread out before him.

“Ah, Hastings!” he said. “You are just in time. I have been
conducting a little investigation on my own account.”

“And what have you found?”

“Several things. For one, this.”

He held up a small, dark object.

“What is it?”

“It is a piece of coal, my friend.”

“Coal?” I stared at him. “What on earth has that got to do with
the case?”

“That is what we have to find out. I found it on the floor of the
Opalsens’ bedroom, near the fire-place.”

“But there was a fire in the room, wasn’t there?”

“There was. But this piece of coal was not in the fire-place. It
was on the floor, some distance away.”

“Well, what of it? It might have fallen out of the scuttle.”

“Perhaps. But it is a very small piece of coal—very small indeed.
And there is something else.”

He held up another object—a small, bright piece of metal.

“What’s that?”

“It is a piece of a watch-spring, Hastings.”

“A watch-spring? But what——”

“Wait, my friend. I have not yet finished. There is also this.”

He produced a small, white object.

“A piece of cotton-wool?”

“Exactly. And finally, there is this.”

He held up a small, glass bottle.

“Medicine?”

“No, Hastings. It is not medicine. It is oil—fine, lubricating
oil.”

I stared at him in bewilderment.

“But what does it all mean, Poirot?”

“It means, my friend, that we are on the track of a very clever
criminal. A very clever criminal indeed!”

“But who is it?”

“Ah, that is what we have to find out. But I think I have a clue.
Come, Hastings, we will go and see the manager.”

We found the manager in his office. He looked very worried.

“Any news of the pearls, Mr. Poirot?” he asked.

“Not yet, monsieur. But I have a request to make. I should like to
see the chambermaid again—the one who was in the room when the
pearls were stolen.”

“Certainly, if you wish. I’ll send for her at once.”

A few minutes later the chambermaid appeared. She looked nervous
and uneasy.

“You wished to see me, sir?”

“Yes, my girl. I have a few questions to ask you. When you were in
the Opalsens’ room yesterday evening, did you notice anything
unusual?”

“No, sir. Nothing at all.”

“You did not see anyone else in the room?”

“No, sir. Only the French maid, as I told the inspector.”

“And you didn’t notice anything on the floor?”

“On the floor, sir? No, I don’t think so.”

“Not a piece of coal, for instance?”

The girl’s face changed. She looked startled.

“Coal, sir? Well, I do remember seeing a small piece of coal on the
carpet, near the dressing-table. I picked it up and put it in the
scuttle.”

“I see. And did you notice anything else?”

“No, sir. Nothing else.”

“Thank you, that will do.”

The girl left the room. Poirot turned to the manager.

“And now, monsieur, I have another request. I should like to see
the room next door again—the one occupied by Mr. and Mrs. Saunders.”

“But the inspector has already searched it!”

“I know, I know. But I should like to see it for myself.”

The manager sighed.

“Very well, Mr. Poirot. I’ll come with you.”

We went up to the first floor and knocked at the door of the Saunders’
suite. It was opened, as before, by Mr. Saunders.

“Oh, it’s you again!” he said, looking surprised. “Is there anything
the matter?”

“I should like to have another look at your room, monsieur—if you
have no objection.”

“None at all—none at all. But I’m afraid you won’t find anything.”

We entered the room. Mrs. Saunders was still lying on the sofa, her
face turned away from us. Poirot walked across to the communicating
door and examined the bolt. Then he turned back to the room.

“Mr. Saunders,” he said, “I see you have a small clock on the
mantelpiece. Is it in working order?”

“Yes, I believe so. Why do you ask?”

“I was just wondering. It seems to have stopped.”

Mr. Saunders walked across to the mantelpiece.

“So it has! I hadn’t noticed it. It must have run down.”

“Or perhaps,” said Poirot, “someone has been meddling with it.”

“Meddling with it? What do you mean?”

“I mean, monsieur, that someone has taken the works out of it!”

He stepped forward and opened the back of the clock. It was empty.

“What’s the meaning of this?” cried Mr. Saunders. “Who has done
this?”

“I think,” said Poirot, “that I can tell you.”

He turned to the sofa.

“Madame,” he said, “would you have the kindness to stand up?”

The woman on the sofa did not move.

“Madame!” said Poirot again, his voice rising.

Still there was no answer. Poirot walked across to the sofa and
touched the woman’s shoulder. She rolled over onto the floor.

It was a large, stuffed doll!

“A doll!” I cried. “But where is Mrs. Saunders?”

“There is no Mrs. Saunders,” said Poirot. “There never was a Mrs.
Saunders.”

He turned to Mr. Saunders, who was cowering in a corner.

“And now, monsieur, perhaps you will tell us where the pearls are?”

“I don’t know what you’re talking about!” cried the man. “I haven’t
got any pearls!”

“We shall see,” said Poirot.

He walked over to the dressing-table and began to search the
drawers. In the bottom drawer he found a small, leather-covered box.
He opened it. It was full of jewellery.

“But these are not the pearls!” I said.

“No, Hastings. These are the jewels that were stolen from the hotel
in London last week. The pearls are here.”

He reached into the back of the drawer and pulled out a small, silk
bag. He opened it, and a string of magnificent pearls fell out onto
the table.

“The pearls!” cried the manager. “But how did they get there?”

“It was very simple,” said Poirot. “Mr. Saunders—or whatever his
real name is—is a very clever thief. He and his accomplice, the
chambermaid, had it all planned out. She was to steal the pearls
while the French maid was out of the room, and then pass them to
him through the communicating door.”

“But the door was bolted on both sides!” I objected.

“So it appeared,” said Poirot. “But in reality, the bolts had been
tampered with. Mr. Saunders had removed the works from the clock
and used the spring to make a clever little device that allowed
him to draw back the bolt on the other side of the door. The
piece of coal I found was used to wedge the door open so that the
chambermaid could pass the pearls through. The oil was to make
the bolt slide silently, and the cotton-wool was to deaden the
sound.”

“And the doll?”

“The doll was to take the place of the imaginary Mrs. Saunders.
It was a very clever idea—but it did not deceive Hercule Poirot!”

Mr. Saunders was led away by the police, and the chambermaid was
also arrested. The pearls were restored to Mrs. Opalsen, who was
overjoyed.

“Oh, Mr. Poirot!” she cried. “I don’t know how to thank you! You
are wonderful—simply wonderful!”

Poirot bowed.

“It was nothing, madame. A mere matter of the little grey cells.”

“But how did you know?” I asked, as we were walking back to our
own room.

“It was the piece of coal, Hastings. It was out of place—and in
the world of Hercule Poirot, everything must be in its place. And
then there was the clock—a clock that does not go is always
suspicious. But the most important thing of all was the chambermaid.”

“The chambermaid?”

“Yes, Hastings. She was too anxious to be searched. An honest girl
would have been indignant—but she was too eager. It was a sure sign
of guilt.”

“I see,” I said. “Well, Poirot, I must say you’ve done it again.”

“Yes, Hastings. I have done it again. And now, I think we will
have a little dinner—a very good dinner—to celebrate our success.”

Poirot crossed to the drawer, took out the jewel-case, unlocked
it, and returned with the imaginary booty.

“Thirty-five seconds,” I announced.

“_Voilà_,” said Poirot with a flourish. “And that, mind you, with
the knowledge of where the pearls were. The thief, whoever he was,
must have had a search for them.”

The inspector’s face had fallen several inches.

“I’m afraid I’ll have to ask you to allow me to search the lady
herself,” he began.

“I have no objection,” said Mrs. Opalsen, with much more
readiness than I should have expected. “But I assure you it’s no
use.”

The inspector, however, proceeded with his task. He searched
thoroughly, but without result. Mrs. Opalsen’s massive form was
unencumbered by anything so substantial as a pearl necklace.

The inspector’s face grew more and more puzzled.

“But if she didn’t do it—who did?” he asked at last.

Poirot turned his gaze slowly upon Mr. Opalsen. The latter started,
and his face went several shades paler.

“You—you don’t suspect _me_?” he stammered.

“Monsieur,” said Poirot softly, “I suspect everyone—until I am
convinced of their innocence.”

“But—but I was downstairs all the time.”

“You say so,” said Poirot. “But who is to prove it?”

“Hastings here—he can prove it.”

“I’m afraid I can’t,” I said. “You left us, you remember, when
the page-boy brought you that message.”

“Exactly!” said Poirot. “And where did you go?”

“To—to see the manager. He wanted to speak to me.”

“Did he?” Poirot’s eyes were like two green lights. “We shall
see.”

He went to the door and spoke to a passing waiter. A few minutes
later the manager appeared.

“You sent for me, Mr. Opalsen?”

“No,” said Poirot, “I did. Will you have the kindness to tell us
what you wanted to see Mr. Opalsen about a little while ago?”

The manager looked surprised.

“I didn’t want to see Mr. Opalsen. I haven’t seen him since
this afternoon.”

Mr. Opalsen’s face was now a ghastly grey.

“But—but the page-boy said——”

“We will have the page-boy,” said Poirot.

The boy was sent for. He appeared, looking very much frightened.

“Did you take a message to Mr. Opalsen a little while ago?” asked
the inspector.

“Yes, sir.”

“Who gave it to you?”

“A gentleman, sir. At least, I think it was a gentleman. He was
sitting in the lounge, and he called me over and gave me a
shilling to take the message to Mr. Opalsen.”

“What was the message?”

“‘Mr. Opalsen’s compliments, and would he step upstairs,’ sir.”

“You’re sure of that?”

“Yes, sir.”

“And you don’t know who the gentleman was?”

“No, sir.”

The inspector looked at Poirot.

“This is very extraordinary,” he said.

“On the contrary,” said Poirot, “it is very simple. The thief
wanted Mr. Opalsen out of the way for a few minutes, that’s all.”

“But why?”

“Because he knew that if Mr. Opalsen were there, he wouldn’t be
able to get into the room.”

“But the door was locked!”

“Was it?” Poirot’s eyes sought the inspector’s.

“The lady said she locked it when she went down to dinner.”

“No,” said Poirot, “she said she locked the _jewel-case_—not the
door.”

“But even if the door were unlocked, anyone coming in would have
been seen by the maid.”

“Unless,” said Poirot, “it was someone the maid _expected_ to see.”

“What do you mean?”

“I mean,” said Poirot, “that there is only one person who could
have entered that room without the maid’s being surprised—and
that is Mr. Opalsen himself.”

“But I tell you I didn’t!” cried the unfortunate man.

“Then who did?” asked the inspector.

“I—I don’t know.”

“Perhaps,” suggested Poirot, “the chambermaid could tell us.”

The chambermaid was recalled. She looked more frightened than ever.

“Now then,” said the inspector, “did you see anyone enter this
room while you were here this evening?”

“No, sir—nobody at all.”

“You’re sure of that?”

“Yes, sir.”

“Did you leave the room at all?”

“Only for a minute, sir, to get some fresh towels.”

“And you didn’t see anyone then?”

“No, sir.”

The inspector turned to Poirot.

“It seems we’re just where we were,” he said.

“Not quite,” said Poirot. “We have at least eliminated several
possibilities. For instance, we know that the thief must have had
a duplicate key to the jewel-case.”

“Yes, that’s certain.”

“And we also know that he must have been someone who knew where
the jewel-case was kept.”

“Yes.”

“And lastly, we know that he must have been someone who could
enter the room without being seen.”

“But we don’t know who that is!”

“Oh, yes, we do,” said Poirot. “There is only one person who
fulfils all those conditions.”

“Who?”

“The person,” said Poirot, “who has the duplicate key.”

“But we don’t know who that is either!”

“Don’t we?” Poirot’s eyes were fixed on Mr. Opalsen’s face. “I
think we do.”

“You—you mean _me_?” gasped the stockbroker.

“I mean,” said Poirot, “the person who gave that message to the
page-boy.”

“But I didn’t give it!”

“Then who did?”

“I—I don’t know.”

“Perhaps,” said Poirot, “the person who gave it is the person
who has the pearls.”

“But who is it? Who is it?”

“That,” said Poirot, “is what we have to find out.”

He turned to the inspector.

“I think,” he said, “that if you were to search Mr. Opalsen’s
pockets, you might find something of interest.”

“Mr. Opalsen’s pockets!” The inspector stared.

“If you please,” said Poirot.

Mr. Opalsen made a movement as if to escape, but the inspector’s
hand was on his shoulder.

“Now then, sir,” he said, “if you’ve no objection.”

Mr. Opalsen’s face was now a greenish white. He submitted to the
search in silence.

The inspector’s hand went into one pocket after another. At last,
from the pocket of his evening coat, he drew out a small, blue
velvet case.

He opened it. Inside, coiled up like a snake, was a magnificent
string of pearls.

“My pearls!” shrieked Mrs. Opalsen.

There was a moment of dead silence. Then Mr. Opalsen burst into
tears.

“I did it!” he sobbed. “I did it! I was desperate—I had to have
the money. Things have been going wrong lately—I thought I could
pawn them and then buy them back again when things improved. I
didn’t think she’d miss them so soon.”

“So that was it!” said the inspector. “Well, I’m afraid you’ll
have to come along with me, sir.”

“One moment,” said Poirot.

He had been looking at the pearls with a very curious expression.

“These are the pearls, madame?” he asked, turning to Mrs. Opalsen.

“Yes, yes—of course they are! Oh, Ed, how could you? How could you?”

“Are you quite sure?” asked Poirot.

“Of course I’m sure! Do you think I don’t know my own pearls?”

“And yet,” said Poirot, “it is very strange.”

“What is strange?” asked the inspector.

“That they should be so light,” said Poirot.

He held the necklace out on his hand.

“See,” he said. “They weigh almost nothing.”

“What do you mean?” asked the inspector.

“I mean,” said Poirot, “that these are not the real pearls. They
are only a very clever imitation.”

“An imitation!” Mrs. Opalsen’s voice rose to a shriek. “An
imitation! But they can’t be! They were worth twenty thousand
pounds!”

“They _were_,” said Poirot. “But these are worth—perhaps ten
shillings.”

“But—but how could they have been changed?” asked the inspector.

“That,” said Poirot, “is what we have to find out.”

He turned to Mr. Opalsen, who was staring at the necklace in a
sort of daze.

“Did you know they were imitations?” he asked.

“No—no! I thought they were the real ones. I—I never thought of
anything else.”

“Then,” said Poirot, “it seems that someone else had the same
idea as you—and got there first.”

“But who? Who could it be?”

“That,” said Poirot, “is what we are going to find out.”

He turned to the manager, who was still standing by the door.

“Will you have the goodness,” he said, “to send the chambermaid
here again?”

The chambermaid was brought back. She looked more terrified than
ever.

“Now then,” said Poirot, “tell me—where did you get those
towels?”

“The towels, sir?” The girl stared.

“Yes, the fresh towels you went to get. Where did you get them
from?”

“From the linen cupboard, sir.”

“And where is the linen cupboard?”

“At the end of the corridor, sir.”

“I see. And did you see anyone as you were going there?”

“No, sir.”

“And as you were coming back?”

“No, sir—only the gentleman.”

“What gentleman?”

“The gentleman who was coming out of this room, sir.”

“Coming out of this room! Who was he?”

“I don’t know, sir. I’d never seen him before.”

“What did he look like?”

“He was a tall gentleman, sir, with a dark moustache.”

“A tall gentleman with a dark moustache,” repeated Poirot. “And
what did he do?”

“He just walked past me, sir, and went down the stairs.”

“I see. And did you notice anything else about him?”

“No, sir—except that he was carrying a small black bag.”

“A small black bag,” said Poirot. “Thank you. That will do.”

The chambermaid went out. Poirot turned to the inspector.

“You see?” he said. “The tall gentleman with the dark moustache.
He is the man we want.”

“But who is he?” asked the inspector.

“That,” said Poirot, “is what we have to find out.”

He turned to the manager.

“Have you any guests in the hotel who answer to that
description?”

“No,” said the manager, “none at all.”

“I see. Then he must have been someone from outside.”

“But how could he have got into the room?”

“The door was unlocked,” said Poirot.

“But the maid was there!”
