“She went into her own room twice,” Poirot reminded him. “Once for
a reel of cotton, and once for her scissors. That would have given
him plenty of time.”

“But he’d have to have a duplicate key!”

“Precisely,” said Poirot. “And that is where our friend Mr.
Opalsen comes in.”

“Me?” gasped the stockbroker.

“Yes,” said Poirot. “You had a duplicate key made, did you not?”

“Yes—yes, I did.”

“And where did you have it made?”

“At a shop in the City—a little place in a side-street.”

“I see. And did you give your name and address?”

“No—I just paid for it and took it away.”

“And did you notice the man who served you?”

“No—not particularly.”

“I see. Well, I think we may assume that the man who served you
is our friend with the dark moustache.”

“But how did he know about the pearls?”

“He probably saw you in the shop,” said Poirot. “And he probably
followed you here. It would be easy enough for him to find out
which room you were in, and to watch for his opportunity.”

“But the imitations!” said the inspector. “Where did they come
from?”

“He probably had them ready,” said Poirot. “He would know that
it would be much safer to leave something in the jewel-case, so
that the robbery wouldn’t be discovered at once. He couldn’t know,
of course, that Mr. Opalsen would be so obliging as to steal the
imitations himself!”

“It’s incredible!” said the inspector. “Absolutely incredible!”

“On the contrary,” said Poirot, “it is very simple. It is only
the little grey cells that are needed.”

He turned to Mrs. Opalsen, who was still weeping.

“Do not distress yourself, madame,” he said. “We shall find your
pearls—I, Hercule Poirot, promise it!”

And with a magnificent gesture, he led the way out of the room.

Poirot went to the dressing-table, opened the drawer, took out the
jewel-case, unlocked it, and returned it to its place.

“How long, Hastings?”

“Twenty-eight seconds.”

“And to take the pearls out and lock the case again?”

“Nearly forty.”

“Exactly. So you see, monsieur l’inspecteur, even if she had them
ready to her hand, she had not the time to perform the operation.
And to have them ready to her hand, she must have had a duplicate
key. No, believe me, it was not the maid.”

The inspector looked at him doubtfully.

“Then who was it?”

“Ah!” said Poirot, with a dramatic gesture. “That is the question!”

The inspector shrugged his shoulders.

“Well, at any rate, I’m going to have a good look round before I
give up. It’s my belief they’re in the room still.”

“That is possible,” said Poirot, “but I do not think so.”

He walked to the window.

“The window is also bolted. I think we must look elsewhere.”

He turned to Mr. Opalsen.

“You have another room, monsieur?”

“Yes, our sitting-room. It’s just across the passage.”

“May I see it?”

“By all means.”

Mr. Opalsen led the way, and Poirot and I followed.

The sitting-room was a large and comfortably furnished apartment.
Poirot walked to the window and looked out.

“The same view as from the bedroom,” he remarked. “And no balcony.
Well, that is that.”

He turned and looked round the room. On a side-table was a large
tray with some glasses and a syphon of soda-water.

“You have been having some refreshment, monsieur?”

“Only a syphon of soda-water. I’m a teetotaller myself.”

Poirot’s eyes wandered to the mantelpiece, where a large French
clock stood between two bronze figures. He walked across to it and
examined it closely.

“A fine clock,” he remarked. “But it does not go.”

“It hasn’t gone since we’ve been here,” said Mr. Opalsen.

Poirot took out his watch and compared it with the clock.

“Ten minutes past ten,” he murmured. “And my watch says half-past.
A difference of twenty minutes. A large difference, monsieur!”

“I daresay,” said Mr. Opalsen indifferently. “But what has that
to do with the pearls?”

“Perhaps nothing,” said Poirot. “But in these cases one must
neglect nothing. One must have a system—a method! To me, the
slightest detail——”

He was interrupted by the entrance of the inspector.

“Nothing,” he said shortly. “I’ve been over every inch of the
room. The pearls aren’t there.”

“Then,” said Poirot, “I think we may say they are no longer in
the hotel.”

“But how did they get out?”

“That,” said Poirot, “is what I am going to find out.”

He turned to Mr. Opalsen.

“You will permit me to have a few words with the chambermaid?”

“Certainly. I’ll send for her.”

The chambermaid appeared, looking somewhat flustered.

“You want me, sir?”

“Yes, my girl. I want you to tell me exactly what you did when
you came into the room this evening.”

“Well, sir, I came in as usual to turn down the beds. The French
mademoiselle was there, as she always is. I didn’t take no more
than three or four minutes, and then I went out.”

“Did you notice anything unusual?”

“No, sir. Everything was just as usual.”

“You didn’t see the jewel-case?”

“No, sir. I didn’t look in the drawer.”

“And you’re sure you didn’t see anyone else in the passage?”

“No, sir.”

“Thank you. That will do.”

The girl retired. Poirot stood for a moment in thought. Then he
turned to the inspector.

“I should like to see the room next door,” he said. “The one with
the communicating door.”

“It’s vacant at present,” said the inspector. “The people who had
it left this morning.”

He led the way to the door and opened it with a master-key. The
room was a small one, and was at present unoccupied.

Poirot walked across to the communicating door and examined it.

“Bolted on this side too,” he remarked.

He turned and looked round the room. His eyes fell on a small
table by the bed. On it was a glass of water.

He walked across to it and picked up the glass.

“A glass of water,” he murmured. “And someone has been drinking
out of it.”

He looked at the inspector.

“You say this room has been vacant since this morning?”

“Yes.”

“Then who has been drinking out of this glass?”

The inspector shrugged his shoulders.

“One of the servants, I suppose.”

“Perhaps,” said Poirot.

He set down the glass and walked to the window.

“Again no balcony,” he remarked.

He stood for a moment looking out, then turned and walked back into
the Opalsens’ bedroom.

“Well,” said the inspector, “I don’t see that we’re any further.”

“On the contrary,” said Poirot, “we are a great deal further.”

“You think so?”

“I am sure of it.”

“Then you know who took the pearls?”

“I have a very good idea,” said Poirot.

He turned to Mr. Opalsen.

“Monsieur, I should like to have a few words with your wife—alone.”

“Certainly,” said Mr. Opalsen. “I’ll go and see how she is.”

He left the room, and a few minutes later Mrs. Opalsen entered.
She had recovered somewhat from her hysterics, but her eyes were
still red with weeping.

“You wanted to see me, Mr. Poirot?”

“Yes, madame. I want you to tell me if you have any enemies.”

“Enemies? Why, no, I don’t think so.”

“No one who might wish to do you a bad turn?”

“No, I’m sure there isn’t. Everyone’s always been very kind to
me.”

“And your maid—Célestine? You have confidence in her?”

“The greatest confidence. She’s been with me for five years, and
I’ve always found her perfectly honest.”

“I see. And the chambermaid? You know nothing of her?”

“Nothing but what I’ve seen of her here. She seemed a very nice,
respectable girl.”

“I see,” said Poirot again.

He stood for a moment in thought, then he turned to me.

“Hastings, I think we will go for a little stroll.”

“A stroll?” I said in surprise. “But what about the pearls?”

“The pearls,” said Poirot, “will keep. At present, I want to
think.”

I followed him out of the room and down the stairs. In the hall,
he stopped and spoke to the hall-porter.

“Can you tell me,” he asked, “if anyone has left the hotel this
evening?”

“Only one gentleman, sir. A Mr. Raymond. He left about half an
hour ago.”

“Mr. Raymond. I see. And did he take much luggage with him?”

“Only a small suit-case, sir.”

“Thank you,” said Poirot.

He turned to me.

“You see, Hastings? The plot thickens.”

“You think this Mr. Raymond had something to do with it?”

“It is possible. But we must not jump to conclusions. First, we
must have the facts.”

We walked out of the hotel and along the front. The night was fine,
and the sea was calm. Poirot walked in silence for some time, his
head bent in thought.

“Hastings,” he said at last, “what do you make of it?”

“Well,” I said, “it seems to me that the maid must have done it,
in spite of what you say about the time. She’s the only one who
could have had a duplicate key, and she was in the room all the
time.”

“But the time, Hastings! The time!”

“She might have had it all ready,” I suggested.

“No, no! I have demonstrated that it was impossible. Besides, why
should she hide them in the room? She would know that the police
would search it.”

“Then who could it have been?”

“That is what we have to find out. But I think I have a clue.”

“A clue?”

“Yes. Do you remember the glass of water in the next room?”

“The glass of water? What has that to do with it?”

“Everything, my friend. Everything!”

He refused to say any more, and we walked back to the hotel in
silence.

The next morning, Poirot was up early. When I came down to breakfast,
he was already there, looking very pleased with himself.

“Well,” I said, “any news?”

“I have been busy, Hastings. Very busy.”

“What have you been doing?”

“I have been making inquiries. And I have found out something
very interesting.”

“What is it?”

“Mr. Raymond, who left the hotel last night, was not Mr. Raymond
at all.”

“Then who was he?”

“He was a well-known jewel-thief, known to the police as ‘Gentleman
Jim’.”

“Then he did it!” I exclaimed.

“It would seem so. But there is one thing that I do not
understand.”

“What is that?”

“How did he get into the room? The door was locked, and the
communicating door was bolted on both sides.”

“He might have had a skeleton key.”

“Even so, he could not have drawn the bolt on the other side of
the door.”

“Then how did he do it?”

“That is what I am going to find out,” said Poirot.

He rose from the table.

“And now, Hastings, we will go and see Mr. Opalsen.”

We found Mr. Opalsen in the sitting-room. He looked tired and
worried.

“Any news, Mr. Poirot?” he asked.

“I have some news, monsieur. I have found out who took the pearls.”

“You have? Who was it?”

“It was the man who called himself Mr. Raymond.”

“The man who left last night?”

“Exactly. He is a well-known jewel-thief.”

“But how did he get them? He wasn’t in the room.”

“He was in the room next door,” said Poirot.

“But the door was bolted!”

“Exactly,” said Poirot. “It was bolted. But—it was not bolted
on the other side!”

“What do you mean?”

“I mean, monsieur, that someone had unbolted it.”

“But who could have done that?”

“Someone who had access to the room.”

“You mean—the maid?”

“No,” said Poirot, “I do not mean the maid.”

“Then who?”

“I mean,” said Poirot, “the person who had the best opportunity
of all. The person who could go in and out of the room as they
pleased.”

“You don’t mean—my wife?”

“No,” said Poirot, “I do not mean your wife.”

“Then who do you mean?”

“I mean,” said Poirot, “you, monsieur!”

“Me?” Mr. Opalsen stared at him in amazement. “You must be mad!”

“I am not mad, monsieur. I am very much in my senses. It was you
who took the pearls.”

“But why should I take my own wife’s pearls?”

“Because, monsieur, you needed the money. You told us yourself
that money was ‘confoundedly tight in the City’. You needed a
large sum of money, and you saw a way to get it. You took the
pearls and gave them to your accomplice, ‘Gentleman Jim’, who
was waiting in the next room. He had already unbolted the door
on his side, and you unbolted it on yours. You handed him the
pearls, and he left the hotel with them.”

“But the jewel-case was locked!”

“You had a duplicate key, monsieur. It was easy for you to have
one made. And you chose a time when the maid was in the next
room, so that the suspicion would fall on her.”

Mr. Opalsen sank into a chair, his face pale.

“It’s a lie!” he gasped. “A wicked lie!”

“It is the truth, monsieur. And I can prove it.”

“How?”

“By the glass of water,” said Poirot. “You see, monsieur, I noticed
that someone had been drinking out of it. And on the glass were
your fingerprints!”

Mr. Opalsen stared at him for a moment, then his head fell forward
into his hands.

“It’s true,” he groaned. “I was desperate. I didn’t know which
way to turn. I thought if I could get the insurance money——”

“I see,” said Poirot. “It was a bold plan, monsieur. But you
forgot one thing.”

“What was that?”

“You forgot Hercule Poirot!”

And that was the end of the mystery of the pearls. Mr. Opalsen
was arrested and charged with the theft, and the pearls were
eventually recovered. As for Célestine, she was released with an
apology, and Mrs. Opalsen, though much shaken by her husband’s
treachery, soon found another hobby to occupy her mind.

“Well, Poirot,” I said, as we sat in the train on our way back
to London, “it was a clever piece of work.”

“It was a simple case, Hastings. A very simple case. But it shows
the importance of method—and of the little grey cells!”

Poirot sprang across to the dressing-table, opened the drawer,
unlocked the case, took out a small object, relocked the case,
shut the drawer, and returned to my side.

“Thirty seconds!” I announced.

“You see?” said Poirot. “The chambermaid could not have done it
in the time, even if she had known where to find the key and had
had a duplicate. For the maid it would have been even more
difficult, for she would have had to do it while her back was
turned to the room. I do not see how it could have been done
unless she had the case in her own room. Let us see!”

He went into the small room and stood looking at the chest of
drawers.

“Yes,” he said, “from here one could not see into the other room.
But it is not here that the pearls were hidden. Let us look
further.”

He began to poke about among the ornaments on the mantelpiece.
Suddenly he stopped, and his face lit up. He held up a small
cardboard box.

“Aha!” he cried. “What have we here?”

The inspector sprang forward and snatched it from him.

“French powder!” he exclaimed.

“_Précisément_,” said Poirot. “And inside?”

The inspector opened the box. It was empty. He looked crestfallen.

“Nothing,” he said.

“Wait!” Poirot took the box from him, and, turning it over,
pointed to a small hole in the bottom.

“You see? It has been used for some other purpose. Let us see
what!”

He took a pin from his coat-sleeve, and, inserting it into the
hole, began to fish. In a moment he had produced a small piece
of paper. He smoothed it out and handed it to the inspector.

“A receipt!” the latter exclaimed. “From a firm of jewellers in
Bond Street. For a pearl necklace!”

He looked at the name. “Mrs. Opalsen!”

There was a moment’s silence. Then Mr. Opalsen spoke.

“That is the receipt for my wife’s pearls,” he said. “I gave it
to her to keep.”

“And it was in this box?” asked the inspector.

“I—I don’t know,” said Mrs. Opalsen. “I suppose so. I put it
away with some other things.”

The inspector’s face cleared.

“Well, that’s that!” he said. “It doesn’t help us much, though,
does it? We knew the pearls were gone.”

“But it shows they were here!” Poirot reminded him. “And it shows
something else too.”

“What’s that?”

“That the person who took them was in no hurry. He had time to
empty the box and hide the receipt.”

The inspector looked at him doubtfully.

“I don’t see that that gets us much further,” he said. “We’ve
searched the maid and we’ve searched her room, and we haven’t found
the pearls. If she didn’t take them, who did?”

“That is the question,” said Poirot. “But I think I can answer it.”

He turned to Mr. Opalsen.

“Monsieur, I have a request to make. Will you allow me to search
you?”

“Search me?” Opalsen’s face went purple. “What the devil do you
mean?”

“Only a little experiment,” said Poirot. “To satisfy my own mind.”

“I’ll be damned if I do!” said Opalsen.

“Oh, Ed!” his wife cried. “Do let him! It’s only a form.”

“A form, is it?” Opalsen turned on her angrily. “I tell you I
won’t have it. It’s an insult!”

“Then I must ask the inspector to do it,” said Poirot quietly.

The inspector looked from one to the other.

“I don’t see any reason for searching Mr. Opalsen,” he said
hesitantly.

“Don’t you?” said Poirot. “Then I will tell you one. Mr. Opalsen
has been in this room since the pearls were missed. He has had
ample opportunity to hide them—on his own person.”

“But why should he?” asked the inspector. “They’re his own pearls—or
at least his wife’s.”

“Exactly,” said Poirot. “And he told us just now that money was
tight in the City. A very good reason for—shall we say—realizing
on his wife’s jewels?”

“It’s a lie!” shouted Opalsen. “A damned lie!”

“Is it?” said Poirot. “Then why did you refuse to be searched?”

Opalsen glared at him for a moment, then his face suddenly
collapsed.

“Oh, all right,” he said. “Search me if you want to. You won’t
find anything.”

He submitted to the search with a bad grace. The inspector was
thorough, but the result was nil.

“There!” said Opalsen triumphantly. “Are you satisfied now?”

“Perfectly,” said Poirot. “I have learned what I wanted to know.”

“And what’s that?” asked the inspector.

“That the pearls are not on Mr. Opalsen’s person,” said Poirot
calmly.

The inspector snorted.

“We could have told you that before,” he said. “Well, if that’s
all, I’ll be getting along. I’ve got to see about that girl.”

He left the room, followed by the plain-clothes man. Mr. Opalsen
threw himself into a chair.

“Well,” he said, “of all the tomfoolery——! I hope you’re satisfied,
Mr. Poirot?”

“Not yet,” said Poirot. “But I am getting there. Hastings, my
friend, will you have the kindness to go downstairs and ask the
manager if he can spare me a few moments?”

I went, and in a few minutes returned with the manager. Poirot
greeted him with his usual politeness.

“Monsieur, I have a small favour to ask of you. Would it be
possible for me to see the register of the hotel?”

“Certainly, M. Poirot. If you will come down to the office.”

We followed him downstairs. Poirot spent some time poring over the
register. At last he closed it with a snap.

“Thank you, monsieur. That is all I want to know.”

He turned to me.

“And now, Hastings, we will go for a little stroll.”

“A stroll?” I said. “But the pearls?”

“The pearls will keep, my friend. They will not run away. And the
air of Brighton is so bracing!”

I followed him out of the hotel, feeling somewhat mystified. Poirot
seemed in no hurry. He sauntered along the front, stopping now and
then to admire the view. At last he turned into a small side-street
and stopped in front of a modest-looking house.

“What are we doing here?” I asked.

“We are going to pay a visit, Hastings. A visit to an old friend.”

He rang the bell, and the door was opened by a neat-looking maid.

“Is Mrs. Higgins at home?” asked Poirot.

“Yes, sir. Will you come this way?”

She led us into a small, primly furnished parlour. In a few minutes
a stout, motherly-looking woman entered the room.

“Why, Mr. Poirot!” she exclaimed. “This is a surprise! And how
are you, sir?”

“I am well, Mrs. Higgins, I thank you. And you?”

“Oh, I can’t complain, sir. But what brings you to Brighton?”

“A little matter of business, Mrs. Higgins. A very small matter.
I wonder if you could help me?”

“I’m sure I’d be glad to, sir, if I can.”

“It’s about a young woman who was staying here a few weeks ago.
A Miss—let me see—Miss Robinson?”

Mrs. Higgins shook her head.

“No, sir. I don’t remember any Miss Robinson.”

“Perhaps I have the name wrong,” said Poirot. “A tall, dark young
woman—very good-looking.”

“Oh, you mean Miss Leigh! Yes, she was here for a fortnight. A
very nice young lady she was, too.”

“And she had a friend with her?”

“Yes, a Mr.—Mr. Smith, I think it was. A very pleasant gentleman.”

“I see,” said Poirot. “And did they say where they were going when
they left here?”

“They said they were going to London, sir. But I haven’t heard
from them since.”

“Thank you, Mrs. Higgins. You have been most helpful.”

He took his leave, and we walked back towards the hotel.

“What was all that about?” I asked. “And who are Miss Leigh and
Mr. Smith?”

“They are the people who stole the pearls, Hastings.”

“What!” I exclaimed. “But I thought you said——”

“I said many things, my friend. Some of them were true, and some
of them—well, not so true. But now we must hurry. We have much to
do.”

When we got back to the hotel, Poirot went straight to the manager’s
office.

“Monsieur, I have a request to make. Would it be possible for me
to see the chambermaid who was in Mrs. Opalsen’s room this evening?”

“Certainly, M. Poirot. I will send for her at once.”

In a few minutes the girl appeared. She looked pale and nervous.

“You wanted to see me, sir?”

“Yes, my child. I want to ask you a few questions. You were in
Mrs. Opalsen’s room this evening when she came up to fetch her
pearls?”

“Yes, sir.”

“And the maid, Célestine, was there also?”

“Yes, sir.”

“Now, tell me—did you notice anything unusual while you were in the
room?”

The girl hesitated.

“Well, sir—there was one thing. But I don’t know if it’s important.”

“Tell me,” said Poirot encouragingly.

“Well, sir, while I was turning down the beds, I saw Célestine
go into her own room. And she stayed there for quite a long time.”

“How long?”

“Oh, I don’t know, sir. Three or four minutes, perhaps.”

“And what was she doing?”

“I don’t know, sir. The door was shut.”

“I see,” said Poirot. “Thank you, my girl. That is all.”

When she had gone, Poirot turned to me.

“You see, Hastings? The evidence is beginning to accumulate.”

“But I thought you said she couldn’t have done it in the time!”

“I said she couldn’t have done it while she was in the room. But
if she was out of the room for three or four minutes——”

“Then you think she did take them?”

“We shall see, Hastings. We shall see.”

He went back to the Opalsens’ suite. The inspector was there,
looking more cheerful than when we had left him.

“Well, M. Poirot,” he said. “I think we’ve got her.”

“Indeed?”

“Yes. We’ve found the pearls.”

“Where?”

“Hidden in the bottom of a box of chocolates in her room. Clever,
wasn’t it? But not clever enough for us.”

Poirot looked at him thoughtfully.

“In a box of chocolates?” he murmured. “How very interesting!”

“Yes. She must have slipped them in there when she went into her
room to fetch the cotton. She thought we wouldn’t think of looking
there.”

“And the chocolates—were they her own?”

“Yes. She bought them this afternoon, it seems.”

“I see,” said Poirot. “Well, that seems to settle it, does it
not?”

“I should think so,” said the inspector. “We’re taking her off
to the station now.”

“One moment,” said Poirot. “Before you go, I should like to ask
Mademoiselle one question.”

He went into the small room where Célestine was waiting, her face
swollen with crying.

“Mademoiselle,” he said gently, “did you buy those chocolates
yourself?”

The girl looked up at him, her eyes wide with terror.

“No, monsieur! I did not! They were a gift.”

“A gift? From whom?”

“From—from a gentleman I met on the front this afternoon.”

“A gentleman? Do you know his name?”

“No, monsieur. He just spoke to me, and we walked a little way
together. And then he gave me the chocolates.”

“I see,” said Poirot. “And what did he look like?”

“He was tall, monsieur, and very handsome. He had a dark
moustache.”

“Thank you, mademoiselle. That is all.”

He went back into the other room.

“Well?” asked the inspector. “What did she say?”

“She says the chocolates were a gift from a stranger,” said Poirot.

The inspector laughed.

“They all say that!” he said. “Well, I’m off. Good-night,
gentlemen.”

He left the room, followed by his subordinates and the weeping
Célestine. Mrs. Opalsen began to sob again.

“My poor pearls!” she wailed. “To think they were in a box of
chocolates all the time!”

“Don’t cry, madame,” said Poirot. “You have your pearls back,
and that is the main thing.”

“But the girl!” she said. “I can’t believe she would do such a
thing. She seemed so honest.”

“Appearances are often deceptive, madame,” said Poirot sententiously.

He turned to Mr. Opalsen.

“And now, monsieur, I think we will bid you good-night. It has
been a long evening.”

“Good-night, M. Poirot. And thank you for all you’ve done.”

We went back to our own rooms.

“Well, Poirot,” I said, as he began to undress. “That’s over.
But I must say I’m disappointed. I thought there was more in it
than that.”

“More in it, Hastings? What do you mean?”

“Well, it all seemed so simple. Just a common or garden theft by
a maid. I expected something more—more dramatic from you.”

Poirot smiled.

“My dear Hastings, life is not always dramatic. Sometimes it is
very simple indeed. But tell me—did you notice anything peculiar
about that box of chocolates?”

“No,” I said. “It looked like any other box of chocolates to me.”

“And yet there was something very peculiar about it. Something
that the inspector did not notice.”

“What was that?”

“The box was full, Hastings. Quite full.”

“Well, what of it?”

“Only this—that if the pearls had been put into the box, some of
the chocolates would have had to be taken out to make room for
them. And yet there were no chocolates missing.”

I stared at him.

“By Jove, Poirot! You’re right! I never thought of that.”

“And there was something else too. The box was wrapped in paper
and tied with string. And the string had not been untied.”

“Then how——?”

“Exactly, Hastings. How? That is the question.”

“But if the pearls weren’t in the box, where were they?”

“They were in the box, my friend. The inspector found them there.”

“Then I don’t understand.”

“It is quite simple, Hastings. The pearls were put into the box
_before_ it was wrapped up.”

“But Célestine said she got the box from a stranger on the front!”

“Exactly. And the stranger was the thief.”

“But how did he get the pearls? Célestine hadn’t even taken them
then!”

“That is where you are wrong, Hastings. The pearls were taken
_before_ Célestine went out for her walk.”

“But Mrs. Opalsen said she saw them just before she went down to
dinner!”

“She _thought_ she saw them, Hastings. But what she actually saw
was a very clever imitation.”

“An imitation?”

“Yes. The real pearls had been taken some time before—probably
during the afternoon, when the room was empty.”

“But who could have taken them?”

“That is what we have to find out, my friend. But I think I have
an idea.”

He wouldn’t say any more, and I had to go to bed with my curiosity
unsatisfied.

The next morning, Poirot was up early. He seemed very busy, and
spent some time on the telephone. At last he came into my room,
looking very pleased with himself.

“Well, Hastings, the case is complete! I have all the pieces of
the puzzle in my hand.”

“Tell me!” I cried.

“Not yet, my friend. First we must go to the police station.”

When we got there, we found the inspector in his office. He looked
rather glum.

“Morning, M. Poirot,” he said. “I suppose you’ve come about that
girl?”

“Yes,” said Poirot. “How is she?”

“Oh, she’s still protesting her innocence. But it’s no use. The
case against her is too strong.”

“Is it?” said Poirot. “I wonder.”

“What do you mean?”

“I mean, monsieur, that I have reason to believe that the girl
is innocent.”

The inspector stared at him.

“Innocent? But the pearls were found in her room!”

“I know. But they were put there by someone else.”

“Who?”

“That is what I am going to show you. If you will come with me
to the hotel, I think I can promise you a surprise.”

The inspector looked sceptical, but he agreed to come. When we got
to the hotel, Poirot led the way to the Opalsens’ suite. Mr. and
Mrs. Opalsen were there, looking very surprised to see us.

“Now, M. Poirot,” said the inspector. “What’s all this about?”

“It is very simple, monsieur,” said Poirot. “I have discovered
how the pearls were stolen.”

He turned to Mr. Opalsen.

“Monsieur, you told us last night that money was tight in the City.
Is that not so?”

“Yes,” said Opalsen. “But what’s that got to do with it?”

“A great deal, monsieur. Because it was you who stole the pearls!”

“What!” shouted Opalsen. “You’re mad!”

“Am I? Let us see. You were in need of money. You knew your wife’s
pearls were worth a fortune. So you decided to steal them and
replace them with an imitation.”

“It’s a lie!”

“Is it? Then perhaps you can explain why you were seen in a
jeweller’s shop in London a few days ago, buying a string of
imitation pearls?”

Opalsen turned pale.

“I—I don’t know what you’re talking about,” he stammered.

“I think you do, monsieur. And I think you also know that you
gave those imitation pearls to your wife, and she, poor lady, never
suspected the difference.”

“But the real pearls!” cried Mrs. Opalsen. “What did he do with
them?”

“He kept them, madame. He was waiting for a favourable opportunity
to sell them. But then he had a better idea. He would stage a
robbery, and then he could claim the insurance money as well!”

“It’s not true!” said Opalsen. “You can’t prove anything!”

“Can I not? I have already found the shop where you bought the
imitation pearls. And I have also found the man to whom you sold
the real ones.”

Opalsen collapsed into a chair, his face buried in his hands.

“All right,” he groaned. “I did it. But I was desperate—I didn’t
know what else to do.”

“And the girl?” asked the inspector. “How did the pearls get into
her room?”

“I put them there,” said Opalsen. “I knew she’d be suspected,
and I thought it would be a good way to get rid of them. I gave
her the box of chocolates on the front, and I slipped the pearls
inside when she wasn’t looking.”

The inspector shook his head.

“Well, Mr. Opalsen, I’m afraid I’ll have to ask you to come along
with me. This is a very serious matter.”

He led Opalsen away, and Mrs. Opalsen followed, weeping. Poirot
turned to me with a smile.

“Well, Hastings, what do you think of my little case now?”

“It was brilliant, Poirot! Simply brilliant! But how did you
know?”

“It was the coffee-cups, my friend. When I arranged them in a
neat row, I realized that one of them was missing. And that cup
was in Mr. Opalsen’s room. He had used it to—how do you say?—‘dose’
his wife’s coffee, so that she would sleep soundly while he
exchanged the pearls.”

“But the box of chocolates?”

“Ah, that was his one mistake. He was so anxious to incriminate
the girl that he overreached himself. He forgot that a box of
chocolates that has been tampered with is always suspicious.”

“And the stranger on the front?”

“There was no stranger, Hastings. It was Opalsen himself, in
disguise. He is a very clever man—but not clever enough for
Hercule Poirot!”

I shook my head in admiration.

“You’re a marvel, Poirot! A positive marvel!”

“It is nothing, my friend. Nothing at all. But now, I think we
will have some lunch. All this excitement has given me an appetite.”

As we walked down to the dining-room, I couldn’t help thinking
that Brighton was, after all, a very interesting place.

Poirot walked over to the dressing-table. With a sure, steady hand
he unlocked the drawer, drew out the jewel-case, unlocked it,
lifted the velvet tray, searched it, and returned the case to its
place, locking the drawer and the case as he did so.

“Well, Hastings?” he demanded, as he concluded.

“One minute and a half,” I replied.

“And Célestine’s longest absence was fifteen seconds! Even allowing
for her being slightly more expert than myself—it is impossible.
Besides, to search for a hidden treasure—that also takes time.
No, no, it was not Célestine.”

“Then it must have been the chambermaid,” said the inspector.

“Wait!” Poirot held up a thin, elegant hand. “You forget, monsieur,
that she also was never alone in the room.”

“But Célestine _did_ leave it.”

“For fifteen seconds. Not enough for even the most accomplished
thief to do what I have just done—and you have seen for yourselves
it is the work of a few moments only. No, the pearls were not
stolen between the time Mrs. Opalsen went down to dinner and her
return.”

“Then when were they stolen?” asked the inspector, staring.

“Ah, that is the question!”

“But they were there when Mrs. Opalsen went down to dinner?”

“You are sure of that, madame?” asked Poirot, turning to her.

“Quite sure. I’ve already told the inspector so.”

“And you locked the case yourself?”

“Yes.”

“And you have the key still?”

“Yes.”

“Then no one could have opened it except with a duplicate key?”

“That is so.”

“And no one had such a key?”

“How should I know? I suppose it would be easy enough to get one
made.”

“Not so easy as you think, madame. It is a very complicated lock.”

Poirot’s eyes wandered to the window.

“And the windows were closed?”

“Yes.”

“And the door into the next room was bolted?”

“Yes.”

“Then,” said Poirot, “if the pearls were not stolen after you went
down to dinner, they must have been stolen _before_.”

“But I saw them, I tell you!”

“_When_ did you see them?”

“Just before I went down. I was undecided whether to wear them or
not. I took them out of the case—I have it here—and then I decided
on the emeralds, and put the pearls back and locked the case.”

“And you are _sure_ they were the pearls?”

“Why, of course! What else should they be?”

“A very good imitation, perhaps?”

“Mr. Poirot!” Mrs. Opalsen rose in her wrath. “Do you suggest that
I don’t know my own pearls? Why, they’re worth five thousand
pounds!”

“Precisely, madame. That is why I suggest it. A thief who could
steal five thousand pounds would not hesitate to spend a few
pounds on a good imitation.”

“But I should have known!”

“Would you, madame? Are you an expert in pearls?”

“Well—no, but——”

“Exactly. Now, if we suppose that some time—say this morning—the
pearls were removed and the imitation ones substituted, the whole
thing becomes clear. The thief would then have plenty of time to
dispose of the real pearls, and the discovery would not be made
until you yourself opened the case.”

“But who could have done it?”

“That,” said Poirot, “is what we have to find out.”

He turned to the inspector.

“I should like to have a few words with the chambermaid, if I may.”

“Certainly. I’ll send for her.”

The chambermaid appeared, looking somewhat sullen.

“Now, my girl,” said Poirot pleasantly, “I want you to tell me
exactly what you did when you came into this room after dinner.”

“I just turned down the beds, sir, and saw to the fire. Célestine
was here all the time.”

“You didn’t go near the dressing-table?”

“No, sir.”

“You’re sure?”

“Quite sure.”

“And you didn’t see anything unusual?”

“No, sir.”

“Did you go into the maid’s room at all?”

“No, sir.”

“Thank you. That will do.”

As the girl left the room, Poirot turned to the inspector.

“I should like to see the room next door.”

“Certainly. It’s No. 24. It’s vacant at present.”

He led the way out into the corridor and opened the door of the
next room. It was a smaller room than the one we had just left,
but similarly furnished. Poirot walked straight to the door
communicating with Mrs. Opalsen’s room. He examined the bolt
carefully.

“As I thought,” he murmured. “The bolt is a new one. And see—it
has been recently oiled.”

He turned to the inspector.

“I think, monsieur, that if you examine the floor here, you will
find something of interest.”

The inspector knelt down and looked closely at the carpet.

“There’s a small stain here,” he said, “just by the door.”

“Precisely. A stain of oil. And if you look at the door-handle,
you will find that it also has been oiled.”

“What does that mean?” asked Mr. Opalsen.

“It means,” said Poirot, “that the door has been opened from this
side.”

“But it was bolted on the other side!”

“Exactly. But a bolt is a very simple thing to move—if you have the
right instrument. A piece of wire—a little patience—and the thing
is done.”

“But who could have done it?”

“Someone who had access to this room. Someone who knew that it was
vacant.”

“The chambermaid!” cried Mr. Opalsen.

“Perhaps. But there is another possibility.”

He turned to the inspector.

“I should like to see the hotel register.”

“Certainly.”

They went downstairs together. A few minutes later Poirot returned,
his eyes sparkling with excitement.

“Hastings,” he whispered, “I have it! The occupant of No. 24
yesterday was a Mr. Henri Blanchard. He left this morning.”

“And you think he is the thief?”

“I am sure of it! He is a well-known international thief. I have
long had my suspicions of him. And now—to find him!”

“But he has left!”

“He will not have gone far. He will be at one of the other hotels.
Come, we must lose no time!”

He hurried out of the hotel, and I followed him. We visited several
hotels, but without success. At last, at the _Metropole_, Poirot’s
search was rewarded.

“Mr. Henri Blanchard? Yes, he is staying here. He is in the lounge
at the present moment.”

Poirot led the way into the lounge. A tall, dark man was sitting in
a chair by the window, reading a newspaper. As we approached, he
looked up.

“Mr. Blanchard?” said Poirot.

“That is my name. What can I do for you?”

“I am Hercule Poirot. I think you know me?”

The man’s face changed. He rose to his feet.

“I have heard of you, monsieur. What is it you want?”

“I want the pearls of Mrs. Opalsen.”

The man laughed.

“I’m afraid you’ve made a mistake, Mr. Poirot. I know nothing of
any pearls.”

“We shall see. Hastings, call a policeman.”

“Wait!” The man’s face went white. “You have no proof.”

“I have all the proof I need. The oil on the floor—the duplicate
key—your presence in No. 24 yesterday. It is enough.”

The man hesitated for a moment, then he put his hand into his
pocket and drew out a small leather case.

“Here they are,” he said, handing it to Poirot. “I knew it was a
risk—but I thought I could get away with it.”

Poirot took the case and opened it. Inside, shimmering in the light,
was a magnificent string of pearls.

“I think these are the ones, Hastings,” he said, with a smile.

We returned to the _Grand Metropolitan_, where the news of the
recovery of the pearls was received with a chorus of delight. Mrs.
Opalsen was almost hysterical with joy.

“Oh, Mr. Poirot, how can I ever thank you?” she cried, as she
clasped the pearls round her neck.

“It is nothing, madame—nothing at all. A little matter of the
little grey cells—that is all.”

Later, as we were sitting in the lounge, I turned to Poirot.

“But how did you know it was Blanchard?” I asked.

“It was very simple, my friend. The oil on the floor told me that
the door had been opened from the other side. The hotel register
told me who had been in that room. And my own knowledge of
international thieves did the rest.”

“But the duplicate key?”

“He must have made that some time ago. He has been watching the
Opalsens for weeks, no doubt. It was a well-planned robbery—but
he did not reckon with Hercule Poirot!”

And Poirot leaned back in his chair, a look of supreme satisfaction
on his face.

The mystery of the stolen pearls was solved.

With almost incredible swiftness, Poirot wrenched open the drawer
of the dressing-table, extracted the jewel-case, fitted the key in
the lock, opened the case, selected a piece of jewellery, shut and
locked the case, and returned it to the drawer, which he pushed to
again. His movements were like lightning.

“Well, _mon ami_?” he demanded of me breathlessly.

“Forty-six seconds,” I replied.

“You see?” He looked round. “There would not have been time for
the chambermaid even to take the necklace out, far less hide it.”

“Then that settles it on the maid,” said the inspector with
satisfaction, and returned to his search. He passed into the maid’s
bedroom next door.

Poirot was frowning thoughtfully. Suddenly he shot a question at
Mr. Opalsen.

“This necklace—it was, without doubt, insured?”

Mr. Opalsen looked a trifle surprised at the question.

“Yes,” he said hesitatingly, “that is so.”

“But what does that matter?” broke in Mrs. Opalsen tearfully. “It’s
my necklace I want. It was unique. No money could be the same.”

“Of course, of course, madame!” Poirot spoke soothingly. “One
can see that for oneself. Now, another question, if you permit.
When did you last see the pearls?”

“Just before we went down to dinner, Mr. Poirot. I was half-minded
to wear them, but then I changed my mind.”

“And you put them back in the jewel-case?”

“Yes.”

“And you locked the case?”

“Yes.”

“Wait a moment, I think you said you put them back in the drawer.”

“I did—in the jewel-case in the drawer.”

Poirot thought a moment.

“I see. Now, Monsieur Opalsen, you were here at the time?”

“I was dressing in my own room. The door was open, and I saw my
wife put the pearls away.”

“Was the maid, Célestine, in the room?”

“She was—putting some things away in the wardrobe.”

“And the chambermaid?”

“She came in to turn down the beds as we were going out.”

“I see. Now, another thing. Where did the chambermaid go after
you left the room?”

“She was still in the room when we went out,” said Mrs. Opalsen.
“Célestine was there too. We left them together.”

“And they both remained there until your return?”

“Célestine did, I know. As for the chambermaid, I don’t know.
Wait! I think I saw her go out just as I was getting into the
lift.”

“I see. Now, another thing. Where does this door lead to?”

Poirot pointed to the door by the window.

“To the next room, as the inspector said. It’s occupied by a
gentleman and his wife—Mr. and Mrs. Reed, I think the name is.”

“Ah!” Poirot looked thoughtful. “A gentleman and his wife. I
wonder if they are in?”

“I believe they’ve gone to the theatre,” said Mr. Opalsen. “At
least, I saw them going out just after dinner.”

“I see. Now, one thing more. This jewel-case—it is a large one?”

“Quite a good size.”

“And you are sure the pearls were in it when you locked it?”

“Of course I’m sure,” cried Mrs. Opalsen. “I handled them.”

“Pardon me, madame, I was not doubting your word. I was merely
wishing to make sure. Well, there seems nothing more for me to do
here at present.”

He turned to the door, and I followed him.

“Well, Poirot,” I said, as we went down the corridor, “what do
you think of it?”

“Think of it? I think it is a very interesting case, Hastings.
Very interesting indeed!”

“You think the maid did it?”

“It would seem so, would it not? And yet——”

“And yet what?”

“There are one or two things that puzzle me. For instance, why
did she not hide the pearls in her own room?”

“Perhaps she did,” I suggested.

“The inspector has already searched it.”

“He may have missed them.”

“Possibly. And yet—I have an idea, Hastings, that we shall find
those pearls in a very unexpected place.”

“Where?”

“Ah, that I cannot tell you yet. We must wait and see.”

He refused to say any more, and we went down to the lounge, where
we found a crowd of people discussing the robbery.

It seemed that the news had spread like wildfire. Everyone was
talking about it.

“The pearls of Mrs. Opalsen!” I heard one woman say. “They say
they’re worth twenty thousand pounds!”

“More than that!” said another. “Thirty thousand, at least!”

“And the maid’s been arrested!”

“The French girl? I always thought she looked a suspicious character!”

And so on, and so on.

I noticed that Poirot was listening intently to all that was being
said. He seemed particularly interested in a group of people who
were sitting near us.

“The chambermaid’s a very pretty girl,” one of them was saying.
“I saw her this morning. Quite a superior-looking girl.”

“Yes, isn’t she?” said another. “I wonder if she’s had anything to
do with it?”

“They say not. The inspector says it’s the French maid.”

“Well, I wouldn’t be too sure. These chambermaids are often
not what they seem.”

I looked at Poirot. He was smiling to himself.

“You see, Hastings?” he murmured. “The chambermaid has her
supporters!”

We stayed in the lounge for some time, and then Poirot suggested
that we should go for a stroll on the front.

“The night air will do us good,” he said. “And it will give me
time to think.”

We walked for about half an hour, Poirot remaining silent all the
time. At last he spoke.

“Hastings, I want you to do something for me.”

“What is it?”

“I want you to find out for me the name of the people in the next
room—the ones Mr. Opalsen mentioned.”

“Mr. and Mrs. Reed?”

“Yes. Find out all you can about them.”

“Certainly. But what have they to do with it?”

“Perhaps nothing—and perhaps a great deal. One never knows. And
also, Hastings, find out if anyone else has a key to that door.”

“The door between the two rooms?”

“Yes.”

“I’ll do my best,” I promised.

We returned to the hotel, and I set about my task. It was not
difficult to find out about the Reeds. They were a young couple
who had arrived a few days previously. Mr. Reed was said to be
something in the City. They seemed quiet, unassuming people, and
no one appeared to know much about them.

As for the door, I found that it was a double door, and that it
was locked on both sides. The key of the Opalsens’ side was in
the lock, but the key of the other side was missing.

I reported my findings to Poirot.

“Aha!” he said. “The key is missing, is it? That is very
interesting. Very interesting indeed!”

“But what does it mean?” I asked.

“It means, my friend, that we are getting nearer to the truth.
Much nearer!”

He refused to say any more, and we retired to bed.

The next morning, Poirot was up early. He seemed in high spirits.

“I have had a thought, Hastings!” he cried. “A most luminous
thought!”

“What is it?”

“I will tell you later. For the present, I must see the manager.”

He was gone for about half an hour. When he returned, he was
radiant.

“It is as I thought!” he cried. “Everything is as I thought!”

“What is as you thought?”

“The pearls, Hastings! I know where they are!”

“Where?”

“Come with me, and you shall see!”

He led the way to the lift, and we went up to the first floor.
Instead of going to the Opalsens’ room, however, he went to the
next door—the one occupied by the Reeds.

He knocked, and a voice told him to come in.

We entered. The room was empty, but through the open door of the
bedroom I could see a man and a woman. They were packing their
boxes.

“Ah, Monsieur Reed!” said Poirot. “I am sorry to disturb you,
but I have a little matter of business to discuss with you.”

The man looked up, surprised.

“Business? With me? I don’t think I know you.”

“My name is Hercule Poirot,” said my friend, with a bow.

The man’s face changed. He looked suddenly alert and guarded.

“The detective?”

“At your service.”

“Well, what is it?”

“It is about the pearls of Mrs. Opalsen,” said Poirot quietly.

The man laughed.

“The pearls? What have I to do with them?”

“That is what I am here to find out,” said Poirot. “You see,
Monsieur, I have a theory. A very simple theory.”

“And what is it?”

“I believe,” said Poirot, “that the pearls are in this room.”

The man laughed again, but it seemed to me that his laugh was a
little forced.

“In this room? That’s good! Why should they be in this room?”

“Because,” said Poirot, “it would be the most natural place for
them to be.”

“I don’t follow you.”

“It is very simple. The pearls were stolen from Mrs. Opalsen’s
room. The maid was in the room all the time, except for two
very short intervals. The chambermaid was also in the room for
a few minutes. But neither of them could have hidden the pearls
in the room without being seen.”

“Well?”

“But there was another way out of the room,” said Poirot. “The
door between the two rooms.”

“But that door was locked!”

“On the Opalsens’ side, yes. But the key was in the lock. Any
one could have turned it. And on this side, the key was missing.”

“Well, what of it?”

“If someone had a key to this side,” said Poirot, “they could
have opened the door, taken the pearls, and then locked the door
again. And no one would have been any the wiser.”

“But who could have had a key?”

“That,” said Poirot, “is what I asked myself. And then I remembered
something. I remembered that you, Monsieur Reed, are something in
the City. And I also remembered that you have been here for a
few days.”

“Well?”

“It would have been very easy for you to obtain a key to that
door,” said Poirot. “A little bribery—a little persuasion—and the
thing is done.”

The man’s face was now very pale.

“This is preposterous!” he cried. “You have no proof—no proof at
all!”

“On the contrary,” said Poirot, “I have the best proof in the
world.”

“What is it?”

“The pearls themselves,” said Poirot.

He walked over to one of the boxes that the man had been packing.
It was a large, heavy-looking box.

“I think,” said Poirot, “that we shall find them in here.”

“You shall not touch that box!” cried the man, stepping forward.

But Poirot was too quick for him. With a sudden movement, he
wrenched open the lid.

Inside, among a heap of clothes, was a small, black jewel-case.
Poirot picked it up and opened it.

A string of magnificent pearls lay inside.

“The pearls of Mrs. Opalsen!” I cried.

“Exactly,” said Poirot.

The man made a sudden dash for the door, but I was too quick for
him. I caught him by the arm and held him fast.

“No you don’t!” I said.

A few minutes later, the police arrived and the man was taken
away. His wife, who had been watching in silence, was also
arrested.

“Well, Poirot,” I said, as we sat in the lounge later that
morning, “you’ve done it again! But how did you know? How did
you know the pearls were in that box?”

“I didn’t know, Hastings. I only suspected. But when I saw the
man’s face when I mentioned the pearls, I knew I was right.”

“But how did he get the pearls? You said the maid was in the
room all the time.”

“She was—except for those two short intervals. And it was during
one of those intervals that the theft was committed.”

“But how? He couldn’t have got in and out in twelve seconds!”

“No, but he didn’t have to. You see, Hastings, the man who stole
the pearls was not Monsieur Reed.”

“Not Monsieur Reed? But the pearls were in his box!”

“Exactly. He was the one who was going to dispose of them. But
he was not the one who stole them.”

“Then who was?”

“Think, Hastings! Who was the only person who could have stolen
the pearls and handed them to Monsieur Reed through that door?”

“The maid?”

“No. The maid was being watched by the chambermaid.”

“The chambermaid?”

“Exactly! The chambermaid!”

“But you said she couldn’t have done it in the time!”

“I said she couldn’t have hidden them in the room. But she could
easily have handed them through the door to Monsieur Reed, who
was waiting on the other side. It would only take a second.”

“I see! And then she went back to her work as if nothing had
happened.”

“Exactly. And that is why she was so anxious for the police to
search her. She knew they wouldn’t find anything!”

“And the maid? Why was she so upset?”

“Because she knew she would be suspected. And she was right!”

“Well, Poirot,” I said, “it’s a wonderful piece of work. Truly
wonderful!”

“It was a simple matter, Hastings. A very simple matter. But it
was interesting—yes, it was very interesting!”

He leaned back in his chair and lit another of his tiny Russian
cigarettes.

“And now,” he said, “I think we might have another cup of coffee.
It is very good coffee in this hotel.”

I agreed, and we sat there in silence, watching the people go by.

It had been a memorable week-end, and one that I should not
easily forget. Thanks to Poirot, the pearls of Mrs. Opalsen had
been restored to their rightful owner, and a clever pair of
thieves had been brought to justice.

As I looked at my friend, I could not help feeling a sense of
pride. He might be small in stature, and his methods might be
unusual, but there was no doubt about it—Hercule Poirot was a
very great man indeed.

“No, I understand that, madame. But if it was insured, it would
be for a very large sum, I imagine. One does not insure such things
as toys.”

Mr. Opalsen nodded.

“For fifty thousand pounds, as a matter of fact. I can’t see what
that has to do with the matter, though.”

“It is a large sum,” said Poirot meditatively. “Very large.”

At this point the inspector returned. His face was a study in
puzzled disappointment.

“I’ve turned the place upside down, and I can’t find a trace of
the pearls,” he confessed. “They’re not in the maid’s room either.
I don’t know where else to look.”

Mr. Opalsen turned to Poirot.

“What do you suggest, Mr. Poirot?”

“The little grey cells, they have been working. Let us consider
the facts once more. Mademoiselle Célestine is certain she did not
leave the room except for those two very brief periods, during
which the chambermaid was present. If the pearls were in the box
when Madame went down to dinner, they must have been stolen between
then and her return. But if—ah, if they were _not_ in the box?”

Mrs. Opalsen gave a little cry.

“But they _were_! I’m certain of it.”

“How certain, madame?” Poirot’s eyes were fixed on her face.

“I—I put them back. I’m quite sure I did.”

“You did not, perhaps, merely _think_ you had done so?”

Mrs. Opalsen hesitated.

“I—well, it was just before we went down. Ed was calling me—wasn’t
you, Ed? And I was in a hurry. I—I suppose it’s _possible_ I
didn’t actually put them in the box.”

“And if you did not?” Poirot’s voice was very soft.

“Why, then they’d be—they’d be on the dressing-table.”

“And they are not there?”

“No.”

“Then,” said Poirot, “if they were not in the box, and they are
not on the dressing-table, where are they?”

There was a silence. The inspector looked at Poirot with interest.

“You’ve got an idea, sir?”

“I have a very small idea,” admitted Poirot. “It is so small that
it is hardly an idea at all. But I should like to ask Monsieur
Opalsen one or two questions.”

The stockbroker looked at him with a certain amount of suspicion.

“Well, what is it?”

“You are a very rich man, Monsieur Opalsen?”

The other’s face cleared.

“I’m doing pretty well, thank you.”

“You have had a very successful year?”

“Not so bad—not so bad.”

“But money is tight in the City, you say?”

“Well, that’s only a way of speaking. Things are a bit quiet,
that’s all.”

“I see.” Poirot nodded. “And the pearls—they were bought some time
ago?”

“About a year. I gave twenty thousand for them then. They’re worth
a lot more now.”

“Exactly. And you have the receipt for them?”

“Of course I have. Why?”

“It would be interesting to see it.”

Mr. Opalsen’s face darkened.

“I don’t see what that’s got to do with you,” he said shortly. “If
the police want to see it, that’s another matter.”

“Oh, quite—quite,” said Poirot smoothly. “I merely thought it
might help. However, it does not matter. There is another little
point. The necklace was not a very long one?”

“No—about sixteen inches, I should say.”

“Thank you. And the pearls were all of a size?”

“No—graduated. The centre one was a beauty—as large as a hazel-nut.”

“A hazel-nut. _Tiens_, that is large. And the others?”

“They were all fine stones—all of them.”

“Thank you, Monsieur Opalsen.” Poirot turned to the inspector.
“I think, monsieur, that if you will allow me to have a few words
with you in private——”

The two men went into the small room next door. In a few minutes
they returned. The inspector’s face was still puzzled, but he
seemed to have acquired a new respect for Poirot.

“Well, Mr. Poirot,” he said, “I’ll do as you say. It seems a bit
unlikely to me, but there’s no harm in trying.”

He turned to Mr. Opalsen.

“I’m afraid I’ll have to ask you to come with me to the police
station, sir. There are one or two formalities——”

“To the police station? What for?” Mr. Opalsen’s face was a study
in indignant surprise.

“Just a matter of form, sir. If you’ll just step this way.”

Mr. Opalsen followed him, still protesting. As the door closed
behind them, Mrs. Opalsen turned to Poirot.

“What does it mean? Why have they taken Ed away?”

“Do not distress yourself, madame. It is, as the inspector said,
a mere formality. In the meantime, I should like to have another
look at that jewel-case.”

He picked it up from the dressing-table and examined it minutely.
Then he took a small magnifying glass from his pocket and peered
at the lock.

“_Tiens_!” he murmured. “That is very curious.”

“What is it?” I asked, leaning over his shoulder.

“The lock, Hastings. It has been tampered with—but not from the
outside.”

“Not from the outside?” I exclaimed. “Then——”

“Then it must have been from the inside,” said Poirot. “And as
the case was locked, it could only have been done by someone who
had a key.”

“But Mrs. Opalsen has the only key!”

“Precisely,” said Poirot. “That is what makes it so interesting.”

He turned to Mrs. Opalsen.

“Madame, I must ask you a very important question. Have you ever,
at any time, let that key out of your possession?”

“Never!” she declared. “I always wear it round my neck, as I told
you.”

“And at night?”

“I put it under my pillow.”

“I see. And you have never had a duplicate made?”

“Never.”

“Then,” said Poirot, “the case is even more interesting than I
thought.”

He sat down and began to think, his brow furrowed with the effort.
Suddenly his face cleared.

“I have it!” he cried. “Hastings, my friend, we have been blind—all
of us! The truth is as plain as the nose on your face—and that,
_mon ami_, is saying a good deal!”

He sprang to his feet and began to pace the room.

“Regard!” he cried. “The pearls are stolen. The maid is suspected.
The chambermaid is suspected. The room is searched—and nothing is
found. Why? Because the pearls are not there. We knew that already.
But _why_ are they not there? Because they have been taken out of
the room. But how? The maid did not leave the room—the chambermaid
did not leave the room. Then who did? There is only one person who
could have taken them out of the room—and that is the person who
_did_ take them!”

“But who was it?” I asked.

“The person who had the key, Hastings! The person who could open
the jewel-case at any time!”

“You mean Mrs. Opalsen?” I gasped.

“No, no, my friend. Think! Who else had the opportunity? Who else
was in the room?”

“The inspector?”

“No, no! Think again! Who was it that came into the room just
before the robbery was discovered?”

“The page-boy?”

“No, no! The person who came to tell Mr. Opalsen that his wife was
ill!”

“But that was the page-boy!”

“Was it? Are you sure, Hastings? Did you see his face?”

“No—he had his back to me.”

“Exactly. And he spoke in a low voice. And what did he say? ‘Mr.
Opalsen’s compliments, and would you step upstairs.’ But Mr. Opalsen
was _with_ us! It was the other way round—‘Mrs. Opalsen’s
compliments.’ And why should she send for him if she was coming
down herself in a few minutes?”

“I see!” I cried. “It was a ruse to get him away!”

“Precisely. And who would want to get him away? Someone who wanted
to get into the room—and who knew that he would be there.”

“But the room was not empty! The maid and the chambermaid were there.”

“Exactly. And that is why the pearls were not stolen then. They
were stolen _before_!”

“But when?”

“When Mrs. Opalsen was dressing for dinner. That was the only time
the room was empty.”

“But she said she saw them then!”

“She said she _thought_ she saw them. She was in a hurry—her husband
was calling her. She did not actually look into the case.”

“Then who took them?”

“The person who had the duplicate key, Hastings! The person who
knew where the pearls were kept, and who had plenty of time to take
them and get away before anyone else came into the room.”

“And who was that?”

“The person who has been playing a part all the evening, Hastings!
The person who has been pretending to be someone else!”

“But who?”

“The ‘page-boy,’ Hastings! The boy who was not a boy at all, but
a man in disguise! And who is that man? There is only one man who
could have done it—the man who has been behind the whole thing from
the start!”

“You don’t mean——”

“I mean Mr. Opalsen, Hastings! The ‘rich’ stockbroker who is on the
verge of ruin—and who has stolen his wife’s pearls to save himself!”

“But the insurance?” I gasped.

“That was the master-stroke, my friend! He would get the money for
the pearls—and the insurance money as well! It was a grand coup!”

“But how did you find out?”

“The receipt, Hastings! He would not show it to me. Why? Because
it would have shown that the pearls were not worth fifty thousand
pounds—nor twenty thousand either! They were paste, Hastings—paste!”

“Paste!” I cried.

“Yes. He had the real pearls sold months ago, and replaced them with
paste. Then he waited for a good opportunity to ‘steal’ them, and
claim the insurance. It was a very pretty little plot—but he forgot
Hercule Poirot!”

“And the ‘page-boy’?”

“An accomplice, of course. Probably his valet. He will be found
in due course. In the meantime, I think we may congratulate the
inspector on his capture.”

“But the pearls?”

“They will never be found, Hastings. They do not exist! But Mr.
Opalsen will go to prison—and that, after all, is the great thing!”

He smiled and lit another cigarette.

“A very interesting little case, Hastings—very interesting indeed.
And now, I think, we might go and have some supper. All this talk
of pearls has made me hungry!”

I looked at him in admiration. Once again, the little grey cells
had triumphed!

Poirot nodded with sympathy. He began to pace the room with his
hands behind his back, his head bent, his eyes fixed on the floor.
At the foot of the bed, he stopped and looked down. I saw something
glistening on the carpet. He stooped and picked it up. It was a
tiny fragment of white silk.

“You see?” he said to me. “A tiny piece of a lady’s glove, I should
say.”

He carried it to the window and examined it.

“And here, too,” he went on, moving across to the washstand.

I followed him.

“What is it?” I asked.

“A drop of water—on the floor. And another here, on the marble top
of the washstand. Curious, is it not?”

I did not see anything particularly curious in a few drops of water
in a bedroom, and I said so.

“No, no; but see how they lie. They are quite fresh.”

He went on to examine the washstand. On it stood a large basin and
ewer, the latter full of water. Beside them was a soap-dish, and
a small bottle of some scent.

Poirot picked up the bottle.

“_Eau-de-Cologne_,” he remarked. “Madame’s?”

“No,” said Mrs. Opalsen. “It’s Célestine’s. She’s very fond of it.”

Poirot put it down again.

“I should like to ask you one question, madame. Where was Célestine
standing when you first came into the room?”

“She was by the dressing-table, monsieur. She had just finished
putting away some things of mine.”

“And the chambermaid?”

“She was by the bed, I think. She was just turning it down.”

“I see. Thank you, madame.”

Poirot turned to the inspector, who had just returned from the
next room.

“Have you found anything?”

“Not a sign of them, monsieur. And yet I’ve searched every inch
of the place. It’s my belief they’re hidden in some place we’ve
missed. We’ll have another look in the morning.”

“Wait!” Poirot’s voice was authoritative. “I should like to see
the chambermaid.”

“Why?”

“I have a question to ask her.”

The inspector looked doubtful, but he went to the door and called
the girl. She came in, looking a trifle sulky.

“Did you, by any chance, see this little piece of silk?” asked
Poirot, holding out the fragment he had picked up.

The girl shook her head.

“No, sir. I didn’t see nothing.”

“You are sure?”

“Quite sure.”

“And you did not see any water on the floor?”

“Water? No, sir.”

“Thank you. That is all.”

The girl went out, and Poirot turned to the inspector.

“I think, monsieur, it would be as well if you were to search the
corridor.”

“The corridor? But they can’t be there!”

“Still—it is possible. One never knows.”

The inspector shrugged his shoulders.

“Very well, if you wish it. But I don’t see what you expect to
find.”

He went out, and we heard him moving about in the corridor.
Presently he returned.

“Nothing,” he said laconically.

Poirot did not seem surprised. He sat down on a chair, his head on
his hand, his eyes closed.

“Let me think,” he murmured. “Let me think.”

We waited in silence. Mr. Opalsen was getting restless. He looked
at his watch.

“Well,” he said at last, “I suppose there’s nothing more to be
done tonight. We’d better go to bed, I think. We’ve had a pretty
trying evening.”

“Wait!” Poirot’s voice was sharp. “I have it!”

He sprang to his feet.

“The pearls! I know where they are!”

“Where?” we all cried in chorus.

Poirot did not answer. He was looking at the door which led into
the next room.

“Is that room occupied?” he asked the inspector.

“No. It’s empty at present.”

“Then we will go in there.”

The inspector led the way, and we followed him. The room was
exactly like the one we had just left. Poirot went straight to
the bed. He pulled aside the clothes, and there, lying on the
mattress, was a magnificent string of pearls!

“My pearls!” cried Mrs. Opalsen, falling on them with a cry of
joy. “Oh, Mr. Poirot, how can I ever thank you!”

“But how did they get there?” asked the inspector, staring.

“That,” said Poirot, “is what I am going to tell you.”

He led the way back into the other room.

“You remember,” he said, “that there were two doors to this room—the
one leading into the corridor, and the one leading into the next
apartment. Both were bolted on the inside. But the door into the
next apartment was also bolted on the other side. Now, if someone
had a duplicate key to that door——”

“But it was bolted!” I cried.

“Exactly. But it is possible to shoot a bolt from the other side.
A piece of wire—a little ingenuity—and the thing is done.”

“But who did it?” asked Mr. Opalsen.

“Ah!” Poirot smiled. “That is the question. Not the maid, for she
was in the room the whole time. Not the chambermaid, for she also
was under observation. Who then?”

He looked round the room.

“There is only one person who could have done it. One person who
was not under observation. One person who had the opportunity—and
the motive.”

He paused, his eyes fixed on Mr. Opalsen.

“Mr. Opalsen!” he said. “It was you!”

The stockbroker fell back as though he had been struck.

“I!” he cried. “You must be mad! Why should I steal my own wife’s
pearls?”

“Because,” said Poirot quietly, “as you told us yourself, money is
‘confoundedly tight in the City.’ Because you needed money—and
needed it badly. Because the pearls were heavily insured. If they
were stolen, you would get the insurance money—and you would still
have the pearls!”

For a moment there was a dead silence. Then Mr. Opalsen broke into
a laugh.

“A very pretty theory, Mr. Poirot! But you have forgotten one
thing. I was downstairs in the lounge with you and Captain
Hastings when the pearls were stolen.”

“Were you?” Poirot’s voice was silken. “Are you sure of that? You
remember that a page-boy came to you with a message. You left us
abruptly. You said your wife had been taken ill. But she had not
been taken ill. You went upstairs—not to your wife’s room, but to
the room next door. You had already provided yourself with a
duplicate key. You entered the room, shot the bolt of the
communicating door, and waited. When your wife came up and went
to her drawer, you were ready. As soon as she had gone out again,
you opened the door, took the pearls, and returned to the next
room. Then you shot the bolt again from the other side, and went
downstairs. It was simple—very simple.”

“It’s a lie!” shouted Opalsen. “A damned lie!”

“Is it?” Poirot’s voice was stern. “Then perhaps you can explain
this.”

He held out the fragment of white silk.

“I found this at the foot of the bed. It is a piece of a man’s
white evening glove. And here,”—he pointed to the drops of water
on the washstand—“are the marks where you washed your hands after
the deed. You were in a hurry, monsieur—you were not quite careful
enough.”

For a moment Opalsen stood as though turned to stone. Then, with
a sudden movement, he turned and dashed for the door. But the
inspector was too quick for him.

“No, you don’t!” he said, gripping him by the arm. “I think you’d
better come with me, sir.”

As the door closed behind them, Mrs. Opalsen burst into fresh
tears.

“Oh, Mr. Poirot!” she sobbed. “To think that Ed could do such a
thing! And he was always so kind to me!”

Poirot patted her hand soothingly.

“Be comforted, madame. It is a sad world, but there are always the
pearls! And now, Hastings, I think we will go to bed. It has been
an exhausting evening.”

As we walked down the corridor, I turned to Poirot.

“You’re a wonderful man, Poirot,” I said admiringly. “I should
never have thought of Opalsen.”

“No?” Poirot smiled. “But then, you see, Hastings, you do not use
your little grey cells as I do. To me, it was quite simple. From
the first, I saw that it must be an ‘inside’ job. And when I found
that the maid and the chambermaid were both innocent, there was
only one person left.”

“But how did you know they were innocent?”

“Because, my friend, I timed them! And I saw that it was impossible
for either of them to have done it. Therefore, it must have been
someone else. And who else was there?”

“I see,” I said thoughtfully. “Yes, I see.”

We reached our rooms and Poirot turned to me with a smile.

“Good night, Hastings. And remember—the little grey cells! They
are the only things that matter in this world!”

And with a wave of his hand, he disappeared into his room.

“But the money would be better than nothing,” said Poirot
soothingly. “Is it not so? And you, Monsieur Opalsen, you have no
suspicions?”

“I don’t know what to think. The maid’s been with us for five
years. She’s always seemed honest—but then you never can tell.”

“You are right, monsieur. You never can tell. Now, if you will
pardon me, I will have a little talk with the chambermaid.”

The inspector, having finished his search, came back into the
room.

“Nothing there, either,” he admitted. “I’ll go and have another
word with the girl.”

He went out, followed by Mr. Opalsen.

“I’m going to stay with my poor wife,” said the latter, “till she’s
composed herself.”

Poirot and I left the room also.

“Well, Hastings, what do you think of it all?” asked my friend,
as we went down the stairs.

I shrugged my shoulders.

“It seems simple enough. Either the maid or the chambermaid, and
from what you’ve just shown us it must be the maid.”

“But you do not think so?”

“No. To tell the truth, I’m not sure. Both of them looked
thoroughly frightened, and neither of them looked like a thief.”

“My friend, the thief does not always look like a thief. That is
one of the most difficult things about my profession.”

“Still, if they aren’t on either of them, and if they aren’t in
the room——”

“Ah!” said Poirot. “Then the problem becomes interesting!”

“But if the maid never left the room?”

“That is what she _says_,” said Poirot dryly. “Now, Hastings, I’m
going to find that chambermaid. I want to ask her a question.”

We found her in the linen-room on the third floor. She was still
very much upset.

“I’ve never been so insulted in my life,” she said, her eyes
flashing. “Search me, indeed! As if I’d touch their dirty jewels!”

“Calm yourself, my good girl,” said Poirot, “I have only one
question to ask you. When you were in Mrs. Opalsen’s room, did
you see anyone else?”

“Anyone else? Why, no, sir. Only the maid.”

“You are sure?”

“Of course I am.”

“And you did not hear anything? No sound from the next room, for
instance?”

“The next room? No, sir. It was as quiet as the grave.”

“Thank you.” Poirot turned away.

“Wait a minute, sir. Now I come to think of it, I _did_ hear a
sound. A sort of click.”

“A click? Where did it come from?”

“I couldn’t say, sir. It was just a click.”

“Was it from the direction of the door into the next room?”

“It might have been. I didn’t notice particularly.”

“I see. Thank you.”

Poirot walked away, his brow furrowed.

“What was that click, Poirot?” I asked.

“Ah! If I knew that, Hastings, I should know everything!”

He stood for a moment, lost in thought.

“Come!” he said suddenly. “We will go and see the manager.”

The manager was in his office. He was a small, dapper man, who
looked harassed and overworked.

“A most unfortunate occurrence,” he said, when Poirot had
introduced himself. “Most unfortunate! It will do the hotel a
great deal of harm.”

“I have no doubt of it,” said Poirot. “But I want to ask you a
question. The room next to Mrs. Opalsen’s—No. 22, I believe—who
occupies it?”

The manager turned to his books.

“No. 22? Let me see. Ah, yes! A Mr. and Mrs. Robinson. They arrived
this afternoon.”

“Mr. and Mrs. Robinson. I see. And are they in now?”

“I believe they are out. They went out almost immediately after
arriving.”

“I see. Thank you.”

Poirot turned to me.

“Come, Hastings!”

We went out into the hall.

“Where are we going now?” I asked.

“To No. 22,” said Poirot.

“But the manager said they were out.”

“Exactly. That is why we are going there.”

“But we can’t go into their room if they’re not there!”

“Why not? I have my own methods, Hastings.”

He produced a small bunch of keys from his pocket, and a few
minutes later we were inside No. 22.

It was a room very similar to Mrs. Opalsen’s, but it was in a
state of some disorder. Two suitcases stood on the floor, and a
lady’s evening dress was lying across the bed.

Poirot went straight to the door communicating with the Opalsens’
room. He examined it carefully. Then he turned his attention to
the suitcases. They were both locked, but Poirot soon had them
open.

“Nothing here,” he said, after a brief search.

He turned to the dressing-table. On it were a few toilet articles
and a small cardboard box. Poirot opened the box. It contained a
few pieces of inexpensive jewellery.

“Nothing here, either,” he said.

He stood looking round the room, his eyes bright and questioning.

“What are you looking for, Poirot?” I asked.

“I am looking for a click, Hastings!”

He walked over to the washstand. It was one of the old-fashioned
kind, with a marble top and a cupboard underneath. Poirot opened
the cupboard. Inside were a basin and a jug. Poirot took them
out and examined the cupboard.

“Aha!” he said suddenly.

“What is it?” I asked, peering over his shoulder.

In the back of the cupboard was a small hole, about the size of
a penny. Poirot put his finger into it.

“You see, Hastings? This hole has been newly made. And it goes
right through the wall into the next room.”

“But what for?”

“To see through, of course! Someone in this room could watch
everything that was happening in the next.”

“Then the Robinsons are the thieves!” I cried.

“It would seem so,” said Poirot. “But we must be sure. We must
be sure!”

He looked round the room again.

“Ah!” he said. “I think I have it!”

He went over to the bed and picked up the evening dress. It was
a dress of black sequins, very shimmering and elegant. Poirot
examined it closely.

“You see, Hastings? One of the sequins is missing. And here, on
the floor, is another.”

He picked it up and held it out to me.

“What does that prove?” I asked.

“It proves that the person who wore this dress was in Mrs.
Opalsen’s room tonight!”

“But how do you know?”

“Because, my friend, when I was in Mrs. Opalsen’s room, I found
this!”

He produced a small piece of black sequin from his pocket.

“I found it on the floor, just by the dressing-table. I didn’t
say anything about it at the time, because I wanted to be sure.”

“Then it’s the Robinsons!” I cried. “We must tell the police at
once!”

“Wait a minute, Hastings. We must be careful. We don’t want to
make any mistakes.”

He stood for a moment, lost in thought.

“Come!” he said suddenly. “We will go back to the lounge.”

We went downstairs and sat in a corner of the lounge. Poirot
seemed to be watching the door.

“Who are you waiting for?” I asked.

“For the Robinsons, of course!”

We waited for about half an hour. Then a man and a woman entered
the hotel. They were both well-dressed and distinguished-looking.
The man was tall and dark, with a small moustache, and the woman
was slim and fair, with a very graceful carriage.

“Is that them?” I whispered.

“Yes,” said Poirot. “That is them.”

He rose and went towards them.

“Pardon, monsieur,” he said, bowing to the man. “But I believe you
have dropped something.”

He held out his hand. In it was the black sequin he had found in
No. 22.

The man looked at it, and then at Poirot.

“I don’t think so,” he said coldly.

“But surely, monsieur? It is from madame’s dress, is it not?”

He turned to the woman.

“I believe you were wearing a dress of black sequins this evening,
madame?”

The woman’s face turned pale.

“I—I don’t know what you mean,” she stammered.

“I think you do, madame. I think you know very well.”

The man stepped forward, his eyes flashing.

“What is the meaning of this?” he demanded. “Who are you?”

“My name is Hercule Poirot,” said my friend, “ and I am
investigating the theft of Mrs. Opalsen’s pearls.”

The man’s face changed. He looked round him, as though seeking a
way of escape. But at that moment the inspector and Mr. Opalsen
appeared in the doorway.

“Aha!” said Poirot. “I think we have our thieves!”

The inspector came forward.

“What’s this, Mr. Poirot?” he asked.

“These are the Robinsons, inspector. And I believe you will find
the pearls in their possession.”

The man made a sudden movement, as though to run, but the
inspector was too quick for him. He grabbed him by the arm.

“Not so fast, my friend!” he said.

The woman uttered a cry and sank into a chair.

“It’s no use, James,” she sobbed. “He knows everything!”

The inspector turned to Poirot.

“How did you find out?” he asked.

“It was the click, inspector! The click of the door into the next
room. And the hole in the cupboard. And the black sequin.”

He explained his discoveries.

“But where are the pearls?” asked Mr. Opalsen.

“I think you will find them in madame’s evening dress,” said
Poirot. “In the hem, no doubt.”

The inspector took the woman into the manager’s office, and a few
minutes later he returned with the pearls.

“You were right, Mr. Poirot!” he said. “They were in the hem of
the dress.”

Mr. Opalsen was overjoyed.

“Mr. Poirot, I don’t know how to thank you!” he said. “You’ve
been wonderful!”

“It was nothing,” said Poirot modestly. “A little matter of the
little grey cells, that is all.”

Later that evening, as we were sitting in our rooms, I asked
Poirot how he had known about the hole in the cupboard.

“I didn’t know, Hastings. I only suspected. But when I saw the
sequin on the floor of Mrs. Opalsen’s room, I knew that someone
had been in there who shouldn’t have been. And when I found the
other sequin in No. 22, I knew who it was. The hole in the
cupboard was just a confirmation.”

“But why did they make the hole?”

“To watch Mrs. Opalsen, of course! They knew she had the pearls,
and they wanted to know where she kept them. They waited until
she went down to dinner, and then they went into her room and
stole them.”

“But the maid was there!”

“Ah! That was the clever part. They knew the maid would be in the
room, so they waited until she went into her own room for a
moment. It only took a few seconds, as I demonstrated. They had
it all timed to a second.”

“And the click?”

“That was the sound of the door being opened. The maid didn’t
hear it because she was in her own room, but the chambermaid
heard it.”

“It was very clever of you, Poirot,” I said.

“Yes,” said Poirot, “it was a very pretty little case. And now,
Hastings, I think I will have a little sleep. My little grey
cells are very tired!”

Poirot went into the next room, and stood watching the inspector
at his task. He was turning out the clothes from the maid’s chest
