of drawers. One of the men was still with him.

“I’m afraid I’ll have to trouble you for your keys, sir,” the
inspector said.

Mr. Opalsen handed them over with a grunt of annoyance.

“The room’s quite a small one,” observed Poirot. “One would have
said that it did not contain many hiding-places.”

“Quite so,” agreed the inspector. “But we’re doing it thoroughly,
all the same.”

He was as good as his word. Every nook and corner was explored,
but with no result. He came back to the bedroom, and stood
reflectively in the middle of it.

“Well, that’s that!” he said. “If they’re here, I don’t know where
they are. I’ll just have a talk with the manager, and then we’ll
be going.”

He left us, after an exchange of civilities with Poirot.

Mr. Opalsen looked at my friend.

“Well, Poirot, what do you think of it?”

Poirot shrugged his shoulders.

“I will tell you, monsieur, when I have had time to think.”

“I’ve a good mind to offer a reward. What do you think?”

“A very good idea. What sum were you thinking of?”

“A couple of hundred—or even five. It’s a very valuable necklace.”

“Wait a little,” said Poirot. “I would not be in too great a hurry.
Wait until tomorrow morning.”

“Well, as you like.” Mr. Opalsen looked at his watch. “It’s late.
I think we’ll be getting to bed. We shall see you in the morning,
no doubt?”

“I shall be delighted, monsieur.”

He took my arm and led me away. We went down to the lounge, which
was now almost empty. Poirot sat down and began to think. He
remained so for some time, with his eyes closed and his hands
clasped in front of him. I did not care to disturb him. Finally
he opened his eyes and looked at me.

“Well, Hastings?” he said.

“I was wondering what you were thinking about,” I answered.

“I was thinking of a certain small object that I saw on the floor
of the maid’s room just now.”

“What was it?”

“A piece of coal, Hastings.”

“A piece of coal!” I repeated.

“Exactly. It was lying near the fireplace. It had evidently fallen
out of the grate. And yet—it was a very small piece.”

“I don’t see what that has to do with the necklace,” I said
testily.

“Perhaps not, my friend. And yet, it was a very small piece—very
small indeed.”

He rose and walked towards the lift. I followed him, wondering.
When we reached our floor, he stopped.

“I think I will just have another look at that room,” he said.
“The Opalsens will be in bed by now, but I have a pass-key.”

He led the way along the corridor, and we entered the room. It
was in darkness, but Poirot switched on the light. He went straight
to the fireplace and knelt down.

“Ah!” he said, with a cry of satisfaction.

He rose, and held out his hand. In the palm of it lay a tiny piece
of coal.

“You see, Hastings?”

“I see the coal,” I said, “but I don’t see the necklace.”

Poirot smiled.

“Wait a little, my friend.”

He went to the washstand and, taking a sponge, damped it
thoroughly. Then he returned to the fireplace and began to rub the
coal with the wet sponge.

As he did so, the black coating began to disappear, and a
marvellous white light shone out from beneath it.

“The pearls!” I gasped.

“Precisely,” said Poirot.

He held the necklace up. It was indeed a magnificent thing.

“But how did you know?” I asked.

“My friend, it was the coal that told me. It was too small—much
too small. It had not the appearance of a piece of coal that had
fallen from the fire. And then I remembered that the maid had
been to the fireplace to fetch her scissors.”

“But how did they get there?”

“That is what we have to find out,” said Poirot. “But I think I
can guess.”

He put the necklace in his pocket and we left the room.

The next morning we met the Opalsens at breakfast. Poirot did not
at once reveal his discovery. He waited until we were alone in
the lounge with them. Then he drew the necklace from his pocket.

“Is this your necklace, madame?” he asked.

Mrs. Opalsen gave a cry of joy.

“My pearls! Oh, Mr. Poirot, how can I ever thank you?”

“It was nothing, madame—a mere trifle.”

“But where did you find them?” asked Mr. Opalsen.

Poirot told them.

“And now,” he said, “I have a little surprise for you.”

He went to the door and beckoned. A few minutes later the
chambermaid entered the room, followed by the inspector. The girl
looked pale and frightened.

“I have asked this young woman to come here,” said Poirot, “because
I have something to say to her. Mademoiselle,”—he turned to the
chambermaid—“you have been very much maligned. I have discovered
the truth.”

The girl looked at him with wide, staring eyes.

“The pearls were not stolen by the maid,” Poirot went on. “They
were stolen by—_yourself_.”

The girl gave a gasp of terror.

“It’s a lie!” she cried. “I never touched them.”

“It is no lie,” said Poirot sternly. “I have proof. You took the
pearls while the maid was in the other room. You had a duplicate
key to the jewel-case. You then hid them in the fireplace, having
first coated them with a preparation of coal-dust. You intended
to recover them later, when the search was over.”

The girl burst into tears.

“I didn’t do it!” she sobbed. “I didn’t do it!”

“It is no use denying it,” said Poirot. “The evidence is too
strong.”

He turned to the inspector.

“I think you will find the duplicate key in her possession,” he
said.

The inspector stepped forward and searched the girl. In a few
minutes he produced a small key.

“Is this it?” he asked.

Poirot nodded.

“And now,” he said, “there is one more thing.”

He turned to Mr. Opalsen.

“Monsieur,” he said, “I think you owe this young woman an apology.”

Mr. Opalsen looked taken aback.

“An apology? What for?”

“For suspecting her of a crime she did not commit,” said Poirot.

“But you just said she did it!” I exclaimed.

Poirot smiled.

“No, Hastings. I said she took the pearls. But she did not steal
them.”

“I don’t understand,” I said.

“It is quite simple,” said Poirot. “The pearls were stolen—by
Mr. Opalsen.”

There was a moment of dead silence. Mr. Opalsen’s face turned a
ghastly grey.

“What do you mean?” he gasped.

“I mean,” said Poirot, “that you were in need of money. You had
insured the pearls for a large sum. You decided to steal them
yourself and claim the insurance money. You employed this young
woman to help you. She was to take the pearls and hide them, and
you were to find them later. But you did not count on Hercule
Poirot!”

Mr. Opalsen made a desperate effort to recover himself.

“It’s a lie!” he shouted. “A damnable lie!”

“Is it?” said Poirot. “Then perhaps you can explain how this
duplicate key came into your possession?”

He held up a second key which he had taken from his pocket.

“I found this in your room this morning,” he said. “It is the
duplicate of the one found on the chambermaid.”

Mr. Opalsen collapsed into a chair.

“It’s no use,” he groaned. “You’ve got me.”

“And now,” said Poirot, turning to Mrs. Opalsen, “I think you
will find that your husband has something to say to you.”

He took my arm and we left the room.

“Well, Poirot,” I said, when we were outside, “that was a clever
piece of work.”

“It was nothing, Hastings—nothing at all. A simple case of
deduction.”

“But how did you know about Mr. Opalsen?”

“My friend, it was the coal. As I told you, it was too small. No
one but a man would have thought of such a clumsy hiding-place.
And then there was the insurance. It was all very simple.”

“And the chambermaid?”

“She was merely his tool. He had promised her a large sum of
money to help him. She was not a professional thief.”

“Well,” I said, “it’s a good thing you were there.”

“Yes,” said Poirot, “it is a good thing for Mrs. Opalsen. But for
her husband—well, that is another matter!”

He sighed.

“It is a sad world, Hastings. But at least we have had a pleasant
week-end!”

“I comprehend, madame,” said Poirot soothingly. “I comprehend
perfectly. To _la femme_ sentiment is everything—is it not so? But
monsieur, who has not the so fine susceptibility, will doubtless
find some slight consolation in the fact.”

“Of course, of course,” said Mr. Opalsen rather uncertainly.
“Still——”

He was interrupted by a shout of triumph from the inspector. He
came in dangling something from his fingers.

With a cry, Mrs. Opalsen heaved herself up from her chair. She was
a changed woman.

“Oh, oh, my necklace!”

She clasped it to her breast with both hands. We crowded round.

“Where was it?” demanded Opalsen.

“Maid’s bed. In among the springs of the wire mattress. She must
have stolen it and hidden it there before the chambermaid arrived
on the scene.”

“You permit, madame?” said Poirot gently. He took the necklace from
her and examined it closely; then handed it back with a bow.

“I’m afraid, madam, you’ll have to hand it over to us for the time
being,” said the inspector. “We shall want it for the charge. But
it shall be returned to you as soon as possible.”

Mr. Opalsen frowned.

“Is that necessary?”

“I’m afraid so, sir. Just a formality.”

Mrs. Opalsen looked slightly annoyed. “Must I?” she queried.

“I’m afraid so, madam. I’ll give you a receipt for it, and it will
be quite safe with us.”

He sat down and wrote out a receipt in his notebook. He then handed
it to Mrs. Opalsen.

“I’ll take the necklace now, madam, and the jewel-case also. It’s
all required for evidence. No doubt I shall hear from you later
about the insurance?”

Mr. Opalsen nodded.

The inspector took the pearls and the case, and departed.

“Well!” said Mrs. Opalsen, sinking back into her chair. “I’m thankful
I’ve got them again. Though what I’m to do for a maid I don’t
know! Célestine seemed so honest, too.”

Poirot did not speak for a few minutes. He was looking at his hands.
Then he looked up.

“Monsieur,” he said, “I think I have an idea. Your wife’s pearls
are back in her hands, or rather in those of the law; the thief
is—er—in the hands of the law likewise. All is as it should be.
But—I have an idea.”

“Yes?” Opalsen looked at him expectantly.

“I have an idea that the case is not yet complete. I should like
to have a few words with the chambermaid.”

“The chambermaid? But she didn’t do it!”

“_Vraiment_,” said Poirot, with a slight smile. “But I should
like to see her for all that.”

“Anything you like, Mr. Poirot,” said Mr. Opalsen, ringing the bell.
“I’m sure I’m very much obliged to you for your help.”

The chambermaid appeared. She was still very red and indignant.

“The gentleman wants to speak to you, my girl,” said Mr. Opalsen.

Poirot rose and bowed to her.

“You have a grievance, mademoiselle? I do not blame you. To be
suspected is not pleasant. But I, Hercule Poirot, know that you
are innocent. It was not you who stole the pearls.”

“I should think not, indeed!” she cried. “I never saw them.”

“Quite so. Now, tell me, when you came in to turn down the beds,
was the French girl here?”

“Yes, she was sitting by the window with her sewing.”

“And she didn’t leave the room?”

“Not once—except for those two times she told about.”

“And you were in the room how long?”

“About five minutes, I should say. I was just finishing the second
bed when the lady come in.”

“I see. And during that five minutes—you did not notice anything
unusual?”

“No, sir.”

“You did not see anyone else in the room?”

“No, sir.”

“Think again. No one?”

“Well, now you mention it, there was a man——”

“A man!”

The exclamation came from all of us.

“Who was he?” asked Poirot.

“I don’t know, sir. He just looked in at the door for a minute
and then went away again.”

“What did he look like?”

“I couldn’t say, sir. It was only for a second. I didn’t take much
notice of him.”

“Was he a guest in the hotel?”

“I couldn’t say, sir. He wasn’t a waiter, I’m sure of that.”

“And what did he do?”

“He just looked in, as I say, and then went away.”

“He didn’t say anything?”

“No, sir.”

“Which door was it?”

“The one from the corridor.”

Poirot looked thoughtful.

“Thank you, mademoiselle. That is all I wanted to know.”

The girl retired.

“Now, what do you make of that?” asked Mr. Opalsen.

“I make of it,” said Poirot, “that there is someone else in this
business besides the French girl. I must find out who that man was.”

“But the pearls were found in Célestine’s bed!” cried Mrs. Opalsen.

“_C’est vrai_,” said Poirot. “That is the difficulty. But we shall
see—we shall see. Hastings, my friend, we will go for a little
stroll on the front.”

I followed him out of the room. As we walked down the corridor,
he stopped at a door and looked at the number.

“Number 24,” he murmured. “And Mrs. Opalsen’s is Number 22. This
must be the room next door.”

He tried the handle. The door was locked.

“I wonder who lives there?” he said.

“What does it matter?” I asked. “The door is bolted on the other
side, as the inspector said.”

“Is it?” said Poirot. “I wonder.”

He took a small instrument from his pocket and inserted it into
the keyhole. In a moment the door swung open.

“Poirot!” I exclaimed. “You can’t do that!”

“Peace, my friend. I am but making an investigation. It is
necessary for the cause of justice.”

He entered the room and I followed him. It was a bedroom, very
similar to the one we had just left. Poirot walked across to the
communicating door and examined the bolt.

“Aha!” he said. “As I thought. Look, Hastings.”

I looked. The bolt was shot, but it did not enter the socket in
the door-frame. Instead, it had been cleverly filed down so that
it only appeared to be shot.

“You see?” said Poirot. “The door could be opened from this side
at any time. Now, who is the occupant of this room?”

He looked round and his eyes fell on a suitcase lying on a chair.
He opened it and turned over the contents.

“Aha!” he said again. “A man’s clothes. And here—what have we here?”

He held up a small bottle.

“Chloroform!” I whispered.

“Precisely. Now, my friend, I think we are beginning to see light.
Let us go.”

We left the room and Poirot relocked the door.

“Now, Hastings,” he said, “we will go to the manager.”

We found the manager in his office. Poirot asked him who was the
occupant of Number 24.

“A Mr. Edward Opalsen, sir,” was the reply.

“Mr. Opalsen!” I cried. “But that’s the man himself!”

“Exactly,” said Poirot. “And now, monsieur, if you will be so good
as to give me the key of Number 26.”

“Certainly, sir.”

The manager handed him the key and we went upstairs again. Number
26 was the room on the other side of Number 24.

Poirot opened the door and we entered. This room was also a bedroom,
but it was empty.

“Now, Hastings,” said Poirot, “I want you to go into Number 24 and
bolt the door from that side. Then I will try to open it from here.”

I did as he requested. The door was firmly bolted.

“Now,” said Poirot, “I will try my little experiment.”

He took out his instrument again and worked at the lock for a
minute or two. Then he gave a push and the door flew open.

“You see?” he said. “The bolt is useless. It has been filed down
on this side too. So you see, anyone in Number 26 could enter
Number 24, and from there enter Number 22.”

“But who was in Number 26?” I asked.

“That is what I am going to find out,” said Poirot.

He went back to the manager’s office.

“Who was in Number 26 this evening?” he asked.

The manager consulted his books.

“A Mr. and Mrs. Robinson, sir. They left about half an hour ago.”

“Left!” cried Poirot. “In a hurry?”

“Well, they said they had been called away unexpectedly.”

“I see. And what did they look like?”

“The gentleman was tall and dark, and the lady was very pretty—a
blonde.”

“Thank you,” said Poirot. “That is all.”

As we walked away, he turned to me.

“Well, Hastings, what do you think of it?”

“It seems clear enough,” I said. “The Robinsons were the thieves.
The man the chambermaid saw was Robinson. He must have entered
the room while Célestine was in her own room, taken the pearls,
and then hidden them in her bed to throw suspicion on her.”

“And the chloroform?” asked Poirot.

“I suppose they intended to use it if anyone interrupted them.”

“Perhaps. But why did they leave so suddenly?”

“Because they knew the police were coming, I suppose.”

“But how did they know?”

“I don’t know. Perhaps they saw them arrive.”

“Perhaps. But there is one thing that puzzles me.”

“What is that?”

“The necklace. Why did they leave it behind? If they had it, why
did they hide it in Célestine’s bed and then go away without it?”

“I suppose they were afraid of being caught with it on them.”

“Perhaps. But it seems very strange. A necklace worth thousands
of pounds—and they leave it behind! No, Hastings, there is
something here I do not understand.”

He was silent for a moment, then he said:

“I think I will have another look at that necklace.”

“But the inspector has it!”

“_C’est vrai_. I must go to the police station.”

We took a taxi and drove to the police station. We found the
inspector in his office.

“Ah, Mr. Poirot!” he said. “You’ve come to see how we’re getting
on? Well, the girl’s in a cell, and we’re going to charge her
to-morrow.”

“I see. And the necklace? Could I see it for a moment?”

“Certainly.”

He took the necklace out of a drawer and handed it to Poirot.
The latter looked at it closely for a few minutes, then handed it
back.

“Thank you,” he said. “And the jewel-case?”

The inspector produced it. Poirot examined it with equal care.

“Thank you,” he said again. “I am very much obliged to you.”

As we left the police station, I asked him if he had found out
anything.

“Yes,” he said, “I have found out several things. One of them is
that the pearls the inspector has are not the real ones.”

“What!” I cried. “False pearls?”

“Exactly. They are very good imitations, but they are false.”

“Then the real pearls are still missing?”

“So it would appear.”

“But who could have changed them?”

“That is the question, my friend. It might have been the Robinsons.
Or it might have been—someone else.”

“Who?”

“We shall see. But first, I must find the Robinsons.”

“But they have gone!”

“Not very far, I think. A tall dark man and a pretty blonde woman—they should not be difficult to find in Brighton.”

We spent the next hour or two searching the various hotels, but
without success. At last, we returned to the _Grand Metropolitan_.

As we entered the hall, Poirot’s eyes fell on a man who was
standing by the reception desk. He was a tall, dark man, and he
was talking to the clerk.

“Aha!” whispered Poirot. “Look, Hastings!”

He went up to the man and touched him on the shoulder.

“Mr. Robinson, I believe?” he said.

The man turned round.

“Yes,” he said. “What of it?”

“I should like to have a few words with you, if you please.”

The man looked at him suspiciously.

“Who are you?” he asked.

“My name is Hercule Poirot. I am a private detective.”

The man’s face changed.

“Oh,” he said. “I’ve heard of you. What do you want?”

“I want to talk to you about the pearls of Mrs. Opalsen.”

The man laughed.

“The pearls? What have I got to do with them?”

“That is what I want to find out. Shall we go into the lounge?”

We went into the lounge and sat down.

“Now, Mr. Robinson,” said Poirot, “I will be frank with you. I know
that you and your wife were in Number 26 this evening. I also know
that the doors between your room and Mrs. Opalsen’s were—er—not
quite as they should be. And I know that you were seen in Mrs.
Opalsen’s room about the time the pearls were stolen.”

Robinson looked at him for a moment in silence. Then he laughed
again.

“You’re a clever man, Mr. Poirot,” he said. “I’ll admit that.
Yes, we were in Number 26, and I did go into Number 22. But I
didn’t steal the pearls.”

“Then why were you there?”

“Well, if you must know, I’m an agent for an insurance company.
We’d heard that there was likely to be an attempt on those pearls,
and I was sent down to keep an eye on them.”

“I see. And did you see the attempt?”

“Yes, I did. I saw someone go into the room and take the pearls.”

“Who was it?”

“It was the maid—Célestine.”

“You saw her?”

“Yes. I was looking through the door—the one from Number 24.
I saw her take the pearls out of the case and hide them in her
bed.”

“And why didn’t you stop her?”

“Because I wanted to see where she’d hide them. And besides, it
wasn’t my business to interfere. My business was just to report
what I saw.”

“I see. And then you and your wife left the hotel?”

“Yes. We’d seen what we came for, and there was no need to stay.”

“I see,” said Poirot again. “But there is one thing I don’t
understand. If Célestine stole the pearls, how is it that the
pearls the police found are false?”

Robinson looked surprised.

“False? Are you sure?”

“Quite sure.”

“Well, that’s news to me. I suppose she must have changed them
beforehand.”

“Perhaps. But if she had the real pearls, why did she hide the
false ones in her bed?”

“I don’t know. Perhaps she thought they were the real ones.”

“Perhaps. But it seems very strange.”

Poirot was silent for a moment, then he said:

“Thank you, Mr. Robinson. That is all I wanted to know.”

Robinson rose and left the room.

“Well, Poirot,” I said, “what do you make of that?”

“I think,” said Poirot, “that Mr. Robinson is a very clever man.
But I do not think he is an insurance agent.”

“Then who is he?”

“I think he is a thief. And I think he has the real pearls.”

“But he said he saw Célestine take them!”

“Precisely. He said so. But that does not mean it is true. I think
he took them himself, and then put the false ones in the bed to
make it look as if she had stolen them.”

“But how did he get the false pearls?”

“He must have had them ready. He probably came here for the
purpose of stealing the pearls and replacing them with false ones.”

“But why did he leave the false ones behind?”

“To throw suspicion on Célestine, as I said. If the pearls were
found in her bed, everyone would think she had stolen them.”

“But why didn’t he take the real ones with him?”

“He did. He has them now.”

“Then we must catch him!”

“Yes, Hastings, we must catch him. But first, I must be sure.”

He was silent for a moment, then he said:

“I think I will have another word with Mr. Opalsen.”

We went back to the Opalsens’ room. Mr. Opalsen was alone.

“Ah, Mr. Poirot!” he said. “Found out anything?”

“Yes, monsieur,” said Poirot. “I have found out that the pearls
the police have are false.”

“False!” cried Opalsen. “But how can that be?”

“It is very simple, monsieur. Someone changed them.”

“But who? The maid?”

“I do not think so. I think it was someone else.”

“Who?”

“I think it was—your wife.”

“My wife!” Opalsen stared at him in amazement. “You must be mad!”

“Not at all, monsieur. Consider the facts. Your wife loves
jewellery. She also loves money. You said yourself that money was
tight in the City. Is it not possible that your wife, seeing a
chance to get a large sum of money from the insurance company,
decided to steal her own pearls?”

“It’s impossible! She’d never do such a thing!”

“Is it? Think, monsieur. She knew you had insured the pearls.
She knew that if they were stolen, you would get the money. And
she would still have the pearls—or at least the money from them.”

“But she was with us all the time!”

“Was she? She went upstairs to fetch the pearls, did she not?
She was away for several minutes. That was when she could have
done it.”

“But the maid was there!”

“The maid was in her own room for part of the time, as she
admitted. And the chambermaid was there too, but she only saw
someone look in at the door. That someone could have been your
wife.”

“It’s preposterous! I won’t believe it!”

“As you wish, monsieur. But it is a possibility.”

Poirot was silent for a moment, then he said:

“There is one way to find out. If your wife has the pearls, she
must have hidden them somewhere. If we can find them, we shall
know the truth.”

“But where could she have hidden them?”

“That is what I am going to find out.”

He began to search the room, but this time he did not look in the
obvious places. Instead, he examined the various small objects
on the dressing-table.

Suddenly, he picked up a large cake of soap.

“Aha!” he said. “What have we here?”

He took a small knife from his pocket and cut the soap in half.
Inside, embedded in the soap, was a string of pearls.

“My God!” cried Opalsen. “The pearls!”

“Exactly,” said Poirot. “The real pearls.”

He handed them to Opalsen.

“Now, monsieur, what do you say?”

Opalsen looked at the pearls in silence for a moment. Then he
sighed.

“I suppose you’re right, Mr. Poirot. I never would have believed
it of her. But—well, she always was a bit flighty.”

“I understand, monsieur,” said Poirot. “It is a great shock to
you. But you must face the facts.”

At that moment, the door opened and Mrs. Opalsen entered. She
looked from one to the other of us in surprise.

“What’s the matter?” she asked. “What are you doing with my soap?”

“We have found your pearls, madame,” said Poirot.

“My pearls? But the inspector has them!”

“No, madame. The inspector has the false pearls. These are the
real ones.”

Mrs. Opalsen turned pale.

“I—I don’t know what you mean,” she stammered.

“I think you do, madame,” said Poirot. “You stole your own pearls
and replaced them with false ones, so that you could claim the
insurance money.”

Mrs. Opalsen burst into tears.

“It’s not true! I didn’t do it! I only did it because Ed was so
worried about money. I thought it would help him.”

“So you admit it?” said Poirot.

“Yes, I admit it. But I didn’t mean any harm. I just wanted to
help.”

“I see,” said Poirot. “Well, madame, it is not for me to judge
you. But I think you have made a great mistake.”

He turned to Opalsen.

“And now, monsieur, I think we will leave you. I have no doubt
you will be able to settle this matter with the police.”

We left the room and walked down the corridor.

“Well, Poirot,” I said, “that was a surprise! I never would have
suspected Mrs. Opalsen.”

“No?” said Poirot. “I did. From the first.”

“Why?”

“Because, my friend, she was too anxious to show me the pearls.
And she was too upset when they were stolen. It was all a little
too—theatrical.”

“And the Robinsons?”

“They were just a complication. Robinson was a thief, as I
suspected, but he was not the one who stole the pearls. He was
only there to see if he could steal them himself.”

“And the chloroform?”

“That was probably for use on the maid, if she had interrupted
him.”

“And the filed bolts?”

“He probably did that himself, so that he could get into the room
easily.”

“I see. Well, it was a clever piece of work, Poirot.”

“Thank you, Hastings. But it was simple—very simple. It only
required a little thought, and the use of the little grey cells.”

We walked out of the hotel and into the bright sunlight of the
Brighton front.

“And now, Hastings,” said Poirot, “I think we will have a little
lunch. I am quite hungry.”

“So am I,” I said. “Where shall we go?”

“I think,” said Poirot, “we will go to the _Ship_. They have very
good omelettes there.”

And so, talking of omelettes and other things, we walked away
along the front.

“Well, well, I suppose you’re right. But it seems hard that my wife
is to lose her necklace twice in the same evening!”

The inspector laughed.

“She’ll have it back before long, sir. It’s all right. We must
just get the girl’s confession, if we can.”

“Wait a moment!” said Poirot. “Where did you find it? In the
bed-springs?”

“Yes, sir.”

“Near the head or the foot?”

“In the middle.”

“Ah!” Poirot’s face showed interest. “That is most curious! And
it was wrapped in something?”

“A piece of old newspaper.”

“Truly? Now that is more than ever curious!”

“I don’t see that,” said the inspector. “She didn’t want the thing
to be seen. That’s all.”

“And why a piece of newspaper?”

“Because it happened to be handy, I suppose.”

“Exactly. It happened to be handy. Now, where did she get a piece
of newspaper from?”

“I don’t know. I’ll ask her.”

“Do, my friend. It may be instructive.”

The inspector turned to the door.

“Well, good-night, gentlemen. I’m off now.”

“One moment,” said Poirot. “I think I have a few words to say
first. You will have to go into the next room, if you don’t mind.
I want to speak to Mr. and Mrs. Opalsen.”

The inspector looked a trifle surprised.

“If you wish it, monsieur. But don’t be long. I must get away.”

He closed the door behind him. Poirot turned to the others.

“Monsieur and madame, I have a little confession to make. I am a
very inquisitive man. Just now, while the inspector was out of the
room, I looked at that necklace!”

Mrs. Opalsen’s face flushed.

“You don’t mean to say——”

“Yes, madame. It is—as I suspected—a very good imitation. It is
not the original necklace at all.”

Mrs. Opalsen sank back into her chair with a groan.

“What!” she gasped. “Not—not the real one?”

“No, madame.”

“Then where is it?”

“That is what I propose to find out,” said Poirot. “But first, I
must ask you one or two questions.”

He turned to Mr. Opalsen.

“Monsieur, you have the good heart, I know. You would not wish an
innocent girl to be punished for a crime she did not commit?”

“Certainly not. But she’s guilty right enough. The pearls were
found in her bed.”

“_Exactly_. And that is just why I am sure she did not put them
there!”

“What do you mean?”

“The pearls were found in the middle of the bed-springs. Now,
to put them there, she would have had to unmake the bed. Did she
do that? No, the chambermaid did that, later in the evening. If
Célestine had hidden them there, she would have had to do it
_before_ the chambermaid came in. But she had no reason to hide
them then. She did not know they were going to be missed. No, the
person who hid those pearls there was someone who wanted them to
be found in the maid’s room.”

“The chambermaid!” I cried.

“No, Hastings. The chambermaid would have hidden them in her own
room, not the maid’s. No, it was someone who wanted to throw the
guilt on Célestine.”

“But who?”

“That is what we have to find out. Now, Mr. Opalsen, I want you
to tell me the truth. Is it not a fact that you have been in
considerable financial difficulties lately?”

Mr. Opalsen’s face turned a dull red.

“What business is that of yours?” he demanded.

“None at all,” said Poirot smoothly. “Except that it might explain
a good deal. For instance, why you should have suggested that your
wife should bring her pearls down for me to see tonight.”

“I didn’t! It was her own idea.”

“Pardon me, monsieur. I think you will find that it was you who
suggested it. You said, ‘I’d like to show them to you.’ And she
went at once.”

“Well, and what if I did? What are you suggesting?”

“I am suggesting, monsieur, that you had already disposed of the
real pearls, and that you had a very good imitation made in their
place. You then arranged this little scene so that the imitation
should be stolen, and you could claim the insurance money.”

“It’s a lie!” shouted Opalsen. “A damnable lie!”

“Is it?” said Poirot. “Then perhaps you will explain why you have
this in your pocket?”

He held out his hand. In it was a small piece of newspaper.

“I found it on the floor just now,” he said. “It is a piece of
the _Financial Times_ of two days ago. And it is exactly the same
shape and size as the piece the imitation pearls were wrapped in!”

For a moment there was silence. Then Mr. Opalsen broke into a
harsh laugh.

“You’re too clever by half, Mr. Poirot! But you’ve no proof—none
whatever.”

“Haven’t I?” said Poirot. “We shall see. Hastings, would you be
so good as to ask the inspector to step in here for a moment?”

I did so. The inspector entered, looking curious.

“Well, monsieur?”

“I have a little discovery to communicate to you,” said Poirot.
“This gentleman, Mr. Opalsen, has been so kind as to inform me that
the necklace which was found just now is an imitation. The real
one was stolen some time ago.”

The inspector’s jaw dropped.

“An imitation! Then—then who’s got the real one?”

“That,” said Poirot, “is what I am about to show you.”

He walked across to the dressing-table and picked up a small
bottle of hair-wash.

“You see this, monsieur? It is a very excellent preparation. It
was on the dressing-table when we came in. But I noticed one thing
about it. The cork did not fit quite tightly. I took the liberty
of examining it. And what do you think I found?”

He unscrewed the top of the bottle and poured the contents into a
basin. As the liquid ran out, something else followed it—a long
string of shimmering white pearls!

“The real necklace!” cried Mrs. Opalsen.

“But—but how did it get there?” gasped the inspector.

“It was put there,” said Poirot, “by the only person who could
have done it. The person who had the key of the jewel-case, and
who could go in and out of the room as she liked.”

He turned to the door.

“Mademoiselle Célestine, will you be so good as to come in?”

The French girl entered, looking pale and defiant.

“It is no use, mademoiselle,” said Poirot. “The pearls have been
found. You stole them from the jewel-case, and hid them in the
hair-wash bottle. Then, when you found that the robbery was
discovered sooner than you expected, you became frightened. You
took the imitation necklace which Mr. Opalsen had so thoughtfully
provided, and hid it in your own bed, hoping that it would be found
there and that you would be able to claim that you had been
‘planted.’ It was a clever trick, but not quite clever enough for
Hercule Poirot!”

Célestine burst into a torrent of French, but it was no use. The
evidence was too strong against her.

“But how did you know?” I asked, as we sat in the lounge later that
evening.

Poirot smiled.

“It was the piece of newspaper that gave me the clue, Hastings.
You see, it was a piece of the _Financial Times_. Now, who would
be likely to have a copy of the _Financial Times_? Not a lady’s
maid, surely? No, it must have been Mr. Opalsen. And when I found
another piece of the same paper in his pocket, I knew I was on the
right track. He had had the imitation made, and was only waiting
for a good opportunity to have it ‘stolen.’ Célestine merely
forestalled him. She stole the real pearls, and then, when the
alarm was raised, she tried to throw the guilt on the chambermaid
by hiding the imitation ones in her own bed. She thought that if
they were found there, everyone would think they had been put there
by someone else.”

“But the hair-wash bottle?”

“Ah, that was where she made her mistake. She thought it was a
safe place to hide the real pearls for the time being. But she
forgot that Hercule Poirot has a very sharp nose! I smelt the
hair-wash, and it didn’t smell quite right. There was a faint
odour of—shall we say—dishonesty about it?”

I laughed.

“Well, Poirot, I must hand it to you. You’ve done it again.”

“It was nothing, my friend,” said Poirot modestly. “A mere matter
of the little grey cells. But I think, all the same, that we have
earned our week-end at Brighton!”

“The law is the law,” said Poirot. “I myself have had a great deal
to do with the law, and I know how impossible it is to circumvent
her.”

Mrs. Opalsen wiped away her tears.

“I’m sure I’m very much obliged to you, Mr. Inspector,” she said,
turning towards him. “If it hadn’t been for your cleverness, I’d
never have seen my pearls again.”

The inspector smiled, his vanity quite restored.

“Oh, that’s all right, madam. Glad we could be of some use. If
we’d been five minutes later, though, I don’t know what would have
happened.”

“Quite so,” said Poirot. “Five minutes later and the thief—where
would he have been? And the pearls—where would _they_ have been?”

He looked round with an air of complete and absolute satisfaction.

“I am very glad to have been of even the smallest assistance,”
he continued. “But I have no doubt that, as the inspector says,
the matter would have come to the same conclusion in the end.”

He bowed with much ceremony.

“And now, Hastings, if you are ready?”

I was more than ready. I followed him out of the room, and we walked
slowly down the corridor.

“Well, that’s a very good thing,” I said. “Poor woman! She was
quite heart-broken.”

Poirot did not answer for a moment. Then he said slowly:

“Hastings, did you notice that necklace?”

“Notice it? Of course I did. It was a beauty.”

“And you saw me examine it?”

“Yes.”

“Well?”

“Well, what? I suppose it was all right?”

“No, Hastings, it was _not_ all right.”

“What do you mean?”

“It was a very good imitation—but an imitation nevertheless.”

“But—but Mrs. Opalsen wouldn’t have a fake necklace!”

“Ah, but someone else might!”

“You mean the maid had changed them?”

“Perhaps.”

“But she hadn’t the time!”

“No, she hadn’t the time.”

“Then who did?”

“That is what I propose to find out,” said Poirot.

He stopped at the top of the stairs.

“Suppose we go and have another word with the manager? I should
like to know something about that chambermaid.”

“But the inspector said she was all right!”

“The inspector is an excellent man, no doubt,” said Poirot, “but
his head is of a wood most solid. He does not use his little grey
cells. Now, I—Hercule Poirot—I use them!”

The manager was in his office. He looked up as we entered.

“Yes, gentlemen? What can I do for you?”

Poirot leaned forward over the desk.

“I should like to ask you a question,” he said. “That chambermaid—how
long has she been with you?”

“About three months. Why?”

“And her character?”

“Excellent. She came to us from a lady in the North—a Mrs.
Pendleton. I have her reference here.”

He pulled out a drawer and produced a letter. Poirot took it and
read it carefully.

“I see,” he said. “I see. Well, thank you very much.”

He handed it back.

“By the way,” he added, as we were leaving the room, “where was
the necklace found?”

“In the maid’s bed—in the springs of the mattress.”

“Ah, yes. I remember. Thank you.”

He walked out into the hall.

“Hastings,” he said, “I think I will go for a little walk.”

“I’ll come with you.”

“No, no, _mon ami_. I would prefer to be alone. I have much to
think of. Do you go and have a game of billiards. I shall be back
before long.”

He walked away with his quick, bird-like step. I watched him out of
sight, then turned towards the billiard-room. I did not feel like
billiards, however, so I wandered out on to the front. The sea
was calm and the moon was shining. It was a beautiful night. I
strolled along for some time, and then sat down on a seat.

I was thinking of Poirot’s words. A fake necklace! Who could have
changed it? And why?

Suddenly I saw a figure approaching. It was Poirot. He was walking
quickly, and his head was bent as though in deep thought. I got up
and went towards him.

“Well?” I asked. “What news?”

He looked up and smiled.

“I have seen the chambermaid,” he said.

“The chambermaid? But I thought you said she was all right?”

“I said that the inspector thought so. I did not say that I
thought so.”

“But you said she hadn’t time!”

“I said she hadn’t time to take the necklace out of the case. I
didn’t say she hadn’t time to put another one in.”

“But she was only in the room for three minutes!”

“Three minutes is a long time, Hastings—if you are prepared.”

“But she didn’t know the pearls were there!”

“Didn’t she? I wonder.”

He relapsed into silence. We walked back to the hotel together.

“What are you going to do?” I asked.

“I am going to wait,” said Poirot. “To wait—and to see.”

We entered the hotel and went up to our rooms. As we passed the
Opalsens’ door, we saw Mr. Opalsen coming out. He looked very
agitated.

“Oh, Mr. Poirot,” he said, “I’m so glad I’ve met you. My wife’s
in a terrible state. She’s just heard about the fake necklace.”

“Indeed?” said Poirot. “And how did she hear that?”

“The inspector told her. He’s just been here. He said that when
they got to the station they examined the necklace and found it
was only an imitation.”

“Ah!” said Poirot. “And what did he say then?”

“He said he was going to re-arrest the maid. He thinks she must
have hidden the real pearls somewhere else.”

“I see,” said Poirot. “Well, I should not worry too much if I
were you. I have a feeling that everything will be all right.”

Mr. Opalsen looked at him doubtfully.

“I hope so,” he said. “I’m sure I hope so.”

He turned and went back into the room.

Poirot and I went on to our own rooms.

“What do you think of it all, Poirot?” I asked, as we were undressing.

“I think, Hastings, that it is a very interesting case—a very
interesting case indeed. There are several points that are not
at all clear.”

“Such as?”

“Well, for one thing, why should the maid have hidden the fake
necklace in her own bed? If she had stolen the real pearls, why
not hide _them_? And if she hadn’t stolen them, why hide the fake?”

“Perhaps she didn’t hide it. Perhaps someone else did.”

“Exactly, Hastings! Someone else! But who?”

“The chambermaid?”

“Perhaps. But if so, why?”

“To get the maid into trouble?”

“But why should she want to do that? She didn’t know the maid.”

“She might have had a grudge against her.”

“Perhaps. But it seems unlikely.”

He was silent for a moment, then he said:

“And there is another thing. Why should anyone want to steal a
fake necklace?”

“They didn’t know it was a fake!”

“Perhaps not. But if they didn’t, why change it for another fake?”

“I don’t understand.”

“Neither do I, Hastings. Neither do I. But I have a little idea—a
very little idea. We shall see if it is correct.”

He turned out the light and was soon fast asleep. I, however, lay
awake for a long time, thinking of the problem. It seemed to me
that the more one thought of it, the more complicated it became.

The next morning Poirot was up early. He was in a very cheerful
mood.

“Well, Hastings,” he said, “the sun is shining, the birds are
singing—it is a beautiful day! Let us go and have breakfast.”

After breakfast we went out on to the front again. We had not gone
far when we saw Mr. Opalsen coming towards us. He looked even more
agitated than he had done the night before.

“Mr. Poirot,” he said, “I must speak to you. Something very serious
has happened.”

“Indeed?” said Poirot. “What is it?”

“My wife’s jewels—the real ones—have been found!”

“Found? Where?”

“In the chambermaid’s room!”

“In the chambermaid’s room? Whereabouts?”

“In her box. They were hidden in the lining.”

“Ah!” said Poirot. “And the chambermaid?”

“She’s been arrested. She’s at the police station now.”

“I see,” said Poirot. “Well, that is very satisfactory, is it
not?”

“Satisfactory? I don’t know. My wife’s in a terrible state. She’s
convinced that the chambermaid is innocent.”

“Innocent? But the pearls were found in her box!”

“I know. But she says she never saw them before. She says someone
must have put them there.”

“Naturally she would say that,” said Poirot. “But what does the
inspector think?”

“Oh, he’s quite sure she’s guilty. He says it’s a clear case.”

“I see,” said Poirot. “Well, perhaps he is right. We shall see.”

Mr. Opalsen went on his way, and we continued our walk.

“Well, Poirot,” I said, “that seems to settle it. The chambermaid
is the thief after all.”

“Does it, Hastings? Does it?”

“Why, of course! The pearls were found in her box!”

“True. But does that prove she put them there?”

“Who else would have put them there?”

“That is the question, Hastings. That is the question.”

He was silent for a moment, then he said:

“I think, Hastings, that I will go and have another word with the
inspector.”

“I’ll come with you.”

“No, no, _mon ami_. I would prefer to be alone. I shall be back
soon.”

He walked away again, and I was left to my own reflections. I must
confess that I was beginning to get a little tired of Poirot’s
mysteriousness. It seemed to me that the case was a very simple
one, and that there was no need for all this mystery.

However, I knew from experience that it was no use trying to get
anything out of him until he was ready to speak. So I waited
patiently for his return.

It was nearly lunch-time when he came back. He looked very pleased
with himself.

“Well?” I asked. “What did the inspector say?”

“Oh, he was very communicative—very communicative indeed. He is
quite sure that he has got the right person.”

“And you?”

“I? Oh, I am not so sure. In fact, I am quite sure that he has
got the wrong person.”

“The wrong person? But the pearls——”

“The pearls, Hastings, are not everything. There are other things
to be considered.”

“What other things?”

“Well, for one thing, there is the question of the reference.”

“The reference? What reference?”

“The reference that the chambermaid brought with her from her last
place.”

“What about it?”

“Well, I have been making a few inquiries, and I find that there
is no such person as Mrs. Pendleton.”

“No such person? But the manager said——”

“The manager said what he believed to be true. But he was deceived.”

“Deceived? By whom?”

“By the chambermaid—or by someone who was acting with her.”

“Then she _is_ guilty after all!”

“Perhaps. But there is another thing. Do you remember the sketch
I made of the room?”

“Yes.”

“Do you remember the door that led into the next apartment?”

“Yes. You said it was bolted on both sides.”

“I did. But I didn’t say it was _always_ bolted on both sides.”

“What do you mean?”

“I mean, Hastings, that it is possible to unbolt a door from the
outside—if you know how.”

“But how would that help?”

“It would help a great deal—if you wanted to get into the room
without being seen.”

“I don’t understand.”

“You will, Hastings. You will. But now let us go and have lunch.”

After lunch we went back to our rooms. Poirot spent the afternoon
in deep thought. He did not speak a word to me, and I did not like
to disturb him.

About five o’clock he suddenly got up.

“Hastings,” he said, “I have it!”

“Have what?”

“The solution! It is all quite clear now.”

“Who is it? Who is the thief?”

“Wait a moment, Hastings. I must make sure. I must make quite
sure.”

He went to the telephone and asked for a number. He spoke for a
few minutes in a low voice, then hung up.

“Yes,” he said, “it is as I thought. Everything fits in
perfectly.”

“Well, tell me! Who is it?”

“Not yet, Hastings. Not yet. I must first speak to Mr. Opalsen.”

He went out of the room and I followed him. We found Mr. Opalsen
in the lounge. He looked very surprised to see us.

“Mr. Poirot!” he said. “What is it?”

“Mr. Opalsen,” said Poirot, “I have some news for you. I know who
stole your wife’s pearls.”

“You do? Who is it?”

“If you will come with me to your room, I will tell you.”

Mr. Opalsen followed us upstairs. When we were in the room, Poirot
closed the door and turned to him.

“Mr. Opalsen,” he said, “I have a very unpleasant duty to perform.
I must tell you that your wife’s pearls were stolen by——”

He paused for a moment, then he said:

“By you!”

“By me?” Mr. Opalsen stared at him in amazement. “Are you mad?”

“No, monsieur, I am not mad. I am very sane. And I know that you
stole the pearls.”

“But that’s ridiculous! Why should I steal my own wife’s pearls?”

“Because, monsieur, you were in need of money. You told us yourself
that money was ‘confoundedly tight in the City.’ And you knew that
the pearls were insured for a large sum.”

“But—but I didn’t steal them! They were found in the chambermaid’s
box!”

“Exactly, monsieur. You put them there.”

“I? How could I have put them there? I didn’t even know which was
her room!”

“Didn’t you? I think you did. You had been watching her for some
time, had you not? You knew when she went to her room, and you knew
when she was out of it.”

“But—but what about the fake necklace?”

“That was a very clever touch, monsieur. You knew that if the real
pearls were stolen, the insurance company would make a very
thorough investigation. So you decided to make it look as though
someone else had stolen them. You bought a fake necklace, and you
arranged for it to be found in the maid’s bed. You knew that would
point the suspicion towards her. Then you waited for a few hours,
and you put the real pearls in the chambermaid’s box. You knew
that would clinch the matter.”

“But how did I get into the chambermaid’s room?”

“Through the door that led from your wife’s room. You unbolted it
from this side, and then you went through into the next apartment,
which happened to be vacant. From there you could easily get into
the corridor and into the chambermaid’s room.”

“But the door was bolted on the other side as well!”

“Only when someone was in the room, monsieur. When the room was
vacant, it was only bolted on this side.”

Mr. Opalsen was silent for a moment. He looked very pale.

“It’s a lie!” he said at last. “A wicked lie!”

“Is it, monsieur? Then perhaps you can explain this?”

Poirot held out a small piece of paper.

“What is it?” asked Mr. Opalsen.

“It is a receipt, monsieur. A receipt for a fake pearl necklace,
bought by you at a shop in London two weeks ago.”

Mr. Opalsen stared at the paper. His face went white.

“How—how did you get this?” he whispered.

“I have my methods, monsieur,” said Poirot. “And now, if you will
be so good as to come with me to the police station——”

Mr. Opalsen did not move. He stood staring at the paper for a long
time. Then, suddenly, his shoulders slumped.

“All right,” he said. “I’ll come. I—I didn’t think you’d find
out.”

“Hercule Poirot finds out everything, monsieur,” said Poirot.

He turned to me.

“Well, Hastings, what do you think of that?”

“I’m amazed,” I said. “Simply amazed. I never would have suspected
him.”

“No,” said Poirot. “That is because you do not use your little grey
cells. If you did, you would see that the simplest explanation is
usually the right one.”

We led Mr. Opalsen down the stairs and out of the hotel. At the
police station, Poirot explained the whole matter to the inspector,
who was even more amazed than I had been.

“Well, Mr. Poirot,” he said, “I must take my hat off to you. You’re
a clever one, and no mistake.”

“I am Hercule Poirot,” said my friend. “And now, Hastings, let us
go and have some tea. I am very thirsty.”

As we walked back to the hotel, I asked him one more question.

“What about the reference?” I said. “The one for the chambermaid?”

“Oh, that?” said Poirot. “That was quite true. There was no such
person as Mrs. Pendleton. The chambermaid had made it up herself.
She was not a very honest girl, I’m afraid. But she was not a
thief—at least, not in this case.”

“And Célestine?”

“Célestine is a very good girl. She was only a little bit foolish.
She should not have left the room, even for a few seconds.”

“Well,” I said, “it’s a very strange case.”

“Yes,” said Poirot. “A very strange case indeed. But it just shows
you, Hastings—it just shows you that you should never judge by
appearances.”

We reached the hotel and went into the lounge. Poirot sat down and
ordered tea.

“And now, Hastings,” he said, “let us talk of something else. Let
us talk of—Brighton!”

I smiled. It was good to see Poirot his old self again.

“Yes,” I said. “Let’s talk of Brighton.”

And we did.

The End.

The inspector departed with his prize. After the police had gone,
the atmosphere became less tense. Mr. Opalsen looked a little
dubious, but Poirot was all smiles.

“Well, monsieur, let me congratulate you on the recovery of your
jewels. It has been a pleasure to be of any assistance to you.”

“You are very kind,” returned Opalsen. “And I hope you will let
me offer you some little acknowledgment of your services?”

Poirot waved his hand.

“No, no, I entreat you. My friend Hastings here, he would tell you
it is against my principles. I work for the love of the chase—for
the exercise of my little grey cells. It is a hobby, you understand?”

Opalsen bowed.

“Still, if there is anything I can do for you——”

Poirot hesitated.

“Well, since you are so kind—I should like to have a look at the
jewel-case.”

Opalsen brought it from the drawer and handed it to him. Poirot
turned it over and over, examining it with the greatest care. Then
he looked up at Mr. Opalsen.

“And the key, monsieur?”

Opalsen produced it from his pocket.

“My wife had it on a chain round her neck, but I’ve got the spare
one here.”

Poirot compared the two keys for a moment, then handed them back.

“A simple lock, as the inspector said,” he remarked. “But there
is one thing that interests me. The necklace was in the jewel-case
when you went down to dinner, madame?”

“Oh, yes!” cried Mrs. Opalsen.

“And you are certain it was there when you came up?”

“But I didn’t see it. I only saw it _wasn’t_ there!”

Poirot nodded.

“Quite so. And now, madame, if I may be so bold, I will ask you
a very strange question. Where did you first buy this necklace?”

Mr. Opalsen answered for her.

“I bought it in Paris two years ago.”

“From a reputable firm, monsieur?”

“One of the best in the Rue de la Paix.”

“I see.” Poirot’s eyes were twinkling. “Well, I will not detain
you any longer. I have been most interested.”

He bowed himself out of the room. I followed him, and we walked
slowly down the corridor.

“Well, Poirot,” I said, “I must say you’ve been very helpful.
If it hadn’t been for your experiment with the watch, the
chambermaid might have been suspected.”

“My friend,” said Poirot, “I am not so sure of that.”

“What do you mean?”

“I mean, Hastings, that things are not always what they seem.
You have a great deal to learn.”

“But the maid had the pearls!”

“Precisely. She had them. But how did they get there?”

“Why, she put them there, of course!”

“Perhaps. But consider, Hastings. The maid is no fool. If she
had stolen the pearls, would she have hidden them in her own bed?
A place where they were certain to be found?”

“She may have been interrupted.”

“Perhaps. But it is not likely. And there is another thing. Did
you notice the necklace, Hastings?”

“Well, it looked very fine to me.”

“To you, yes. But to me—well, I have seen many pearls.”

“You don’t mean to say they were false?”

“I will not go so far as that. But I will say that they were not
the pearls I should have expected a man like Mr. Opalsen to buy
for his wife. They were—how shall I put it?—a little too perfect.”

I stared at him.

“You mean they were a copy?”

“It is possible. But let us go and have another look at that
chambermaid.”

“Why?”

“Because, Hastings, I am interested in her. She is a very pretty
girl—is she not?”

“I didn’t notice particularly.”

“Ah, you have no eye for beauty! But I, who am an artist, I notice
these things. And she has a very interesting face—very interesting
indeed.”

We found the girl in the linen-room. She looked up at us with a
start.

“Well, my dear,” said Poirot, “and how are you feeling after your
unpleasant experience?”

“I’m all right, thank you, sir.”

“You are a very brave girl,” said Poirot. “Most girls would have
been in hysterics.”

“I’ve nothing to be afraid of,” she said defiantly.

“I am sure of that,” said Poirot. “And now, if you will be so
kind, I should like you to show me the way to the room next to
Mrs. Opalsen’s.”

“The one that’s bolted, sir?”

“Yes.”

“It’s empty at present, sir. I’ll get the key.”

She fetched the key and led us to the room. It was a replica of
the one we had just left, but the furniture was arranged
differently. Poirot walked across to the door that led into Mrs.
Opalsen’s room.

“This is the door, is it not?”

“Yes, sir.”

Poirot tried the bolt. It was shot home. He looked at it for a
moment, then turned to the girl.

“And who occupied this room last night?”

“A gentleman, sir. He left this morning.”

“I see. And his name?”

“I don’t know, sir. I’ll find out for you.”

She went away and returned in a few minutes.

“The name was Mr. Robinson, sir.”

“Robinson,” murmured Poirot. “A very common name. And he left
this morning, you say?”

“Yes, sir.”

“I see. Well, thank you very much.”

He gave her a tip and we went back to our own rooms.

“What on earth are you after, Poirot?” I asked.

“I am looking for a thief, Hastings.”

“But the thief has been caught!”

“Has he? I wonder.”

“But the pearls were found in the maid’s bed!”

“Exactly. In the maid’s bed. But how did they get there?”

“I told you—she put them there herself!”

“And I told you—it was a very stupid place to hide them. No,
Hastings, I think there is something more in this than meets the
eye.”

He sat down in an armchair and closed his eyes. I knew he was
thinking, and I did not disturb him. After a few minutes he opened
his eyes and looked at me.

“Hastings,” he said, “I have a little task for you.”

“What is it?”

“I want you to go down to the office and find out if there is a
man named Robinson staying in the hotel.”

“But the girl said he’d left!”

“I know. But I want you to make sure. And if he has left, find out
where he went.”

“All right,” I said.

I went down to the office and made inquiries. The clerk told me
that Mr. Robinson had indeed left that morning, and had given an
address in London.

I went back and told Poirot.

“I see,” he said. “And did you find out anything else about him?”

“No. He seems to have been a very ordinary sort of person.”

“I see. Well, Hastings, I think we will go to London.”

“To London? But we’ve only just come!”

“I know. But I have a feeling that we shall find what we are
looking for in London.”

“But what about the Opalsens?”

“Oh, they will be all right. I have left a little note for Mr.
Opalsen. And now, let us pack our bags.”

I was bewildered, but I knew it was no use arguing with Poirot
when he had that look in his eyes. We packed our bags and took
the next train to London.

When we arrived at Victoria, Poirot called a taxi.

“Where to?” I asked.

“To the address Mr. Robinson gave at the hotel.”

The taxi took us to a quiet street in Bloomsbury. We stopped in
front of a small, neat house. Poirot got out and rang the bell.

The door was opened by a middle-aged woman.

“Is Mr. Robinson in?” asked Poirot.

“No, sir. He’s out at present.”

“Do you know when he will be back?”

“I couldn’t say, sir. He’s only just moved in.”

“I see. Well, perhaps we could wait for him?”

“I’m afraid not, sir. I’m just going out myself.”

“I see. Well, thank you very much.”

He turned away and we walked back to the taxi.

“What now?” I asked.

“Now, Hastings, we will go to my rooms in Jane Street. I have
some thinking to do.”

We went back to Poirot’s rooms, and he spent the rest of the
evening in deep thought. I tried to talk to him, but he only
shook his head and told me to be quiet.

The next morning he was up early.

“Hastings,” he said, “I want you to go to the shop of a certain
jeweller in Bond Street. I will give you the address. I want you
to show him this.”

He handed me a small piece of paper with a drawing on it.

“What is it?” I asked.

“It is a sketch of the necklace Mrs. Opalsen lost. I want you to
ask him if he has ever seen it before.”

“But Poirot, he’s a jeweller! He must have seen hundreds of
necklaces like that.”

“Not like that, Hastings. Not like that. Believe me.”

I went to the jeweller’s and showed him the sketch. He looked at
it for a moment, then his face changed.

“Where did you get this?” he asked.

“A friend of mine asked me to show it to you,” I said.

“I see. Well, your friend is very clever. This is a sketch of a
very famous necklace. It was stolen from a lady in Paris about a
year ago.”

I was thunderstruck.

“Stolen?” I gasped.

“Yes. It was never recovered. The lady was very distressed about
it.”

“And you are sure this is the same necklace?”

“I am positive. I made it myself.”

I thanked him and hurried back to Poirot.

“Poirot!” I cried. “You were right! The necklace was stolen!”

“I know,” said Poirot calmly.

“But how did you know?”

“I did not know. I only suspected. And now, Hastings, we must
go back to Brighton.”

“To Brighton? But we’ve only just come from there!”

“I know. But the play is not yet over. And the actors are waiting
for us.”

We took the train back to Brighton and went straight to the Grand
Metropolitan. Poirot asked to see Mr. Opalsen.

We were shown up to his room. He was sitting at a table, looking
very morose.

“Well, Mr. Poirot,” he said, “what can I do for you?”

“I have come to tell you that I have found your necklace,” said
Poirot.

Opalsen jumped up.

“You have? Where is it?”

“It is in a very safe place,” said Poirot. “But before I give it
to you, I want to tell you a little story.”

“A story? What do you mean?”

“Listen, monsieur. About a year ago, a very famous necklace was
stolen from a lady in Paris. It was a very beautiful necklace,
composed of the finest pearls in the world. The thief was never
caught, and the necklace was never recovered.”

Opalsen’s face had gone very pale.

“What has this to do with me?” he asked.

“A great deal, monsieur. Because that necklace was the one you
bought for your wife.”

“I—I don’t know what you’re talking about!”

“Oh, yes you do, monsieur. You bought it from a man in Paris—a
man named Robinson.”

Opalsen sank back into his chair.

“How did you know?” he whispered.

“I did not know. I guessed. And then I made some inquiries. It
was a very clever scheme, monsieur. You bought the stolen necklace
for a fraction of its value, and then you insured it for its full
worth. Then you arranged for it to be stolen again, so that you
could claim the insurance money.”

“It’s a lie!” cried Opalsen.

“Is it, monsieur? Then perhaps you can explain how the pearls
came to be in the maid’s bed?”

“She stole them, of course!”

“No, monsieur. She did not steal them. You put them there yourself.”

“I? That’s ridiculous!”

“Is it? You were the only person who could have done it. You had
the key to the jewel-case, and you knew where the maid’s bed was.
You waited until the room was empty, and then you slipped the
pearls into the bed. You knew they would be found, and you knew
the maid would be blamed. It was a very neat little plan.”

“But why should I do such a thing?”

“Because, monsieur, you needed the money. You told me yourself
that money was ‘confoundedly tight in the City.’ And you knew that
the insurance company would pay up without any trouble if the
thief was caught.”

Opalsen was silent for a moment. Then he looked up at Poirot.

“You are very clever, Mr. Poirot,” he said. “But you have no proof.”

“Oh, but I have, monsieur. I have the word of the jeweller who
made the necklace. And I have the word of the chambermaid, who
saw you come out of the maid’s room yesterday morning.”

“The chambermaid? But she said she didn’t see anything!”

“That was because she was afraid. But when I talked to her, she
told me the truth. She saw you, monsieur. And she will testify
against you in court.”

Opalsen’s face crumbled.

“All right,” he said. “You’ve got me. What are you going to do?”

“I am going to call the police,” said Poirot.

And that was the end of the case. Mr. Opalsen was arrested and
charged with insurance fraud and theft. The pearls were returned
to their rightful owner in Paris, and Mrs. Opalsen—well, she was
a very unhappy woman for a while, but I have no doubt she soon
found another hobby to occupy her time.

As for Poirot, he was as modest as ever.

“It was nothing, Hastings,” he said, as we sat in the train on
our way back to London. “A very simple case. But it shows you
that even the cleverest criminals make mistakes.”

“But Poirot,” I said, “how did you know it was Opalsen? I mean,
it could have been the maid, or the chambermaid.”

“My friend, I knew it was not the maid because she would not have
been so stupid as to hide the pearls in her own bed. And I knew it
was not the chambermaid because she had no motive. But Mr. Opalsen—he
had a motive, and he had the opportunity. And when I saw the
necklaces—well, I knew then that there was something wrong.”

“But how did you know they were stolen?”

“Because, Hastings, pearls like that are not found every day.
They were too perfect—too beautiful. And when I heard that Mr.
Opalsen had bought them in Paris—well, I began to put two and two
together.”

“You are a marvel, Poirot,” I said.

“No, no, Hastings. I am only a man who uses his little grey
cells. And now, if you will excuse me, I think I will have a
little nap. It has been a very tiring weekend.”

And with that, he closed his eyes and was soon fast asleep.

“The jewels are returned—is it not so?” said Poirot smoothly. “All
is well. But I—I have the so great curiosity. Monsieur,”—he turned
to the inspector—“it would be a great favour if you would allow
me to have a few words with the maid. It is possible, I think,
that she may be induced to—er—confess.”

The inspector shook his head.

“Not a hope. We have her in the next room now, and she’s as
obstinate as a mule. Still, if you wish——”

“You are very kind, monsieur.”

Poirot followed the inspector into the adjoining room, and after
a few moments they both returned. Célestine was with them, still
sobbing, but no longer defiant.

“The girl insists she’s innocent,” the inspector said with a
shrug. “It’s the usual story. But she admits she has no idea how
the necklace got into her bed.”

He turned to Mrs. Opalsen.

“And now, madam, we’ll have to be moving. If you’ll just give me
the necklace for a few minutes while I make a note of it.”

Mrs. Opalsen held it out reluctantly.

“I suppose you must,” she said. “But mind you don’t lose it.”

“Don’t you worry about that, madam.”

The inspector took it and walked over to the dressing-table. He
stood for a moment with his back to us, then turned.

“Well, that’s that. If you’ll just sign this, sir.” He held out
a paper to Mr. Opalsen.

The latter complied, and the official with his subordinate left
the room. Mrs. Opalsen sank into a chair, still weeping.

“To think of it!” she moaned. “And I’ve always been so kind to
her. I can’t believe she’d do it.”

Mr. Opalsen patted her shoulder.

“There, there, my dear. Don’t take it so much to heart. After
all, you’ve got the necklace back. That’s the main thing.”

Poirot was standing by the window, looking out. Suddenly he
turned.

“Monsieur,” he said, addressing Mr. Opalsen. “You have, I think,
the so great good sense. Would it be possible for me to have a
word with you—privately?”

“Certainly. If you will come into the sitting-room.”

He led the way, and Poirot and I followed him. Mr. Opalsen closed
the door and looked at Poirot inquiringly.

“Well, Mr. Poirot?”

“Monsieur,” began the little Belgian, “I will be brief. I have
not the so great confidence in the police of your country.”

“Eh? What’s that?”

“They are—how shall I say it?—too simple. They see what is before
their eyes, and they look no further. It is not so that Hercule
Poirot works.”

“I see. And what have you found out?”

“Monsieur, I have reason to believe that the necklace found in the
maid’s bed is—how you say?—a ‘dud’.”

“What!” Mr. Opalsen’s face went white.

“It is as I say. The real necklace is elsewhere.”

“But—but—how do you know?”

“I have my methods. And, monsieur, I will go further. I will tell
you where it is.”

“Where?”

“In the pocket of that inspector of police who has just left the
room.”

“The inspector!” Mr. Opalsen gasped.

“Exactly. It was a very clever trick. He is no inspector of police,
but a very dangerous and well-known thief. He knew the necklace was
stolen, and he knew it would be searched for. He came here with his
accomplice, who was dressed as a police searcher. It was she who
found the necklace—which was already in her possession—and placed
it in the maid’s bed while she was searching her. Then the
so-called inspector ‘found’ it, and—presto!—he has walked off with
the real one, leaving a worthless imitation in its place.”

“But—but—this is incredible!” cried Mr. Opalsen. “The man was in
uniform.”

“It is not difficult to obtain a uniform,” said Poirot dryly. “And
his subordinate—the plain-clothes man—was also an accomplice. They
have managed it very well.”

“But what are we to do? We must stop them! We must call the police!”

“Wait, monsieur. I have already taken my precautions. I have
telephoned to the real police, and they are even now on their way.
But there is one thing I must ask of you. You must not say a word
to your wife. It would only agitate her further.”

“I see. Yes, you are right. But—but—are you sure of all this?”

“Monsieur, I am Hercule Poirot. I am never wrong.”

And with a little bow, Poirot led the way back into the bedroom.

“Oh, let him take it, Ed!” cried his wife. “I’d feel safer if he
did. I shouldn’t sleep a wink thinking some one else might try and
get hold of it. That wretched girl! And I would never have believed
it of her.”

“There, there, my dear, don’t take on so.”

I felt a gentle pressure on my arm. It was Poirot.

“Shall we slip away, my friend? I think our services are no longer
needed.”

Once outside, however, he hesitated, and then, much to my surprise,
he remarked:

“I should rather like to see the room next door.”

“What, the room on the other side? But I thought you said it was
bolted on both sides?”

“So it is. But I should like to see it for all that.”

He turned back and spoke to the inspector.

“I may go into the next room?”

“If you like, monsieur. It’s empty, but the door is locked from the
corridor.”

He produced his key-ring. Poirot and I followed him.

The room was exactly similar to the one we had just left, and
presented a most ordinary appearance. The door connecting with
the Opalsens’ suite was, as Poirot had said, bolted on both sides.

Poirot walked to it and drew back the bolt.

“Wait!” he said, and went out.

He entered the Opalsens’ room, and I heard him drawing the bolt on
the other side of the door.

“_Maintenant_!” he cried, when he returned.

He tried the handle, but the door refused to move.

“You see?” he said. “It is as the inspector says. Bolted on both
sides.”

I looked at him in some perplexity.

“Then how do you think it could have been done?”

“I don’t think it, my friend. I _know_.”

He looked round the room.

“There is no fireplace here,” he remarked. “Only the steam-radiator.
Nothing could be hidden there. And the bed—not much chance of
hiding anything there. It is a brass one, with no hangings. No,
I don’t see any place of concealment here.”

“Then you think the pearls are not in this room?”

“I am sure they are not.”

“Then why are you looking for them?”

“Because, my friend, I am not looking for the pearls.”

“What are you looking for, then?”

“A little piece of soap.”

“A piece of soap!” I gasped. “What on earth for?”

“Oh, just a whim of mine—a little whim! Ah, here it is.”

He picked up a small fragment of soap from the floor near the door,
and looked at it with an expression of intense satisfaction.

“But what does it mean?” I asked.

“It means, my friend, that I was right.”

“Right about what?”

“Everything!”

He led the way back into the corridor.

“Let us find our host and hostess,” he said. “I think they will
be in the lounge.”

We found the Opalsens there. Mr. Opalsen was looking somewhat
gloomy, but his wife had recovered her spirits.

“I’m just telling Ed,” she said, “that it’s all been a lesson to
me. I shall never leave my jewels about again.”

“A very wise resolution, madame,” said Poirot. “And now, if you
will permit me, I should like to ask you one or two questions.”

“Why, certainly, Mr. Poirot.”

“The necklace—it was composed of very fine pearls, I believe?”

“Magnificent! The colour was perfect.”

“And the clasp?”

“A large emerald, surrounded by diamonds.”

“Ah!” Poirot nodded. “And the pearls themselves—were they all of
the same size?”

“No, they were graduated. The largest was in the middle, and they
got smaller towards the ends.”

“I see. And you are quite sure that the necklace the inspector
showed you just now was your own?”

“Why, of course! I’d know it anywhere.”

“You are quite sure?”

“Of course I am! Why, what do you mean?”

“Only this, madame.” Poirot leaned forward, and his voice sank to
a whisper. “_The necklace the inspector found in the maid’s bed was
a faked one_!”

Mrs. Opalsen fell back in her chair.

“A fake! You mean—it wasn’t my necklace at all?”

“Exactly, madame.”

“But—but how do you know?”

“Because, madame, the real necklace is at this moment in the
possession of your husband.”

There was a moment’s dead silence. Mr. Opalsen went a dull, brick-red
colour.

“What—what the devil do you mean?” he stammered.

“I mean, monsieur, that it is you who have robbed your wife.”

“It’s a lie!” shouted Opalsen. “A damned lie! Why, the man’s mad!”

“I think not,” said Poirot quietly. “Consider the facts. You were
in need of money. You told my friend Hastings that money was ‘tight
in the City.’ You decided to stage a robbery. You had a duplicate
key made for the jewel-case. You also had a duplicate necklace
made—a clever imitation. You waited until your wife went down to
dinner. Then you went up to the room, opened the jewel-case, took
out the real necklace, and put the fake one in its place. Then you
went down to dinner as though nothing had happened. You knew that
your wife would discover the loss when she went to fetch the pearls
to show me. You also knew that the maid would be the first person
to be suspected. You had already hidden the fake necklace in her
bed, so that when the police searched the room they would be sure
to find it. The fact that the maid had never left the room would
make her guilt seem all the more certain. It was a very clever
plot, monsieur—very clever indeed.”

“It’s a lie!” repeated Opalsen, but his voice lacked conviction.

“Then how do you explain the piece of soap?” asked Poirot.

“The soap? What soap?”

“The piece of soap I found in the next room. You used it to rub
the bolts of the door between the two rooms, so that they would
slide easily and silently. You entered the room from the corridor,
drew back the bolt on your side, and then, with the help of a small
pair of pliers, you turned the bolt on the other side through the
keyhole. It is a well-known trick. Then you entered your wife’s
room, substituted the necklaces, and returned the way you came,
bolting the door behind you. It was very simple—once one had
thought of it.”

Mr. Opalsen made a sudden movement, but Poirot was too quick for
him.

“It is no use, monsieur. I have already informed the manager, and
he is waiting outside with the police. I think you had better go
quietly.”

For a moment Opalsen looked as though he would show fight; then his
shoulders slumped, and he buried his face in his hands.

“I had to do it!” he groaned. “I was desperate. If I couldn’t get
the money, I was ruined.”

Mrs. Opalsen burst into tears.

“Oh, Ed!” she sobbed. “How could you? And to think I should have
suspected poor Célestine!”

The manager and the police inspector entered the room, and Mr.
Opalsen was led away.

Mrs. Opalsen turned to Poirot.

“I don’t know how to thank you, Mr. Poirot. If it hadn’t been for
you, I should never have known the truth.”

“It was nothing, madame,” said Poirot, with a modest wave of his
hand. “A mere matter of the little grey cells.”

“But how did you know it was him?” I asked, as we walked back to
our own room.

“My friend,” said Poirot, “there were several things that pointed
that way. In the first place, there was the question of the time.
As I demonstrated, it would have been impossible for the maid to
have hidden the pearls in the time at her disposal. Then there was
the fact that the necklace was found so easily. A real thief would
have hidden it more securely. And finally, there was the husband’s
manner. He was too anxious to believe in the maid’s guilt. It is
always a mistake to be too anxious, Hastings.”

“And the soap?” I asked.

“Ah, the soap! That was the finishing touch. I knew that the door
must have been opened somehow, and the soap provided the clue. It
is a small thing, but it is the small things that count.”

He sighed.

“And now, my friend, let us go to bed. I find that these cases of
domestic treachery are always very fatiguing.”

I looked at him with admiration.

“Poirot,” I said, “you are a genius!”

“I know it,” said Poirot simply. “It is a great misfortune.”

“The room next door? But why?” I asked in surprise. “It was bolted
on both sides.”

“Yes, yes. But, all the same, I have a little curiosity.”

He tried the handle of the door. To my surprise it opened.

“Why, it’s not bolted!” I cried.

“It was bolted,” said Poirot calmly. “The inspector said so. But
the bolt was on _our_ side. We have opened it ourselves.”

He looked into the room. It was a well-appointed bedroom, similar
to the one we had just left. Poirot walked across to the windows.

“Aha!” he said. “They are wide open. That is where she did not
look.”

“Who?”

“The chambermaid.”

“But what does that matter? The necklace was found in the maid’s
bed.”

“Was it?”

“Of course it was!” I retorted. “We saw it.”

“I do not doubt that, my friend. It was found. It is a fact. But
the fact remains—the necklace was there!”

“Of course it was there!” I said again. “The inspector found it.”

“Yes, yes. But the fact remains—the necklace was there.”

“What _do_ you mean?”

“Only that I find it very interesting,” said Poirot. “And now, if
you please, I should like to see the chambermaid.”

“The chambermaid? But the inspector said she was all right.”

“_Évidemment_. It is for that reason I should like to see her.
A woman who is ‘all right’—it is a rarity, is it not so? And
besides, I want to ask her a question.”

“What question?”

“That, my friend, is my own little secret. But I think she can
answer it for me.”

We found the chambermaid in the passage. She was still very much
upset, but Poirot’s manner was so sympathetic that she soon regained
her composure.

“Tell me, my girl,” he said, “is it you who have charge of this
room?” He indicated the one we had just left.

“Yes, sir.”

“Then you must have seen many things. For example, have you seen
any one else go into Mrs. Opalsen’s room lately?”

“Only the maid, sir, and—well, once or twice the master.”

“Mr. Opalsen?”

“Yes, sir.”

“And no one else?”

“No, sir.”

“Not even a page-boy?”

“No, sir.”

“Thank you.”

Poirot turned away.

“Well, Hastings, what do you think of it?”

“I don’t know what to think,” I said. “It seems a very simple case.”

“It is simple,” said Poirot, “very simple. So simple that it might
almost be too simple.”

“You mean you think the maid is innocent?”

“I do not say that. But there are one or two little things that
I should like to clear up.”

“Such as?”

“Such as the question of the insured pearls.”

“But Mr. Opalsen said they were insured.”

“Yes, yes. But I should like to know for how much.”

“I don’t see that that has anything to do with it.”

“Do you not? Well, perhaps not. But it is an interesting point.
And there is another.”

“What is that?”

“The question of the chambermaid.”

“But you said herself she was ‘all right’!”

“So I did. But all the same, she is an interesting study.”

“I don’t understand you at all.”

“Never mind, my friend. Let us go and have a little walk on the
front. The night air will do us good.”

As we walked along, Poirot was very silent. He seemed to be deep
in thought. Suddenly he stopped.

“Hastings, I have it!”

“Have what?”

“The solution! It is so simple—so very simple!”

“You know who stole the pearls?”

“I know who stole the pearls, and I know where they are.”

“But the inspector has them!”

“Has he? Are you sure of that?”

“Of course he has! We saw him take them.”

“We saw him take _a_ necklace. But was it _the_ necklace?”

“What do you mean?”

“Wait and see, my friend. Wait and see.”

He would say no more, and we returned to the hotel in silence.
As we entered the hall, we saw Mr. Opalsen coming towards us.
He looked very much agitated.

“Mr. Poirot,” he cried, “I’ve been looking for you everywhere.
A most extraordinary thing has happened.”

“What is it?”

“The pearls—they are gone again!”

“Gone again?” I cried. “But the inspector had them!”

“Yes, yes. But they have been stolen from him!”

“Stolen from the inspector? But how?”

“I don’t know. He was taking them to the police station in a
cab, and when he got there they were gone!”

“This is indeed serious,” said Poirot gravely. “But do not
