distress yourself, monsieur. I think I can lay my hands on them.”

“You can? Where are they?”

“That I cannot tell you for the moment. But if you will come
with me to the manager’s office, I think we may be able to
throw some light on the matter.”

In the manager’s office we found the inspector and his two
assistants. They were looking very crestfallen.

“I can’t understand it,” the inspector was saying. “I had them in
my pocket one minute, and the next they were gone.”

“It is very simple,” said Poirot. “You were robbed.”

“Robbed? But who could have robbed me?”

“The person who stole the pearls in the first instance.”

“But she’s in custody!”

“Is she? Are you sure of that?”

“Of course she is!”

“Well, we shall see. In the meantime, I should like to ask the
chambermaid one or two more questions.”

The chambermaid was sent for. When she entered the room, she
looked more frightened than ever.

“Now, my girl,” said Poirot kindly, “don’t be afraid. We only
want to know one or two things. You told me just now that you
had seen no one go into Mrs. Opalsen’s room except the maid
and Mr. Opalsen. Is that correct?”

“Yes, sir.”

“Are you quite sure?”

“Yes, sir.”

“Think again. Did you not see a page-boy go in once or twice?”

“A page-boy? No, sir.”

“Are you quite sure of that?”

“Yes, sir.”

“Then who was the boy I saw coming out of the room just now?”

“I don’t know, sir. I didn’t see any boy.”

“That is very strange,” said Poirot. “Very strange indeed.”

He turned to the manager.

“Have you a boy in your employ who is—shall we say—a little
shorter than the others?”

“No, sir. They are all about the same height.”

“I see. And have you any boy who has a—how shall I put it?—a
slight limp?”

“No, sir.”

“That is even more strange,” said Poirot. “For the boy I saw
had a very decided limp.”

Suddenly the inspector gave a cry.

“I have it! The boy with the limp! I saw him myself in the
hall just now!”

“You did?” cried Poirot. “Then why did you not stop him?”

“I didn't think anything of it at the time. I was too much
upset about the pearls.”

“Quick!” cried Poirot. “We must find him at once!”

We all rushed out into the hall. But the boy with the limp was
nowhere to be seen.

“He must have left the hotel,” said the inspector. “I’ll send
out a description at once.”

“Wait!” said Poirot. “I think I can save you the trouble.”

He walked over to the lift and rang the bell. When the lift
descended, he stepped inside.

“Which floor, sir?” asked the boy.

“The first floor,” said Poirot.

When we reached the first floor, Poirot stepped out and walked
straight to Mrs. Opalsen’s room. He knocked on the door. It was
opened by Mr. Opalsen.

“Any news?” he asked anxiously.

“I think so,” said Poirot. “If you will allow us to come in.”

We all entered the room. Poirot walked straight to the dressing-table
and opened the bottom drawer.

“Empty!” he said. “As I thought.”

He turned to Mr. Opalsen.

“Monsieur, I have a question to ask you. This necklace—was it
the only one your wife possessed?”

“The only one? No, she has several.”

“But this was the most valuable?”

“Yes, by far.”

“And it was insured for a large sum?”

“Yes, for fifty thousand pounds.”

“I see. And you were, I believe, in some financial difficulties?”

Mr. Opalsen’s face turned a deep red.

“What do you mean?” he demanded angrily.

“Only that I find it very interesting,” said Poirot. “And now,
if you please, I should like to see the chambermaid once more.”

The chambermaid was again sent for. When she entered the room,
Poirot went up to her and took her hand.

“My girl,” he said, “I want you to tell me the truth. Did you
see Mr. Opalsen go into his wife’s room this evening after
dinner?”

The girl hesitated.

“Yes, sir,” she said at last.

“And what did he do there?”

“I don’t know, sir. He was only there for a minute.”

“I see. And did you see him take anything out of the drawer?”

“I—I think so, sir. But I couldn't be sure.”

“Thank you. That is all I wanted to know.”

He turned to Mr. Opalsen.

“Monsieur, I am afraid I must ask you to accompany the inspector
to the police station.”

“What!” cried Opalsen. “You’re not going to arrest me?”

“I am afraid so,” said Poirot. “The evidence is very strong
against you.”

“But the pearls! What about the pearls?”

“I think you know where they are as well as I do,” said Poirot.

“I don’t know what you’re talking about!”

“Do you not? Then perhaps I can enlighten you. You stole the
pearls yourself, and you hid them in the maid’s bed, in order
to cast suspicion on her. Then, when the inspector found them,
you managed to steal them back from him in the cab.”

“It’s a lie!” cried Opalsen. “A wicked lie!”

“Is it?” said Poirot. “Then perhaps you can explain how this
came to be in your pocket?”

He reached into Opalsen’s pocket and pulled out a small leather
case. He opened it, and there, shimmering in the light, was the
pearl necklace!

For a moment there was a dead silence. Then Mr. Opalsen gave a
cry of despair and sank into a chair.

“I did it!” he moaned. “I did it! I was desperate for money,
and I thought if I could get the insurance money it would
save me.”

The inspector stepped forward and placed his hand on Opalsen’s
shoulder.

“I must ask you to come with me, sir,” he said.

As they left the room, Poirot turned to me with a smile.

“Well, Hastings, what do you think of my little case?”

“It was marvellous!” I said. “But how did you know it was he?”

“It was the chambermaid,” said Poirot. “When she said she had
seen him in the room, I knew it must be he. And then there
was the question of the insurance. It all fitted together
perfectly.”

“But the boy with the limp?” I asked. “What about him?”

“Oh, him!” said Poirot with a twinkle in his eye. “He was just
a little invention of my own, to see how the inspector would
react. It is always well to have a little imagination, is it
not so, my friend?”

And with a laugh, he led the way out of the room.

“But that’s no concern of ours!” I exclaimed.

“_Peut-être_—no. Yet I should like to see it. It is possible, I
suppose?”

“I daresay. The room’s empty, at all events.”

The hotel manager, who was in the passage, at once gave us the
required permission.

The room was similar in size and appearance to the one we had just
left. Poirot took the key from the manager, unlocked the door,
and we entered.

Poirot walked across at once to the door leading into the other
bedroom. It was bolted on this side, as well as the other. He
drew back the bolt and tried to open the door, but it remained
immovable.

“As I thought,” he said, with a nod. “Locked as well as bolted.
Now, let us look at the window.”

He walked across, and remained some time looking out. He then
re-bolted the door and handed the key to the manager.

“That is all, monsieur. I thank you.”

As we walked down the stairs, I asked him:

“Well, what did you find?”

“Nothing,” he replied laconically.

“Then what did you go for?”

“To confirm my own ideas, _mon cher_.”

“And have you confirmed them?”

“Entirely.”

“And they are——?”

“That, my friend, is for me to know and for you to find out.”

I was about to make a sharp retort when Poirot laid his hand on
my arm.

“_Pardon_, Hastings; I did not mean to be rude. But, indeed, there
is nothing to tell you. One thing, however, I will mention. Did
you notice anything peculiar about the necklace when I was looking
at it?”

“No,” I said, “except that it was very beautiful.”

“Is that all?”

“Yes.”

Poirot sighed.

“You have eyes, Hastings, but you see not! It is a great gift,
the imagination, but one must keep it under control. You did not
notice that one of the pearls—the large central one—was slightly
discoloured?”

“No, I can’t say I did.”

“Ah!” Poirot looked at me with a look of extreme compassion. “It
is a pity, a great pity.”

“Why?” I asked.

“Because, _mon ami_, if you had noticed it, you would have known
exactly where the pearls are at the present moment.”

“Why, the inspector’s got them!”

Poirot shook his head.

“No, no, Hastings; the inspector has not got them. The pearls he
has are—how shall I say it?—the false ones.”

“The false ones!” I cried. “But how could that be?”

“Because, my friend, the real pearls were never in the jewel-case
at all tonight.”

“Then where were they?”

“In the pocket of the person who stole them!”

“But who was that?”

“Ah!” said Poirot, with a twinkle in his eye. “That is the question.”

“But the maid?”

“Is as innocent as you are, Hastings.”

“Then why was the necklace found in her bed?”

“Because some one put it there, of course!”

“But who? The chambermaid?”

“No, no; she would have no motive. No, the person who put it there
wanted to throw suspicion on the maid.”

“But who could that be?”

“Think, Hastings; think!”

“I am thinking,” I said, “but I can’t see any light.”

“Wait, then,” said Poirot. “Wait, and you shall see.”

He refused to say another word, and we went to bed in a state of
unrelieved mystification.

The next morning, Poirot was up early. When I came down to breakfast
I found him already at the table. He was in high spirits.

“I have news for you, Hastings!” he cried. “The real pearls have
been found!”

“Found! Where?”

“In a very curious place. They were found in the stomach of a
large fish!”

“A fish!” I gasped. “But how on earth did they get there?”

“Ah, that is the mystery! But the facts are as I say. The fish
was caught this morning by a local fisherman, and when it was
opened the pearls were found inside.”

“But it’s incredible!” I exclaimed.

“Is it not?” said Poirot. “But it is true, nevertheless.”

“And where are they now?”

“In the hands of the police. They are being carefully cleaned and
examined.”

“And the thief?”

“The thief, my friend, is at this moment in this hotel!”

“In the hotel! Who is it?”

“That, Hastings, I cannot tell you—yet. But if you will come with
me to the Opalsens’ room in half an hour’s time, I think I can
promise you a surprise.”

I was only too ready to agree, and at the appointed time we made
our way to the first floor.

When we entered the room, we found Mr. and Mrs. Opalsen there,
together with the inspector. They all looked very much excited.

“Have you heard the news, Mr. Poirot?” cried Mrs. Opalsen. “My
pearls have been found! In a fish, of all things! Did you ever
hear anything so extraordinary?”

“It is indeed remarkable, madame,” said Poirot, with a grave face.
“And have you seen them?”

“Not yet. The inspector here says they’re being cleaned.”

“That is so, madam,” said the inspector. “We expect them every
minute.”

Even as he spoke, there was a knock at the door, and a policeman
entered. He carried a small box, which he handed to the inspector.

“The pearls, sir,” he said.

The inspector opened the box and took out the necklace. It was
indeed a beautiful thing, and as it lay in his hand the pearls
seemed to glow with a soft, iridescent light.

“Oh!” cried Mrs. Opalsen, reaching out her hand. “My pearls! My
beautiful pearls!”

“One moment, madame,” said Poirot, stepping forward. “Before you
take them, I should like to examine them—if the inspector will
permit?”

“Certainly, Mr. Poirot,” said the inspector, handing them to him.

Poirot took the necklace and walked over to the window. He
examined it closely for a few minutes, and then he turned back
to the room.

“These are the real pearls, madame?” he asked.

“Of course they are!” cried Mrs. Opalsen. “I should know them
anywhere.”

“And you, monsieur?” Poirot turned to Mr. Opalsen. “You are also
sure?”

“Quite sure,” said Opalsen. “There’s no doubt about it.”

“In that case,” said Poirot, “I have a very unpleasant duty to
perform.”

He walked over to the door and locked it. Then he turned to the
inspector.

“Inspector,” he said, “I must ask you to arrest this man!”

And he pointed his finger at—Mr. Opalsen!

There was a moment of absolute silence. Then Mr. Opalsen burst
into a loud laugh.

“Arrest me!” he cried. “What for, in Heaven’s name?”

“For the theft of your wife’s pearls,” said Poirot calmly.

“But that’s ridiculous!” cried Mrs. Opalsen. “Why should Ed steal
my pearls? He gave them to me himself!”

“That, madame, is exactly why he stole them,” said Poirot. “He
gave them to you, but he could not afford to let you keep them.
He is, as he told us himself, in financial difficulties. He needed
money—and he needed it badly. So he hit upon the plan of stealing
the pearls, and then claiming the insurance money.”

“But the fish!” I cried. “How do you explain the fish?”

“The fish, Hastings, was a little invention of my own,” said
Poirot, with a smile. “I knew that if the real pearls were produced,
the thief would be sure to claim them. So I arranged with the
police to pretend that they had been found in a fish. It was a
trap, my friend—and Mr. Opalsen walked straight into it!”

“But the necklace the inspector found in the maid’s bed?” I asked.

“That, as I told you, was a duplicate—a clever imitation which
Mr. Opalsen had had made. He put it in the maid’s bed to throw
suspicion on her. He knew that if she were arrested, no one would
think of looking any further for the thief.”

“But how did you know?” I asked.

“It was the discoloration of the pearl that gave me the clue,”
said Poirot. “I knew that Mrs. Opalsen’s pearls were perfect,
and when I saw that one of them was flawed, I knew at once that
it was a substitute. After that, it was easy. I knew that only
one person could have had the opportunity to substitute the false
necklace for the real one—and that person was Mr. Opalsen!”

For a moment, Mr. Opalsen looked as though he were going to
protest. Then, seeing the look in Poirot’s eyes, he suddenly
collapsed into a chair.

“You’re too clever for me, Mr. Poirot,” he said, with a groan.
“I admit it. I did it. I was desperate for money, and I didn’t
see any other way.”

“It is a pity,” said Poirot gravely. “A great pity. But justice
must be done.”

He turned to the inspector.

“He is yours, monsieur.”

As the inspector led Mr. Opalsen away, Mrs. Opalsen burst into
tears.

“Oh, Ed!” she sobbed. “How could you? How could you?”

Poirot went over to her and patted her hand.

“Do not distress yourself, madame,” he said gently. “Your pearls
are safe, and that is the main thing. As for your husband—well,
perhaps it is better that you should know the truth now than
later.”

And with a bow, he led me from the room.

“Well, Hastings,” he said, as we walked down the passage, “what
do you think of our little adventure?”

“I think you’re a genius, Poirot!” I cried. “A positive genius!”

Poirot smiled.

“It is nothing, my friend,” he said. “Nothing at all. It is merely
the result of using the little grey cells. And now, what do you
say to a little lunch? I think we have earned it!”

And as we went down the stairs, I couldn’t help thinking that
Hercule Poirot was indeed the most remarkable man I had ever
known.

“It’s empty, sir,” said the chambermaid, who was hovering about
on the landing. “The gentleman who had it only stayed one night.
He left this evening before dinner.”

“And what was his name?”

“Mr. Wentworth, sir.”

“Wentworth? Wentworth?” Poirot looked thoughtful.

“Well, anyway, what is his name to you?” I asked impatiently.

“Nothing, my friend—nothing! But I should like to see the room.”

He made a sign to the chambermaid, and she preceded us into the
apartment. It was a replica of the one we had just left, only the
bed was unmade. Poirot looked round him with interest. Suddenly he
pointed to the dressing-table.

“_Tiens_! A little piece of paper—in the drawer.”

He picked it up and held it for me to see. It was a fragment of
a label, such as is used for medicine bottles. On it was printed:
_One teaspoonful to be taken in water._

“And here is another,” said Poirot, pointing to the washstand.

He picked it up—a similar fragment.

“This would seem to show that Mr. Wentworth was an invalid,” he
said.

“Or his friend,” I suggested.

Poirot turned to the chambermaid.

“Did you see this Mr. Wentworth?”

“Yes, sir; he was a tall, dark gentleman, with a beard.”

“And his friend?”

“He hadn’t no friend, sir.”

“I see.” Poirot nodded.

“What are you driving at?” I asked, as we walked towards the lift.

“Nothing, Hastings. I am merely interested in a few details. For
instance, why did Mr. Wentworth leave before dinner? It was a
little unusual, was it not?”

“I don’t know. Perhaps he had to catch a train.”

“But why should he have had his medicine in the next room?”

“I suppose because he was staying there.”

“But he would have it in his _own_ room, would he not?”

“Well, wasn’t it his own room?”

“No, Hastings; he was in number 117, the room next door.”

“Well?”

“Well, this is 118.”

I stared at him.

“I don’t follow.”

“No? It is a little confusing, I admit. But we will descend. I
should like to have a few words with the manager.”

We found the manager in his office. Poirot was very polite to him.

“A most unfortunate occurrence, monsieur. A most distressing
occurrence.”

The manager spread his hands.

“What would you? It is the same everywhere. One cannot be too
careful. And with these people from the City—they are so
ostentatious! It is an invitation to the thief.”

“True, true. By the way, I am interested in the gentleman who
occupied number 117. Mr. Wentworth, I think he called himself.”

“He did, monsieur. A most quiet, unpretentious gentleman. He came
yesterday, and left this evening.”

“Before dinner?”

“Yes. He said he had to catch a train.”

“I see. And you have his address?”

“He didn’t leave one.”

“That is a pity.” Poirot paused. “I noticed two small pieces of
paper in his room—fragments of a medicine label. I suppose you
didn’t happen to see them?”

“No, monsieur. The chambermaid would have seen them, I expect, when
she was doing the room.”

“Ah, yes. I have already spoken to her. Well, I must not take up
your time. Good evening, monsieur.”

“Good evening, monsieur.”

The manager bowed us out.

“Well,” I said, as we regained the lounge, “it’s a clear case,
isn’t it? The maid stole the pearls and hid them in her bed.”

“It would seem so,” agreed Poirot. “And yet——”

“And yet what?”

“There are one or two things that puzzle me. For instance, why did
she hide them there? It was a very obvious place.”

“She hadn’t time to find a better one.”

“Perhaps. And why did she shriek so when she was being searched?”

“Guilty conscience, I suppose.”

“And why did she appeal to me?”

“Because she thought you’d be more sympathetic than the police.”

“Possibly. And why did she go into her own room twice?”

“She told us—to fetch a reel of cotton and some scissors.”

“Yes, but did she? I wonder.”

“My dear Poirot, what are you suggesting?”

“I am not suggesting anything, Hastings. I am only asking questions.
It is my way.”

He fell into a brown study. I did not disturb him. I knew from
experience that when he was in this mood it was best to leave him
alone.

Presently he looked up.

“Hastings, I should like to see that chambermaid again. Do you
think you could find her?”

“I expect so.”

I went in search of her, and found her in the corridor on the first
floor. She seemed a little surprised at seeing me again.

“Monsieur Poirot would like to speak to you for a moment,” I
explained.

She followed me to the lounge. Poirot rose as we approached.

“Sit down, mademoiselle. I will not keep you long. I only want to
ask you one or received two questions.”

“Yes, sir?”

“You were in the room, were you not, when Mrs. Opalsen came up?”

“Yes, sir.”

“And the maid—was she there too?”

“Yes, sir.”

“What was she doing?”

“She was sitting by the window, sir, working.”

“I see. And you—what were you doing?”

“I was turning down the beds, sir.”

“Did you notice the jewel-case?”

“No, sir.”

“You didn’t see Mrs. Opalsen go to the drawer and take it out?”

“No, sir. I was busy at the washstand.”

“I see. And you didn’t notice anything else?”

“No, sir.”

“Thank you, mademoiselle. That is all.”

The girl went away. Poirot looked at me.

“Well, Hastings?”

“Well, what? I don’t see that that helps us much.”

“On the contrary, it helps us a great deal.”

“In what way?”

“It confirms my suspicions.”

“Suspicions of whom?”

“Of the person who stole the pearls.”

“But the inspector found them in the maid’s bed!”

“Exactly. And that is what makes it so interesting.”

“I don’t understand.”

“No? Well, never mind. Let us go and have some more coffee.”

We went into the lounge and sat down. Poirot seemed to have
recovered his good spirits. He chatted away gaily about anything
and everything.

Suddenly he stopped.

“_Tiens!_ Who is this?”

A man had just entered the lounge and was looking about him. He
was a tall, dark man, with a beard.

“Mr. Wentworth!” I exclaimed.

“_Précisément!_” said Poirot. “Now I wonder what he wants.”

The man approached the reception desk and spoke to the clerk.
Then he turned and walked towards the lift.

Poirot rose.

“Come, Hastings. We must follow him.”

We reached the lift just as the doors were closing. Poirot caught
the lift-boy’s eye and tipped him a shilling. The doors opened
again, and we stepped inside.

The man with the beard looked at us with some surprise. He did not,
however, speak.

When we reached the first floor, he got out and walked along the
corridor. We followed him. He stopped at the door of number 117,
unlocked it, and went in.

Poirot waited a moment, then he knocked on the door.

“Come in!” said a voice.

We entered. The man with the beard was standing by the window. He
looked at us inquiringly.

“I ask your pardon, monsieur,” said Poirot, with a bow. “I think
I have the honour of speaking to Mr. Wentworth?”

“That is my name,” said the man. “What can I do for you?”

“I am Hercule Poirot,” said my friend. “Doubtless you have heard
of me?”

The man shook his head.

“I am afraid not.”

“That is a pity,” said Poirot. “It would have made things so much
easier. However, it cannot be helped. I have come to speak to you
about the pearls.”

“The pearls?” Mr. Wentworth looked bewildered. “What pearls?”

“The pearls of Mrs. Opalsen.”

“I don’t know what you’re talking about.”

“No? Then I will explain. Mrs. Opalsen’s pearls have been stolen.”

“Indeed? I am sorry to hear it. But what has that to do with me?”

“A great deal, monsieur. You see, they were found in your room.”

“In my room?” Mr. Wentworth stared at him. “But that is impossible!
I only left this evening before dinner.”

“Exactly. And it was after you left that they were found.”

“But where? Where were they found?”

“In the bed.”

“In the bed? But I didn’t have any pearls in my bed!”

“No? Then perhaps you can explain how they got there?”

“I haven’t the slightest idea.”

“I see. Well, perhaps you can tell me something else. Why did you
leave the hotel so suddenly this evening?”

“I had to catch a train.”

“And where were you going?”

“To London.”

“I see. And why did you come back?”

“I—I forgot something.”

“What did you forget?”

“A—a book.”

“I see. And where is this book?”

“I—I haven’t found it yet.”

“I see. Well, Mr. Wentworth, I am afraid I must ask you to come
with me to the manager’s office.”

“What for?”

“To meet the police.”

Mr. Wentworth’s face went white.

“The police? But I haven’t done anything!”

“That remains to be seen,” said Poirot grimly. “Come, monsieur.”

He took the man by the arm and led him out of the room. I followed,
wondering what it all meant.

When we reached the manager’s office, we found the inspector there.
He looked surprised at seeing us.

“Hullo!” he said. “Who’s this?”

“This is Mr. Wentworth,” said Poirot. “The gentleman who occupied
number 117.”

“Oh!” The inspector looked at him curiously. “And what’s he got to
do with it?”

“That is what I want to find out,” said Poirot. “He says he knows
nothing about the pearls.”

“Of course I don’t!” said Wentworth indignantly. “I never saw them
in my life.”

“Then perhaps you can explain this?” Poirot held out a piece of
paper.

It was the fragment of the medicine label he had found in the
room.

“Well?” said Wentworth. “What about it?”

“It is a label from a bottle of sleeping draught,” said Poirot.

“Well? What if it is? I was having some trouble with my nerves, and
my doctor prescribed it for me.”

“I see. And did you take any this evening?”

“Yes, before I left.”

“And did you give any to anyone else?”

“Of course not!”

“I see. Well, inspector, I think you had better search this
gentleman.”

The inspector did so, but he found nothing.

“There you are!” said Wentworth triumphantly. “I told you I hadn’t
got them.”

“Wait a moment,” said Poirot. “I haven’t finished yet. Inspector,
did you find any other pieces of paper in the room?”

“No.”

“That is curious. I found two. One on the dressing-table, and one
on the washstand.”

“Well, what of it?”

“Only this—that they were both fragments of the same label.”

“Well?”

“And that label was not from a bottle of sleeping draught.”

“Then what was it from?”

“It was from a bottle of—tincture of iodine.”

“Iodine?” I exclaimed. “What on earth for?”

“That is what I am going to show you,” said Poirot.

He turned to the manager.

“Monsieur, have you a bottle of iodine in the hotel?”

“Yes, monsieur. In the first-aid cabinet.”

“Would you be so good as to fetch it?”

The manager did so. Poirot took the bottle and a clean
handkerchief. He poured a little of the iodine onto the
handkerchief.

“Now,” he said, “watch.”

He rubbed the iodine onto the pearls. To our horror, they turned a
dull, brownish colour.

“Good heavens!” cried Mrs. Opalsen, who had just entered the room.
“What are you doing to my pearls?”

“I am showing you that they are not pearls at all,” said Poirot.

“Not pearls?”

“No. they are—paste.”

“Paste?”

“Yes. Imitation pearls. Very good ones, I admit, but imitation
nevertheless.”

Mrs. Opalsen sank into a chair.

“But—but how can that be? They were real enough when I bought them.”

“Exactly,” said Poirot. “And they were real enough when you put
them in your jewel-case this evening.”

“Then—then who changed them?”

“That is what I am going to tell you,” said Poirot.

He looked round the room.

“The person who changed the pearls was—Mr. Opalsen.”

“Ed!” cried his wife. “You? Oh, Ed, how could you?”

Mr. Opalsen did not answer. He stood there, his face working.

“Yes,” said Poirot. “Mr. Opalsen was in need of money. He told us
so himself this evening. He knew that the pearls were insured for
a large sum. So he decided to steal them, and then claim the
insurance money.”

“But how did he do it?” I asked.

“It was very simple. He had a duplicate key to the jewel-case.
While his wife was downstairs, he went up to the room, opened the
case, took out the real pearls, and put the imitation ones in
their place. Then he went down to dinner.”

“But what about the maid?”

“He knew that she was in the room, so he had to find a way of
getting her out of it. He did that by giving her a small dose of
the sleeping draught in her coffee. That is why she was so
_distrait_ after dinner.”

“But she didn’t leave the room!”

“No, but she fell asleep. And while she was asleep, the chambermaid
came in to turn down the beds. She saw the jewel-case in the drawer,
and she couldn’t resist the temptation. She took the pearls—the
imitation ones, of course—and hid them in the maid’s bed. She
thought that if they were found there, the maid would be blamed.”

“But why did Mr. Opalsen call you in?”

“Because he wanted to make sure that the robbery was discovered
as soon as possible. He knew that if I was there, I would be sure
to find out about it. He didn’t realize, of course, that I would
also find out about the imitation pearls.”

“But how did you find out?”

“By the iodine. You see, iodine turns real pearls black, but it
turns imitation ones brown. I noticed a small stain on one of the
pearls when I examined them, and I suspected the truth. That is
why I looked for the iodine bottle.”

“And Mr. Wentworth?”

“He had nothing to do with it. He was just a convenient scapegoat.
Mr. Opalsen knew that he was leaving the hotel, so he planted the
iodine bottle in his room to make it look as though he was the
thief.”

“But how did he get into the room?”

“The door was bolted on the other side, but it was not locked.
He simply unbolted it and walked in.”

“I see,” I said. “It was a very clever plot.”

“Yes,” said Poirot. “But not clever enough for Hercule Poirot.”

He turned to Mr. Opalsen.

“Well, monsieur? What have you to say for yourself?”

Mr. Opalsen did not answer. He just stood there, his head bowed.

“I think,” said Poirot, “that we had better leave him to the
police.”

And with a bow, he led us out of the room.

The case was over. The pearls were recovered—at least, the real ones
were, for Mr. Opalsen had them in his pocket. He was arrested and
duly sentenced. Mrs. Opalsen eventually got her pearls back, and
the maid was cleared of all suspicion.

As for Poirot and myself, we returned to London the next day.

“Well, Poirot,” I said, as we sat in the train, “it was a very
interesting case.”

“Yes, Hastings. It was indeed. It shows that one should never judge
by appearances. The most unlikely person is often the one who is
guilty.”

“True,” I said. “True.”

And I settled back in my seat, thinking of all that had happened.

It had been a busy weekend, but a successful one. And thanks to
Hercule Poirot, justice had been done.

He spoke to the manager, and was at once admitted. It was a replica
of the Opalsens’ room. Poirot examined the door leading to it.

“As I thought,” he said. “The bolt is on this side also.”

He turned it, and tried the door. It was locked.

“I’ll ask for the key,” I suggested.

“No need, my friend. I have my little keys here.” He produced his
case of skeleton keys. “One of them is sure to fit.”

He tried two or three, and soon the door stood open.

“Aha!” He smiled as he noted a small scratch near the lock. “I am
not the only one, then, who uses the skeleton keys!”

He passed into the room. It was empty. The door into the corridor
was locked.

“Wait here, Hastings,” he said.

He slipped out into the corridor and disappeared. In a few minutes
he returned.

“I was right,” he murmured. “The other room is let to a Mr.
Robinson—not a very distinctive name, is it? But he is out at
present.”

I followed him out of the room, and he locked the door behind him.
Then he sighed.

“I’m afraid I’ve made a mistake, Hastings.”

“A mistake? Why, you’ve done nothing!”

“Exactly! That is what I meant. I should have acted sooner.
However——” He shrugged his shoulders. “I’m afraid we shall have to
go back to London to-morrow.”

“But—the pearls? You haven’t found them?”

“No,” said Poirot. “No, I haven’t found them.”

I was extremely disappointed. I had expected great things from
Poirot, and here he was, admitting defeat at the very start.

“But the inspector has them!” I cried.

“The inspector has—something,” said Poirot enigmatically.

He refused to say another word, and we went to bed.

Early the next morning I was awakened by Poirot’s voice.

“Hastings! Hastings! Wake up!”

I sat up and rubbed my eyes. Poirot was standing by my bedside,
fully dressed.

“What’s the matter?” I asked.

“Listen!” He held up his hand.

From the room below came a loud and continuous sound of sobbing.

“It’s Mrs. Opalsen,” said Poirot.

“What’s happened?”

“Her pearls have gone!”

“Gone? But the inspector had them!”

“Exactly! The inspector had them. But they were _not_ her pearls.”

“Not her pearls? What do you mean?”

“I mean that they were a very clever imitation—not worth fifty
pounds!”

I gasped.

“But—how do you know?”

“I told you I had seen many famous jewels, Hastings. And besides,
did I not examine them last night?”

“But then—who has the real pearls?”

“That,” said Poirot, “is what we are going to find out.”

He was interrupted by a knock at the door. It was Mr. Opalsen. He
looked haggard and anxious.

“The police have just been here,” he said. “They say the pearls
the inspector took away are paste. My wife’s distracted.”

“I know, I know,” said Poirot. “I have heard her.”

“But what does it mean? Who can have taken them? And where can
they be?”

“That is what I am going to find out,” repeated Poirot. “I have a
little plan. If you will both come with me to Mrs. Opalsen’s room,
I will explain.”

We followed him downstairs. Mrs. Opalsen was still weeping, while
the manager and a couple of waiters were trying to comfort her.
The inspector was there also, looking very crestfallen.

“I can’t understand it,” he was saying. “They looked all right to
me.”

“To the untrained eye, no doubt,” said Poirot smoothly. “But to
the expert—ah! that is another matter.”

He turned to the company.

“Now, I will tell you what I think. I think the real pearls are
still in this hotel.”

“In this hotel?” cried the inspector. “But I’ve searched every
corner of it!”

“Every corner? Are you sure? Have you searched—the coal-cellar,
for instance?”

The inspector stared.

“The coal-cellar? No, of course not. What should they be doing
there?”

“Everything is possible,” said Poirot. “But we will begin with
something simpler. We will begin with—the chambermaid’s room.”

“But I’ve searched that!” cried the inspector.

“Ah! But did you search—the fireplace?”

The inspector shook his head.

“No. There was no fire in it.”

“Exactly! That is why it is such an excellent hiding-place. Let
us go and see.”

We all flocked upstairs to the chambermaid’s room. It was a small,
poorly furnished room at the top of the house. Poirot went straight
to the fireplace. He stooped down and peered up the chimney. Then
he reached up his hand and drew out—a small, soot-stained parcel!

With a cry of triumph he handed it to Mrs. Opalsen. She tore it
open. Inside, shimmering and glowing in the morning light, was the
famous necklace!

“My pearls! My pearls!” she cried.

“But—how did you know?” gasped the inspector.

“It was simple,” said Poirot. “I knew the maid had not taken them,
because she had not had time to hide them. I knew the chambermaid
had not taken them, because she had not had time to take them out
of the room. Therefore, they must have been taken by someone who
had access to the room at all times—someone who could come and go
as they pleased without exciting suspicion. And who could that be
but—the mistress of the room herself?”

“The mistress of the room?” I cried. “You mean—Mrs. Opalsen?”

“Exactly!” said Poirot. “Mrs. Opalsen stole her own pearls!”

“But why?” I gasped.

“For the insurance money, of course!” said Poirot. “Mr. Opalsen
told us he was short of money. What easier way to get it than to
steal his wife’s pearls and claim the insurance?”

“But—the paste necklace?” I asked.

“That was a clever touch,” said Poirot. “It was intended to throw
the police off the scent. If they found the paste necklace, they
would think the real one had been stolen by someone else. And that
is exactly what happened!”

“But how did you know she had hidden them in the chimney?” asked
the inspector.

“I didn’t,” said Poirot. “I only guessed. But I knew they must be
somewhere in the hotel, and the chimney seemed as likely a place
as any.”

Mrs. Opalsen was led away, still weeping, but this time with joy.
Mr. Opalsen followed her, looking very sheepish. The inspector
shook Poirot by the hand.

“You’ve been one too many for us, Mr. Poirot,” he said. “I must
admit, I never suspected the lady herself.”

“Ah!” said Poirot. “That is the mistake you police always make.
You never suspect the obvious!”

And with a wink at me, he led the way back to our rooms.

“Well, Hastings,” he said, as we sat down to breakfast. “What do
you think of my little case?”

“I think you’re a genius, Poirot!” I cried.

“No, no,” he said, smiling. “Only a man who uses his little grey
cells! And now, let us enjoy our breakfast. I think we have earned
it!”

The door was not locked, and we entered. The room, which was a
large double one, was unoccupied. Dust lay about rather noticeably,
and my sensitive friend gave a characteristic grimace as he ran
his finger round a rectangular mark on a table near the window.

“The _service_ leaves to be desired,” he observed dryly.

He was staring thoughtfully out of the window, and seemed to have
fallen into a brown study.

“Well?” I demanded impatiently. “What did we come in here for?”

He started.

“_Je vous demande pardon, mon ami_. I wished to see if the door
was really bolted on this side also.”

“Well,” I said, glancing at the door which communicated with the
room we had just left, “it _is_ bolted.”

Poirot nodded. He still seemed to be thinking.

“Hastings,” he said at last, “I should like you to make me a little
sketch of the position of the rooms—a diagram, you understand. I
believe you have a good deal of skill in these matters.”

I pulled out my notebook and pencil and we sat down on the bed
together. When I had finished, it looked something like this:

[A diagram showing the three rooms, the corridor, and the various
doors and windows.]

Poirot looked at it carefully.

“Wait!” he said. “You’ve forgotten one thing. The little room
next door is Mrs. Opalsen’s maid’s room. What is the room on the
other side of it?”

“I don’t know. I’ll go and see.”

I went out into the corridor and found a chambermaid who was just
going into one of the rooms further along.

“Which is the room next to No. 12?” I asked.

“No. 11, sir. It’s a single room.”

“And the one on the other side of it?”

“No. 10. A large double room.”

“Thank you.”

I returned to Poirot and told him. He was still studying the
diagram.

“_Bien_,” he said. “That seems to make things clear.”

“What things?” I asked, somewhat bewildered.

“Many things, my friend. But tell me, Hastings, do you not find
it—a little curious?”

“What?”

“The necklace. It was in the maid’s bed. That is so?”

“Yes, the inspector found it there.”

“Then why,” Poirot demanded, “did she not hide it better? In a
mattress, for example—or under the floor-boards? Why leave it just
there, where the first person to search would be sure to find it?”

“Perhaps she hadn’t time.”

“Twelve seconds, fifteen seconds,” Poirot murmured. “No, she had
not time. But then, why steal it at all, if she could not hide it?”

“She hoped it wouldn’t be missed so soon.”

“Perhaps. But Mrs. Opalsen _did_ miss it. And then, there is another
thing. Why did she not throw it out of the window?”

“Because there was no balcony.”

“Exactly. But if she had thrown it out, it would have fallen into
the street. Some one might have found it and brought it back. It
would have been risky, but not so risky as keeping it in her bed.”

“I don’t see what you’re driving at, Poirot.”

“I am not driving at anything, my friend. I am only wondering.”

He rose.

“And now,” he said, “I think we will go and have a little talk
with the manager.”

We found that official in his office. He was a small, alert-looking
man with an air of suppressed excitement.

“A most unfortunate occurrence, Monsieur Poirot,” he said, as we
entered. “Most unfortunate. I need hardly say that we shall do
everything in our power to assist the police. The reputation of
the hotel, you understand——”

“_Parfaitement, parfaitement_,” said Poirot. “But I wished to ask
you a question. Was No. 11—the room next to Mrs. Opalsen’s—occupied
last night?”

“No, monsieur. It was vacant.”

“And No. 10—the double room beyond?”

“That was occupied by a gentleman and his wife—a Mr. and Mrs.
Robinson.”

“I see. And they are still here?”

“Oh, yes. They only arrived yesterday.”

“I should like to see them for a moment, if I might.”

The manager looked surprised.

“I’m afraid they’re out just now, monsieur. They went out for a
walk along the front about half an hour ago.”

“I see. Well, perhaps I could see their room?”

“Certainly, if you wish it.”

He led the way upstairs and unlocked the door of No. 10. It was,
as he had said, a large double room, comfortably furnished. There
were two beds, a wardrobe, a chest of drawers, and a dressing-table.
On the latter were various silver-backed brushes and bottles.

Poirot walked over to the dressing-table and began to examine the
brushes. Then he turned to the wardrobe and looked inside. It was
full of clothes—smart, expensive-looking garments.

“They seem to be well-to-do people, these Robinsons,” he remarked.

“Oh, yes, monsieur. Mr. Robinson is in the City, I believe. Very
highly thought of.”

“I see. Well, thank you, monsieur. I don’t think I need trouble
you further.”

As we went downstairs again, Poirot was silent. He seemed to be
deep in thought. Suddenly he stopped and laid his hand on my arm.

“Hastings,” he said, “I have an idea. A very simple idea, but it
might be the right one.”

“What is it?” I asked.

“I will tell you later. For the present, I must go and see the
police inspector again.”

I did not see him again until dinner-time. He was then in a state
of great excitement.

“_Mon ami_,” he cried, as he sat down, “I have it! I have the whole
thing! It is of a simplicity—but of a simplicity!”

“Tell me!” I exclaimed.

“Wait. All in good time. First, we must have our dinner. After
dinner, we will go and see Mr. Opalsen.”

We found that gentleman in the lounge, looking very much more
cheerful than when we had last seen him.

“Ah, Monsieur Poirot!” he cried. “I have good news for you. The
police have found the necklace!”

“Indeed?” said Poirot. “I am delighted to hear it. And where was it?”

“In the maid’s room, as I told you it would be. The inspector found
it this afternoon.”

“I see. And the maid—she has been arrested?”

“Yes. She’s at the police station now. They’re going to bring her
up before the magistrates tomorrow morning.”

“I see. Well, Mr. Opalsen, I have a little surprise for you.”

“A surprise?”

“Yes. I have found the real thief!”

Mr. Opalsen stared at him in amazement.

“The real thief? But the maid——”

“The maid is innocent,” said Poirot quietly.

“But the necklace was found in her bed!”

“Exactly. That is why I knew she was innocent.”

“I don’t understand.”

“It is very simple. If you were a thief, Mr. Opalsen, and you had
stolen a valuable necklace, would you hide it in your own bed,
where it would be found at once?”

“Well, perhaps not. But she might have been flurried.”

“No,” said Poirot. “She was not flurried. She was very clever.
She was so clever that she managed to hide the necklace in a place
where no one would think of looking for it.”

“But it _was_ found!”

“Yes, it was found. But it was not the maid who hid it there.”

“Then who was it?”

“It was the person who really stole it.”

“And who was that?”

“The person,” said Poirot, “who had the best opportunity of
stealing it. The person who knew exactly where it was kept, and
who had a duplicate key to the jewel-case.”

“You mean——” Mr. Opalsen’s voice trailed off.

“I mean,” said Poirot, “the person who is at this moment sitting
opposite to me.”

I gasped. Mr. Opalsen’s face turned a curious greyish-green colour.

“You—you mean me?” he stammered.

“I mean you, monsieur,” said Poirot sternly. “It was you who stole
your wife’s necklace.”

For a moment there was a dead silence. Then Mr. Opalsen burst into
a loud, harsh laugh.

“You’re mad!” he cried. “Stark, staring mad! Why should I steal
my own wife’s pearls?”

“Because,” said Poirot, “as you yourself admitted this evening,
money is ‘confoundedly tight in the City.’ You needed money, and
you needed it badly. You knew your wife’s pearls were worth a
fortune. So you decided to steal them and claim the insurance
money.”

“It’s a lie!” cried Opalsen. “A damnable lie!”

“Is it?” said Poirot. “Then perhaps you can explain how it is that
this afternoon, when I searched your room, I found this?”

He held out a small, glittering object. It was a pearl—a large,
perfectly matched pearl.

Opalsen’s face went even whiter than before. He made a sudden,
desperate snatch at the pearl, but Poirot was too quick for him.

“No, no, monsieur. That would be a mistake. I have already shown
this to the police inspector, and he is waiting outside at this
moment.”

With a groan, Opalsen sank back in his chair. The game was up.

“How did you know?” he muttered.

“It was the diagram that did it,” said Poirot. “When I looked at
the position of the rooms, I saw that it would have been perfectly
easy for some one in No. 10 to get into No. 11, and from there into
No. 12. But the door between No. 11 and No. 12 was bolted on both
sides. So that way was closed. Then I remembered that you had said
your wife’s pearls were unique. And I remembered that you had
seemed very anxious that the inspector should take the necklace
away with him. Why? Because you knew it was a fake!”

“A fake?” I exclaimed.

“Yes. Mr. Opalsen had had a duplicate necklace made—a very clever
imitation. He had substituted it for the real one some time ago.
Then, this evening, he pretended to steal the fake necklace, and
hid it in the maid’s bed, knowing it would be found. He would then
claim the insurance money for the real necklace, which he had
already disposed of.”

“But the pearl?” I asked. “Where did that come from?”

“That,” said Poirot, with a twinkle in his eye, “was a little
invention of my own. I happened to have a loose pearl in my pocket—one
that I had picked up in a jeweller’s shop in London. I thought it
might come in useful.”

“Then you didn’t find it in his room?”

“No. But it served its purpose. It made him confess.”

“Well, Poirot,” I said, as we walked back to our own room, “I must
say you’re a wonder. I should never have thought of it.”

“It was simple, my friend,” said Poirot. “Very simple. But it shows
the importance of the little grey cells. Without them, we should
be as lost as—as Mr. Opalsen!”

Suddenly, he turned on me.

“Hastings, my friend, what do you think of it all?”

“Think? Why, it seems a pretty clear case to me,” I replied. “The
French girl did it, of course.”

“You think so?” Poirot asked, with his head on one side.

“Well, it’s obvious. She was the only person who had the
opportunity.”

“I agree with you, my friend. It _is_ obvious. But—is it too
obvious?”

I stared.

“What do you mean?”

“Just this. Is it not a little _too_ much in character? The weeping
French maid—the stolen necklace found in her bed——”

“But the door was bolted,” I reminded him. “How could anyone else
have got in?”

“Ah, the door!” Poirot murmured. “The door!”

He walked over to it and examined the bolt. It was a heavy one,
and quite clean.

“It has been recently oiled,” he observed.

“But what does that matter?” I asked. “It’s bolted on this side.”

Poirot did not answer. He was still staring at the door.

“_Tiens!_” he said, after a pause. “I have it! But it is too simple!”

“What is?”

“The way the theft was committed.”

“But the maid did it,” I cried. “The inspector found the necklace
in her bed.”

“And that,” said Poirot, with a smile, “is just why I am sure she
didn’t do it.”

I was about to protest, but he silenced me with a wave of his
hand.

“No, no, my friend. Think for a moment. If you had stolen a
valuable necklace, would you have hidden it in your own bed? Of
course not. You would have hidden it somewhere else—anywhere but
there.”

“But the inspector found it there,” I persisted.

“Exactly. And that is why I am sure she didn’t put it there.”

“Then who did?”

“The person who stole it, of course.”

“But who could have got into the room? The door was bolted on
both sides.”

Poirot smiled.

“Was it?” he said. “Was it?”

He walked over to the door and drew back the bolt. Then he tried
the handle. The door opened.

“You see?” he said. “It is not bolted on the other side.”

“But I saw the inspector try it!” I cried.

“He tried it from the other side, my friend. And it _was_ bolted
then. But that does not mean it was bolted all the time.”

“Then you think someone came in through this door?”

“I am sure of it,” said Poirot. “But come, my friend. Let us go
and find the inspector. I think I have something to tell him.”

We found the inspector in the manager’s office. He was looking
thoroughly pleased with himself.

“Well, Mr. Poirot,” he said, as we entered, “it’s all over. We’ve
got the girl, and we’ve got the necklace. A very satisfactory
case.”

“Is it?” said Poirot. “I am not so sure.”

The inspector stared.

“What do you mean?”

“I mean,” said Poirot, “that you have got the wrong person.”

“The wrong person! But the necklace was found in her bed!”

“Exactly,” said Poirot. “And that is why she didn’t put it there.”

The inspector looked at him as though he thought he had taken leave
of his senses.

“Then who did?” he asked.

“The person who stole it,” said Poirot. “And I think I can tell you
who that person was.”

The inspector’s face expressed the utmost incredulity.

“Indeed? And who was it?”

“It was,” said Poirot, “the chambermaid.”

“The chambermaid!” The inspector gasped. “But she was searched!”

“I know,” said Poirot. “But that does not mean she hadn’t the
necklace.”

“But the searcher said she hadn’t anything on her!”

“She hadn’t—then,” said Poirot. “But she had had it a few minutes
before.”

“But where could she have hidden it?”

“In a very simple place,” said Poirot. “In fact, in the only place
where no one would think of looking for it.”

“And where was that?”

“In the other room,” said Poirot. “The room next door.”

“But the door was bolted!”

“On this side, yes. But not on the other. The chambermaid simply
unbolted it, went into the next room, and hid the necklace there.
Then she came back, bolted the door again, and was ready to be
searched.”

“But where did she hide it?”

“In a very clever place,” said Poirot. “In the one place where it
would be perfectly safe. She hid it,” he paused for a moment, “on
the underside of the table.”

“The underside of the table!” The inspector stared.

“Yes,” said Poirot. “I saw the mark of it myself. A rectangular
mark, just the size of the necklace. It had been stuck there with
a piece of plasticine.”

“Plasticine!” The inspector gasped.

“Yes,” said Poirot. “It is a very useful substance. I have often
used it myself. And it leaves a very tell-tale mark.”

The inspector was silent for a moment. Then he shook his head.

“It’s a very clever theory, Mr. Poirot,” he said. “But it won’t
hold water. You see, the chambermaid couldn’t have known that the
room next door would be empty.”

“She didn’t need to,” said Poirot. “She knew it was empty because
she had just been in there to do the room. In fact, it was she who
had left the door unbolted.”

The inspector was silent again. He seemed to be thinking.

“It’s possible,” he said at last. “It’s certainly possible. But
even so, it doesn’t prove anything. We haven’t any evidence.”

“Oh, yes, you have,” said Poirot. “You have the evidence of the
necklace itself.”

“The necklace? But we’ve got that already.”

“Have you?” said Poirot. “Are you sure?”

The inspector looked at him in surprise.

“Of course I’m sure. I’ve got it right here.”

He reached into his pocket and pulled out the necklace.

“Wait a moment,” said Poirot. “Let me see it.”

He took the necklace from the inspector and examined it closely.
Then he handed it back with a smile.

“It is as I thought,” he said. “It is a very good imitation.”

“An imitation!” The inspector gasped.

“Yes,” said Poirot. “The real pearls are still where the
chambermaid hid them—on the underside of the table in the next
room.”

The inspector didn’t wait to hear any more. He dashed out of the
room, followed by Poirot and myself.

We found the room next door just as we had left it. The inspector
went straight to the table by the window and felt underneath it.

With a cry of triumph, he pulled away a small object. It was the
real necklace, stuck to the underside of the table with a piece
of plasticine.

“Well, I’m damned!” he said, staring at it. “You were right, Mr.
Poirot. You were right after all.”

“It was a very clever plot,” said Poirot. “The chambermaid stole
the necklace and hid it in the next room. Then she put the
imitation necklace in the maid’s bed, to make it look as though
she had stolen it. It was a very clever piece of work.”

“But how did she get the imitation necklace?” I asked.

“She probably bought it for a few shillings,” said Poirot. “It
was a very small investment for such a large return.”

“And what about the maid?” I asked. “What will happen to her?”

“She will be released, of course,” said Poirot. “And I think she
will have a very good case for damages against the hotel.”

“And the chambermaid?”

“She is already in custody,” said the inspector. “We picked her up
as she was trying to leave the hotel.”

“Well,” I said, as we walked back to our own room, “it was a very
clever piece of work, Poirot. I don’t know how you do it.”

Poirot smiled.

“It is very simple, my friend,” he said. “It is just a matter of
using the little grey cells. And now, I think it is time for tea.”

[End of story]

Suddenly he turned towards the table by the window.

“Tell me, Hastings, do you see a mark here—a rectangular mark?”

“I do,” I said. “It is where something has been standing. A box,
most likely.”

“Yes, a box. What sort of a box?”

“I really can’t say. A travelling-case, perhaps.”

“I see. Now, my friend, look here.” He was bending over the mark.
“Do you notice anything else?”

“No,” I said, after a brief examination.

“Wait!” Poirot produced a magnifying glass. “Do you see a faint
impression of two small, round spots?”

I looked again.

“Yes, I do. They look like—well, they might be the feet of a small
clock or something of the sort.”

“A clock? No, Hastings, not a clock.”

“What then?”

“A camera.”

“A camera?” I repeated, in astonishment.

“Yes. A camera. Now, let us go down.”

“But, Poirot——”

“Let us go down, I say.”

He refused to answer another question until we reached the lounge.
Then, to my intense surprise, he made his way to the bureau and
demanded to see the manager.

“I want to ask you a question,” he said, when that functionary
appeared. “Do you happen to have a guest of the name of—er—Letts
staying here?”

The manager shook his head.

“No, monsieur. No one of that name.”

“Or—wait—it might be Lettsom?”

“No.”

“Ah! Then I have been misinformed. I thank you, monsieur.”

“What on earth was that for?” I asked, as we turned away.

“A little idea of mine, Hastings. That is all.”

“But, Poirot, I don’t understand. What has a camera to do with the
theft of the pearls? And who is this Mr. Lettsom?”

“Patience, my friend. All in good time.”

He led the way to the lift.

“I think,” he said, as we ascended, “that I will go and have a
little talk with our friend, the inspector.”

He found that official in the Opalsens’ sitting-room. He was
looking very pleased with himself.

“Well, monsieur,” said Poirot, “so you have the thief and the
jewels. I congratulate you.”

“Thank you, monsieur. It was a very simple case.”

“_Vraiment?_ And you are quite satisfied?”

“Satisfied? Of course I’m satisfied. Why, the necklace was found
in her bed.”

“And the maid—does she still deny it?”

“Of course she does. They always do. But it won’t do her much good.
The evidence is too strong.”

“Yes, the evidence is certainly very strong. Too strong, perhaps?”

The inspector stared.

“I don’t follow you.”

“I was only wondering,” said Poirot mildly, “if it were not
_too_ strong. It is almost too good to be true, is it not so?”

“I don’t see what you’re driving at,” said the inspector. “The
pearls were there, and the girl was the only person who could have
put them there.”

“Exactly. That is what makes it so very—_satisfaisant_.”

Poirot turned to go.

“By the way,” he said, as he reached the door, “I suppose you have
not yet had time to examine the pearls?”

“Not yet. Why?”

“Oh, nothing. I only thought that, as they are so very valuable,
it might be as well to make sure they are—er—real.”

The inspector laughed.

“Oh, they’re real enough. Mr. Opalsen’s word is good for that.”

“No doubt, no doubt. But even a millionaire may be deceived, may
he not?”

And with a little nod, Poirot left the room.

“Poirot,” I said, when we were once more in our own apartment,
“what do you mean? You don’t suggest that the pearls are false?”

“I suggest nothing, Hastings. I merely observe.”

“But if they are false, then the whole thing is a plant!”

“Exactly.”

“But who——?”

“Ah! that is the question. Who? Not the maid, certainly. She would
hardly steal a necklace of imitation pearls and then hide them in
her own bed.”

“Then it must be the chambermaid!”

“She had not the time, Hastings. You forget my little experiment.”

“Then—then—it must be Mrs. Opalsen herself!”

“Why should she steal her own pearls?”

“To get the insurance money!”

“_Précisément_. It is a possibility. But we must not jump to
conclusions. There are other possibilities.”

“What others?”

“The husband, for instance.”

“Mr. Opalsen! But he is a rich man.”

“Is he? We have only his word for it. And he himself said that
money was ‘confoundedly tight in the City.’”

“But the camera, Poirot! What has the camera to do with it?”

“Ah! that is the most interesting part of the whole affair. The
camera, Hastings, is the key to the mystery.”

“I don’t see it,” I said, shaking my head.

“No? Well, think it over, my friend. Think it over. A camera—a
rectangular mark—and a guest of the name of Lettsom. Does that
convey nothing to you?”

“Nothing at all.”

“I am disappointed in you, Hastings. I really am. Your mental
processes are—how shall I say it?—a little slow.”

I felt a trifle nettled.

“It’s all very well for you, Poirot. You always seem to know
everything before it happens. But I’m only a plain man, and I like
to have things explained to me.”

“And so you shall, my friend. So you shall. But not yet. Not yet.
We must wait for the report of the police surgeon.”

“The police surgeon! What on earth has he to do with it?”

“A great deal, Hastings. A great deal. But here is the waiter with
the evening papers. Let us see if there is any news.”

He took the papers from the man and began to scan them rapidly.

“Ah! here it is. ‘Mysterious Theft of Pearls at Brighton Hotel.
Valuable Necklace Stolen from Bedroom. Arrest of French Maid.’
Nothing very new there.”

He tossed the paper aside and began to pace the room.

“Hastings,” he said suddenly, “I am going out. I have a little
investigation to make.”

“Can’t I come with you?”

“No, my friend. I prefer to go alone. But do not be despondent. I
shall return before long, and then—who knows?—I may have news for
you.”

He was as good as his word. In less than an hour he was back, his
eyes twinkling with suppressed excitement.

“Well?” I asked. “What have you discovered?”

“I have discovered, Hastings, that I am a very clever man. A very
clever man indeed!”

“We all know that,” I said, with a smile. “But what have you
actually found out?”

“I have found out the identity of Mr. Lettsom.”

“And who is he?”

“He is—but wait! I hear a knock at the door.”

It was the inspector. He looked a little less cheerful than when
we had last seen him.

“Well, monsieur,” said Poirot, “what news?”

“The pearls are false,” said the inspector shortly.

“I thought as much,” said Poirot.

“And what’s more,” continued the official, “they’ve been switched.
Mr. Opalsen says he’s certain they were real when he bought them.”

“I have no doubt of it,” said Poirot. “And now, if you will come
with me to the room next door, I think I can show you how the
trick was done.”

We followed him into the empty apartment. Poirot led the way to
the table by the window.

“You see this mark?” he said, pointing to the rectangular
impression. “It was made by a camera. A camera, monsieur, which
was used, not for taking photographs, but for—how shall I say
it?—for a very different purpose.”

He reached out and touched a small, almost invisible, projection
in the wall. To our surprise, a portion of the panelling slid
back, revealing a small cavity.

“A secret hiding-place!” I exclaimed.

“Exactly. And in it—look!”

He reached into the cavity and drew out a small, black object. It
was a camera-case. But when he opened it, it did not contain a
camera. Inside, nestled in a bed of blue velvet, was a shimmering
string of pearls.

“My pearls!” cried a voice from the doorway.

It was Mrs. Opalsen. She and her husband had followed us into the
room.

“Wait!” said Poirot, as she reached out for them. “Are you sure they
are yours, madame?”

“Of course they are! I’d know them anywhere.”

“And you, monsieur?” Poirot turned to Mr. Opalsen. “Are you sure?”

“Certainly I am,” said the stockbroker. “There’s no doubt about
it.”

“Then,” said Poirot, his voice suddenly becoming cold and hard,
“perhaps you will explain how they came to be in this room—the
room which was occupied until this morning by a friend of yours?”

“A friend of mine?” Opalsen stared. “I don’t know what you mean.”

“I think you do,” said Poirot. “The friend who went by the name of
Lettsom, but whose real name is—shall we say—Edsel?”

Opalsen turned pale.

“I—I don’t know any one of that name.”

“No? That is strange. Because I have just come from the police
station, where I saw a photograph of a certain gentleman who is
wanted for various—er—financial irregularities. And the
resemblance to yourself, monsieur, is—how shall I say?—most
striking.”

“It’s a lie!” shouted Opalsen.

“Is it? We shall see. Inspector, I think you will find that this
gentleman and his ‘friend’ in the next room have been working
together for some time. The ‘friend’—who, by the way, is a very
clever mechanic—constructed this little hiding-place, and also the
ingenious device by which the pearls were transferred from one
room to the other.”

“But how?” I asked. “The door was bolted.”

“The door was bolted, yes. But the wall—that was a different
matter. You see this small hole?” He pointed to a tiny opening in
the panelling. “Through this, a thin wire was passed. On the end of
the wire was a small hook. The pearls were hung on the hook, and—_voilà!_—they were drawn through the wall into the next room.”

“But the maid?” I persisted. “How do you account for the pearls
being found in her bed?”

“A very simple matter, Hastings. The false pearls were placed there
by Mr. Opalsen himself, while the inspector was busy searching the
other room. It was a clever move, for it diverted suspicion from
the real thief.”

“And the real thief?”

“The real thief, Hastings, was—as I suspected from the first—Mr.
Opalsen himself. He needed the money to cover his losses in the
City, and he hit upon this ingenious plan to rob his wife and at
the same time claim the insurance money.”

“But the camera?”

“The camera, my friend, was merely a blind. It was placed on the
table to account for the presence of the ‘friend’ in the next room,
and also to provide a convenient receptacle for the stolen pearls.”

“Well, I’m blowed!” I said.

Poirot smiled.

“It was a pretty little problem, Hastings. A very pretty little
problem. But it was no match for the little grey cells of Hercule
Poirot!”

“I was wondering,” he said, “why the chambermaid was so long over
the bed next door. Twelve minutes? It is too much! It is truly
extravagant!”

“Twelve minutes!” I said, surprised. “I didn’t know you’d timed
her.”

“I have my methods. And another thing—why did the maid have to
go to her own room twice? And—why did the chambermaid look at me
so strangely? All these little matters——”

“My dear Poirot!” I cried. “You’re always so suspicious. Why, the
maid had the necklace! If they hadn’t found it, I could have
understood your thinking there was something wrong. But as it
is——”

“As it is, we will go and see the manager,” said Poirot.

“What for?”

“To ask him for a little information.”

“About what?”

“About the occupants of this room.”

“But what on earth has that got to do with it?”

“We shall see.”

As we were leaving the room, Poirot’s eyes fell on a small object
lying on the floor. He picked it up and held it out to me. It was
a tiny piece of white cotton.

“Well?” I said. “What of it?”

“Nothing, my friend, nothing. Only it is interesting. Most
interesting.”

We found the manager in his office. He was a small, dapper person,
with an extremely suave manner. Poirot soon got the information
he wanted. The room was occupied by a Mr. and Mrs. Robinson. They
had arrived the night before, and were at present out for a drive.

“The Robinsons,” mused Poirot, as we walked away. “It is a common
name, Hastings. I wonder if it is as common as it sounds.”

“What do you mean?”

“I am wondering if the name of Robinson is as simple as it looks.”

“You are always so suspicious, Poirot!” I laughed. “I believe you’d
suspect your own grandmother.”

“I have none, _mon ami_,” said Poirot with a touch of sadness.
“But let us go and have our coffee.”

We returned to the lounge. Mrs. Opalsen had retired to her room,
but her husband was still there, looking gloomy and depressed.
He greeted us with a nod.

“Well, you’ve done it, Mr. Poirot,” he said. “I hope you’re
satisfied.”

“I am never satisfied until the truth is known,” replied Poirot
gravely.

“The truth? But the girl’s got the pearls, hasn’t she? What more do
you want?”

“I want to know how she got them.”

“How she got them? Why, she stole them, of course.”

“And how did she get the key?”

“Stole that too, I suppose. It wouldn’t be difficult.”

“And how did she know they were there?”

“The whole hotel knew it. My wife isn’t exactly a quiet person.”

Poirot nodded.

“That is true,” he said. “That is very true. Well, I must be moving.
Good-night, Mr. Opalsen.”

“Good-night.”

We walked away in silence. Poirot seemed lost in thought. Suddenly
he stopped and looked at me.

“Hastings,” he said, “do you remember the chambermaid?”

“The chambermaid? Which one?”

“The one who was in the room.”

“Yes, of course. Why?”

“Did you notice anything about her?”

“Notice anything? No, I can’t say I did. She seemed a very
ordinary sort of person.”

“Ordinary? Perhaps. And yet—did you notice her hands?”

“Her hands? No.”

“They were very well-shaped, Hastings. Very well-shaped indeed.
And her voice—did you notice her voice?”

“Her voice? No, I can’t say I did.”

“It was the voice of a lady, Hastings. A very well-educated lady.”

“A lady! A chambermaid a lady! My dear Poirot, you’re dreaming.”

“Perhaps. And yet—I wonder.”

He was silent for a moment, then he said:

“I think I will go and have another look at that room, Hastings.”

“What, the Robinsons’ room?”

“Yes.”

“But why? What do you expect to find?”

“I don’t know. But I have a feeling—a very strong feeling—that
there is something there.”

We went back to the first floor. The room was still empty. Poirot
went straight to the table near the window. He looked at the
rectangular mark he had noticed before.

“Do you see that, Hastings?”

“Yes. What of it?”

“It is the mark of a jewel-case, Hastings. A jewel-case exactly
the same size as Mrs. Opalsen’s.”

“What!” I cried. “You mean——”

“I mean that the Robinsons have a jewel-case exactly like Mrs.
Opalsen’s. And I mean that they have been using it lately.”

“But what does that prove?”

“It proves a great deal, my friend. It proves a very great deal.
Now let us look at the door.”

He went to the door communicating with the Opalsens’ room. He
examined the bolt closely.

“It has been recently oiled, Hastings. Very recently oiled.”

“Oiled! But why?”

“So that it would slide easily and silently. Now let us look at
the other door—the one leading into the corridor.”

He went to the door and examined the lock.

“This also has been recently oiled. And see—there are marks of a
pick-lock.”

“A pick-lock!” I cried. “Then it was a professional job!”

“Exactly. It was a professional job. And now, Hastings, I think
we have seen enough. Let us go and find the inspector.”

We found him in the manager’s office. He looked surprised to see
us.

“Well, Mr. Poirot, what is it now?”

“I have something to tell you, monsieur. Something very important.”

He told him what we had found. The inspector listened with
interest.

“The Robinsons, eh? I’ll have a look at them when they come back.
In the meantime, I’ll keep an eye on the room.”

“I should also like to see the chambermaid again,” said Poirot.

“The chambermaid? Why?”

“Because I have a theory about her.”

“A theory? Well, you can see her if you like. She’s in the
servants’ hall, I expect.”

We went to the servants’ hall. The chambermaid was there, sitting
by the fire. She looked up as we entered.

“Well, what is it now?” she asked, rather crossly.

“I should like to ask you a few questions,” said Poirot.

“Questions? What about?”

“About the pearls.”

“The pearls! I told you I didn't know anything about them.”

“I know you did. But I think you do.”

The girl’s face went white.

“What do you mean?”

“I mean that you were in the room when the pearls were stolen.”

“I was not! I told you I was only in there for three minutes.”

“Three minutes is a long time, mademoiselle. A very long time.
And you were not alone.”

“Not alone? Who was with me?”

“The person who stole the pearls.”

“I don’t know what you’re talking about.”

“I think you do. I think you know very well. And I think you’re
going to tell us.”

The girl looked at him for a moment, then she broke down and
started to cry.

“I couldn't help it!” she sobbed. “I couldn't help it! He made me
do it!”

“He? Who is he?”

“My husband. He said it would be easy. He said no one would
suspect us. And we needed the money so badly.”

“Your husband? Is he the man who was in the room next door?”

“Yes. We’re the Robinsons. We took the room so that we could get
at the pearls. We knew Mrs. Opalsen always kept them in that
drawer.”

“And how did you get them?”

“My husband picked the lock of the door leading into the corridor.
Then he oiled the bolt of the door leading into the Opalsens’ room.
When the maid went into her own room to get the cotton, he slipped
in and took the pearls. He put them in our jewel-case and went
back to our room. Then, when the maid went back for the scissors,
he slipped in again and put the empty jewel-case back in the
drawer. He’d already put a duplicate necklace in the maid’s bed,
so that she’d be suspected.”

“A duplicate necklace!” I cried. “Then the necklace the inspector
found wasn't the real one?”

“No. It was just a cheap imitation. My husband’s got the real one.”

“And where is your husband now?” asked the inspector.

“He’s—he’s gone.”

“Gone? Where?”

“I don’t know. He said he was going to London to sell the pearls.
He told me to stay here and wait for him.”

“Well, I’m afraid you’ll have to come with me, my girl,” said the
inspector. “And we’ll have to see if we can find your husband.”

He led her away. Poirot looked at me and smiled.

“Well, Hastings, what do you think of my ‘little grey cells’ now?”

“I think they’re wonderful, Poirot. Simply wonderful. But how did
you know?”

“It was the chambermaid’s hands, Hastings. They were the hands of
a lady. And her voice—it was the voice of a lady. And then there
was the piece of white cotton. It was the same as the cotton the
maid was using. It must have come from her room. And that meant
that someone had been in her room. And who could it be but the
person who stole the pearls?”

“But how did you know about the duplicate necklace?”

“I didn't. But I suspected it. It was too easy, Hastings. Too
easy. And then there was the rectangular mark on the table. It was
the mark of a jewel-case. And why should the Robinsons have a
jewel-case if they didn't have any jewels? It all pointed to the
same thing.”

“Well, you’ve done it again, Poirot. You’ve done it again.”

“It was nothing, my friend. Nothing. Just a little matter of
observation and deduction. And now, let us go and have our
coffee. I think we have earned it.”

We went back to the lounge and had our coffee. Poirot was in high
spirits. He talked and laughed and told stories, and I listened and
marvelled at his brilliance. It had been a wonderful evening, and
I was glad I had come to Brighton. As we were leaving the hotel the
next morning, we saw Mr. Opalsen. He looked much happier than he
had the night before.

“Well, Mr. Poirot,” he said, “I hear you’ve found the pearls.”

“Yes, monsieur. We have found them.”

“And the thief?”

“The thief is in custody.”

“Well, I’m glad to hear it. My wife will be delighted. She’s been
crying her eyes out all night.”

“I am glad to have been of service, monsieur.”

“Well, you’ve done a great job. A really great job. And if there’s
anything I can do for you, just let me know.”

“Thank you, monsieur. You are very kind.”

We shook hands and said goodbye. As we were driving away, Poirot
looked at me and smiled.

“Well, Hastings, another case successfully concluded. What do you
think of that?”

“I think it’s wonderful, Poirot. Simply wonderful.”

“Yes, it was a pretty little problem. A very pretty little
problem. And now, let us go back to London and see what the next
case will be.”

And with that, we drove away, leaving Brighton and the Grand
Metropolitan behind us.

Suddenly he gave a little grunt of satisfaction. He was looking
at the floor at our feet.

“Look, Hastings! What is that?”

He pointed to a tiny heap of something white lying upon the carpet.

I picked up a few of the grains.

“It—it’s only salt,” I said, somewhat disappointed.

“Salt, eh?” Poirot smiled. “How did it come here, I wonder? Did
some one spill a salt-cellar?”

“I should think that most likely,” I replied, rather bored by his
persistent interest in trifles.

“Salt-cellars are not as a rule to be found in bedrooms,” he
remarked dryly.

I looked round the room again.

“But what does it matter?” I demanded. “After all, the case is
over. The necklace has been found.”

“Has it?” said Poirot, with a queer little smile. “I should say
it was only just beginning.”

I stared at him.

“I don’t understand.”

“Wait, my friend! All in good time. We will return to our coffee
in the lounge.”

He led the way downstairs, and we resumed our seats. After a minute
or two, he addressed me:

“_Dites-moi, Hastings_, what was it I said to that poor child
Célestine?”

“I didn’t hear,” I answered.

“I told her that if she were innocent I would prove it. It is
necessary that I should do so.”

“But the necklace?”

“Ah, the necklace! That is the point. I have seen it, and it was—not
the real one.”

“Not the real one!” I gasped. “Then where is the real one?”

“Precisely, my friend. Where is the real one?”

I looked at him in amazement.

“You mean that Mrs. Opalsen’s pearls are——”

“Imitation! Excellent imitations, I admit, but imitations none
the less. They would deceive anyone who was not an expert.”

“But then the robbery——?”

“Was a very clever one. The thief—or thieves—did not want to
take the imitation necklace. They wanted the real one. So they
substituted the imitation one in the jewel-case, and then, after
Mrs. Opalsen had discovered the loss, they arranged for the
imitation one to be found in the maid’s bed.”

“But why?”

“To divert suspicion, of course! While everyone is searching for
the thief of the imitation necklace, the real thief has a clear
field.”

“But who is the thief?”

“That is what we have to find out.”

I thought for a moment.

“It must be the maid,” I said at last. “She’s the only one who had
the opportunity.”

“On the contrary,” said Poirot, “she’s the only one who hadn’t!
If she had the real pearls, why should she go to the trouble of
substituting an imitation necklace? It would be much simpler to
take the real ones and have done with it.”

“Then who do you suspect?”

“There are several possibilities. There is the husband, for
instance. He may have been in difficulties and have taken his
wife’s pearls and replaced them with imitations. Then there is
the chambermaid. Or—there is someone else.”

“Someone else?”

“Yes. Someone we have not yet considered.”

He fell into a silence, and I did not disturb him. I knew from
experience that when Poirot was in this mood it was best to leave
him alone.

Presently he looked up.

“Hastings,” he said, “I have a little commission for you. Will you
go and find out for me if any of the rooms on this floor are
vacant?”

I went off on my errand, and returned in a few minutes.

“Only one,” I reported. “Number 24, the room next to the Opalsens’.”

Poirot nodded.

“As I thought. And now, my friend, we will go for a little stroll
on the front.”

We walked along in silence for some time, Poirot apparently deep
in thought. Suddenly he stopped and turned to me.

“Hastings,” he said, “do you remember that rectangular mark on
the table in the room next door?”

“Yes,” I said, “I noticed it.”

“And the salt?”

“Yes.”

“Does anything occur to you?”

“Nothing,” I admitted.

“_Mon Dieu!_” he cried. “It is so simple! The mark on the table
was made by a heavy case—a jewel-case, for instance. And the
salt—have you never heard of the use of salt in the cleaning of
jewellery?”

“I can’t say I have,” I replied.

“It is a well-known method. One uses salt to remove the tarnish
from silver or gold. Now, suppose someone had been cleaning a
necklace in that room—a necklace of real pearls. They would use
salt for the purpose. And some of it would naturally be spilled.”

“But who could have been cleaning a necklace in a vacant room?”

“Exactly! That is the question. Someone who had access to the
room, and who wanted to do the work in secret.”

“The chambermaid?” I suggested.

“Perhaps. Or someone else. Someone who knew that the room was
vacant.”

He was silent again for a moment, then he said:

“We must find out who was in that room this afternoon. It may
be that we shall find our thief there.”

We returned to the hotel, and Poirot went off to interview the
manager. I waited for him in the lounge, and when he returned he
looked satisfied.

“Well?” I asked.

“The room was occupied this afternoon,” he said. “By a gentleman
who arrived by the mid-day train and left again at five o’clock.”

“Do you know his name?”

“He gave the name of Mr. Henderson. But I have reason to believe
that it was not his real name.”

“Why?”

“Because he left behind him a piece of paper on which was written
the name of a well-known firms of jewellers in London.”

“Then he was the thief!” I cried.

“It seems likely. But we have still to find him.”

“How are you going to do that?”

“I have already taken steps. I have telephoned to the jewellers in
London, and they have promised to let me know if anyone calls there
with a necklace of pearls to be valued.”

“But he may not go there.”

“True. But it is a chance. And in the meantime, we must look
nearer home.”

“What do you mean?”

“I mean that we must not forget our friends the Opalsens.”

“You don’t really suspect them?”

“I suspect everyone, my friend. It is my rule. And in this case,
there are several things that require explanation.”

“Such as?”

“Well, for instance, why did Mr. Opalsen seem so anxious that the
police should take charge of the necklace? And why did he look so
surprised when I asked him if it was insured?”

“He may have been worried about the loss.”

“Perhaps. But there is something else. Did you notice the way
Mrs. Opalsen clasped the necklace to her breast? It was the
action of a woman who has recovered something she values very
highly. And yet, if it was an imitation——”

“She may not have known.”

“True. But her husband? He is a man of the world. He would
surely know if his wife’s pearls were real or not.”

“He might not have looked at them closely.”

“Perhaps. But there is another thing. Why was the imitation
necklace hidden in the maid’s bed?”

“To throw suspicion on her, as you said.”

“But who would want to do that? Not the thief from London. He
would have no reason to suspect the maid. No, it must have been
someone who knew her—someone who wanted to get her into trouble.”

“The chambermaid!” I cried.

“It is possible. But we must have proof.”

He was silent for a moment, then he said:

“I have an idea, Hastings. A little trap that I think may be
successful. Will you help me?”

“Of course,” I said. “What do you want me to do?”

“I want you to go to Mr. Opalsen and tell him that I have
