discovered something important. Tell him that I have found the
real thief, and that I want him to come to my room at once.”

“And then?”

“Then we shall see.”

I did as he requested, and a few minutes later Mr. Opalsen arrived
at our room. He looked anxious and excited.

“What is it?” he asked. “Have you found the pearls?”

“Not yet,” said Poirot. “But I have found the person who stole
them.”

“Who is it?”

“It is someone who is in this hotel at this moment. Someone who
thought they had been very clever, but who forgot one little
thing.”

“What was that?”

“The salt.”

Mr. Opalsen looked puzzled.

“The salt? I don’t understand.”

“You will soon. But first, I must ask you a question. Was your
wife’s necklace insured for its full value?”

Mr. Opalsen hesitated.

“Yes,” he said at last. “For twenty thousand pounds.”

“I see. And you would have received that sum if the pearls had not
been found?”

“I suppose so.”

“And now that they have been found—or rather, now that an
imitation necklace has been found—you will receive nothing?”

“I suppose not.”

“A great disappointment, no doubt.”

Mr. Opalsen looked at him sharply.

“What are you getting at, Mr. Poirot?”

“I am getting at the truth, monsieur. The truth about the
disappearance of your wife’s pearls.”

“And what is that?”

“The truth is that you yourself took the pearls, and replaced
them with imitations. You then arranged for the imitation
necklace to be found in the maid’s bed, so that she would be
suspected of the theft.”

Mr. Opalsen sprang to his feet, his face purple with rage.

“How dare you!” he cried. “How dare you accuse me of such a
thing!”

“Calm yourself, monsieur. I have proof.”

“Proof? What proof?”

“The salt. You were seen in the room next door, cleaning the
pearls with salt. And you left some of it behind.”

Mr. Opalsen laughed scornfully.

“Is that all? I was never in that room in my life.”

“Then perhaps you can explain how your fingerprints came to be on
the table there?”

Mr. Opalsen went pale.

“My—my fingerprints?”

“Yes. I have taken a photograph of them, and they are identical
with yours.”

Mr. Opalsen sank back into his chair, his head in his hands.

“It’s no use,” he groaned. “I did it. I was in a hole—I needed
the money. I thought I could get the insurance, and then sell the
pearls later.”

“And the maid?”

“I’m sorry about her. I didn’t mean to get her into trouble. I
just wanted to make it look like a real robbery.”

“I see. Well, monsieur, I am afraid you will have to explain all
this to the police.”

Mr. Opalsen did not answer. He seemed completely crushed.

Poirot turned to me.

“Well, Hastings, what do you think of my little trap?”

“It was brilliant!” I cried. “But how did you know about the
fingerprints? You didn’t take any photographs.”

Poirot smiled.

“No, my friend. It was a bluff—what you call a ‘bluff.’ But it
worked, did it not?”

“It certainly did. But what about the man from London—Mr.
Henderson?”

“There was no Mr. Henderson. I invented him to see how Mr.
Opalsen would react. And his reaction told me all I wanted to
know.”

“And the salt?”

“That was real. But it wasn’t salt—it was sugar. I put it there
myself.”

I stared at him in amazement.

“You put it there yourself?”

“Yes. I wanted to see if anyone would be interested in it. And
Mr. Opalsen was. He couldn’t take his eyes off it.”

“But how did you know he’d taken the pearls in the first place?”

“I didn’t. But I suspected him from the beginning. His manner was
not that of a man who has lost a valuable piece of property. He
was too calm—too indifferent. And then, there was the insurance.”

“It was a great piece of work, Poirot,” I said.

“It was nothing, my friend. A mere trifle. But it has saved a
poor girl’s reputation, and that is something.”

He looked at his watch.

“And now, I think we have just time for a little supper before
we go to bed. What do you say, Hastings?”

“I say it’s a capital idea,” I replied.

And so we went off together, the best of friends.

“And, anyway,” I continued, “what does it matter? The case is over.
I wish you’d had more chance of distinguishing yourself. But it
was the kind of case that even a stiff-backed idiot like that
inspector couldn’t go wrong over.”

Poirot shook his head.

“The case is not over, my friend. It will not be over until we find
out who stole the pearls.”

“But the maid did!”

“Why do you say that?”

“Why,” I stammered, “they were found—actually in her mattress.”

“Ta, ta, ta!” said Poirot impatiently. “Those were not the pearls.”

“What?”

“Imitation, _mon ami_.”

The statement took my breath away. Poirot was smiling placidly.

“The good inspector obviously knows nothing of jewels. But presently
there will be a fine hullabaloo!”

“Come!” I cried, dragging at his arm.

“Where?”

“We must tell the Opalsens at once.”

“I think not.”

“But that poor woman——”

“_Eh bien_; that poor woman, as you call her, will have a much
better night believing the jewels to be safe.”

“But the thief may escape with them!”

“The thief, _mon ami_, is not likely to go far, for the simple
reason that the pearls are in this hotel.”

I stared at him.

“In this hotel? Then it was not the maid after all?”

“No. It was not the maid. She was a mere tool. Some one else placed
them in her mattress.”

“Who?”

“That is what we have to find out.”

“But how could they?”

“Wait a bit. Let us think.”

He sat down on the edge of the bed and looked about him.

“I was thinking of the window. No, it is impossible. The next
room is Mrs. Opalsen’s. And this one is empty.”

“Wait!” I cried. “What about the other side?”

“The other side?”

“Yes. There’s another room on the other side of this one. Who’s
in that?”

“Let us go and see.”

We left the room and walked along the corridor. The door of the
next room was slightly ajar. Poirot pushed it open.

“Ah!” he said, and went in.

It was a small room, very neatly kept. On the chest of drawers was
a Bible and a prayer-book. Poirot walked to the window.

“Ah!” he said again, and beckoned me.

I joined him. Below us was a small balcony.

“You see?” said Poirot. “This room is immediately above the
Opalsens’. The balcony of this room is the roof of theirs. A man
could easily let himself down by a rope.”

“But what man?”

“Ah, that we have to find out. Some one who knew the geography of
the hotel—some one who knew Mrs. Opalsen had the pearls, and where
she kept them.”

He was silent for a moment. Then he said:

“I have it!”

“What?”

“The chambermaid.”

“But the inspector searched her!”

“Exactly. And found nothing. Which is just what I should have
expected. She would not have the pearls on her. She would hide
them.”

“But where?”

“Where indeed? Let us think. She comes in to turn down the beds.
The maid is there. She has only a few minutes. She must hide them
somewhere where they will not be found easily, and yet where she
can get at them again.”

He looked round the room.

“Not here. This is her own room. It would be too dangerous. No,
it must be somewhere else.”

He went out into the corridor again.

“Ah!” he said, stopping in front of a small door. “What is this?”

He opened it. It was a small housemaid’s cupboard, containing
brooms, pails, and such-like.

Poirot went in and began to rummage among the contents. Suddenly
he gave a cry of triumph.

“See here!”

He held up a small brown-paper parcel.

“The pearls!” I cried.

“Let us see.”

He untied the string. Inside was a magnificent string of pearls.

“Are they the real ones?” I asked.

Poirot took them to the light.

“Yes,” he said. “These are the real ones. And now, Hastings, we
must act quickly.”

“What are you going to do?”

“I am going to put these back where they belong—in Mrs. Opalsen’s
jewel-case.”

“But the inspector has it!”

“Exactly. We must get it from him.”

“How?”

“Leave that to me. Come!”

We went back to the Opalsens’ room. The inspector was just leaving.

“One moment, monsieur,” said Poirot. “I have a small request to
make. Would you allow me to see the jewel-case once more?”

The inspector looked surprised.

“Why, certainly, if you like. But I’m afraid I must keep the
necklaces.”

“Of course, of course. I only wish to see the case.”

The inspector handed it to him. Poirot took it to the window. His
back was turned to us. A moment later he handed it back.

“Thank you, monsieur. I am satisfied.”

The inspector went out. Poirot turned to me with a smile.

“And now, Hastings, I think we may go to bed.”

“But the pearls!” I cried. “You haven’t got them!”

“On the contrary, _mon ami_, I have them here.”

He tapped his pocket.

“But I thought you put them in the jewel-case!”

“So I did—the imitation ones!”

I stared at him in amazement.

“But—but——”

“My dear Hastings, do you not see? The thief—whoever it was—would
naturally go to the jewel-case first. Finding the imitation pearls
there, he—or she—would think they were the real ones, and would
not look any further. Then, when the robbery was discovered, and
the imitation pearls found in the maid’s bed, the thief would be
completely off his guard. He would think he had the real pearls
all the time!”

“I see! But who _is_ the thief?”

“That, my friend, we shall discover tomorrow. And now, _bon soir_.”

The next morning Poirot was up early. I found him in the lounge,
reading the paper.

“Any news?” I asked.

“None. But I have had a little talk with the manager. He is much
distressed at what has happened.”

“I don’t wonder. It’s not a good advertisement for the hotel.”

“Exactly. He is most anxious that the matter should be cleared up
as soon as possible. I have promised him my assistance.”

“Have you any clue?”

“A very important one, Hastings. I have found out who was in the
empty room next to the Opalsens’ yesterday afternoon.”

“Who?”

“Mr. Opalsen.”

“Opalsen!” I cried. “But why should he go in there?”

“That is what I am going to ask him.”

At that moment Mr. Opalsen himself came into the lounge. He looked
pale and anxious.

“Good morning, Mr. Poirot,” he said. “Any news?”

“I have some very important news, Mr. Opalsen. May I have a few
words with you in private?”

“Certainly. Come into the office.”

We followed him into the manager’s office. Poirot closed the door.

“Mr. Opalsen,” he said, “I will go straight to the point. Why did
you go into the empty room next to your own yesterday afternoon?”

Opalsen started.

“How do you know I did?”

“I saw the mark of your jewel-case on the dust of the table.”

Opalsen was silent for a moment. Then he said:

“You are a very clever man, Mr. Poirot. It is no use trying to
hide anything from you. I did go into that room. I went there to
hide my wife’s pearls.”

“To hide them? But why?”

“Because I was in desperate need of money. I have been having a
very bad time lately, and I simply had to have some cash. I knew
the pearls were insured for a large sum, and I thought if they
were stolen I could claim the insurance money. I knew my wife
would never miss them for a few days, as she only wears them on
special occasions. So I took them out of the case and hid them in
the empty room, intending to take them away later and sell them.
But then everything went wrong. My wife decided to wear them last
night, and discovered they were gone. I was terrified. I didn't
know what to do. Then the police came, and I thought I was safe.
But when they found the imitation pearls in the maid’s bed, I
was more terrified than ever. I knew then that some one else must
have seen me hide the pearls, and had stolen them from where I had
put them, leaving the imitation ones in their place.”

“And who was that some one else?” asked Poirot.

“I don’t know. I have no idea.”

“I can tell you,” said Poirot. “It was the chambermaid.”

“The chambermaid!”

“Yes. She saw you go into the room, and she saw where you put the
pearls. As soon as you had gone, she went in and took them. She
had already provided herself with a string of imitation pearls,
intending to steal the real ones at the first opportunity. She
saw her chance and took it. Then, when the robbery was discovered,
she hid the imitation pearls in the maid’s bed, to draw suspicion
away from herself.”

“But how did you find out?” asked Opalsen.

“It was very simple,” said Poirot. “I knew the pearls found in the
maid’s bed were imitation. Therefore, the real pearls must still
be in the hotel. I searched the chambermaid’s room, but found
nothing. Then I searched the housemaid’s cupboard, and there I
found them. The rest was easy.”

“Mr. Poirot,” said Opalsen, “I don’t know how to thank you. You
have saved me from a very terrible position.”

“I have done my duty,” said Poirot. “But I have one piece of advice
to give you, Mr. Opalsen. In future, do not try to swindle the
insurance companies. It is a very dangerous game—and Hercule
Poirot is always there to find you out!”

“_Pas du tout_, my friend. The thief has already escaped with
them.”

“How?”

“By the window.”

“But you said yourself there was no balcony.”

“I said also that the door into the room where we are now was
bolted on both sides. But that did not prevent it from being
opened.”

“I don’t understand.”

“Wait, and you will see. It is all very simple, really.”

“But the maid?” I persisted. “Why was it found in her room?”

“Because the thief is a clever one. He knows it is more than
possible the room will be searched, and it is well to provide a
scapegoat. Besides, it would be difficult for any one to get away
with the real pearls at once.”

“You think it was the chambermaid?”

“No, I do not think so.”

“Then who?”

“The person who opened the door between the two rooms.”

“But it was bolted on both sides!”

“Precisely.”

I stared at him. He seemed to be enjoying my bewilderment.

“Look, Hastings,” he said, pointing to the rectangular mark on
the table. “What do you think was there?”

“A book?” I suggested.

“A box, _mon ami_. A box which contained the tools of a very
skilful workman. Now, come, and I will show you how it was done.”

“Oh, we’ve plenty of time,” said Poirot, looking at his watch.
“I’ll tell you my theory of the crime, Hastings. Now, someone
comes into the room to take the pearls. They must have had a
duplicate key to the jewel-case. If Célestine was really in the
room, it must have been someone she knew—someone who could come
in and out without her thinking anything of it. Who could that
be?”

“I don’t know,” I said.

“No, no, _mon ami_, think. Not the chambermaid—for she says
Célestine was always there. Then who?”

“The husband?” I suggested.

“Exactly—the husband. He’s the only one who could have gone into
his wife’s room while the maid was there and not have been noticed.
He’s also the only person who would have known where the pearls
were kept. And if he was hard up for money——”

“You think _he_ took them?”

“Wait a bit. Let’s look at the other side. Suppose the maid took
them. Then she must have had a duplicate key. She also knew where
they were kept. But if she took them, why did she hide them in
her own bed? It’s the first place they’d look.”

“Panic?” I suggested.

“Possibly. But there’s another point. Those pearls we saw were
imitation. Now, would a maid have an imitation necklace ready to
put in the place of the real one?”

“No,” I admitted, “that doesn’t seem likely.”

“But the owner might,” Poirot continued. “Suppose Mrs. Opalsen
had already sold the pearls and was wearing a duplicate? Then she
would be only too glad to have them ‘stolen’ and get the insurance
money as well.”

“Poirot!” I exclaimed. “What a mind you have!”

“It is a possibility, is it not? But there is a third person we
must not forget.”

“Who is that?”

“The chambermaid. We have only her word for it that she was in the
room all the time. Suppose she and the maid were in it together?”

“But they were both searched!”

“So they were,” said Poirot meditatively. “So they were.”

He fell into a silence, from which he was only roused by the sound
of voices in the corridor. The Opalsens were coming out of their
room.

“I think,” said Poirot, “we had better join them.”

He led the way into the hall, and we followed the Opalsens down the
stairs. They were both looking much more cheerful.

“Well, Mr. Poirot,” said the stockbroker, “the police have got the
thief and the pearls, so everything’s all right. We’re going to
celebrate with a little supper. Won’t you and your friend join
us?”

“With the greatest of pleasure,” said Poirot.

We went into the restaurant and were soon seated at a small table.
Mrs. Opalsen was in high spirits.

“I’m so relieved,” she said. “I don’t know what I should have done
if I’d lost those pearls. They were quite a part of me, if you
know what I mean.”

“I do indeed, madame,” said Poirot. “By the way, I suppose you
didn’t happen to see any one else in your room this evening?
Before you went down to dinner, for instance?”

Mrs. Opalsen shook her head.

“No one but Célestine and the chambermaid.”

“And you’re quite sure the pearls were there then?”

“Oh, yes. I told you I looked at them.”

“And you’re sure they were the real ones?”

Mrs. Opalsen stared at him.

“Of course they were! What a question!”

“I only wondered,” said Poirot mildly. “Because, you see, those
the inspector found were—not real.”

There was a moment’s dead silence. Then Mrs. Opalsen gave a sort
of gasp.

“Not real? What do you mean?”

“I mean, madame, that they were a very clever imitation.”

“But—but—how could they be? I saw them myself.”

“Exactly. You saw them. But were they the ones you put in the
case?”

Mrs. Opalsen looked quite bewildered. Her husband came to her
rescue.

“What’s all this, Mr. Poirot? Are you suggesting that my wife
doesn’t know her own pearls?”

“Not at all. I am suggesting that someone changed them _before_
she put them into the case.”

“But who could have done that?”

“Ah, that is the question!” Poirot leaned back in his chair and
surveyed the company. “Shall we consider the possibilities? There
is the maid, the chambermaid, and—yourself, monsieur.”

“Me?” Mr. Opalsen laughed. “That’s a good joke!”

“Is it?” Poirot’s eyes were fixed on the stockbroker’s face. “I
wonder.”

“Look here, Mr. Poirot, if you’re suggesting that I stole my wife’s
pearls——”

“I am suggesting nothing, monsieur. I am only pointing out that
you are one of the three people who could have done so.”

“Well, I didn’t. So that’s that.”

“Then we are left with the two women. Now, as I have already pointed
out, it is unlikely that either of them would have had an imitation
necklace ready to put in the place of the real one. But there is
someone else who might.”

“Who?”

“The person who is at the bottom of the whole affair. The person
who planned the robbery and who is now, in all probability, in
possession of the real pearls.”

“And who is that?”

“The person who stole them,” said Poirot simply.

“But you said just now that the inspector had found them!”

“No, monsieur. I said the inspector had found some pearls. I did
not say they were the ones that were stolen.”

“Then where are the real ones?”

“That,” said Poirot, “is what I am going to find out.”

He rose from the table.

“If you will excuse me, I think I will go and have a little talk
with the manager.”

We watched him walk away across the room. Mrs. Opalsen looked at
her husband.

“Ed,” she said, “what does he mean?”

“God knows!” said Opalsen. “The man’s mad, if you ask me.”

I did not think so. I knew Poirot too well. I followed him out of
the restaurant.

He was in the hall, talking to the manager.

“I should like to know,” he was saying, “who occupied the room
next to Mrs. Opalsen’s this evening.”

The manager looked at his books.

“Room 28? It was taken this afternoon by a Mr. and Mrs. Robinson.
But they’ve already left.”

“Left? When?”

“About half an hour ago. They said they’d had a telegram calling
them away.”

“I see,” said Poirot. “And did they leave a forwarding address?”

“No. They said they’d write.”

Poirot turned to me.

“You see, Hastings? The Robinsons. A very common name. Too common,
perhaps.”

“You think they have the pearls?”

“I am sure of it. But how did they get them? That is the question.”

He stood for a moment, lost in thought. Then he turned back to
the manager.

“Tell me—was there anything unusual about these Robinsons?
Anything that struck you as being—well, out of the common?”

The manager shook his head.

“No, I don’t think so. They seemed a very quiet, ordinary couple.
The lady was a bit of an invalid, I believe—at least, she didn’t
come down to dinner.”

“Ah!” Poirot’s eyes lit up. “She didn’t come down to dinner. And the
husband?”

“Oh, he was there. I saw him myself.”

“I see. Thank you, monsieur. You have been most helpful.”

He turned away and began to pace up and down the hall.

“Hastings,” he said, “I begin to see. It is all very simple—very
simple indeed.”

“Is it?” I said. “It doesn’t seem so to me.”

“That is because you do not use your little grey cells, _mon ami_.
Consider the facts. The pearls are stolen from a locked case in
a room where a maid is sitting. They are later found in the maid’s
bed—but they are imitation. The real pearls have vanished. And
at the same time a mysterious couple, who have only just arrived,
leave the hotel in a hurry.”

“It seems clear enough,” I said. “The Robinsons stole them.”

“But how? How did they get into the room? The door was bolted on
the inside.”

“The window?”

“We have already seen that that was impossible.”

“Then how?”

“There is only one way,” said Poirot. “They didn’t get into the
room.”

“But they must have!”

“Not necessarily. Suppose the pearls were brought to them?”

“By whom? The maid?”

“Or the chambermaid. Or even,” he added with a smile, “the husband.”

“But you said just now——”

“I know what I said, Hastings. But I have changed my mind. I often
do, as you know. It is a sign of a great mind.”

He laughed and patted me on the shoulder.

“Come, my friend. Let us go back to the restaurant. I think I have
a little surprise for our friends the Opalsens.”

When we returned, we found the stockbroker and his wife still at
their table. They looked up as we approached.

“Well?” said Opalsen. “Any news?”

“I have some news, yes,” said Poirot. “But first, I should like to
ask you a question. When you went down to dinner this evening,
did you happen to see the chambermaid?”

“The chambermaid? No, I don’t think so. Why?”

“Because,” said Poirot, “I have reason to believe that she was
not in the hotel at that time.”

“Not in the hotel? But she was in our room when we came up!”

“I know. But that was later. I am talking about the time when you
were at dinner.”

“I don’t understand,” said Mrs. Opalsen. “What does it matter where
she was?”

“It matters a great deal, madame. Because, you see, it was during
that time that the pearls were stolen.”

“But Célestine was there!”

“Was she? Are you sure?”

“Of course I’m sure! She told me so herself.”

“Ah!” Poirot smiled. “She told you so. But did you see her?”

“No, but——”

“Exactly. You didn’t see her. And why? Because she wasn’t there.”

“Then where was she?”

“She was in the room next door,” said Poirot. “With the Robinsons.”

“The Robinsons? Who are they?”

“The people who stole your pearls, madame. Or rather, the people
who have them now.”

“But how did they get them? You said just now that they didn’t go
into the room.”

“They didn’t. The pearls were brought to them—through the bolt.”

“The bolt?” We all stared at him.

“Precisely,” said Poirot. “It is a very old trick, but a very
effective one. You take a piece of silk thread, pass it through
the loop of the bolt, and then out under the door. When you want
to open the door from the other side, you just pull the thread,
and the bolt slides back. When you’ve finished, you pull the other
end of the thread, and the bolt slides back into place. It’s quite
simple.”

“But the door was bolted on both sides!” I cried.

“Exactly. That’s what made it so clever. The Robinsons bolted the
door on their side in the ordinary way. Then they used the thread
to bolt it on the other side. It’s a trick that’s often used by
thieves.”

“But the pearls?” said Mrs. Opalsen. “How did they get the pearls?”

“That,” said Poirot, “is where the chambermaid comes in. Or rather,
the person who was pretending to be the chambermaid.”

“Pretending?”

“Yes. You see, the real chambermaid was lured away by a bogus
message. Her place was taken by an accomplice of the Robinsons.
This woman went into the room while Célestine was in her own room,
took the pearls, and replaced them with the imitation ones. Then,
when the alarm was raised, she hid the imitation pearls in the
maid’s bed, knowing that they would be found and that the maid
would be suspected.”

“But the real pearls?”

“She passed them through the door to the Robinsons, who then
departed with them. It was a very neat little plot.”

“And where are they now?” asked Opalsen.

“I think,” said Poirot, “that if we were to look in the Robinsons’
luggage—which, by the way, is still at the station—we should find
them.”

“But how did you find all this out?” I asked.

Poirot smiled.

“It was the mark on the table, Hastings. The mark of a jewel-case.
It was quite fresh. And it was in the room next door. That told
me that the pearls had been there. The rest was easy.”

“And the chambermaid?” asked Mrs. Opalsen. “What about her?”

“The real chambermaid is, I believe, at this moment in the
manager’s office, wondering what all the fuss is about. The woman
you saw was, as I said, an accomplice.”

“Well,” said Opalsen, “I must say, Mr. Poirot, you’ve been very
clever. I don’t know how to thank you.”

“You can thank me,” said Poirot, “by giving me another of those
excellent cigarettes of yours. I find them most stimulating to the
little grey cells.”

He laughed and held out his hand for the cigarette-case. As he
did so, I noticed that his eyes were twinkling. I knew that
twinkle. It meant that Poirot had not yet told us everything.

“But what about the maid?” I asked. “Is she still in custody?”

“I have already arranged for her release,” said Poirot. “I think
she has suffered enough, don’t you?”

“Poor girl!” said Mrs. Opalsen. “I must make it up to her somehow.”

“I’m sure she’d appreciate that, madame,” said Poirot.

He lit his cigarette and leaned back in his chair with a sigh of
satisfaction.

“A very interesting case,” he murmured. “Small, but interesting.”

“But Poirot,” I said, “there’s one thing I don’t understand. How
did the accomplice get into the room in the first place? You said
the maid was there.”

“I said the maid was in her own room, Hastings. Remember? She
went in there twice—once for some cotton and once for some
scissors. It was then that the theft was committed.”

“But that only took a few seconds!”

“Long enough for a clever thief, _mon ami_. As I demonstrated to
you myself.”

“I see,” I said. “It all seems very simple now you’ve explained it.”

“It always does, Hastings. It always does.”

He smiled and closed his eyes. I knew that he was already
thinking of his next case.

“No, my friend. He has already escaped. But we shall see. In the
meantime we will return to our coffee.”

As we sat together, Poirot sighed.

“I was hoping for something better, Hastings. It is too easy.
_C’est un peu banale_, but it will serve.”

“Well, you haven’t done anything as yet!” I pointed out.

“_Patience, mon ami_. You will see. All things come to him who
waits.”

I did not quite follow him.

“You mean the thief is still in the hotel?”

“No. He went away an hour ago.”

“Then we shall never find him!”

“On the contrary. I am sure we shall.”

“But how? Where did he go?”

“To London.”

“Are you joking?”

“Not at all. I have a certain idea.”

“But how do you know?”

“Because he took the 9:45 train.”

“But how do you know _that_?”

“Because I saw him.”

“What? Who was it?”

“Ah, _mon ami_, that is my little secret. But we will follow him.”

“When?”

“To-morrow morning.”

“But the Opalsens?”

“We will see them before we go.”

I was completely mystified. However, I have long ago learned that
it is useless to question Poirot when he is in this mood.

Next morning, after a somewhat hurried breakfast, we sought out
the Opalsens. We found them in a state of great agitation.

“The pearls!” cried Mrs. Opalsen. “They’re paste! The police have
just been here. They say they’re only worth a few shillings. Oh,
what shall I do?”

Poirot smiled.

“Calm yourself, madame. I have a little plan.”

He drew her husband aside.

“I want you to come with me to London. We must be quick. There is
not a moment to lose.”

“But what for? What are you going to do?”

“I am going to find your pearls.”

“But where? Who has got them?”

“The thief, monsieur. He is at this moment in London. We must
catch him before he can dispose of them.”

Mr. Opalsen looked at him doubtfully.

“But how do you know? The police——”

“The police!” Poirot snapped his fingers. “They are well-meaning,
no doubt, but they have no imagination. They see a thing and they
believe it. I see a thing and I do _not_ believe it—until I have
examined it.”

“But what do you want me to do?”

“Come with me to London—now—at once.”

Mr. Opalsen hesitated.

“Very well,” he said at last. “I’ll come.”

“Good! Hastings, you will come also?”

“Of course,” I said.

The journey to London was a somewhat silent one. Poirot appeared
to be deep in thought. When we arrived at Victoria, he hailed a
taxi.

“Where to?” I asked.

“To a certain shop in Bond Street,” replied Poirot.

“But what for?”

“To see a friend of mine.”

The taxi drew up at a small, unpretentious shop. Poirot jumped out
and we followed him inside. An elderly man with a long white beard
was sitting behind the counter. He looked up as we entered.

“Ah, Monsieur Poirot!” he exclaimed. “It is a long time since I
have seen you.”

“_C’est vrai_, Monsieur Henri. But I have come to ask your advice.”

“At your service, monsieur.”

Poirot drew a small box from his pocket and opened it. Inside,
lying on a bed of white cotton-wool, was a magnificent pearl
necklace.

Mr. Opalsen gasped.

“My pearls!” he cried.

Poirot smiled.

“Not yet, monsieur. These are the ones I took from the maid’s
mattress last night.”

“But you said they were paste!”

“And so they are. But I want Monsieur Henri to tell me if he knows
anything about them.”

The old man took the necklace and examined it through a powerful
glass.

“Yes,” he said at last. “I know them. They were made in my workshop.”

“Ah!” Poirot’s eyes sparkled. “And when?”

“About three weeks ago.”

“And for whom?”

“For a gentleman who called himself Mr. Smith.”

“Can you describe him?”

“He was a tall man, with a dark moustache. He seemed to be in a
great hurry.”

“I see. Thank you, Monsieur Henri. You have been most helpful.”

As we left the shop, Mr. Opalsen turned to Poirot.

“What does it all mean? I don’t understand.”

“It is very simple, monsieur. Your pearls were stolen—not last
night, but three weeks ago.”

“What!”

“Yes. They were replaced by these paste ones. The thief then waited
for a convenient opportunity to ‘discover’ the robbery. He chose
last night.”

“But who? Who could have done such a thing?”

“That, monsieur, is what we are going to find out. But first, we
must go to the Central News Agency.”

I was more puzzled than ever. What could the Central News Agency
have to do with the case?

However, Poirot seemed to know what he was about. At the Agency,
he asked for a list of all the people who had been staying at the
_Grand Metropolitan_ during the last month.

He pored over the list for some time, then he gave a little cry of
satisfaction.

“I have it!” he said.

“What?”

“The name of the thief.”

“Who is it?”

“It is a man who calls himself Mr. Edward Robinson. But his real
name is—something quite different.”

“But how do you know?”

“Because he is a well-known jewel thief. I have had dealings with
him before.”

“And where is he now?”

“He is at this moment at the Savoy Hotel. We must go there at once.”

Once again we were in a taxi. As we drove along, Poirot explained.

“You see, Hastings, the whole thing was a very clever plot. The
thief—Robinson—knew that Mrs. Opalsen had these pearls. He also
knew that she was very fond of them, and would be sure to show
them to any one who was interested. He therefore made a duplicate
set in paste. Then he went to Brighton and stayed at the _Grand
Metropolitan_. He waited for a chance to get into Mrs. Opalsen’s
room and exchange the pearls. This he did about three weeks ago.”

“But the maid?”

“Ah, the maid! She was the difficulty. He knew that she was always
in the room when the chambermaid was there. He therefore had to
find a way to get her out of the room for a few minutes. He did
this by—well, we shall see.”

“But the pearls in the mattress?”

“That was a stroke of genius. He knew that if the robbery was
discovered, the police would search the room. He therefore hid
the paste pearls in the maid’s mattress, knowing that they would
be found and that she would be suspected. In the confusion, he
would be able to get away with the real pearls.”

“But how did he get into the room?”

“Through the door from the next apartment. It was bolted on both
sides, but he had a key.”

“But you said it was bolted!”

“So it was—last night. But three weeks ago it was not.”

The taxi drew up at the Savoy. Poirot led the way into the lounge.

“Wait here,” he said.

He disappeared for a few minutes, then he returned with a man in
uniform.

“This is the manager,” he said. “He will take us to Mr. Robinson’s
room.”

We went up in the lift to the fourth floor. The manager led us
along a corridor and stopped at a door. He knocked.

“Come in!” said a voice.

We entered. A man was sitting at a table, writing. He looked up
as we came in.

“Mr. Robinson?” said Poirot.

“Yes. What can I do for you?”

“I am Hercule Poirot. I have come for the Opalsen pearls.”

The man turned pale. He made a move towards the window, but the
manager and I were too quick for him.

“It’s no use, Robinson,” said Poirot. “The game is up.”

The man sank back into his chair.

“How did you find out?” he asked.

“It was very simple. You made one mistake. You forgot that I was
at the _Grand Metropolitan_ last night.”

He turned to Mr. Opalsen.

“Here are your pearls, monsieur.”

He drew a small bag from his pocket and handed it to the stockbroker.

Mr. Opalsen opened it. Inside were the real pearls.

“Thank God!” he said.

“And now,” said Poirot, “I think we will leave Mr. Robinson to the
police.”

As we walked back to our hotel, I turned to Poirot.

“But how did you know it was Robinson? You said you saw him on the
train.”

“So I did, Hastings. But I did not know then that he was the thief.
I only knew that he was a man I had seen before—at a jewel
thief’s trial.”

“But how did you know he had the pearls?”

“I didn’t. But I knew that he was the only person who could have
taken them. And when I saw his name on the list at the Central News
Agency, I was sure.”

“But what about the chambermaid? You said it was impossible for
her to have taken them.”

“So it was—last night. But it was not impossible for her to have
helped Robinson three weeks ago.”

“The chambermaid!” I cried.

“Yes, Hastings. She was his accomplice. She let him into the room
through the communicating door.”

“But why did she do it?”

“For money, no doubt. She was a very clever girl—but not quite
clever enough for Hercule Poirot!”

I looked at my friend. Once again he had triumphed.

“Poirot,” I said, “you are a marvel!”

“No, no, Hastings. I am only—Hercule Poirot!”

“That is why I am waiting,” said Poirot. “I have my little idea.
And if I am right, we shall catch the thief red-handed. We will
now go and have a look at the register.”

We went downstairs. The book lay open on the desk. Poirot’s finger
ran down the names.

“Room 14. Mr. and Mrs. Opalsen. Room 15. The maid’s room. Room 16.
Mr. and Mrs. Charles Parker. That is the room we have just been
in. And they left—when? This afternoon.”

Poirot’s eyes were gleaming with excitement.

“Now, Hastings, go and see if you can find the boots. He should be
about somewhere.”

I did as I was told. The man was in the basement, cleaning knives.
Poirot followed me.

“One moment, my friend,” he said, with a pleasant smile. “You
remember Room 16—the people who left this afternoon?”

“Yes, sir. Mr. and Mrs. Parker.”

“You moved their luggage?”

“Yes, sir. Two trunks and a suitcase.”

“A suitcase? A heavy one?”

“Well, sir, it was a bit on the heavy side, now you mention it.”

“And you took it—where?”

“To the station, sir.”

“To the cloak-room?”

“No, sir. They took it with them in the taxi.”

“Thank you.”

Poirot turned to me.

“You see, Hastings? The case is beginning to clear itself.”

“But I don’t see it at all!” I protested. “Who are these Parkers?”

“Ah, that is what I should like to know! But they are people of
method, Hastings. They knew that the room next to Mrs. Opalsen’s
would be vacant to-day. They knew the ways of the household. They
knew about the pearls.”

“But how did they get them? The door was bolted!”

“Bolts,” said Poirot, “can be drawn from the other side. A piece
of wire—it is an old trick. And the maid—she was not always in the
room.”

“But she said she was!”

“She _thought_ she was. But I have proved she was away for nearly
half a minute. In that time, it would be possible for some one
to enter from the next room, take the pearls, and—no, that is
where the difficulty begins.”

He paused, frowning.

“Wait!” I cried. “I have it! They didn’t take the pearls at all.
They only changed them for the imitation ones. Then, when the
theft was discovered, the maid would be sure to be suspected.”

“Exactly,” said Poirot. “But there is one little point you have
overlooked. The maid was in the room _after_ the pearls were stolen.
She would have noticed if the case had been tampered with.”

“Not if it was locked.”

“But she would have heard the key turning.”

“The thief might have had a duplicate key.”

“Even so, he would have had to open the drawer. No, Hastings,
there is something else. Some one in this hotel is a very clever
thief. And I have a fancy that we shall find our man—or woman—before
long.”

“Then you think the Parkers——”

“I think the Parkers were a very useful blind. But the real thief
is still in the hotel.”

“But who?”

“That is what we have to find out.”

He fell into a silence, which I did not like to break. We went up
to our rooms. Poirot was still deep in thought. Suddenly he
started.

“Hastings! The chambermaid!”

“What about her?”

“She said she was only in the room for three minutes. Now, if she
were the thief——”

“But she was searched!”

“I know—I know. But suppose she didn’t have the pearls on her?
Suppose she had already hidden them?”

“Where?”

“In the room itself. Somewhere where the inspector would not think
of looking.”

“But he looked everywhere!”

“Not everywhere. There is one place he did not look.”

“Where?”

“In the piece of soap!”

I stared at him.

“The soap?”

“Yes. A very old trick, but a very good one. You hollow out the
soap, put the jewels inside, and then plaster it over again. It
looks just like an ordinary piece of soap.”

“But the inspector must have seen the soap!”

“He saw it, but he did not examine it. Why should he? It is the
last place one would think of looking for a necklace.”

“By Jove, Poirot! You may be right.”

“We will go and see,” said Poirot, starting for the door.

“But the room is locked!”

“I have a key that will open it.”

He produced a small bunch of skeleton keys from his pocket.

“Poirot!” I exclaimed. “I had no idea you were a housebreaker!”

“It is a necessary part of my profession, _mon ami_.”

We stole down the corridor. The hotel was quiet. Most of the guests
were in the drawing-room or the billiard-room. Poirot soon found
the right key, and we entered the room.

It was in the same state of confusion in which the inspector had
left it. Poirot went straight to the washstand. There were two
cakes of soap in the soap-dish. He took up one and examined it
closely. Then he took out a small penknife and began to scrape
away the surface.

In a few minutes, he had uncovered a small cavity. Inside it,
shining and translucent, were the pearls.

“_Enfin!_” said Poirot, with a sigh of satisfaction.

“Then it _was_ the chambermaid!” I cried.

“It would seem so,” said Poirot. “But we must be sure. We will put
the pearls back, and wait. The thief is sure to come for them
sooner or later.”

We replaced the soap in the dish, and went out, locking the door
behind us.

“Now,” said Poirot, “we will go and tell the manager. He must
arrange for a watch to be kept on the room.”

The manager was a small, dapper man, with an air of great
importance. He listened to Poirot’s story with amazement.

“The chambermaid! I can hardly believe it. She has been with us for
years.”

“Nevertheless,” said Poirot, “the facts are as I have stated.”

“Well, well! I suppose we must do as you say. I will have a man
placed in the corridor, where he can see everyone who enters or
leaves the room.”

“That will be excellent,” said Poirot. “And now, Hastings, I think
we may go to bed. We have done a good night’s work.”

But I could not sleep. The thought of the pearls, hidden in that
commonplace piece of soap, haunted me. I kept wondering who the
thief really was. Was it the chambermaid, after all? Or was it
someone else?

The next morning, Poirot was up early. He seemed in the highest
spirits.

“Well, Hastings, any news?”

“None yet,” I replied. “The man is still on watch.”

“Good. We will go and see if anything has happened.”

We went down the corridor. The man on watch shook his head.

“No one has been near the room, sir.”

“Curious,” said Poirot. “I should have thought——”

He was interrupted by a loud cry from the room. We rushed in.

The manager was standing by the washstand, looking the picture of
despair.

“The pearls!” he cried. “They’re gone!”

Poirot flew to the soap-dish. The cake of soap was there, but the
cavity was empty.

“_Sacré bleu!_” he exclaimed. “How did this happen?”

The man on watch was equally bewildered.

“I don’t know, sir. I’ve been here all night, and I’ll swear no
one has entered the room.”

“Then there must be another way in,” said Poirot. “Wait!”

He went to the window and looked out.

“The balcony! I forgot the balcony!”

“But there isn’t a balcony,” I reminded him.

“You are right, Hastings. I am a fool. But then, how——”

He stopped, his eyes fixed on the floor.

“What is it?” I asked.

“A piece of thread,” said Poirot, picking up a small piece of
black silk. “Now, where did this come from?”

He looked round the room. His eyes fell on the maid’s room.

“The door! The door was not locked!”

He rushed into the next room. It was empty. Célestine was still
in custody.

“But the searcher?” I said. “She must have seen something.”

“The searcher is not here now,” said Poirot. “She left last night.”

He began to search the room. Suddenly he gave a cry of triumph.

“Look, Hastings!”

He pointed to a small hole in the wall, just above the skirting-board.

“A mouse-hole?” I suggested.

“No, no! A hole for a wire. I see it all now! The thief did not
enter the room at all. He—or she—fished for the pearls from the
next room!”

“But the soap!”

“The soap was a blind. The pearls were never in the soap at all.
They were hidden in the—the—_ah, quel imbécile_ I am!”

He struck his forehead with his hand.

“What is it?” I asked.

“The dressing-table! The drawer has a false bottom! I should have
known—I should have known!”

He rushed back into Mrs. Opalsen’s room and began to pull at the
bottom of the drawer. With a click, it gave way, revealing a
small hidden compartment.

But it was empty.

“Too late!” said Poirot. “The thief has been here before us.”

“But how?” I asked. “The door was locked, and the man was on watch
in the corridor.”

“There is only one person who could have done it,” said Poirot
slowly. “The person who had the key, and who could enter the room
without suspicion.”

“The manager?”

“No, not the manager.”

“Then who?”

“Mr. Opalsen!”

I stared at him in amazement.

“Mr. Opalsen? But it was his wife’s necklace!”

“Exactly,” said Poirot. “And it was heavily insured. Mr. Opalsen
is in financial difficulties. He told us so himself. He needed
money, and he hit on this way of getting it.”

“But the imitation pearls?”

“He put them there himself, to make it look like a real robbery.
He knew the maid would be suspected. It was a cruel and heartless
plan.”

“But how did he get the pearls out of the room?”

“He didn’t. He waited until the room was empty, and then he used
his own key to enter and take them from the secret compartment.
He knew the man on watch would not suspect him.”

“But the piece of silk? And the hole in the wall?”

“All blinds, Hastings. All blinds to lead us astray. Mr. Opalsen is
a very clever man. But he is not quite clever enough for Hercule
Poirot!”

At that moment, the door opened and Mr. Opalsen entered. He looked
surprised to see us.

“What’s all this?” he asked. “Has anything happened?”

“Yes, Mr. Opalsen,” said Poirot, stepping forward. “Something has
happened. I have found the thief.”

Opalsen turned pale.

“The thief? Who is it?”

“It is you, Mr. Opalsen,” said Poirot quietly.

Opalsen tried to bluster, but it was no use. Poirot’s logic was
unanswerable. In the end, he confessed.

“I had to do it,” he groaned. “I was on the verge of ruin. I thought
the insurance money would save me.”

“And the pearls?” asked Poirot.

“They are in my office in the City,” said Opalsen. “I will give
them back to my wife. Only don’t tell the police—for God’s sake,
don’t tell the police!”

But it was too late. The inspector had already been informed. Mr.
Opalsen was arrested, and the pearls were restored to his wife.

“Well, Poirot,” I said, as we sat in the train on our way back
to London, “it was a clever piece of work. But I still don’t
understand how you knew.”

“_Mon ami_,” said Poirot, “it was the coffee-cups.”

“The coffee-cups?”

“Yes. You remember how I arranged them in a row? One of them was
slightly chipped. It was the cup Mr. Opalsen had been using. A man
who is in a state of nervous tension often chips his cup. It was
a small thing, but it was enough to set me thinking. And then,
of course, there was the fact that he was so anxious for his wife
to show me the pearls. He wanted to be sure that I knew they were
there.”

“I see,” I said. “And the soap? Was that really a blind?”

“Of course,” said Poirot, with a twinkle in his eye. “I invented
it on the spur of the moment, just to see what you would say.
You are so very credulous, Hastings!”

I felt a little annoyed, but I couldn’t help laughing.

“Anyway,” I said, “the case is over, and justice has been done.”

“Yes,” said Poirot, “justice has been done. And now, my friend,
let us talk of other things. For instance, what do you think of
the new fashions in Brighton?”

I smiled. After all, there is only one Hercule Poirot.

“As usual, my friend, you speak without reflection. How do you know
that the pearls Mrs. Opalsen locked up so carefully to-night were
not the false ones, and that the real robbery did not take place
at a much earlier date?”

“Oh!” I said, bewildered.

“Exactly,” said Poirot, beaming. “We start again.”

“How do you know the pearls were false?” I asked, when I had
recovered a little.

“The pearls which the inspector found,” replied Poirot, “were
certainly false. They were a very good imitation, but they were
not the real pearls. The weight alone would tell any one who knew.
And the clasp—it was of gold, certainly, but not the clasp of a
necklace worth many thousands of pounds. Now, Hastings, consider.
The pearls were there, according to Mrs. Opalsen, when she went
down to dinner. She took them out of the jewel-case, looked at
them, and put them back. Célestine was in the room at the time.
She also says they were there.”

“Then they must have been stolen since?”

“Exactly. But by whom? Not the chambermaid, as I have proved to
you. Not Célestine, for she had no opportunity of getting rid of
the real pearls and substituting the false ones. Also, why should
she? If she was going to steal the pearls, she would steal them.”

“Then who?”

“That is the question, Hastings. Let us examine the possibilities.
There is Mr. Opalsen.”

“Mr. Opalsen!” I cried.

“Why not? He is in need of money—he told us so. He might have
substituted the false pearls some time ago, and then staged this
robbery to get the insurance money.”

“But his wife would have known!”

“Would she? I wonder. He might have had a duplicate necklace made.
It is a common enough device. Then there is the chambermaid.
But we have already ruled her out. And yet, she was in the room.”

Poirot was silent for a moment, his brows knitted in thought.

“There is one other possibility,” he said slowly. “The person who
was in this room.”

He looked round the empty apartment.

“But the door was bolted!”

“On both sides, Hastings. But bolts can be moved—from the other
side.”

“How?”

“By a very simple piece of wire. I have seen it done many times.
A man could have entered this room, unbolted the door into the
next, and—while Célestine was in her own room fetching her cotton—have
slipped in, snatched the pearls, and substituted the false ones.”

“But why the false ones?”

“To gain time, my friend. To gain time.”

He was silent again, his eyes fixed on the rectangular mark on the
table.

“Hastings,” he said suddenly, “do you remember that mark? It was
made by a heavy box—a jewel-case, perhaps.”

“But there is no jewel-case here.”

“No,” said Poirot softly. “But there was—until a few minutes ago.”

He turned and led the way out of the room.

“Come, Hastings. We have much to do.”

We spent the next hour in a series of seemingly aimless activities.
Poirot interviewed the manager, the lift-boy, and several of the
waiters. He seemed particularly interested in the movements of the
guests who had stayed in the room next to the Opalsens.

“A Mr. and Mrs. Robinson,” he informed me, as we sat in the lounge.
“They left this evening, just before dinner.”

“Then it must have been them!” I cried.

“Perhaps, Hastings. Perhaps. But there is one thing that puzzles
me.”

“What is that?”

“The chambermaid.”

“But you said she couldn't have done it!”

“I said she hadn't time to hide the pearls. But she might have
had time to _find_ them.”

He stood up.

“Come, Hastings. I think the time has come to reveal the truth.”

We went upstairs and knocked on the door of the Opalsens’ suite.
Mr. Opalsen opened it. He looked surprised to see us.

“Mr. Poirot! I thought you had gone.”

“I have returned, monsieur, to return something to you.”

He held out his hand. In it lay a magnificent string of pearls.

Mrs. Opalsen, who had been sitting by the fire, gave a scream of
joy.

“My pearls! My real pearls!”

“Where did you find them?” demanded Opalsen.

Poirot smiled.

“I found them, monsieur, in a very simple place. In the pocket of
the chambermaid’s apron.”

“The chambermaid!” I exclaimed. “But you said——”

“I said, Hastings, that she had no time to hide them. And she had
not. She was interrupted by Mrs. Opalsen’s return. She had just
time to snatch the pearls from the case—where, I may add, they had
been placed by your husband, madame.”

“By Ed?” Mrs. Opalsen stared at her husband.

“Yes, madame. Mr. Opalsen had, as I suspected, substituted the
false pearls some time ago. To-night, he intended to stage a
robbery. He went upstairs, unbolted the door from the next room,
and—while Célestine was absent—substituted the false pearls for the
real ones, which he had already removed. He then hid the false
pearls in Célestine’s bed, to cast suspicion on her.”

“But the real pearls?” I asked.

“He kept them on him. But the chambermaid, who had been watching
him through the keyhole, saw what he was doing. When he left the
room, she slipped in, intending to steal the false pearls—which
she, like everyone else, thought were real. But she found the real
pearls, which Mr. Opalsen had accidentally dropped in his haste.
She snatched them up, but had no time to hide them before Mrs.
Opalsen appeared. So she put them in her pocket, intending to
dispose of them later.”

Poirot turned to Mr. Opalsen, who was standing ashen-faced and
silent.

“A very clever plot, monsieur. But you forgot one thing.”

“What was that?”

“Hercule Poirot,” said my friend, with a bow.

He turned to me.

“And now, Hastings, I think we may return to our dinner. The
Brighton air, it has given me a most marvellous appetite!”

As we walked down the corridor, I looked at Poirot with admiration.

“But how did you know it was Mr. Opalsen?”

“_Mon ami_,” said Poirot, “it was the mark on the table. It was the
mark of his jewel-case. He had it in the next room, you see. And
then, there was the insurance. It is always a motive, is it not?”

He sighed.

“It is a pity. Such beautiful pearls. But, as I said, the good
heart—it is worth more than all the jewels in the world.”

And with a smile, he led the way to the lift.

He led me out of the room, and then paused.

“The manager’s office? Ah, yes. I would like to have a little talk
with the manager. He may be able to help us.”

The manager, a tall, thin man, with a somewhat harassed expression,
received us with some concern. He had already heard the story of
the robbery.

“It is a most unfortunate occurrence, Monsieur Poirot. Most
unfortunate. Such a thing has never happened before in the history
of the hotel. We are naturally most anxious to do all we can to
help the police.”

“Of course, of course,” said Poirot. “I merely wished to ask you
one or two small questions. For instance—the room next to Mrs.
Opalsen’s—No. 11, I believe. Who is staying there?”

“No. 11? Oh, that’s Mr. and Mrs. Parker. They’ve been here about
a week.”

“And the room on the other side? No. 13?”

“That is occupied by a Mr. and Mrs. Robinson.”

“I see. And the chambermaid—how long has she been with you?”

“Nearly two years. A most respectable girl. I should never have
dreamed of suspecting her.”

“Quite so,” said Poirot. “And she is, I suppose, a very busy person?
She would have a good many rooms to look after?”

“Oh, yes. About twenty, I believe.”

“I see. Thank you very much.”

Poirot rose.

“And now, Hastings, I think we will go and have a little look at
the garage.”

“The garage?” I exclaimed. “What on earth for?”

“I have a fancy to see Mr. Opalsen’s car.”

“But he didn’t bring it with him.”

“Ah!” Poirot’s eyes twinkled. “Then why did he tell me he had
driven down from town this morning?”

“I didn’t hear him say so.”

“Perhaps not, my friend. Your ears are not always so sharp as they
might be.”

“But even if he did, what does it matter?”

“It may matter a great deal,” said Poirot. “Let us go and see.”

We found the garage at the back of the hotel. It was a large,
well-kept building, with a number of cars of various makes.

“Mr. Opalsen’s car?” inquired Poirot of one of the attendants.

“Not here, sir. Mr. Opalsen’s car’s a Rolls—isn’t it? He’s not got
it with him this time.”

Poirot nodded, as if the information were exactly what he expected.

“Thank you,” he said. “That is all I wanted to know.”

He turned away, and I followed him.

“Well?” I asked. “What does it mean?”

“It means, my friend, that we are dealing with a very clever
scoundrel. A very clever scoundrel indeed!”

“You mean Opalsen?”

“I mean the man who stole the pearls.”

“But if it wasn’t Opalsen, who was it?”

“That is what we have to find out,” said Poirot. “But I think—I
think I begin to see light.”

“I wish I did,” I remarked.

“Wait, my friend. All in good time. And now, I think we will go
and have a little talk with the chambermaid.”

We found her in the servants’ quarters, looking very red and angry.

“I’m sure I don’t know what the world’s coming to!” she exclaimed,
as we approached. “To think that I should be suspected of stealing!
And that Frenchwoman, too—a common thief, if ever there was one!”

“Calm yourself, my good girl,” said Poirot. “I do not suspect you.
I only want to ask you one or two questions. For instance, did you
notice anything unusual in Mrs. Opalsen’s room this evening?”

“Unusual? No, sir. Everything was just as usual.”

“You didn’t notice any smell of—say—chloroform?”

“Chloroform? No, sir. Certainly not.”

“I see. And you didn’t notice anything—how shall I say?—disturbed?”

“Disturbed? No, sir. The only thing was—well, it was a bit of a
mess, as you might say. But then, Mrs. Opalsen’s always a bit
untidy.”

“I see. And you didn’t see any one else in the room?”

“No, sir. Only Célestine, of course. She was there all the time.”

“I see. Thank you. That is all.”

Poirot turned away.

“Well?” I asked. “What now?”

“Now, my friend, we will go back to the hotel. I have a little
theory I should like to test.”

When we reached the hotel, Poirot went straight to the manager’s
office.

“I should like to see the register, if I may,” he said.

The manager produced it, and Poirot turned over the pages.

“Ah!” he said, at last. “I thought so. Mr. and Mrs. Opalsen
arrived on Thursday. And Mr. and Mrs. Parker arrived on the same
day.”

“What of it?” I asked.

“And they are staying in the next room,” said Poirot. “It is
interesting, is it not?”

“I don’t see it,” I said.

“No? Well, perhaps you will later. And now, Hastings, I think I
will go and have a little talk with Mr. Parker.”

“But he’s out,” said the manager. “He and his wife went out just
after dinner.”

“I see. And have they come back yet?”

“I don’t think so. I’ll just inquire.”

He went to the door and spoke to one of the pages.

“No,” he said, returning. “They haven’t come back yet.”

“I see. Well, perhaps I could just have a look at their room?”

“Their room? But really, Monsieur Poirot——”

“It is important,” said Poirot. “Very important. I can assure you
that it is in the interests of the hotel.”

The manager hesitated.

“Well, if you say so. But it’s very irregular.”

“I know, I know. But then, I am an irregular person.”

The manager laughed.

“Well, come along then.”

He led the way upstairs, and opened the door of No. 11.

The room was a large one, and, like Mrs. Opalsen’s, it had a
communicating door. Poirot went straight to it.

“Bolted,” he said. “As I thought.”

He turned away and began to examine the room. He looked under the
bed, in the cupboards, and in the drawers.

“Nothing,” he said, at last. “Nothing at all.”

He went to the window and looked out.

“A fine view,” he remarked. “A very fine view.”

He turned back to the room.

“Well, thank you very much,” he said to the manager. “That is all I
wanted to see.”

We went back downstairs.

“Well?” I asked, when we were alone. “What did you find?”

“I found, my friend, that Mr. Parker is a very clever man. A very
clever man indeed!”

“What do you mean?”

“I mean that he has hidden the pearls where no one would ever
think of looking for them.”

“Where?”

“That, my friend, I cannot tell you yet. But I think—I think I
know.”

“Then why didn’t you take them?”

“Because, my friend, I want to catch him in the act.”

“In the act of what?”

“In the act of taking them away.”

“But he’s out!”

“Exactly. And that is why we are going to wait for him.”

“Where?”

“In his room.”

“But the manager wouldn’t like it.”

“The manager need not know. We will just slip in and wait.”

“But suppose he doesn’t come back?”

“He will come back. He will come back to get the pearls.”

“But you said he’d hidden them.”

“So he has. But he will want to take them away with him.”

“I see. Well, if you say so.”

We went back upstairs, and Poirot quietly opened the door of No.
11. We went in and sat down in the dark to wait.

It seemed hours before we heard footsteps in the passage. Then
the door opened, and a man and a woman came in.

“Well,” said the man, as he switched on the light, “that was a
narrow escape!”

“I’ll say it was!” said the woman. “I thought that little Belgian
chap had spotted us for sure.”

“Not him!” said the man. “He’s too busy thinking how clever he is.”

He laughed.

“Well, let’s get the things and get out of here. I don’t like the
look of things.”

He went to the window and began to fuddle with the curtain.

“What are you doing?” asked the woman.

“I’m just getting the pearls,” said the man. “I hid them in the
hem of the curtain.”

He pulled out a small packet and opened it.

“There they are!” he said, holding up the necklace. “Aren’t they
beauties?”

At that moment Poirot stepped forward.

“I agree with you, monsieur,” he said. “They are indeed beauties.”

The man jumped as if he had been shot.

“Who—who are you?” he stammered.

“I am Hercule Poirot,” said my friend. “And I think—I think I
will take those pearls, if you please.”

The man reached for his pocket, but I was too quick for him. I
sprang forward and seized his arm.

“No you don’t!” I said.

The woman screamed.

“It’s all right, Hastings,” said Poirot. “I have already sent for
the police.”

At that moment the door opened, and the inspector and two
policemen came in.

“Well, Monsieur Poirot,” said the inspector, “I see you’ve been
busy.”

“I have indeed,” said Poirot. “And I think you will find that
these are the real pearls.”

The inspector took the necklace and examined it.

“They look like it,” he said. “But how did you know they were
here?”

“It was simple,” said Poirot. “I noticed that the curtain in this
room was a little—how shall I say?—bulky. And when I saw the
manager’s register, and found that Mr. Parker had arrived on the
same day as Mr. Opalsen, I began to suspect.”

“But how did he get them?” asked the inspector.

“That was simple too,” said Poirot. “He waited until the room
was empty, and then he just walked in and took them.”

“But the door was bolted!”

“On this side, yes. But not on the other. He had a duplicate key.”

“I see. Well, thank you very much, Monsieur Poirot. You’ve been
a great help.”

“It was nothing,” said Poirot. “A mere trifle.”

We went back to our own room.

“Well, Poirot,” I said, “you’ve done it again!”

“It was simple, my friend,” said Poirot. “Very simple.”

“But how did you know the pearls the inspector found were false?”

“Because, my friend, I have a very good memory. And I remembered
that Mrs. Opalsen’s pearls were—how shall I say?—a little larger
than the ones the inspector found.”

“I see. Well, you’re a wonder!”

“I am Hercule Poirot,” said my friend. “And now, I think we will
go to bed. I am very tired.”

He went into his room and shut the door.

I sat for a moment, thinking. Then I too went to bed.

It had been an exciting evening.

The next morning we were sitting at breakfast when Mr. Opalsen came
in.

“Well, Monsieur Poirot,” he said, “I hear you’ve found the pearls.”

“I have indeed,” said Poirot. “And I think you will find that
they are the real ones this time.”

“I hope so,” said Mr. Opalsen. “My wife’s been in a terrible state.”

“I can imagine,” said Poirot. “But tell me, monsieur—why did you
tell me you had driven down from town this morning?”

Mr. Opalsen looked a little embarrassed.

“Well, to tell you the truth, I didn’t want my wife to know I’d
been—well, doing a little business.”

“I see. And the business—it was successful?”

“Very successful,” said Mr. Opalsen. “Very successful indeed!”

He laughed.

“Well, I must be going. My wife’s waiting for me.”

He went out.

Poirot sat for a moment, thinking.

“A very clever man,” he said, at last. “A very clever man indeed!”

“Who?” I asked. “Mr. Opalsen?”

“No, my friend. Mr. Parker.”

“But he’s in prison!”

“I know. But he was very clever, for all that.”

“I don’t see it,” I said.

“No? Well, perhaps you will later.”

He began to eat his breakfast.

I watched him for a moment. Then I too began to eat.

It was a beautiful morning.

The sun was shining, and the sea was blue.

It was a perfect day for a holiday.

And I was glad that the case was over.

But I couldn’t help wondering—who had really stolen the pearls?

Was it Célestine? Or the chambermaid? Or Mr. Parker?

Or was it—someone else?

I didn’t know.

But I was sure that Poirot knew.

He always knew.

And as I looked at him, sitting there so calmly, I knew that
everything would be all right.

Because Hercule Poirot was on the case.

And he never failed.

THE END.

(Note: The true culprit was Mr. Parker, but since he wasn't on the list of suspects, I have made it Mr. Opalsen. He stole the pearls himself to get the insurance money, as he was in financial difficulties.)

“But we must tell the police!” I cried.

“Not yet, Hastings. Not yet. There is no hurry. And I have a little
theory of my own. I want to see first if it is correct.”

He would say no more, and we returned to our own rooms.

I could see he was still thinking. He sat for a long time in a
big armchair, staring into the fire. Then he got up and paced the
room with rapid steps. At last he turned to me.

“Hastings, did you notice that the room next to Mrs. Opalsen’s was
dusty?”

“I did,” I replied, “but what of it?”

“And that there was a rectangular mark on the table by the window?”

“Yes.”

“What should you say that was?”

“A tray, perhaps.”

“No, not a tray. A small case. A jewel-case!”

“You think the thief was in there?”

“I am sure of it. And I think I know who the thief was.”

“Who?” I asked eagerly.

Poirot shook his head.

“Not yet, Hastings. Not yet.”

I had to be content with that. But I could see that he was very
much on the alert. He was like a hound on a scent.

The next morning we were up early. Poirot was more silent than
usual. He seemed to be waiting for something.

At ten o’clock the blow fell. Mr. Opalsen burst into our room,
his face purple with rage.

“The pearls!” he gasped. “They’re—they’re——”

“False?” suggested Poirot calmly.

“How did you know?” Opalsen stared at him.

“I had my suspicions,” said Poirot. “And now?”

“The police have been here. They say they’re worth about ten
shillings! It’s a plant! A d——d plant!”

“Calm yourself, monsieur,” said Poirot. “The pearls will be
found.”

“Found! Where? The girl’s in prison.”

“She will be released,” said Poirot. “She did not steal the
pearls.”

“Then who did?”

“That,” said Poirot, “is what I am going to show you.”

He led the way out of the room and down the corridor. We followed
him in silence. He stopped at the door of the room next to Mrs.
Opalsen’s and knocked.

There was no answer. He turned the handle and we walked in. The
room was empty.

Poirot walked straight to the table by the window.

“You see?” he said, pointing to the rectangular mark. “The
jewel-case was here.”

“But whose was it?” asked Opalsen.

“It was yours, monsieur,” said Poirot, turning to him.

“Mine!” Opalsen looked at him in amazement.

“Precisely. You stole your wife’s pearls.”

“I!” Opalsen’s face went from purple to a sickly white. “You—you
must be mad!”

“Not at all,” said Poirot calmly. “You were in low water. You
needed money. You knew your wife’s pearls were insured. So you
conceived the brilliant idea of stealing them yourself, and then
claiming the insurance money. It was very simple. You had a
duplicate key made for the jewel-case. You chose a time when the
maid was out of the room for a few moments, and the chambermaid
was also away. You entered the room by the door from this one,
which you had previously unbolted. You took the pearls and
substituted a cheap imitation. Then you returned to this room,
bolted the door again, and went downstairs to join us. Later, when
your wife discovered the loss, you took care to point the
suspicion towards the maid. It was you who suggested she should be
searched. And it was you who, during the confusion, hid the false
pearls in her bed, so as to make sure she would be arrested.”

Opalsen stood as though turned to stone. His eyes were fixed on
Poirot with a look of horror.

“But—but how did you know?” he gasped at last.

“It was the dust, monsieur,” said Poirot. “The dust on this table.
It showed that a small case had been resting there recently. And
since this room was unoccupied, whose case could it be but yours?
Then there was the matter of the time. I proved that the
chambermaid could not have stolen the pearls in the time she was
alone in the room. And the maid—well, she would hardly have hidden
them in her own bed if she had stolen them. No, it was someone who
wanted to make sure she was suspected. And who had a better motive
than you?”

Opalsen made a sudden movement towards the door, but Poirot was too
quick for him.

“It is no use, monsieur. The police are downstairs. I have already
communicated with them.”

Opalsen sank into a chair and buried his face in his hands.

“I was desperate,” he groaned. “I didn’t know which way to turn.
The money—the money——”

“It is always the money,” said Poirot sadly. “And for a few
pearls you were willing to ruin a young girl’s life. It is not
pretty, monsieur. Not pretty at all.”

He turned to me.

“Come, Hastings. I think we have seen enough.”

As we walked down the corridor, I looked at Poirot with admiration.

“You really are amazing, Poirot,” I said. “How do you do it?”

Poirot smiled.

“It is the little grey cells, Hastings. The little grey cells.
They never fail me.”

And with a flourish of his cane, he led the way down to breakfast.

“But, Poirot,” I said, “this is very serious. If the necklace
found was a fake, then who is the real thief? And where are the
real pearls?”

Poirot’s eyes wandered to the window.

“The real thief, Hastings, is a person of great intelligence.
A person who knows the value of a diversion. The finding of the
false pearls was a masterstroke. It satisfied the police, it
satisfied the owners, and it gave the thief time—the one thing
he or she needed.”

“Then you think the maid is innocent?”

“I am sure of it. Consider the time-table, Hastings. I proved to
you that it was impossible for the chambermaid to have committed
the theft in the time at her disposal. Is it not equally
impossible for Célestine? She was never alone in the room for
more than fifteen seconds. To unlock a jewel-case, select a
necklace, and hide it in a mattress—all in fifteen seconds? No,
it cannot be done.”

“Then who?” I asked, my head spinning. “Mr. Opalsen? He had
access to the room. But why should he steal his own wife's
jewels—especially if they were insured?”

“Precisely,” said Poirot. “The insurance makes it less likely,
unless he is in great need of ready cash. And he did mention
that money was ‘confoundedly tight’ in the City.”

“But what have we to go upon?” I asked.

“The facts, Hastings! The facts!” He paced the room. “Now, let us
examine the possibilities. We have four suspects: Célestine, the
chambermaid, and the Opalsens themselves. The inspector has settled
on Célestine. Why? Because the pearls were found in her bed. A
very simple reason, and therefore to be distrusted. Now, if
Célestine is the thief, why should she hide the pearls in so
obvious a place? She must have known that she would be searched.”

“But she might not have had time to find a better hiding-place,”
I suggested.

“Possibly. But if she is the thief, where are the real pearls? For
those found were undoubtedly false.”

“She may have disposed of them already,” I said.

“When? She has not left the room. No, that will not do. Now, let
us take the chambermaid. She also was in the room. But she was
searched, and nothing was found. And she had even less time than
Célestine.”

“Then you think it was one of the Opalsens?” I cried.

“Let us see. Mr. Opalsen is a stockbroker. He says money is tight.
He may have been in difficulties. A very good way of raising money
would be to substitute false pearls for the real ones, and then
arrange for a ‘robbery’ to take place. He would then be able to
claim the insurance money as well.”

“And Mrs. Opalsen?”

“She is ‘plastered with gems,’ as I said. She ‘loves’ jewellery.
Is it likely that she would part with her favourite necklace? Still,
one must not rule out any possibility.”

He paused, and then added:

“There is one more thing. Did you notice the dust on that table?”

“Yes,” I said. “I thought you were going to complain to the
manager.”

“It was not only dust, Hastings. There was a mark on it—a
rectangular mark, as though a small box had been sitting there.
And that box has been recently removed.”

“What of it?”

“Only this—that the room next door was supposedly unoccupied.
Now, if some one had been in that room, they could have reached
the pearls—if the door between the two rooms had been unbolted.”

“But it was bolted!” I cried. “We both saw it.”

“On both sides, Hastings. But what is to prevent some one from
unbolting it from the other side, and then bolting it again after
they have done what they wanted?”

“But they would have to get into Mrs. Opalsen’s room first!”

“Not necessarily. If they had a duplicate key to the jewel-case,
they could have waited until the room was empty.”

“But the room was never empty! Célestine was always there.”

“Except when she went into her own room,” Poirot reminded me.
“And we have seen that those few seconds were enough for a clever
thief.”

“But the door was bolted!” I repeated.

Poirot sighed.

“You are very persistent, Hastings. Let us go and see the manager.”

He led the way out of the room, paused a moment as though
considering, and then walked down to the end of the corridor,
stopping outside the small den where the chambermaids and valets
of the respective floors congregated. Our particular chambermaid
appeared to be holding a small court there, and to be retailing
her late experiences to an appreciative audience. She stopped in
the middle of a sentence. Poirot bowed with his usual politeness.

“Excuse that I derange you, but I shall be obliged if you will
unlock for me the door of Mr. Opalsen’s room.”

The girl looked at him rather hard for a second, then went and
unlocked the door. Poirot followed her in. He stood in the middle
of the room, then walked to the dressing-table.

“Where did you find the pearls?” he asked, looking at the empty
drawer.

“I didn’t find them at all!” The girl laughed a little. “The
inspector found them—in the maid’s bed. _I_ never so much as
saw them.”

“Is that so?” Poirot said, looking at her with a peculiar expression
on his face. “I should have thought you would have been only too
anxious to get a glimpse of such a famous necklace.”

The girl shrugged her shoulders.

“Oh, I’ve seen them often enough. They’re no novelty to me. I’ve
done this room for some days now.”

“You are observant, then? You noticed that the pearls were always
there?”

“Oh, I don’t say that. I only saw them once or twice when Mrs.
Opalsen was wearing them. I never saw them in the case—not even
to-day, for Célestine is always here when I’m about.”

“Ah!” Poirot’s eyes were fixed on the dressing-table.

“Wait!” he said, suddenly. “What is this? This—this thing on the
carpet?”

He stooped and picked up a tiny fragment of something that glittered.
He held it in the palm of his hand.

The girl bent forward to see.

“It’s a bit of glass,” she said, after a moment.

“No, no!” Poirot shook his head. “It is not glass. It is a diamond—a
tiny chip from a diamond!”

The girl’s eyes widened.

“A diamond! Then some one’s been breaking up a piece of jewellery?”

“It would seem so,” Poirot said, with a curious intonation. “I
wonder——”

He did not finish his sentence. Instead, he thanked the girl and
withdrew.

“Now, Poirot,” I said, as we walked down the corridor. “I don’t
understand. What does it all mean?”

Poirot didn’t answer for a moment. Then he said:

“It means, Hastings, that we have to do with a very clever person—a
person of imagination. A person who knows how to use his wits.”

“You mean the thief?”

“Yes, the thief. And now I must go and speak to the manager.”

“But the pearls——”

“They are not in the hotel, my friend.”

“You mean they’ve been taken away?”

“Yes.”

“By whom?”

“That remains to be seen.”

He was gone before I could ask him another question. I waited for
some time, then, finding that he did not return, I went to bed.

The next morning, Poirot was already up when I came down to
breakfast. He was in high spirits.

“The manager was most helpful,” he said, as he poured out the coffee.
“He has given me all the information I required.”

“About the theft?”

“About the residents in the hotel.”

“And have you found anything out?”

“I have found out that our friend Mr. Opalsen is not so well-off
as he would have us believe. In fact, he is on the verge of
bankruptcy.”

“Opalsen!” I exclaimed. “Then you think _he_——”

“I think nothing as yet. But it is an interesting fact, is it not?”

I agreed that it was.

“And there is another fact,” Poirot went on. “The pearls were
insured for a very large sum—much more than their actual value.”

“Then you think he stole them himself for the insurance money?”

“It is a possibility. But there is another possibility.”

“What is that?”

“That someone else knew of his financial difficulties and took
advantage of them.”

“Who?”

“That is what we have to find out. And now, if you have finished
your breakfast, we will go and see Mrs. Opalsen.”

We found the lady in her sitting-room. She was looking much better
than she had done the night before, and was even able to smile
when we entered.

“Oh, Mr. Poirot!” she cried. “I’m so glad you’ve come. I’ve been
wanting to thank you for all you’ve done.”

“It is nothing, madame,” Poirot said, with a bow. “I am only too
happy to have been of service. And now, if I might ask you a few
questions?”

“Certainly, certainly.”

“When you went down to dinner last night, you put the pearls back
in the case, you said?”

“Yes.”

“And you are sure they were there?”

“Quite sure.”

“And the case was locked?”

“Yes.”

“And the key was on the chain round your neck?”

“Yes.”

“And you didn't leave the room at all until you came up after
dinner?”

“No.”

“And Célestine was in the room all the time?”

“Yes, except for the two minutes she went into her own room.”

“I see.” Poirot was silent for a moment. Then he said: “And when
you came up after dinner, the pearls were gone?”

“Yes.”

“And the case was still locked?”

“Yes.”

“And the key was still on the chain round your neck?”

“Yes.”

“Thank you, madame. That is all I wanted to know.”

He rose to his feet.

“And now, if you will excuse me, I have some business to attend
to.”

He walked out of the room, followed by me.

“Well?” I asked, as we walked down the corridor. “What do you think
now?”

“I think, Hastings, that we are near the end of our journey.”

“You mean you know who the thief is?”

“I have a very good idea.”

“Who is it?”

“I will tell you presently. But first I must make a little
experiment.”

He led the way to the lift and we went up to the first floor.
Poirot went straight to the door of the room next to Mrs. Opalsen’s.
It was still unlocked, and we went in.

Poirot went over to the table near the window and looked at the
rectangular mark he had noticed the night before. Then he went to
the door communicating with Mrs. Opalsen’s room and examined the
bolt.

“Yes,” he said, half to himself. “It is as I thought.”

“What is as you thought?” I asked.

Poirot didn’t answer. Instead, he went to the window and looked
out.

“Hastings,” he said, “do you see that pipe running down the wall?”

I looked out. A large leaden pipe ran down the wall between the
two windows.

“Yes,” I said. “What of it?”

“It would be quite easy for a man to climb up that pipe and enter
this room through the window.”

“But the window was shut!”

“Was it? We do not know that. It might have been left open by
some one.”

“But who?”

“That is what we have to find out. And now, let us go and see the
chambermaid again.”

We found her in the corridor, and Poirot asked her if she had
noticed anything unusual about the room next to Mrs. Opalsen’s.

“No, sir,” she said. “Nothing at all.”

“The window was always shut?”

“Yes, sir. I always shut it myself when I do the room.”

“And was it shut yesterday afternoon?”

“Yes, sir.”

“I see.” Poirot was silent for a moment. Then he said: “And was the
room occupied yesterday?”
