“No, sir. It’s been empty for several days.”

“Thank you.”

Poirot turned away and we walked back to the lift.

“Well?” I asked. “What do you think now?”

“I think, Hastings, that the case is even more interesting than I
thought.”

“But you said you knew who the thief was!”

“I have a theory. But I must be sure before I speak.”

He was silent for the rest of the morning, and I could see that he
was deep in thought.

After lunch, he told me that he was going out for a while, and that
I was to wait for him in the lounge.

I waited for over an hour, and then he returned, looking very
pleased with himself.

“I have it, Hastings!” he cried. “I have it!”

“The thief?”

“Yes, the thief. And the pearls too!”

“Where are they?”

“In a safe-place. But come, we must go and see the manager.”

We found the manager in his office, and Poirot told him that he
had found the pearls and that he knew who the thief was.

The manager was delighted.

“That is wonderful news, Mr. Poirot! Who is it?”

“I will show you,” Poirot said. “But first I must ask you to come
with me to Mrs. Opalsen’s room.”

We all went up to the first floor, and Poirot knocked on the door
of Mrs. Opalsen’s room.

Mr. Opalsen opened it, and Poirot told him that he had found the
pearls.

Mrs. Opalsen was overjoyed.

“Oh, Mr. Poirot! I knew you would find them! Where are they?”

“I will show you,” Poirot said. “But first I must ask you to sit
down.”

We all sat down, and Poirot began to speak.

“When I first heard the story of the theft,” he said, “I was
struck by several things. First, the fact that the pearls were
stolen while the maid was in the room. Second, the fact that the
jewel-case was locked and the key was on the chain round Mrs.
Opalsen’s neck. And third, the fact that the pearls were found in
the maid’s bed.”

He paused for a moment, then went on.

“It seemed to me that there were only two possibilities. Either the
maid had stolen the pearls herself, or some one else had stolen
them and hidden them in her bed to cast suspicion on her.”

“But the pearls were false!” I cried.

“Exactly,” Poirot said. “And that was the most important clue of
all. Why would some one steal a necklace and then replace it with
a false one?”

“To gain time,” I suggested.

“Exactly. To gain time. But who would want to gain time? Only
someone who knew that the theft would be discovered soon.”

“But who could have known that?”

“Only someone who knew that Mrs. Opalsen was going to show the
pearls to me that evening.”

“But that was only decided on at the last moment!”

“Exactly. And that is why the thief had to act quickly. He had
to steal the pearls and replace them with the false ones in a very
short time.”

“But how did he do it?”

“He didn’t do it,” Poirot said. “She did it.”

He pointed his finger at the chambermaid, who was standing by the
door.

The girl’s face turned white.

“Me? I didn’t do it! I swear I didn’t!”

“Oh, yes, you did,” Poirot said. “You stole the pearls several
days ago and replaced them with the false ones. You knew that Mrs.
Opalsen didn’t often look at her pearls, and you thought you would
have plenty of time to get away before the theft was discovered.”

“But how did I do it?” the girl cried. “Célestine was always in
the room!”

“No, she wasn’t,” Poirot said. “She went into her own room for a
few minutes every day, and that was when you did it. You had a
duplicate key to the jewel-case, and you were very quick.”

“But the pearls were found in the maid’s bed!” I cried.

“Yes,” Poirot said. “Because the chambermaid put them there. When
she heard that Mrs. Opalsen was going to show the pearls to me, she
knew that the theft would be discovered. So she took the false
pearls from the jewel-case and hid them in the maid’s bed, hoping
that the police would find them and suspect the maid.”

“But what about the real pearls?” I asked.

“She had already sent them away,” Poirot said. “She sent them to
an accomplice in London.”

“But how do you know all this?” the manager asked.

“Because of the chip of diamond I found on the carpet,” Poirot
said. “It was a tiny piece of one of the diamonds from the
clasp of the necklace. It must have fallen off when the
chambermaid was taking the necklace out of the case.”

“But you said the pearls were not in the hotel!” I cried.

“I was wrong,” Poirot said. “The real pearls were not in the
hotel, but the false ones were. And the chambermaid had hidden
them in the maid’s bed.”

“But where are the real pearls now?” Mrs. Opalsen asked.

“They are in the hands of the police in London,” Poirot said. “I
telegraphed them this morning, and they have arrested the
accomplice and recovered the pearls.”

The chambermaid burst into tears and confessed everything. She was
taken away by the police, and Mrs. Opalsen was reunited with her
pearls.

“Well, Poirot,” I said, as we walked back to our room. “You’ve
done it again. But how did you know it was the chambermaid?”

“Because of the rectangular mark on the table in the next room,”
Poirot said.

“The mark? What had that to do with it?”

“It was the mark of a jewel-case,” Poirot said. “The chambermaid
had taken the case into the next room to change the pearls, and
she had left it on the table. The dust on the table showed where
it had been.”

“But how did she get into the next room?”

“Through the window,” Poirot said. “She climbed along the ledge
from Mrs. Opalsen’s room. It was a dangerous thing to do, but she
was desperate.”

“I see,” I said. “Well, it was a very clever piece of work,
Poirot.”

“Thank you, Hastings,” Poirot said. “But it was only a matter of
using the little grey cells.”

“It’s locked, sir,” she replied, lookin’ a bit surprised. “The
police have got the key.”

“Ah!” Poirot’s face fell. “That is a pity. I wanted to see—what
did I want to see? Oh, yes, I wanted to see if there was a balcony
outside.”

“There isn’t, sir,” she said. “I told you that before.”

“Are you sure?” Poirot’s eyes twinkled. “Now, just think. Are you
_quite_ sure?”

“Why, of course I am, sir. I’ve lived in this hotel for three
years, and I ought to know.”

“True, true. Then that settles it.”

He turned away. I followed him.

“What were you after?” I asked. “You saw for yourself there wasn’t
a balcony.”

“My friend, I am an old man, and sometimes I have fancies. Now,
I have a fancy that there is something to be seen in that room.
But if the police have the key——”

He broke off. We had reached the door of the Opalsens’ bedroom.
To my surprise, the key was in the lock. Poirot turned it softly,
and we entered. The room was empty.

“Wait here,” said my friend, and disappeared into the maid’s room
next door.

He was away for some minutes. When he returned his face was radiant.
He held something in his hand. It was a small, round object.

“What have you found?” I asked.

“Look!”

He held it out to me. It was a piece of white wax.

“Well?” I said, staring at it. “What does that prove?”

“A good deal, my friend. It proves that the thief was not Célestine,
the French maid.”

“Why?”

“Because, Hastings, this is a piece of wax such as is used for
taking impressions of keys.”

“Oh!” I said. “Then the thief must have had a duplicate key!”

“Precisely.”

“Then it must have been the chambermaid, after all!”

“Wait a bit. I am going to have a little talk with the manager.”

He led the way downstairs. The manager was in his office, looking
very harassed.

“Mr. Poirot,” he exclaimed, as we entered, “this is a most
unfortunate affair! A most unfortunate affair! The reputation
of the hotel will be ruined!”

“Calm yourself, monsieur,” said Poirot. “I have some news for you.
Your chambermaid is not a thief.”

“I’m glad to hear it—very glad to hear it. But the pearls——”

“The pearls have been stolen by someone who had a duplicate key.”

“A duplicate key?”

“Exactly. Someone who had access to Mrs. Opalsen’s key. Now, who
would that be?”

“I really can’t say.”

“Think, monsieur. Who would be likely to have a chance of getting
hold of it?”

“The maid, I suppose.”

“Exactly. But we have already decided that it was not the maid.
Now, who else?”

“I’m sure I don’t know.”

“What about the husband?”

“The husband!” The manager stared.

“Why not?” said Poirot. “He knew where the jewels were kept. He
had plenty of opportunities of getting hold of the key. And we
know he’s in low water just now. ‘Money’s confoundedly tight in
the City,’ he said. It would be a very simple way of getting hold
of some ready money, wouldn’t it?”

“But—but his wife!”

“My dear monsieur, husbands have been known to rob their wives
before now. It’s a very common occurrence. And, of course, he’d
see to it that the blame fell on someone else—the maid, for
instance.”

“It’s incredible!”

“Not at all. It’s a very simple and ingenious little plot. He takes
the pearls, replaces them by a cheap imitation, and then, when the
theft is discovered, he makes a great fuss and calls in the police.
The imitation pearls are found in the maid’s room, and everything
seems to point to her. It’s really very clever.”

“But the wax?” I asked. “Where does that come in?”

“Ah!” Poirot smiled. “That was a little mistake on his part. He
dropped it in the maid’s room, and I was lucky enough to find it.
It was a very small thing, but it was enough to show me how the
theft had been committed.”

The manager looked at him with admiration.

“Mr. Poirot,” he said, “you’re a genius! A positive genius!”

“I have my little successes,” said Poirot modestly. “And now, if
you’ll excuse me, I think I’ll go and have a little talk with Mr.
Opalsen.”

He led the way back to the lift. As we went up, I couldn’t help
feeling a little sorry for Mrs. Opalsen. To have your pearls stolen
by your own husband—it was a cruel blow!

We found Mr. Opalsen in the sitting-room. He looked up as we
entered.

“Well?” he asked. “Any news?”

“Yes,” said Poirot. “I have some news for you, monsieur. I know
who stole the pearls.”

“You do?” Opalsen sprang to his feet. “Who was it?”

“It was you, monsieur,” said Poirot quietly.

Opalsen stared at him for a moment, and then burst into a loud
laugh.

“Me! That’s a good one! I like that! And what should I want with
my wife’s pearls, I should like to know?”

“You wanted money, monsieur. You told us yourself that money was
tight in the City.”

“And so you think I’d rob my own wife to get it? You’re a fool,
Mr. Poirot—a positive fool!”

“I think not,” said Poirot. “I have proof, monsieur.”

“Proof! What proof?”

“I have the piece of wax you used for taking an impression of the
key.”

Opalsen’s face changed. He looked at Poirot with a new expression.

“So you found that, did you?” he said slowly. “I thought I’d been
more careful.”

“You were very careful, monsieur—but not quite careful enough.
Hercule Poirot does not miss much.”

“Well,” said Opalsen, “I suppose the game’s up. What are you going
to do about it?”

“That,” said Poirot, “is for your wife to decide.”

He walked to the door and called to Mrs. Opalsen. She came in,
looking very pale and anxious.

“Ed!” she cried. “What is it? What’s happened?”

“Mr. Poirot has something to tell you, madame,” said her husband.

Poirot explained the situation as gently as he could. Mrs. Opalsen
listened in silence, her eyes fixed on her husband’s face. When
he had finished, she turned to Opalsen.

“Is it true, Ed?” she asked.

“Yes,” he said. “It’s true. I’m sorry, Mary—I didn’t think you’d
find out.”

“Oh, Ed!” She burst into tears.

Opalsen went to her and put his arm round her.

“I’m sorry, dear. I’ll make it up to you—I promise I will. As soon
as things get better in the City, I’ll buy you the finest necklace
in London.”

“I don’t want a necklace,” she sobbed. “I only want you to be
honest with me.”

“I will, dear—I will.”

Poirot and I slipped out of the room, leaving them together.

“Well,” I said, as we walked down the corridor, “that’s a sad end
to the story.”

“Yes,” said Poirot. “It is always sad when trust is broken. But
at least the truth is out, and that is something.”

“And the pearls?” I asked. “What’s become of them?”

“Mr. Opalsen has them, no doubt. He will return them to his wife,
and all will be well.”

“I hope so,” I said. “I hope so.”

As we reached our own rooms, Poirot turned to me with a smile.

“And now, my friend,” he said, “I think we have earned our dinner.
Let us go and see what the _Grand Metropolitan_ can provide for
us.”

I followed him into the room, feeling that, after all, a week-end
at Brighton had its excitements.

The girl looked at him rather hard.

“Why, what do you want to go in there for? There’s nobody there
now.”

“It is that I have left my walking-stick,” said Poirot, with an
air of complete candour.

“Oh, very well!”

She led the way along the corridor, and unlocked the door of the
bedroom.

“I’ll wait for you,” she said, as we entered.

Poirot did not waste time. He went straight to the dressing-table,
took out the jewel-case, and, much to my horror, proceeded to
force the lock with a small instrument which he produced from his
pocket.

The lid flew open. He took out the emeralds and the other pieces
of jewellery, and looked at them with a look of intense disgust.

“All false!” he cried. “All false! _Sacré_! What a fool I have
been!”

“What?” I cried.

“_Oui_, it is as I tell you. All imitation!”

He replaced the jewels and locked the case again.

The chambermaid was watching us with interest.

“Find your stick?” she asked, as we came out.

“_Hélas_, no! It must be in the restaurant. I am so sorry to have
deranged you, mademoiselle.”

He turned away, and I followed him.

“Well?” I asked. “What next?”

“Next,” said Poirot, “we will go and see the manager.”

We found that official in his office. He was a small, dapper person,
excessively polite.

“Mr. Opalsen? Yes, he is in the lounge. You will find him there.”

“I do not want Mr. Opalsen,” said Poirot. “I want to see the lady
searcher you sent for just now.”

“The lady searcher?” The manager looked surprised. “But I didn’t
send for any lady searcher.”

“What?”

“Certainly not. I should have been informed if the police had sent
for one.”

“But she came!”

“She may have done, but it was not at my request.”

“_Mon Dieu_!” cried Poirot. “I see it all! Quick! The manager’s
private room! Where can we find the inspector?”

“He is still upstairs, I think.”

“Come, then!”

We raced up the stairs. The inspector was just coming out of the
Opalsens’ room. Poirot caught him by the arm.

“The searcher!” he cried. “Where is she?”

“The searcher? Why, she’s gone. She left some time ago.”

“And the chambermaid?”

“She’s about somewhere, I suppose. Why?”

“Because they are both in it!” cried Poirot. “They’re a pair of
the cleverest thieves in England. Quick! We may catch them yet!”

The inspector looked at him as though he had gone mad.

“What do you mean?”

“I mean that the woman who came here was no searcher, but a
confederate of the chambermaid’s. They’ve got the pearls!”

“But I saw the pearls myself!”

“You saw some imitation ones that they’d planted in the maid’s
bed! The real ones were never there!”

“Then where are they?”

“On the person of the so-called searcher, of course! She took them
from the chambermaid when they were in the room together. Don’t
you see? It was the chambermaid who stole them!”

“But you said yourself it was impossible for her to have hidden
them!”

“So it was—in the time! But she didn’t hide them. She passed them
through the door to her confederate in the next room! The door
that was bolted on both sides!”

“But how could she?”

“The bolt,” said Poirot, “was a dummy! It had been tampered with
beforehand. It looked all right from this side, but it could be
pushed back from the other! The chambermaid took the pearls, passed
them through to her friend, and then she was ready for any amount
of searching! It was the cleverest thing I’ve ever seen.”

“By George!” said the inspector. “I believe you’re right! I’ll
telephone to the station at once.”

He hurried away. Poirot turned to me with a smile.

“You see, Hastings? The little grey cells! They do not fail one.”

“But how did you know?” I asked, full of admiration.

“The dust, my friend! The dust on the table in the next room. There
was a rectangular mark where a jewel-case had been sitting. And yet
the room was supposed to be unoccupied! That set me thinking. And
then the lady searcher—she was a little too professional, was she
not? And the chambermaid—she was a little too ready to be searched!
It was all very well thought out.”

“And the Opalsens?”

“Ah, the Opalsens! I think we will not tell them just yet. It will
be a pleasant surprise for them to-morrow morning.”

“And Célestine?”

“Ah, Célestine! I must go and make my peace with her. The poor girl,
she has had a bad time.”

He did so, and I think Célestine’s forgiveness was not hard to
win.

The next morning the pearls were recovered. The two women were
captured at the railway station, just as they were about to leave
for London. They were well-known criminals, and the police were
delighted at their capture.

Mr. Opalsen was full of gratitude to Poirot.

“I don’t know how to thank you, Mr. Poirot. You’ve been simply
wonderful. If there’s anything I can do——”

“There is one thing,” said Poirot.

“What is that?”

“The next time you have a stroke of luck in the City, monsieur,
you will perhaps buy your wife some real jewels instead of these
excellent imitations?”

Mr. Opalsen went a deep red.

“How did you know?” he stammered.

“_Mon ami_,” said Poirot, “I have eyes. And I have also the little
grey cells. It was a very good imitation, but not quite good
enough for Hercule Poirot!”

And he smiled at me, the most self-satisfied smile I have ever
seen.

“The room I’ve just been in?”

“No, the room where the gentleman sleeps.”

The girl stared at him.

“Why, it’s not the room where the lady’s things are, but the one
on the other side, next the maid’s.”

“Precisely.”

“You mean the gentleman’s dressing-room?”

“Exactly.”

The chambermaid went ahead of us, and Poirot, followed by myself,
entered a smaller room, whose window looked out on the same view
as those of the other two rooms. Poirot began to examine it
minutely. There was no fireplace. He looked behind the wardrobe,
pushed the bed aside, and looked into the drawers of the chest of
drawers. Then he gave a little exclamation of satisfaction.

In the corner of the room, near the window, was a small, round
washstand, on which stood a basin and ewer. Poirot took the basin
and looked into it. It was dry. Then he examined the bottom.

“_Tiens_!” he murmured. “That is curious.”

“What is?” I asked, following him.

“The bottom of the basin is quite clean, yet the ewer is almost
empty.”

He took up the ewer and shook it. There was very little water in
it.

“Perhaps he had a wash,” I suggested.

“No, the towel is quite dry. And there is no water in the glass.
Yet—the ewer is nearly empty.”

He stood for a moment with his eyes closed, and his lips moving
as though in prayer. Then he turned to the window.

“Ah!” he said, and pointed.

There was a small, leaden-headed nail in the window-sill, which
I had not noticed before. Poirot pulled a small, magnifying glass
from his pocket and examined it.

“You see?”

I looked through the glass. Round the head of the nail was a tiny
shred of what looked like silk.

“Well?” I asked.

“What does that suggest to you, Hastings?”

“Someone has been climbing in by the window?”

“No. It was a very fine piece of silk, and it was tied round the
nail. Now, come into the next room.”

We followed him into the maid’s room. He walked straight to the
window.

“Look!”

There, in the window-sill, was another nail, exactly similar to
the first.

“I begin to see,” I cried. “They were lowered from one window to
the other.”

“Exactly. But who lowered them?”

“The maid, of course.”

“And why should she do that, my friend? If she had them, why not
keep them?”

I was silenced. Poirot was looking round the room.

“Is there a fireplace here? No. But there is a ventilator.”

He climbed on to a chair and peered into the small, iron-grated
aperture. Then he gave a little cry of triumph.

“_V’là_! I have it.”

He reached in his hand and drew out a small, heavy object. It was
wrapped in a piece of newspaper. He unfolded it. There, before our
eyes, lay a magnificent string of pearls.

“The real ones!” I cried.

“The real ones, _mon ami_.”

“But how did they get there?”

“That is what we have to find out.”

He looked at the piece of newspaper in which they had been wrapped.
It was a fragment of a French journal.

“_Tiens!_ This is interesting.”

“Then it was the maid after all?”

“Wait, wait!”

He went back into the bedroom, where Mrs. Opalsen was still sitting,
and handed her the pearls.

“Are these yours, madame?”

With a scream of joy she caught them from him.

“My pearls! My own beautiful pearls! Oh, Mr. Poirot, how can I ever
thank you?”

“By being more careful in future, madame.”

“But where did you find them?”

“In the ventilator of the maid’s room.”

“Then it _was_ Célestine!”

“I am not so sure, madame. Will you tell me—is your husband often
in your room?”

Mrs. Opalsen looked a little surprised.

“Why, yes, of course. He often comes in to talk to me while I am
dressing.”

“And he knew where you kept your jewels?”

“Oh, yes. I have no secrets from Ed.”

Poirot nodded.

“I see. And was he in your room this evening, before you went down
to dinner?”

“Yes, he came in for a few minutes.”

“I see,” said Poirot again.

He turned to me.

“Come, Hastings. I have one or two things to say to the inspector.”

We found that official in the hall. Poirot took him aside for a
moment. When he returned his face was grave.

“Well?” I asked. “Is it all over?”

“Not yet, my friend. Not quite yet.”

He led the way out of the hotel.

“Where are we going?”

“To the police station.”

“But why? You’ve found the pearls.”

“I have found the pearls, yes. But I have not yet found the thief.”

“But surely it must be the maid?”

“We shall see, my friend. We shall see.”

At the police station Poirot had a long talk with the
superintendent. When he came out he looked more cheerful.

“And now, Hastings, we will go back to the hotel and have a little
supper. I feel that I have earned it.”

We were halfway through our meal when Poirot suddenly gripped my
arm.

“Look!” he whispered.

I looked in the direction he indicated. Mr. Opalsen was entering
the room. He looked pale and haggard. He walked straight up to our
table.

“Mr. Poirot,” he said, and his voice shook, “I want to thank you.
You have saved me from a very terrible position.”

“How is that, monsieur?”

“My wife has told me everything. She has the pearls. But for you,
that poor girl would have been ruined.”

“It was nothing, monsieur. A mere matter of the little grey cells.”

“But I don’t understand,” I broke in. “If the maid didn’t do it,
who did?”

Mr. Opalsen looked at Poirot.

“Shall I tell him?”

Poirot nodded.

“It was I,” said Mr. Opalsen.

“You!” I cried, in amazement.

“Yes. You see, I was in a very difficult position. I had been
speculating, and things had gone against me. I was in urgent need
of a large sum of money. I knew that my wife’s pearls were insured
for their full value. I—I thought that if they were stolen, the
insurance company would pay, and I should be able to get out of
my difficulties.”

“But the imitation pearls?” I asked.

“I had them made some time ago. I intended to substitute them for
the real ones, and then arrange for a robbery to take place. But
when I heard that Mr. Poirot was in the hotel, I was terrified.
I knew that he would be sure to find me out. So I—I tried to hide
the pearls where they would be found, and the suspicion would
fall on someone else. I am a miserable wretch, Mr. Poirot.”

“It was a grave mistake, monsieur,” said Poirot gravely. “A very
grave mistake. But, since you have confessed, I think we can
arrange things. The pearls have been restored to their owner, and
no harm has been done. I will speak to the inspector.”

Mr. Opalsen thanked him with tears in his eyes, and left us.

“Well!” I said, when he had gone. “I should never have thought it
of him.”

“No?” said Poirot, with a smile. “And yet, to the trained mind,
it was all so simple. The empty ewer—the silk on the nail—the
French newspaper—all pointed to the same thing.”

“But I don’t see——”

“It is very simple, my friend. Mr. Opalsen wished to hide the
pearls where they would be found by the police. He knew that the
maid’s room would be searched. So he lowered the pearls from his
own window to the maid’s window, and then pushed them into the
ventilator with a walking-stick. The empty ewer provided the
weight to lower them, and the silk was used to tie them to the
nail. The French newspaper was a clever touch, designed to throw
suspicion on the maid.”

“But how did you know it was he?”

“Because, my friend, no one else had the opportunity. He was the
only person who could have gone into his own room and the maid’s
room without being suspected. And he was the only person who knew
where the jewels were kept.”

“Well,” I said, “you’ve done it again, Poirot.”

“It was nothing, my friend. A mere trifle. But now, let us finish
our supper. I am strangely hungry.”

And Poirot, with a satisfied smile, returned to his _omelette_.

“_Which_ room? The lady’s or the gentleman’s?”

“The gentleman’s, if you please.”

The girl produced a key and led the way. The room was at the
opposite end of the corridor. She unlocked it and we went in.

Poirot’s first action was to walk straight to the dressing-table.
He stood looking at it for some moments, his head on one side.
Then he began to go through the drawers.

“What on earth are you looking for?” I asked.

“A little something that I do not see. Ah!”

He had pulled out a small drawer at the top and was looking into
it with an expression of intense satisfaction.

“What is it?” I asked, peering over his shoulder.

“A piece of soap, _mon ami_. An ordinary piece of scented soap.”

He held it up for me to see. It certainly appeared quite ordinary.
I could not see anything remarkable about it.

“And now,” said Poirot, “we will go back and see if our friend
the inspector has discovered his mistake yet.”

We were just in time. The inspector, with a very red face, was
in the act of explaining to the Opalsens that the necklace was a
sham.

“But I tell you it’s mine!” cried Mrs. Opalsen, almost in
hysterics. “I’d know it anywhere!”

“I’m afraid not, madam. One of my men has just had it tested by
a jeweller in the town.”

“Then where are the real ones?”

“That’s what we’ve got to find out, madam.”

Poirot stepped forward.

“Perhaps I can help you there,” he said.

The inspector turned on him.

“You!” he said. “What do you know about it?”

“A good deal, my friend. To begin with, if you will have the
goodness to look at the bolt of the door in the next room—the empty
room, I mean—you will find it has been recently oiled.”

“Oiled?”

“Precisely. And if you will examine the piece of soap I have in
my hand, you will find it has a very distinct impression of a key
on one side.”

“A key!” cried the inspector.

“The key of the jewel-case, which, as you remember, Mrs. Opalsen
wore round her neck. It was a simple lock. A duplicate could
easily be made.”

The inspector’s face began to clear.

“I see. Someone got hold of the key, made an impression of it in
soap, and had a duplicate made. Then they entered the room from
next door——”

“But the door was bolted,” I reminded him.

“On _both_ sides,” added Poirot. “But the bolt on the side of the
empty room was quite easily turned from this side by means of a
pair of pincers through the keyhole.”

“Then who did it?” demanded the inspector. “The maid?”

“No,” said Poirot. “The maid was never alone in the room. Even
when she went into her own room for a few seconds, the chambermaid
was there.”

“Then it must have been the chambermaid!”

“But we searched her!” cried the inspector. “And she couldn’t have
hidden them in the other room, for it was empty and we searched
that too.”

“Wait a moment,” said Poirot. “There is one person you have not
searched.”

“Who?”

“Mr. Opalsen!”

A dead silence followed the words. Mr. Opalsen’s face went a
curious grey colour.

“What do you mean?” he gasped. “Are you suggesting——”

“I am suggesting,” said Poirot, “that you were in need of money,
monsieur. You told us so yourself this evening. You had a duplicate
set of pearls made in London, and you also had a duplicate key to
your wife’s jewel-case. This evening, while your wife was at
dinner, you went up to her room—the chambermaid was not there then,
I think?—and substituted the false pearls for the real ones.”

“But the maid was there!” cried the inspector.

“Exactly,” said Poirot. “That is where the cleverness of the plan
comes in. You knew the maid would be there. You wanted her to be
there. You stayed in the room for a few moments, talking to her,
and while her back was turned you made the substitution. Then you
went downstairs and joined us at dinner. Later, when your wife
went up to fetch the pearls, you followed her. You knew she would
discover the loss at once. In the confusion that followed, you
managed to hide the false pearls in the maid’s bed. You knew the
police would search the room and find them there. The maid would
be arrested, and no one would ever suspect you of having the real
pearls in your possession.”

There was a moment’s silence. Then Mr. Opalsen gave a sudden
strangled cry and made a dash for the door. But the inspector was
too quick for him.

“Not so fast, my friend!” he said, catching him by the arm. “I
think you’d better come along with me.”

“And the pearls?” cried Mrs. Opalsen. “Where are my pearls?”

“I think you will find them in monsieur’s pocket,” said Poirot
calmly.

The inspector’s search proved that he was right. A few minutes
later, the real pearls were restored to their owner.

“Well,” I said, as we walked back to our own rooms, “that was a
neat bit of work, Poirot. But how did you know it was Opalsen?”

“_Mon ami_,” said Poirot, “it was the soap. Why should a man like
Mr. Opalsen, who has everything he wants, steal a piece of soap
from a hotel? It was not even a new piece. It had been used. And
then there was the impression of the key. It was clear that someone
had been making a duplicate. And who was more likely to have
access to the key than Mr. Opalsen?”

“But why did he want to steal his wife’s pearls?”

“As he told us, money is ‘confoundedly tight’ in the City just now.
No doubt he hoped to realize a large sum on the pearls, and
replace them later with another duplicate set before his wife
discovered the loss. It was a bold plan, but he did not reckon on
Hercule Poirot!”

And Poirot, with a satisfied smile, began to arrange his
toilet-table with his usual meticulous care.

The woman rose willingly, and we accompanied her down the passage
again. Mr. Opalsen’s room was on the other side of the corridor,
its door facing that of his wife’s room. The chambermaid unlocked
it with her pass-key, and we entered.

As she was about to depart Poirot detained her.

“One moment; have you ever seen among the effects of Mr. Opalsen
a card like this?”

He held out a plain white card, rather highly glazed and uncommon
in appearance. The maid took it and scrutinized it carefully.

“No, sir, I can’t say I have. But, anyway, the valet has most to
do with the gentlemen’s rooms.”

“I see. Thank you.”

Poirot took back the card. The woman departed. Poirot appeared to
reflect a little. Then he gave a short, sharp nod of the head.

“Ring the bell, I pray of you, Hastings. Three times, for the
valet.”

I obeyed, devoured with curiosity. Meanwhile Poirot had emptied
the waste-paper-basket on the floor, and was swiftly going through
its contents.

The man appeared almost immediately. He was a small, dark,
unobtrusive-looking fellow, who looked as if he knew his business.

“I believe you are the valet for this floor, are you not?”

“Yes, sir.”

“I have a small matter I want you to attend to. You may have seen
among Mr. Opalsen’s effects a card like this?”

Again he produced the card. The valet examined it with a flicker
of interest.

“Yes, sir. I have seen one or two about.”

“Where?”

“Usually on the dressing-table, or in one of the drawers. I think
there is one there now, sir.”

He pointed to a small wooden stand on the chest of drawers.

“Ah! Thank you. That is all.”

The man bowed and withdrew.

Poirot picked up the card. It was precisely similar to the one
he held in his hand.

“Well?” I asked. “What does it mean?”

“It means, _mon ami_, that we are at last on the right track.
Let us return to the room of Mrs. Opalsen.”

On our way we were overtaken by the inspector, who looked both
hot and angry.

“Look here, sir!” he exclaimed, as he caught us up. “That necklace
was a fake. Not even a good one! What’s the meaning of it?”

“Ah!” Poirot’s eyes twinkled. “You have made that discovery? I
congratulate you.”

“I’m not in a mood for joking. Where are the real pearls?”

“They are in this hotel, monsieur. If you will come with me I
will show you where.”

The inspector stared at him.

“I hope you’re not fooling me, Mr. Poirot?”

“I have too much respect for the law, monsieur. But I must ask
for your assistance in a small matter. Will you have the goodness
to send for the manager?”

“Certainly.”

He spoke to a passing page-boy, and a few minutes later that
functionary joined us in the corridor.

“You wished to see me, gentlemen?”

Poirot bowed.

“Monsieur, I have a request to make. Will you kindly send for the
chambermaid of this floor, and also for the valet?”

The manager looked surprised, but he gave the necessary orders.
We all moved towards Mrs. Opalsen’s room. In a few minutes the
two servants appeared.

“Now, monsieur,” said Poirot, turning to the inspector, “I will
ask you to be so good as to search these two persons—but
_thoroughly_.”

“What?” The manager’s face was a study. “You can’t mean——”

“I mean exactly what I say, monsieur.”

The inspector’s face had also undergone a transformation. He
stepped forward and took the chambermaid by the arm.

“Now then, my girl, I’m sorry, but I’ve got to do it. Just step
along with me.”

“And the valet also,” said Poirot.

“But this is preposterous!” cried the manager. “I have never
heard of such a thing! My employees——”

“Will you be so good as to be silent, monsieur,” said Poirot, with
an air of authority. “I am acting in the interests of justice.”

The two suspects were led away. We waited in a tense silence.
At last the inspector reappeared. He was carrying something in
his hand.

“Well?” I cried. “Did you find them?”

“I did!” said the inspector. “In the lining of the valet’s
waistcoat. A most ingenious hiding-place.”

He held out a string of magnificent pearls.

“My pearls!” cried Mrs. Opalsen, who had joined us. “Oh, Mr.
Poirot, how can I ever thank you?”

“It was nothing, madame. A mere trifle.”

“But how did you know?” I asked, as we were alone once more.

“It was quite simple, Hastings. You remember that I timed the
actions of the maid and the chambermaid? I found that neither
could have had time to hide the pearls—_in the room_. Therefore
the pearls must have been taken _out_ of the room.”

“But how? The maid never left it, and the chambermaid only for
a few minutes.”

“Precisely. But there was another person who had access to the
room—the valet! He could have entered by the door from the next
apartment—the one I found bolted on both sides.”

“But it _was_ bolted!”

“Yes, but bolts can be moved from the outside—with a piece of
wire and a little ingenuity. The valet is an expert at that kind
of thing. He entered the room while the maid was in her own room,
took the pearls, and substituted the imitation ones. Then he
slipped out again, and bolted the door behind him.”

“But the card?” I asked. “What had that to do with it?”

“Ah, the card! That was a little piece of bluff on my part,
Hastings. I suspected the valet from the first—his manner was
a little too unobtrusive, you understand? I used the card to
test him. If he had been an honest man he would have said he had
never seen it before. But he was a thief, and a thief is always
suspicious. He thought I knew something, and he tried to put me
off the scent by pretending he had seen the card before.”

“I see,” I said. “And the imitation pearls in the maid’s bed?”

“A very clever piece of work, Hastings. The valet put them there
to throw suspicion on the maid. He knew that if the real pearls
were found on him he would be ruined, so he provided a scapegoat.”

“Well,” I said, “it’s been a most interesting case. I’m glad we
came to Brighton after all.”

“So am I, Hastings. So am I. It has given me an opportunity of
using my little grey cells—and that is always a pleasure.”

He smiled at me, and I felt that, after all, Poirot was a very
great man.

“Nothing here,” he said, then added, as though his thought were
somewhat elsewhere: “We must have a look in the maid’s room.”

A heavy-looking man in the uniform of a valet appeared in the
doorway.

“You rang, sir?”

“I should be obliged if you would answer me one or two questions.”
Poirot’s manner was extremely suave. “You were in Mr. Opalsen’s
room after dinner to-night?”

“Yes, sir.”

“About what time?”

“Between half-past eight and nine, sir.”

“I see. Now—did you notice anything unusual?”

The man hesitated.

“Well, sir, if I might make so bold, I did think it rather a
coincidence. You see, sir, as I was coming along the corridor,
I saw a gentleman I know by sight—a Mr. Warrender—come out of the
next door to Mr. Opalsen’s.”

“Which door?”

“Number 24, sir.”

“And what was there unusual in that?”

“Well, sir, only that Mr. Warrender had particularly asked for
the room next to his friends, the Opalsens. And yet I saw him
come out of Number 24, while his own room is Number 28.”

“I see,” said Poirot. “Thank you. That is all.”

He turned to me.

“We’ll go down to the lounge, Hastings.”

“What does it all mean?” I asked, as we descended.

“It means, my friend, that I have a very pretty little case to
hand. One that will be a credit even to Hercule Poirot!”

In the lounge he made for a corner where a small table was
unoccupied, and called a waiter.

“You will bring me, if you please, two glasses of your best Benedictine.”

The waiter departed. Poirot leaned back and half-closed his eyes.
I waited in a fever of impatience.

“And now?” I said, at last. “What does it mean? Who is this Mr.
Warrender? And what has he to do with the pearls? Why did you
come down here instead of telling the police?”

“Wait, wait, my friend! You are so impetuous! All in good time.
Here is our Benedictine. _À votre santé_!”

He sipped the sticky liqueur with great deliberation.

“I will be frank with you, Hastings. I am at a loss. But we shall
see. We shall see.”

“You are at a loss?” I echoed.

“Yes. My little grey cells are not functioning with their usual
precision. But the clue of the card—that was important. Yes, very
important.”

“The card?”

“Yes, the little white card I showed the chambermaid.”

“But where did you get it?”

“I found it, my friend, on the floor of the room next to Mrs.
Opalsen’s—the room which is at present empty.”

“And what does it mean?”

“It means—well, it may mean several things. But first I must make
sure of one or two points.”

He rose, and went across to the bureau. I saw him consult a
large book, and then return to his seat.

“Yes, it is as I thought,” he said, with an air of satisfaction.
“Number 24 is at present unoccupied.”

“But the valet said he saw a Mr. Warrender come out of it!”

“Exactly. And the name of the gentleman who occupies Number 28 is
not Warrender, but—let me see—Johnston.”

“Then the valet was mistaken?”

“Perhaps. Or perhaps not. We shall see.”

He was silent for a few moments, and then said abruptly:

“Tell me, Hastings, what do you think of Mr. Opalsen?”

“Oh, a very pleasant, straightforward kind of man. A bit of a
plunger, I should say. But quite all right.”

“And his wife?”

“A very charming woman, but—well, perhaps a little—what shall I
say?—superficial?”

“You have hit it exactly, Hastings. Superficial! It is a good word.
And now, what do you think of the maid—Célestine?”

“Well, she seemed very much upset. I should say she was a very
devoted servant.”

“And the chambermaid?”

“Oh, a very ordinary type of girl. A bit flighty, perhaps.”

Poirot nodded.

“Yes, yes. It is all very interesting.”

He was silent again. I felt that I was on the verge of a great
discovery.

“Poirot!” I cried. “I have it!”

“You have it? _Félicitations_, my friend! And what is it that
you have?”

“The pearls were never in the jewel-case at all!”

“No?” Poirot’s eyes twinkled. “And where were they, then?”

“In the room next door—Number 24!”

“But why there?”

“Because the thief—whoever he was—had a duplicate key to the
communicating door. He went in, took the pearls, and then bolted
the door again on the other side.”

“And the pearls?”

“He hid them in Number 24, intending to come back for them later.”

“But the room was empty!”

“Exactly. That’s why it was such a good place to hide them.”

“But how did he get into the room?”

“With a pass-key, of course.”

Poirot shook his head.

“No, no, Hastings. It is a good theory, but it will not do. You
forget the card.”

“The card? What has that to do with it?”

“Everything, my friend. Everything.”

He rose.

“And now, I think we will go to bed. I have much to think about.”

“But the pearls?”

“Do not distress yourself, Hastings. We shall find them. I am
certain of it.”

I was far from sharing his confidence, but I knew from experience
that it was useless to question him further.

The next morning Poirot was up early. I found him in the lounge,
absorbed in a newspaper.

“Well?” I asked. “Any news?”

“None. But I have been thinking, Hastings. I have been thinking.”

“And what is the result?”

“The result is that I should like to have another look at that
room—Number 24.”

“But it’s occupied now!” I exclaimed, pointing to the book on the
bureau.

“So I see. A Mr. and Mrs. Robinson. They arrived late last night.”

“Then we can’t go in.”

“On the contrary, my friend. We can—and we will!”

He led the way to the lift.

“But what if they’re there?” I whispered, as we reached the first
floor.

“They will not be there. They are at breakfast. I have made sure
of that.”

He produced a bunch of keys from his pocket, and after one or two
attempts, the door of Number 24 swung open.

The room was in some confusion, as though its occupants had only
just left it. Poirot went straight to the table by the window.

“Ah!” he cried. “It is as I thought!”

He held up a small object. It was a piece of fine wire, about
three inches long.

“What is it?” I asked.

“It is a clue, Hastings. A very important clue.”

He was looking round the room with an air of intense satisfaction.
Suddenly his eyes lighted on a small travel-bag that stood on a
chair. He pounced upon it, and in a moment its contents were
strewn upon the bed.

“Poirot!” I cried. “What are you doing? You can’t do that!”

“Peace, my friend! Peace! I know what I am doing.”

He was feverishly searching through a small leather case. Suddenly
he uttered a cry of triumph.

“Look, Hastings! Look!”

He held out a small, shimmering object. It was a pearl—a large,
beautifully shaped pearl.

“The necklace!” I cried.

“Not the necklace, Hastings. Only one pearl. But it is enough.
It is enough!”

He was rapidly replacing the things in the bag.

“And now, let us depart. Quickly!”

We reached the corridor just as a man and woman came round the
corner. They were a young couple, and looked somewhat surprised at
seeing us. Poirot bowed with his usual politeness.

“A thousand pardons, monsieur. I fear I have mistaken the room.”

He hurried me away before they could reply.

“And now?” I asked, as we reached the lounge.

“And now, Hastings, we will have a little talk with Mr. Opalsen.”

We found the stockbroker in the dining-room. He looked tired and
worried.

“Any news, Mr. Poirot?” he asked eagerly.

“I have found one of the pearls, monsieur.”

“What? Where?”

“In the room next to your wife’s—Number 24.”

“In Number 24? But it’s occupied by some people called Robinson.”

“Exactly. And it is Mr. Robinson who has your pearls.”

“Mr. Robinson? But I don’t know any Mr. Robinson!”

“Perhaps not. But he knows you. Or rather, he knows your wife’s
pearls.”

“But how did he get them?”

“That, monsieur, I will explain to you. But first, we must find
the inspector.”

The inspector was easily found. He was in the manager’s office,
looking very much disgruntled.

“Well?” he asked, as we entered. “Any more ‘experiments’?”

“I have found the pearls,” said Poirot quietly.

The inspector stared.

“You have? Where?”

“In the possession of a Mr. Robinson, who is at present staying in
this hotel.”

“Mr. Robinson? I’ve never heard of him.”

“Possibly not. But if you will come with me, I think I can
convince you.”

We all went up to the first floor. Poirot led the way to Number 24.
He knocked on the door, and it was opened by the young man we had
seen in the corridor.

“What is the meaning of this?” he asked, looking from one to the
other of us.

“The meaning, monsieur,” said Poirot, “is that I have reason to
believe you have in your possession a certain pearl necklace
belonging to Mrs. Opalsen.”

The young man went deathly pale.

“I—I don’t know what you mean,” he stammered.

“We shall see,” said the inspector, pushing past him into the
room.

In a few minutes the whole story was out. The young man, whose
real name was not Robinson, but—of all things—Warrender, had been
in financial difficulties for some time. He had known the Opalsens
for some years, and had been well aware of the value of the
pearls. He had also known of Mrs. Opalsen’s habit of keeping them
in her jewel-case.

He had arrived at the hotel a few days previously, and had
managed to secure the room next to the Opalsens. He had then
provided himself with a duplicate key to the communicating door,
and also to the jewel-case.

On the night of the robbery, he had waited until he saw the
Opalsens go down to dinner. He had then entered their room,
opened the jewel-case, and substituted a clever imitation for the
real pearls. He had then returned to his own room, intending to
leave the hotel the next morning.

But the discovery of the robbery much sooner than he had expected
had upset his plans. He had been afraid to leave the hotel,
fearing that he might be searched. He had therefore hidden the
real pearls in a small travel-bag, intending to dispose of them
later.

But he had not reckoned with Hercule Poirot.

“But how did you know?” I asked, as we sat in the train on our way
back to London.

“It was the card, Hastings. The little white card.”

“But what did it mean?”

“It was a French card, my friend. A card used by certain French
thieves to mark the rooms they intend to rob. When I found it in
Number 24, I knew that the robbery had been planned for some time.
And when the valet told me he had seen a Mr. Warrender come out of
that room, I knew that he was the man.”

“But the pearl in the bag?”

“That was a little piece of luck, Hastings. He must have been
hurried when he was putting the pearls away, and one of them
must have fallen out.”

“Well,” I said, “it was a wonderful piece of work, Poirot. I don’t
know how you do it.”

Poirot smiled.

“It is the little grey cells, my friend. The little grey cells!”

“Nothing here,” he said, with an air of satisfaction, and replaced
the papers in the basket.

The valet appeared. He was a small, pale man, with a discreet and
deferential manner. He looked from me to Poirot with some surprise.

“You rang, sir?”

“Yes, we are with Mr. Opalsen. He is at the moment with the police.
I wished to ask you a question.”

“Yes, sir.”

“Have you ever seen this before?”

Again the white card was produced.

The man’s face changed. He looked at Poirot with an expression of
intense interest.

“Yes, sir. I have.”

“Where?”

“In Mr. Opalsen’s dress-clothes. I found it when I was brushing
them.”

“When was that?”

“This morning, sir.”

“Thank you. That is all I wanted to know.”

The man withdrew, still with that same look of interest and
bewilderment.

“Well?” I asked. “What does that mean?”

Poirot was pacing the room with short, quick steps. Suddenly he
stopped.

“Hastings, did you notice a certain rectangular mark in the dust
on a table in the empty room?”

“I did.”

“And you saw the card I have just produced? It is of the same
dimensions.”

“I see.”

“Is it possible that you see, Hastings? I begin to have hopes of
you. It was a very simple trick—so simple that it escaped the
inspector. The pearls were stolen, not to-night, but some time ago.
Mr. Opalsen’s necklace was insured for its full value—perhaps for
more. And money, as he himself told us, is ‘confoundedly tight in
the City.’”

“You mean he—he stole his own wife’s pearls?” I gasped.

“Precisely. He had an imitation made—a very good imitation. He
put it in the jewel-case, and the real pearls he disposed of
elsewhere. Then he waited for a favourable opportunity. To-night,
when we were all together, he sent his wife to fetch them. The
rest was easy. He had only to make sure that they were found in
the maid’s room, and the thing was done. The card? It was the
business-card of the firm who made the imitation pearls. He must
have dropped it by accident.”

I was speechless. The simplicity of the thing was indeed amazing.

“But how did he get them into the maid’s room?” I asked.

“Through the door into the next apartment—the one we found bolted
on both sides. He had a key to that door. He entered the empty
room, unbolted the door on that side, and waited. When Célestine
went into her own room for the cotton and the scissors, he slipped
in, substituted the imitation pearls for the real ones—no, I am
wrong there—he had already done that. He merely had to place the
imitation pearls where they would be found.”

“But the door was bolted on _this_ side!” I protested.

“Exactly. It is a very old trick, but a very effective one. A
piece of strong silk thread passed round the handle of the bolt,
and the ends passed under the door. A sharp pull from the other
side, and the bolt is shot. Then you have only to draw the thread
towards you, and the thing is done.”

“And the real pearls?”

“He has them, of course. He probably has them on him at this
moment.”

“But we must do something!” I cried. “We must tell the police!”

“Gently, gently, my friend. We must have proof. At present we have
nothing but a theory.”

“But the card——”

“He will say he knows nothing about it. No, we must have more than
that.”

He stood for a moment, lost in thought. Then his face cleared.

“I have it! Hastings, go to the office and find out if Mr. Opalsen
has had any visitors lately—say during the last few days.”

I hurried off to obey his instructions. When I returned, ten
minutes later, I found Poirot waiting for me in the hall.

“Well?”

“He had a visitor yesterday—a Mr. Bernard. They were in the lounge
together for some time.”

“Bernard! I seem to know the name. A tall man, with a dark
moustache?”

“Yes.”

“I thought so. Mr. Bernard is a well-known ‘fence.’ The pearls have
already changed hands. But we may catch them yet. Come, Hastings!”

He led the way out of the hotel and towards the station.

“Where are we going?” I asked.

“To London. We must be there before Mr. Bernard has time to
dispose of the pearls. I think I know where to find him.”

As we were waiting on the platform for our train, a familiar
figure approached us. It was Mr. Opalsen.

“Going back to town?” he asked, with a smile. “I’m doing the same.
Too much excitement for me here. My wife’s still a bit upset, so
I’m leaving her behind for a bit. The police have got the necklace,
of course.”

“Quite so,” said Poirot. “A most interesting case.”

The train came in, and we all three got into a first-class carriage.
Mr. Opalsen was very talkative, and he and Poirot were soon deep
in a discussion of the case. I sat and watched them, marveling at
the way in which Poirot was leading the other on.

Suddenly Poirot leaned forward.

“By the way, Mr. Opalsen, you dropped this.”

He held out the white card.

Opalsen took it, his face turning a ghastly grey.

“I—I don’t know what you mean,” he stammered.

“I think you do,” said Poirot quietly. “And I think you also know
that the pearls the police have are imitation.”

Opalsen made a movement as though to spring from the carriage,
but Poirot’s hand was on his arm.

“It is no use, monsieur. The game is up. I have already informed
the police, and they will be waiting for you at Victoria.”

Opalsen collapsed into his seat, his face a mask of despair.

“How did you know?” he gasped.

“It was the card, monsieur. A very small thing—but it was enough.”

When we arrived at Victoria, two men in plain clothes were indeed
waiting for us. Mr. Opalsen was led away, and Poirot and I were
left alone on the platform.

“Well, Hastings,” said Poirot, with a smile, “another case
successfully concluded. And now, I think, a little supper at the
_Savoy_—to celebrate our return to town.”

“But Poirot,” I said, as we drove off in a taxi, “how did you
really know about the pearls? Was it really only the card?”

Poirot laughed.

“No, my friend. It was the fact that Mr. Opalsen was so very anxious
to tell us how much they were worth. A man whose wife has just been
robbed of a fortune does not usually stop to calculate the exact
value of his loss. And then, of course, there was the insurance.
A very old motive, Hastings—but a very common one.”

“And the real pearls?”

“They were in Mr. Opalsen’s pocket all the time. He had not had
time to hand them over to his friend Mr. Bernard. But I think he
will find it rather difficult to explain their presence there to
the police.”

He leaned back in the taxi, a look of supreme satisfaction on his
face.

“Yes, Hastings, it has been a most interesting case. And it has
taught us one thing—never to underestimate the importance of small
things. Even a piece of white card may be enough to hang a man—or,
at any rate, to send him to prison!”

The valet appeared—a small, dark man, with a furtive and slightly
hang-dog expression. Poirot showed him the card, but he likewise
could give no information on the subject. Poirot dismissed him.

“Well?” I asked.

“The valet has been in the hotel six months. He was previously at
the _Queen’s_, at Eastbourne. He is not a man I should choose to
trust with my clothes. He is too——” Poirot waved his hand
expressively.

“What about the chambermaid?”

“She has been here three years. She is a woman of good character.
She is also, I should imagine, a woman of some common sense.”

“And the maid?”

“She is an old and trusted servant. She has been with Mrs. Opalsen
nearly ten years.”

“Then who could it have been?”

“That is the question, _mon ami_.”

Poirot’s eyes were dancing with excitement. He looked about him,
poking into corners and drawers in his own particular way. Suddenly
he gave a little cry of triumph.

“What is it?”

He held out a small piece of white paper.

“Look at that, Hastings!”

I took it. On it was written in a clerkly hand:

_“With the compliments of the management.”_

“What of it?” I asked.

Poirot chuckled.

“Nothing—except that it was at the bottom of the
waste-paper-basket.”

“Well, where else should it be?”

“True, true. But it is interesting, all the same. Now, Hastings,
we will descend to the hall and have a word with the manager.”

“Are you going to tell him about the pearls?”

“Not yet. Not yet. I have a little idea, that is all.”

The manager was in his office. He looked up as we entered.

“Can I be of any assistance to you, monsieur?”

“It is possible. You have, I believe, a guest of the name of
Opalsen staying here?”

The manager nodded.

“And you have lately had some—er—unfortunate occurrence in
connection with that lady’s jewellery?”

“I have indeed. The police are now in the hotel. It is a most
distressing affair for the management.”

“Quite so. Quite so. Now, monsieur, I want you to be so good as
to do me a little favour. I wish to know if any one has called for
Mr. Opalsen this evening?”

The manager touched a bell, and a page appeared.

“Find out if anyone has called for Mr. Opalsen this evening.”

The boy returned in a few minutes.

“No, sir, no one.”

“You are sure?”

“Quite sure, sir.”

Poirot thanked him and we withdrew.

“Well?” I said. “What now?”

“Now, Hastings, we will go and have a little talk with Mr. Opalsen.”

“In his room?”

“No, I think we will find him in the lounge.”

We found Mr. Opalsen sitting by himself in a corner of the lounge.
He looked up as we approached.

“Ah! Still at it, Mr. Poirot? Found out anything fresh?”

“Not exactly, monsieur. But I have been making a few inquiries.”

“Indeed?” Opalsen’s tone was slightly sarcastic. “And what have
you discovered?”

“I have discovered,” said Poirot, “that no one has called for you
this evening.”

Opalsen stared.

“Of course not! Why should they?”

“Exactly. Why should they? And yet, monsieur, you were called away
from our table by a page who told you someone wished to see you.”

Opalsen laughed.

“Oh, that! That was a mistake, of course. The boy got the names
mixed up.”

“Indeed? And yet he went straight to you.”

“I suppose he did. I didn’t think anything of it at the time.”

“No,” said Poirot, “I suppose not. It was a very simple little
ruse.”

“Ruse? What do you mean?”

“I mean, monsieur, that it was a device to get you away from the
table so that the robbery could be committed.”

“But the robbery was committed upstairs!”

“Was it?” said Poirot.

Opalsen stared at him.

“What do you mean?”

“I mean,” said Poirot, “that the pearls were never in the bedroom
at all.”

“Never in the bedroom? But my wife saw them there!”

“She saw _some_ pearls there, no doubt. But were they the _real_
ones?”

Opalsen turned pale.

“You mean——”

“I mean, monsieur, that the real pearls were stolen some time ago,
and that false ones were substituted for them.”

“But that’s impossible! My wife would have known.”

“Would she? Are you sure? Many of these imitations are very clever
nowadays.”

Opalsen sat silent for a moment, then he said:

“But who could have done such a thing?”

“That,” said Poirot, “is what I am going to find out.”

He turned away and I followed him.

“Poirot,” I said, “what does all this mean?”

“It means, my friend, that we are on the track of a very clever
criminal.”

“But who?”

“Ah, that is the question! But I have a little idea. Yes, I have
a little idea.”

He would say no more, and we went up to our rooms.

The next morning Poirot was up early. I found him in the lounge,
talking to the manager. He seemed to be in high spirits.

“Ah, Hastings! You are late. I have been busy, very busy.”

“What have you been doing?”

“I have been making a few more inquiries. And I think—yes, I think
I am beginning to see light.”

“Who is it?” I asked eagerly.

“Patience, my friend, patience! All will be revealed in good time.
In the meantime, I have a little commission for you.”

“What is it?”

“I want you to go to the police-station and ask for the inspector
who was here last night. Tell him I should be glad if he would
step over to the hotel for a few minutes.”

“Is that all?”

“That is all.”

I did as he requested, and in a short time the inspector arrived.
Poirot was waiting for him in the lounge.

“Ah, inspector! It is good of you to come. I have something to
show you.”

“Indeed?” The inspector looked interested.

“If you will follow me.”

He led the way upstairs to the room next to Mrs. Opalsen’s.

“Now, inspector,” said Poirot, “I want you to look at this table.”

He pointed to the rectangular mark I had noticed the night before.

“Well?” said the inspector. “What of it?”

“Do you not see?” said Poirot. “That mark was made by a jewel-case.
A jewel-case that has been standing there for some time.”

“Well, what if it has? This room has been occupied, I suppose.”

“It has not been occupied for several days,” said Poirot. “The
manager tells me so.”

“Then who put the jewel-case there?”

“That is what I am going to show you.”

He went to the door communicating with Mrs. Opalsen’s room and
drew back the bolt. Then he went to the other side and tried the
door. It was still bolted.

“You see?” said Poirot. “The door is bolted on both sides. And yet,
it is possible to open it.”

“How?”

Poirot took a small instrument from his pocket and inserted it
into the keyhole. There was a faint click, and the door swung open.

“Aha!” said the inspector. “A pick-lock!”

“Exactly,” said Poirot. “A very simple device. And now, if you
will come with me.”

He led the way into Mrs. Opalsen’s room. It was empty. Poirot went
straight to the dressing-table and opened the drawer. He took out
the jewel-case and opened it.

“Look!” he said.

The case was empty.

“But the pearls!” cried the inspector. “I thought you said they
were false!”

“They were,” said Poirot. “But they have been stolen again.”

“Stolen again? But who could have stolen them?”

“The person who stole the real ones,” said Poirot.

“And who is that?”

“I will show you.”

He led the way out of the room and down the corridor to Mr.
Opalsen’s room. He knocked on the door.

“Come in!”

We entered. Mr. Opalsen was sitting at a table, writing. He looked
up as we entered.

“Ah, Mr. Poirot! Found out anything more?”

“Yes, monsieur,” said Poirot. “I have found out who stole the
pearls.”

“Indeed? And who was it?”

“It was you, monsieur,” said Poirot.

Opalsen sprang to his feet, his face livid.

“What? You dare to accuse me?”

“I do,” said Poirot. “And I will tell you how you did it.”

“This is an outrage!” cried Opalsen. “Inspector, I hope you will
take note of this!”

The inspector looked from one to the other, bewildered.

“I think you’d better explain, Mr. Poirot,” he said.

“With pleasure,” said Poirot. “It was a very clever plot,
monsieur. You were in need of money—you told us so yourself. You
stole your wife’s pearls some time ago and substituted false ones.
But you knew that sooner or later she would find out. So you
devised this little plan. You arranged for a page-boy to call you
away from the table—that was easily done by giving him a few
shillings. Then you went upstairs, entered the room next to your
wife’s—which you knew was empty—and opened the communicating door
with a pick-lock. You then took the false pearls from the jewel-case,
and hid them in the maid’s bed, knowing that she would be the first
person suspected. Then you went back to the lounge and waited for
the discovery of the robbery.”

“It’s a lie!” cried Opalsen. “A tissue of lies!”

“Is it?” said Poirot. “Then perhaps you will explain how this
came to be in your waste-paper-basket?”

He held out the piece of paper he had found the night before.

“What is it?” asked the inspector.

“It is a note from the management,” said Poirot, “accompanying a
duplicate key for which Mr. Opalsen had asked. He told them he had
lost his own. With that key he could open his wife’s jewel-case
at any time.”

Opalsen collapsed into a chair, his face ghastly.

“It’s no use,” he muttered. “You’ve got me.”

“And the real pearls?” asked the inspector.

“I’ve—I’ve disposed of them,” said Opalsen hoarsely.

“I think not,” said Poirot. “I think you will find them,
inspector, in the lining of monsieur’s dressing-gown.”

The inspector went to the wardrobe and took out a heavy silk
dressing-gown. He felt along the hem, and then with a cry of
triumph he ripped it open. A string of magnificent pearls fell out.

“Well, Mr. Poirot,” said the inspector, “I must hand it to you.
You’ve been too many for us this time.”

“It was the little grey cells, my friend,” said Poirot, beaming.
“The little grey cells!”

As we walked back to our rooms, I said:

“Poirot, how did you know?”

“My friend, it was the card. The glazed card I showed to the maid
and the valet. It was not a visiting card at all—it was a card
used by jewellers for testing pearls. I found it in Mr. Opalsen’s
room. He had been testing the false pearls to see if they would
pass muster. And then there was the note from the management—that
was the finishing touch. A very clever man, Mr. Opalsen—but he forgot
that Hercule Poirot sees everything!”

“And the chambermaid and Célestine?”

“They were but pawns in the game, Hastings. Pawns in the game!”

“Well,” I said, “it’s been a most interesting weekend.”

“Yes,” said Poirot, “and we have still another day. What do you
say to a little walk on the front, Hastings? The air of Brighton,
it is most invigorating!”

A man in a white jacket came along the passage and entered the
room. He was a small, sallow-faced fellow, with a somewhat
furtive expression.

“You rang, sir?”

“I did,” said Poirot. “I wished to see if you have ever seen this
card.”

He held out the white card once more.

The man took it and looked at it.

“No, sir, I can’t say I have. I have only been here a week.”

“Indeed?” Poirot looked at him with interest. “And you like the
work?”

The man shrughed his shoulders.

“It’s much like any other work, sir. I’m only a temporary—filling
the place of a man who’s ill.”

“I see. Well, that will be all, thank you.”

The man went out. Poirot returned to his search of the
waste-paper-basket. He came upon a torn envelope, and examined it
eagerly. Then he gave a little exclamation of satisfaction.

“I have it, Hastings! Look!”

He held out a torn fragment of paper. On it was written:
‘_...er 24th_.’

“What does it mean?” I asked.

Poirot’s eyes twinkled.

“It means, my friend, that I am right. We will now go and see
Mr. Opalsen.”

In a few moments the valet answered the bell. To him Poirot put
the same question, and handed him the card to examine. But the
response was the same. The valet had never seen a card of that
particular quality among Mr. Opalsen’s belongings. Poirot thanked
him, and he withdrew, somewhat unwillingly, with an inquisitive
glance at the overturned waste-paper-basket and the litter on the
floor. He could hardly have helped overhearing Poirot’s thoughtful
remark as he bundled the torn papers back again:

“And the necklace was heavily insured. . . .”

“Poirot,” I cried,  “I see——”

“You see nothing, my friend,” he replied quickly. “As usual,
nothing at all! It is incredible—but there it is. Let us return to
our own apartments.”

We did so in silence. Once there, to my intense surprise, Poirot
effected a rapid change of clothing.

“I go to London to-night,” he explained. “It is imperative.”

“What?”

“Absolutely. The real work, that of the brain (ah, those brave
little grey cells), it is done. I go to seek the confirmation. I
shall find it! Impossible to deceive Hercule Poirot!”

“You’ll come a cropper one of these days,” I observed, rather
disgusted by his vanity.

“Do not be enraged, I beg of you, _mon ami_. I count on you to do
me a service—of your friendship.”

“Of course,” I said eagerly, rather ashamed of my moroseness. “What
is it?”

“The sleeve of my coat that I have taken off—will you brush it?
See you, a little white powder has clung to it. You without doubt
observed me run my finger round the drawer of the dressing-table?”

“No, I didn’t.”

“Ah! Then you missed the clue. But no matter. You will brush the
coat for me, will you not?”

“I will, with pleasure.”

“_Mille remerciements_, my friend. And now, I must fly for the
train. But I shall return—if all goes well—to-morrow morning. You
will stay here, will you not? I might want you.”

“Of course.”

I saw Poirot off. Then I returned to the hotel and prepared for
rest.

About midnight I was awakened by a light tapping at my door. I sat
up in bed and called out:

“Come in!”

It was Mr. Opalsen. He looked pale and haggard.

“Has Poirot gone?” he asked.

“He has gone to London,” I replied. “To get the final proof, he
said.”

“Proof? Of what?”

The man’s voice was hoarse and agitated. I saw he was terribly
upset.

“Of the theft, I suppose. He’s convinced the pearls were false.”

Mr. Opalsen groaned.

“I know they were! I—it’s no use. I’ve come to make a clean breast
of it. You can tell him when he comes back. I’ve been speculating—losing
money. I was desperate. I took the pearls and put the imitation
ones in their place. I thought I’d be able to pay them back—but things
got worse. And now my wife has found out—and the police——”

He broke off, his head in his hands. I felt a wave of pity for the
man, and I tried to comfort him as best I could.

“Don’t take it so much to heart,” I said. “After all, you’ve told
the truth now. That’s the great thing.”

“The truth!” he groaned. “And the disgrace of it—if it comes out!
I’ve been a fool—a miserable fool!”

He left me, and I lay awake for some time, thinking over this
startling development. So Poirot had been right, after all! His
keen eyes had seen through the deception from the first.

I must have fallen asleep at last, for I was awakened by Poirot’s
return early the next morning. He looked tired but triumphant.

“_Eh bien_, Hastings! All is well. I have the proof. And the
robbery? Has there been a sensation?”

“A sensation indeed!” I replied. “Mr. Opalsen came to me last
night and confessed everything.”

Poirot’s face fell.

“Confessed? What did he confess?”

“That he took the pearls himself, and put the imitation ones in
their place. He’s been speculating and losing money, and he was
desperate.”

Poirot stared at me for a moment in silence. Then he burst into a
fit of laughter.

“Oh, the brave Mr. Opalsen! The clever Mr. Opalsen! He has
deceived even my friend Hastings!”

“What do you mean?” I asked, bewildered.

“I mean, my friend, that Mr. Opalsen did not take the pearls. He
is no more a thief than I am.”

“Then why did he confess?”

“Because he is a very clever man, and he saw that the game was up.
He knew that I was on the track of the real thief, and he thought
to save himself—and his wife’s reputation—by a false confession.”

“Then who _did_ take them?”

“Ah, that is what I went to London to find out. And I have found out!
The pearls were stolen—not by Mr. Opalsen, nor by the maid Célestine,
nor by the chambermaid——”

“Then who?” I cried.

“By a very different person altogether. But come, let us go to the
Opalsens’ room. The inspector will be there by now, and I have
something to say to him.”

“It was most interesting. And the same on the mark on the table
next door. My finger became quite white. And the quality of the
powder—ah, it was _superbe_!”

He laughed with a gleeful chuckle as he went out of the door, and
left me to the uninteresting task of brushing his coat. I could
see no sense in the proceeding.

But it was only the following day that I understood.

A telegram from London reached me about lunch-time. It ran:

“Arrive five o’clock. Case concluded. Meet me at station.
                                               POIROT.”

I was there, waiting for him. I saw him descending from the
Pullman car. He looked radiant. He waved a triumphant hand to me.

“All is well?” I cried.

“The pearls have been recovered?”

“The pearls _are_ recovered, _mon ami_!”

He patted his pocket. “In here—wrapped in cotton-wool.”

“Who had them?”

“Mr. Opalsen.”

“Opalsen!” I cried. “But he’s a millionaire!”

“A very common mistake, Hastings. It was the Mrs. Opalsen who was
wealthy, not the husband. He had used her money for his
speculations. Things were going badly with him—as he told us himself.
He had to have money, and he hit upon the plan of a sham robbery,
and an insurance claim.”

“Then it was he who hid the false pearls in the maid’s bed?”

“Precisely.”

“But the real ones?”

“They were in his pocket all the time. He had a duplicate key to
the jewel-case, and took them before dinner. He relied on being
able to substitute the false ones and to throw the blame on the
maid or the chambermaid.”

“But how did you find out?”

“_Eh bien_, the finger-mark on the table in the empty room! It
corresponded exactly with the rectangular mark of the jewel-case.
And the white powder—the French face-powder that I found in the
drawer—was the same as that on the table in the empty room. It
was clear that the jewel-case had been in both places.”

“But why in the empty room?”

“Because Mr. Opalsen took it there to remove the real pearls and
put in the false ones. He didn’t want his wife to see him doing
it. He must have gone in there by the door from the corridor,
which he probably found unlocked.”

“And the card?”

“Ah, the card! That was my little joke, Hastings. It was just a
piece of highly glazed paper I happened to have in my pocket. I
showed it to the maid and the valet just to make them think I was
searching for some clue I had already found. It is always well to
keep people’s interest alive, is it not so?”

“It was Opalsen, then?” I said, still a little bewildered.

“Yes, my friend. He is now in the hands of the police.”

“And the maid?”

“She has been released, of course. She is very grateful to me.”

“And the pearls?”

“They will be returned to Mrs. Opalsen—minus a small fee for
Hercule Poirot!”

He smiled his most engaging smile.

“After all,” he added, “one must live, _mon ami_. And the little
grey cells, they have worked well, have they not?”

I was forced to admit that they had.

“And now,” said Poirot, “let us go to the _Grand Metropolitan_.
I have a great desire for a good dinner!”

And as we walked away from the station I couldn’t help thinking
that, after all, there was nobody quite like Hercule Poirot.

“A pity, Hastings. Well, the sleeve of my coat is covered with the
dust of the _Grand Metropolitan_. It is possible that in the City
there is a different kind of dust—it may be so.”

He was quite serious, and I did as he requested, taking my task
most seriously also.

He came back the following evening, and brought with him a
remarkable-looking individual with a large black beard and an
enormous nose.

“Allow me,” said Poirot, “to present to you my friend, Monsieur
Papopolous, the world’s greatest expert on precious stones.”

The Greek bowed with a magnificent gesture.

“Monsieur Poirot has asked me to examine a certain necklace of
pearls—a most remarkable specimen, monsieur, of the finest water.”

He took it from a case he was carrying and handed it to Poirot.

“What?” I cried. “Is that the necklace? But the inspector had it
last night!”

Poirot smiled.

“Ah, the inspector—he has a counterfeit, _mon ami_. This is the
original. I found it in—but why should I tell you where? I am
not yet quite sure that the story is ended.”

He turned to the Greek.

“And you think, monsieur, that these are the true pearls?”

“I have no doubt of it. They are worth a king’s ransom. See, the
lustre—the colour—the weight!”

“It was as I thought,” said Poirot. “I thank you, monsieur. You
have been of great service to me.”

The Greek took his leave. Poirot sat silent for a few moments,
then he said, with an air of satisfaction:

“So far so good. Now for the next step.”

“But how did you find them?” I asked, amazed.

“Through the little grey cells, my friend. I used my brains. It
is a most excellent habit, believe me!”

“But I don’t understand——”

“It is not necessary that you should. Wait, and all shall be
revealed to you!”

He would say no more.

The following morning we were sent for to the Opalsens’ room.
There we found the inspector, looking very crestfallen, and the
Opalsens in a state of great agitation.

“The necklace is a fake!” cried Mr. Opalsen, the moment we entered.
“The inspector has just told us so. He’s had it examined by an
expert.”

“It’s a most extraordinary thing,” said the inspector, looking
very unhappy. “I can’t understand it at all. The maid must have
changed it before she hid it.”

“I think not,” said Poirot quietly.

“What do you mean?”

“I mean that the maid never had the necklace at all.”

“Then who stole it?”

“A very clever thief, monsieur—a thief who knew all about Mrs.
Opalsen’s pearls, and who also knew that she was in the habit of
keeping them in that particular drawer.”

“But how could anyone have got into the room?” asked the inspector.
“The door was locked, and the maid was there all the time.”

“Was she?” said Poirot significantly.

“She says she was, except for a few seconds.”

“And it was in those few seconds that the theft was committed.”

“But it’s impossible! No one could have entered the room and
opened the drawer and the jewel-case in that time.”

“No one from the outside, perhaps,” said Poirot. “But what if the
thief was already in the room?”

“In the room?”

“Yes. Hidden, perhaps, in the maid’s room.”

“But the maid would have seen him.”

“Not if she was—asleep.”

“Asleep? But she says she wasn’t.”

“She thinks she wasn’t. But what if she had been drugged?”

“Drugged?”

“Yes. A little white powder—perhaps in her coffee. I found traces
of it on the table in the next room.”

“But who could have drugged her?”

“Someone who had access to her room—someone who knew her habits.
And someone who knew that Mrs. Opalsen would be coming up to fetch
her pearls at that particular moment.”

“You mean——” The inspector stared at him.

“I mean,” said Poirot, “that the person who stole the pearls was
none other than——”

He paused, his eyes fixed on Mr. Opalsen.

“Mr. Opalsen himself!”

A dead silence followed this announcement. Then Mr. Opalsen broke
into a loud laugh.

“Well, of all the absurd ideas! I steal my wife’s pearls? Why should
I do such a thing?”

“To get the insurance money, monsieur,” said Poirot calmly. “You
yourself told us that money was ‘confoundedly tight in the City.’
And the pearls were heavily insured.”

“It’s a lie!” cried Opalsen, his face purple with rage. “A
dastardly lie!”

“Is it?” said Poirot. “Then perhaps you will explain how this
came into your possession?”

He held out the white card he had shown the chambermaid.

“What is it?” asked the inspector.

“A card used by a well-known firm of diamond merchants in
Amsterdam. Mr. Opalsen visited them lately—doubtless to arrange for
the manufacture of the counterfeit necklace which was found in the
maid’s bed.”

“It’s a plant!” shouted Opalsen. “A wicked plant! I’ve never seen
the card before.”

“We shall see,” said Poirot. “In the meantime, I have much
pleasure in restoring the real pearls to Mrs. Opalsen.”

He handed the necklace to the astonished lady.

“But where did you find them?” she gasped.

“In the one place where no one would think of looking for them,”
said Poirot with a smile. “In Mr. Opalsen’s own pyjama pocket!”

The inspector stepped forward.

“I’m afraid I’ll have to ask you to come with me, sir,” he said
to Opalsen.

The latter made a desperate effort to compose himself.

“It’s a mistake—a ghastly mistake! You’ll regret this, all of you!”

But the inspector was firm, and Mr. Opalsen was led away, still
protesting his innocence.

Mrs. Opalsen was dissolved in tears.

“To think of it!” she sobbed. “My own husband! I shall never get
over it—never!”

Poirot patted her hand.

“_Courage, madame_,” he said. “At least you have your pearls.”

“Yes,” she sighed, “I have my pearls.”

When we were alone, I turned to Poirot.

“Poirot,” I said, “you’re a genius! How did you ever suspect
Opalsen?”

“My friend,” he said, “it was the insurance. It is always the
insurance! And then the card—the little card from Amsterdam. It
was the link that was missing.”

“But how did you know the pearls in the maid’s bed were false?”

“Because, Hastings, the thief who is clever enough to steal real
pearls does not hide them where they are sure to be found. He
hides the false ones there, to divert suspicion. It is a very old
trick, but it still works—sometimes.”

“And the drugging of the maid?”

“Ah, that was a little touch of my own! I saw the dust on the table
in the next room—the white powder—and I guessed. It is always
the little things, Hastings, the little things that count!”

I looked at him with admiration. Truly, there is no one like
Hercule Poirot!
