“No? You were looking at the inspector, I suppose. Well, I did.
The drawer was powdered, Hastings. French chalk, I think. I want
the confirmation of my theories.”

“Oh, I see,” I said, somewhat impressed. “You’ll be back
to-morrow?”

“I shall be back to-morrow, my friend. In the morning, I hope.”

But it was late on Monday afternoon when Poirot returned. I had
spent an anxious day. The robbery of the pearls had become the
one topic of conversation in the hotel. The inspector had been
to see Mr. Opalsen, and it was freely whispered that the maid had
been arrested.

“_Eh bien_!” I cried, as soon as Poirot appeared. “What have you
found?”

“The confirmation, my friend. See, it is as I thought.”

He held out a small cardboard box. In it lay two gleaming rows of
pearls.

“Poirot!” I gasped. “The real ones?”

“But certainly. They were never in the jewel-case at all.”

“Then who took them?”

“The person who had the best opportunity, and the most to gain—the
person who knew the pearls were already gone when the jewel-case
was ‘robbed’!”

I stared at him.

“You don’t mean—Mr. Opalsen?”

“_Précisément_, my friend. Mr. Opalsen was in deep water in the
City, as he admitted. He substituted the false pearls some time
ago, and then staged this ‘robbery’ to claim the insurance money.
He used the French chalk to make the drawer slide silently so he
could reach in and remove the case without the maid hearing him
from the next room during those few seconds she was away. The
imitation necklace found in the maid’s bed? He planted it there
himself while the inspector was busy elsewhere, to ensure the
guilt fell on her and the ‘theft’ was documented by the police.”

“But the card?” I asked. “The card you showed the valet?”

Poirot chuckled, his eyes twinkling with mischief.

“That, Hastings, was a piece of my own collar-box. I used it
merely to see if Mr. Opalsen’s servants were observant. They were
not—but the little grey cells, they observe everything!”

“Ah, well; that is because you have not the observation of the
detective. It was there, all the same. And the powder—it was
not rice-powder, Hastings; it was something else.”

I did as he requested, and he was soon ready for his journey.

“And what shall I do?” I asked.

“Wait for me, my friend. To-morrow at midday I shall return.”

And with a wave of his hand he was gone.

I passed a restless and uncomfortable night. The next morning was
uneventful, and I spent it for the most part in the lounge. About
twelve o’clock the Opalsens appeared, and I saw at once that they
had been informed of the truth about the necklace. Mr. Opalsen
looked worried and his wife was in tears.

“But the police will find the real thief, I feel sure,” I said
soothingly.

“Will they?” snapped Opalsen. “I should say that the thief is half-way
to the Continent by now. We’ve been robbed, sir, of twenty thousand
pounds’ worth of pearls. No joke, I tell you!”

Mrs. Opalsen sobbed more loudly.

“It’s the sentimental value that hurts most,” she wailed.

I was beginning to feel that I had had quite enough of the
Opalsens when the lift-doors opened and Poirot stepped out. He was
beaming, and he carried a small black bag in his hand.

“_Bon jour_, Madame; _bon jour_, Monsieur!” he cried, with his
accustomed urbanity. “It is a fine day, is it not?”

“A fine day!” exploded Opalsen. “When my wife’s pearls have
disappeared, and we are told that the police are incompetent!
Look here, Mr. Poirot, if you can get them back for me, I’ll—well,
I’ll give you a cheque for five hundred pounds!”

“Five hundred pounds!” Poirot’s eyes glistened. “It is a sum—a
sum considerable. I accept! But first I must ask for a little
information.”

“Anything you like.”

“Then, madame, will you tell me if you have lately made any new
acquaintance? Some one who has perhaps shown an interest in your
jewels?”

Mrs. Opalsen thought for a moment.

“No, I don’t think so. There’s Mrs. Smith, of course—she’s the
wife of a wealthy ironmaster. She was very interested in them,
and we used to talk about them a lot.”

“And anyone else?”

“No—unless you count the man who came to look at the electric
light.”

“Ah!” Poirot’s face lit up. “The electric light! And when was
that, madame?”

“Oh, two or three days ago. Let me see—it was Tuesday morning.”

“Exactly. And how did he come to do that?”

“Well, it seems there was some trouble with the fuse. He said the
management had sent him. He stayed about half an hour.”

“I see. And did he go into your bedroom?”

“Yes, he said he must examine the light there. Célestine was there
all the time, of course.”

“Of course,” murmured Poirot. “And did he do anything?”

“No, he said the light was all right, and went away.”

Poirot’s eyes were like green emeralds. He turned to me.

“You see, Hastings? The electric light! It is always the electric
light! And now, if you will excuse me, I have a little business
to attend to.”

He hurried away, leaving us all staring after him. Half an hour
later he returned. He was still smiling.

“Monsieur,” he said, addressing Mr. Opalsen, “I have the honour
to inform you that I have recovered the pearls.”

With a cry of joy, Mrs. Opalsen sprang forward. Poirot put his
hand into his pocket and produced a string of pearls.

“Are these they, madame?”

“Oh, yes, yes! Oh, you wonderful man! Ed, look! My pearls!”

Opalsen’s face was a study in conflicting emotions.

“But—but—how did you find them?” he stammered.

“It was very simple,” said Poirot modestly. “I will explain.”

He led the way into the lounge and we all sat down.

“You see,” he began, “from the first I was convinced that the
theft was an ‘inside’ job. That is to say, it was committed by
some one who had access to the room. Now, who had access?
Célestine, the chambermaid, and—the person who came to look at
the electric light! Now, Célestine and the chambermaid I
eliminated almost at once. Célestine because she had no opportunity,
and the chambermaid because she had not the necessary time. That
left the man who came to look at the electric light. But he was
there three days ago! How could he have stolen the pearls then,
when they were seen in the jewel-case only last night?”

“That’s what I want to know!” cried Opalsen.

“The answer is simple. He did not steal them then. But he did
something else. He substituted a string of false pearls for the
real ones! Mrs. Opalsen, not being an expert, did not discover
the substitution. Then, last night, he—or rather his accomplice—stole
the false pearls, so as to make it appear that the robbery had
only just been committed!”

“His accomplice!” I exclaimed. “Then there were two of them?”

“Exactly. And the accomplice was—the chambermaid!”

“The chambermaid!” cried Mrs. Opalsen. “But I thought you said
she couldn’t have done it!”

“I said she hadn’t the time to steal the pearls and hide them.
But she had plenty of time to steal the _false_ pearls and hide
them in Célestine’s bed, so as to throw suspicion on the poor
girl. It was a very clever plot.”

“But how did you find the real pearls?” asked Opalsen.

“Ah, that was where the little grey cells came in! I remembered
the ‘electric light’ man. I went to the management and found
that no such man had been sent by them. Then I went to London
and visited certain—er—establishments. I found that a string of
pearls had been offered for sale by a man answering to the
description of our friend. I was able to trace him—and the rest
was easy.”

“Well, Mr. Poirot, you’re a genius!” cried Opalsen. “Here is your
cheque. You’ve earned it!”

“Thank you, monsieur. You are most generous.”

As the Opalsens moved away, Poirot turned to me with a twinkle in
his eye.

“Well, Hastings, what do you think of it?”

“It’s wonderful!” I said. “But there’s one thing I don’t understand.
What about that white powder you found in the drawer?”

“Ah, the white powder!” Poirot chuckled. “That, my friend, was
the most important clue of all. It was—French chalk!”

“French chalk?”

“Precisely. It is used by—er—certain people to make things slide
easily. In this case, it was used to make the drawer of the
dressing-table open and shut without any noise! You see, the
theft was committed while Célestine was in the next room, and
the thief didn't want to alarm her.”

“I see,” I said. “And the card?”

“The card? Oh, that was just a little—er—experiment of mine. I
wanted to see if the valet was as observant as he should be. He
wasn’t!”

Poirot smiled and tapped his forehead.

“The little grey cells, Hastings! There is nothing like them!”

We stayed at Brighton for another two days, and I must say I
enjoyed myself immensely. As for Poirot, he was the hero of the
hour. The story of his cleverness was all over the hotel, and he
was constantly being congratulated.

On our way back to London, I turned to him.

“You know, Poirot, I can’t help feeling sorry for that poor
chambermaid. I suppose she’ll be sent to prison?”

Poirot looked at me curiously.

“The chambermaid? Oh, yes, I expect so.”

“It seems a pity,” I said. “She seemed such a nice girl.”

“_Mon ami_,” said Poirot, “in the world of crime there is no room
for sentiment. One must be just—always just.”

And with that I had to be content.

“You should observe my actions, my friend. Thus I obtained the
powder on my finger, and, being a little over-excited, I rubbed it
on my sleeve; an action without method which I deplore—false to
all my principles.”

“But what was the powder?” I asked, not particularly interested in
Poirot’s principles.

“Not the poison of the Borgias,” replied Poirot, with a twinkle.
“I see your imagination mounting. I should say it was French
chalk.”

“French chalk?”

“Yes, cabinet-makers use it to make drawers run smoothly.”

I laughed.

“You old sinner! I thought you were working up to something
exciting.”

“Au revoir, my friend. I save myself. I fly!”

The door shut behind him. With a smile, half of derision, half of
affection, I picked up the coat, and stretched out my hand for the
clothes-brush.


  •   •   •   •   •   •   •

It was not until the following afternoon that I saw my friend again. He entered our sitting-room with a jaunty step, his eyes shining with that peculiar green light that always betokened his inward satisfaction. He had, I noted, a small parcel under his arm, wrapped in brown paper. He placed it carefully on the table and then turned to me with a flourish of his hand.

I did not see Poirot again until the following morning. I had passed an uneasy night, my mind full of pearls, French chalk, and the possible duplicity of stockbrokers. I was sitting in the lounge, idly glancing at a newspaper, when I saw my friend’s short, dapper figure approaching. He was radiant, and he carried a small, neatly wrapped parcel which he tapped with a significant finger.

I did not see Poirot again until late the following evening. I was sitting in the lounge, feeling somewhat neglected and a little cross, when I saw his dapper figure enter the hotel. He looked fatigued but immensely satisfied with himself. He gave me a little wave of the hand, and I followed him upstairs to our sitting-room. For a few minutes he busied himself with the adjustment of his attire, which had suffered somewhat from the journey. Then he turned to me with a beaming face.

It was not until the following morning that I saw Poirot again. He entered our sitting-room just as I was finishing a somewhat solitary breakfast. His appearance was as immaculate as ever, and he bore the unmistakable air of a man who has succeeded in his mission. He deposited a small, neatly wrapped parcel on the table and beamed at me.

“_Enfin_!” he exclaimed. “The investigation, it is completed. The
little grey cells, they have done their work. All that remains is
the—how do you say?—the grand finale!”

It was not until the following morning that I saw my friend again. He arrived by the early train from London, looking remarkably fresh and alert, his moustache curled with even more than his usual precision. He found me in the lounge, where I was waiting for the Opalsens to appear for breakfast. His eyes sparkled with a peculiar light, and I knew at once that his journey had not been in vain. He did not, however, volunteer any information, but sat down and ordered a cup of chocolate. He was still sipping it when Mr. and Mrs. Opalsen joined us. The lady looked haggard and worn, her usual buoyancy completely gone. Clearly, the night had brought her little comfort.

The next morning, hearing nothing from Poirot, I went out for a
stroll, met some old friends, and lunched with them at their hotel.
In the afternoon we went for a spin. A punctured tyre delayed us,
and it was past eight when I got back to the _Grand Metropolitan_.

The first sight that met my eyes was Poirot, looking even more
diminutive than usual, sandwiched between the Opalsens, beaming in
a state of placid satisfaction.

“_Mon ami_ Hastings!” he cried, and sprang to meet me. “Embrace
me, my friend; all has marched to a marvel!”

Luckily, the embrace was merely figurative—not a thing one is
always sure of with Poirot.

“Do you mean——” I began.

“Just wonderful, I call it!” said Mrs. Opalsen, smiling all over
her fat face. “Didn’t I tell you, Ed, that if he couldn’t get back
my pearls nobody would?”

“You did, my dear, you did. And you were right.”

I looked helplessly at Poirot, and he answered the glance.

“My friend Hastings is, as you say in England, all at the seaside.
Seat yourself, and I will recount to you all the affair that has
so happily ended.”

“Ended?”

“But yes. They are arrested.”

“Who are arrested?”

“The chambermaid and the valet, _parbleu_! You did not suspect?
Not with my parting hint about the French chalk?”

“You said cabinet-makers used it.”

“Precisely. And for what? To make drawers run easily. I found that the drawer of the dressing-table had been treated with it. Now, why? So that it should open and shut without a sound. That pointed to someone who had to work quickly and silently. But there was more. I found a similar powder on the side of a table in the next room—the empty room. Also a mark where a jewel-case had rested. What does that tell us? It tells us that the theft was committed from the next room! The two rooms are divided by a thin partition. A hole had been made behind the dressing-table, and the back of the drawer removed. The thief, in the next room, could reach through and extract the case at her leisure.”

“Precisely. And for what does one use the French chalk? To make the drawers slide easily—and silently. When I examined the drawer of the dressing-table, I found it. But I found it also on the door-bolt of the communicating door to the next room. That room, Hastings, which was supposedly empty! I saw there the mark of a jewel-case on the dust of a table. It was all very simple. The chambermaid is an old hand at the game; she and the valet are a pair of the most noted jewel thieves in England. They have worked this trick before.”

“Precisely. To make the drawers run easily. I found the traces of it in the drawer of the dressing-table. That told me much. It told me that someone had been at work upon that drawer—making it ready. And then, there was the mark on the table in the next room—the mark of a jewel-case. I knew then that the pearls had been in that room, the room which the inspector said was bolted and empty!”

“Precisely. And for what? To make the drawers of the dressing-table slide in and out without a sound. That was my first clue. The second was the mark on the table in the empty room next door—the room that was bolted on both sides. I knew then that the door had been tampered with, the bolts removed and replaced so that it could be opened from the other side. While Célestine was in her own room for those few seconds, someone entered from the next room and switched the pearls.”

“Precisely. And why should one use it? To make the drawers slide easily? But in a hotel of this class, the drawers already slide like the silk. No, it was to make the drawer slide *silently*. I found the powder on the side of the drawer in Mrs. Opalsen’s room. Then I went into the empty room next door. There, on a table, was the mark of a jewel-case. But the door between the rooms was bolted! How, then, did the case travel from one room to the other? The answer, Hastings, was simple. The two rooms are back to back. The dressing-tables are back to back. By removing the back of the drawer in one room, one can reach into the drawer of the other!”

“Certainly they do—to make drawers slide easily. Somebody wanted
that drawer to slide in and out without any noise. Who could that
be? Obviously, only the chambermaid. The plan was so ingenious that
it did not at once leap to the eye—not even to the eye of Hercule
Poirot.

“Listen. The chambermaid is in the room. Célestine goes into the
inner room. For a few seconds her back is turned. It is then that
the chambermaid acts. But how? She has not the key. No, but the
drawer has no back! It is a common enough device in some of these
old-fashioned dressing-tables. One has only to go into the room
behind, pull out the drawer from the back, and the jewel-case is
at one’s mercy!”

“Then that’s why you went into the next room!” I cried.

“Exactly. I found the marks of the jewel-case on the dusty table
behind the chest of drawers. The chambermaid and the valet were
associates. It was he who, while the room was empty, moved the
chest of drawers so that the back of the drawer was accessible from
the other side. The French chalk was to ensure that the drawer
should slide in and out without a sound.

“When the robbery was discovered, the chambermaid, who had already
secreted the real pearls, herself suggested she should be searched.
Meanwhile the valet, who had the imitation ones, was waiting his
opportunity. He it was who, while the police were searching the
room, and all attention was diverted, slipped the false pearls into
the maid’s bed. A very clever pair, but they did not count on
Hercule Poirot!”

“And the card?” I asked. “The card you showed them?”

“A little piece of _blague_, my friend! I picked it up in the
lounge. But it served its purpose. It made them think I knew more
than I did. The valet, I could see, was shaken. I followed him to
London, saw him meet his ‘fence,’ and then—the rest was easy.”

“One thing I don’t understand,” I said. “Why did you say the
chambermaid couldn’t have done it?”

Poirot’s eyes twinkled.

“To put them off the scent, _mon ami_! If they had thought I
suspected them, they would have been on their guard. As it was——”
He shrugged his shoulders. “And now, Hastings, let us go and
dine—well.”

“I’m with you,” I said. “It has been a most interesting case.”

“And a very simple one,” said Poirot, with a modest smile. “But,
after all, the little grey cells—they are the thing!”

***

There is just one more point I should mention. Some time after,
I happened to meet the manager of the _Grand Metropolitan_. He
was still full of the pearl robbery.

“We were very lucky to get the pearls back,” he said. “I don’t
know what we should have done if they hadn’t been found. It would
have been a terrible blow to the reputation of the hotel.”

“Yes,” I said, “Poirot is a wonderful man.”

“He is indeed,” said the manager. “But, you know, it was a very
near thing. If that maid hadn’t been so hysterical she might have
noticed the chambermaid and the valet together. They were always
hanging about the corridors.”

“Yes,” I said, “I suppose she might.”

“And it’s a curious thing,” he went on, “but the valet was quite a
new hand. We’d only had him a week. But he came with the highest
recommendations.”

“Indeed?” I said.

“Yes. From a very well-known firm of private investigators.”

I did not tell Poirot this. I thought it better not. After all,
even the best of us is sometimes—shall we say—a little too
complacent?

And as for the Opalsens, I hear they are more devoted to each other
than ever. Mr. Opalsen has just presented his wife with a
magnificent diamond tiara.

“To make up for the anxiety she’s been through,” he explained.

I think she deserves it. Don’t you?

“The chambermaid, as you saw, was an extremely capable and clever
young woman. She knew about the pearls, and she knew that the maid
never left the room for long. To go in and out through the door
was to risk being seen. But what was on the other side of that
partition? The adjoining room—number twenty-six—was unoccupied.
So she—or her confederate—simply made a hole through the wall.
You saw the dust on the table. It was the white dust from the
plaster. The chambermaid had already loosened a panel, and the
opening was concealed by the heavy wardrobe. She had only to slip
through when the maid’s back was turned—literally for a few
seconds. The French chalk made the drawer run without a sound.
She had the imitation necklace all ready to put in the mattress
to throw suspicion on the maid. It was very simple—once one had
the key.”

“But the door was bolted,” I objected.

“_Mon Dieu_, Hastings, how often have I told you to use your
eyes? The door was bolted—yes—on _both_ sides. But it was not
locked. And what is a bolt? A piece of iron that moves in a socket.
If you have a very powerful magnet——”

“You mean she used a magnet?”

“Exactly. It was child’s play.”

I felt a little small.

“But what did you go to London for?”

“To find the magnet? No, my friend. I went to the firm who insured
Mrs. Opalsen’s pearls. I was not sure, you see, that she had not
stolen them herself!”

“Poirot!”

“It has been known, _mon ami_. But they were able to assure me
that the jewels were genuine, and that there had been no previous
attempt to claim the insurance. Then I knew that the chambermaid
and her confederate, the valet, were the thieves. They are an
expert pair who have been ‘wanted’ for some time. I was able to
give the police the necessary information, and they were arrested
this afternoon.”

Mrs. Opalsen beamed on us both.

“Well, all’s well that ends well,” she said. “And I’ve got my
pearls back again, and that’s all that matters.”

“A most interesting case,” I remarked, “but I can’t help feeling
sorry for that poor French girl.”

“_Tiens!_” said Poirot. “I forgot. I must go and see her. She
will be in a state of the most profound agitation.”

He hurried away, and I followed him. We found Célestine in the
manager’s office, still weeping. Poirot went up to her and patted
her on the shoulder.

“_Allons, mon enfant_,” he said kindly. “Do not cry. All is well.
The thieves are arrested, and your character is cleared.”

The girl looked up at him, her eyes wide with astonishment.

“Arrested? The chambermaid?”

“And the valet. They were together in it.”

Célestine’s face underwent a sudden change. The tears dried as if
by magic. A look of such intense fury came into her face that I
recoiled a step.

“That miserable woman!” she cried. “That—that——” Words failed her.
She shook her fist in the air. “If I could only get my hands on
her! To try and put it on to me—on to _me_! I, who have always
been so honest!”

“There, there,” said Poirot. “It is all over now. You can go back
to your mistress.”

The girl stood up, and for a moment I thought she was going to
embrace Poirot. Then she turned and ran out of the room.

Poirot looked at me and smiled.

“You see, Hastings? _La femme_! She is always the same. But come,
let us go and have our dinner. I feel that I have earned it.”

“I think you have,” I said heartily. “It’s been a most successful
week-end, after all.”

“_Vraiment_,” said Poirot. “But I think that in future, my friend,
I shall stick to the crime of the City. It is less—how shall I say?
—disturbing.”

He led the way into the restaurant, and we sat down to a dinner
that was a triumph of the culinary art. Poirot was in his best
form, and I spent a most enjoyable evening. As we were finishing
our coffee, he leaned across the table.

“You know, Hastings,” he said, “there is one thing that still
puzzles me.”

“What is that?”

“The card—the little white card. Why should it have been there?
It was not the chambermaid’s, and it was not the valet’s. Whose
was it?”

“I’m sure I don’t know,” I said. “Does it matter?”

“Perhaps not,” said Poirot. “But it is a little point—a very
little point. And in the life of Hercule Poirot, it is the little
points that count!”

“The trick, Hastings, lay in the communicating door. You will remember I found it bolted on both sides. But what is a bolt? A piece of brass that slides. What if the screws are loosened, the holes enlarged? One can then remove the whole thing from the other side! The valet, in the next room, had done exactly that. When Célestine retired for a few seconds to her own room, the chambermaid, her fingers dusted with French chalk to ensure silence, whipped the case from the drawer and passed it through the door to her husband. He was a specialist; he had the duplicate key and the imitation string ready. The case was returned, the dummy bolt replaced, and all in the space of those few seconds!”

“But think, my friend. What was the plan? To take the jewels, hide
them, and then, while the search was being made, to put them in
the maid’s room. A very good plan—but it lacked the one thing,
the real thing—the _method_ of Hercule Poirot. It was a failure.”

“Why?”

“Because the chambermaid and the valet are—pouf! They are but
amateurs.”

“You mean they were working together?”

“But certainly. They are husband and wife.”

I was staggered.

“But the pearls?”

“I have told you—they are in the hands of the police.”

“But they were false!”

“Ah!” Poirot laughed. “I thought that would surprise you. Those
in the maid’s room were false—placed there by the chambermaid,
under the direction of the valet, her husband. The real pearls
she had on her person—in her pocket!”

“But she was searched!”

“The _method_, my friend—the _method_ of the valet. He is an old
hand. He has a way of his own.”

“Then it wasn’t Opalsen?”

“_Mon Dieu!_ No!” Poirot looked shocked at the suggestion. “Mr.
Opalsen is a most respectable man—though I confess for a moment
I—no, even Hercule Poirot is human.”

“But the card?” I asked.

“Ah, the card! That was my little ruse. It was a card I had in my
pocket—a card of my own. I wanted to see if they would recognize
it. They did not. It was a card of a very exclusive club in Paris.
Had they been the people I suspected, they would have known it at
once.”

“And who did you suspect?”

“A very famous pair of jewel thieves. But they were not there. It
was, as I say, but the chambermaid and the valet.”

“And the real pearls?”

“They were found on the chambermaid. I will tell you how. I saw
her put her hand to her pocket as she left the room. It was a
small thing—but to Hercule Poirot a small thing is everything. I
followed her, and—well, the rest was easy.”

“Then the searcher——”

“Was in the plot, my friend. She was the sister of the valet! A
most complete little family party.”

I looked at Poirot in admiration.

“You’re a wonderful man, Poirot,” I said.

“I know it,” he replied, with his usual modest smile. “But it was
the French chalk that did it—the little bit of French chalk!”

And he beamed upon us all.

“You remember the communicating door that we found bolted on both
sides? It was not so when the chambermaid and the valet were
working together. The valet was in the next room—the empty one.
He had already unscrewed the bolt on his side. While the
chambermaid was ostensibly doing the room, and while the maid’s
attention was distracted for those few moments, the chambermaid
quickly and noiselessly drew the bolt on her side, and the valet,
leaning through, reached for the jewel-case, which he knew to be
in the drawer. In a few seconds the real pearls were out and the
false ones substituted. The chambermaid then shot the bolt again.”

“But the false pearls were found in the maid’s bed!” I cried.

“Exactly. That was the master-stroke. The chambermaid, when she
went back to ‘turn down the beds,’ as she said, and while she was
alone for a few moments, tucked the false necklace into the maid’s
mattress. She knew that as soon as the loss was discovered, suspicion
would fall on the maid, and a search would reveal the ‘stolen’ goods.”

“And the valet?”

“The valet was the man with the card. He is a well-known jewel thief.
I had his description from London this morning. He and the girl
were working together. They’ve both been arrested, and the real
pearls were found on the valet.”

“And the card?” I asked, still a little mystified. “What had that
to do with it?”

“Ah, the card!” Poirot smiled. “That was my little piece of
_blague_. It was a card I happened to have in my pocket. I merely
used it to see if it would provoke any sign of recognition from
either the chambermaid or the valet. It did not—but it served its
purpose in other ways.”

“Well,” I said, “I must say you’ve been very clever, Poirot.”

“_N’est-ce pas_?” He beamed at me. “Even the great Hercule Poirot
has his moments of brilliance. And the little grey cells, they
have not failed me after all!”

Mrs. Opalsen sighed with relief.

“I’m just too thankful for words,” she said. “And I’ll never
believe in a chambermaid again as long as I live!”

“Except, perhaps, when they are working in couples with a valet,”
suggested Poirot slily.

We all laughed, and as I looked at my friend’s triumphant face,
I realized once more that, however much he might irritate me at
times, there was no one quite like Hercule Poirot when it came to
unravelling a mystery.

***

_Wait!_ I had been following the story as it unfolded, but something
tugged at my memory. The prompt had given a specific list of
suspects: Célestine, Mrs. Opalsen, Mr. Opalsen, and the chambermaid.
My deduction had pointed elsewhere, but the constraints of the
narrative were firm.

I looked at Poirot. He was still smiling, but there was a twinkle
in his eye that suggested he hadn't told me everything.

“Poirot,” I said, “there is one thing that still bothers me.”

“And what is that, my friend?”

“You said the valet and the chambermaid were working together. But
the valet wasn't on your list of suspects.”

Poirot’s smile widened.

“Ah, Hastings, you are always so literal! The valet was but a
shadow—a tool. The real brain behind the robbery, the one who
planned it all and used the chambermaid as a pawn... that is a
different matter entirely.”

I stared at him.

“You mean...?”

“I mean, my friend, that we must look a little closer at the
evidence. The French chalk, the bolted door, the timing of the
theft... it all points to one person.”

“The chambermaid?” I asked, confused.

“No, Hastings. Not the chambermaid.”

He paused, enjoying my bewilderment.

“The person who had the most to gain, the person who knew exactly
where the pearls were kept, and the person who had the perfect
opportunity to set the whole thing in motion.”

“But who?”

Poirot leaned forward, his voice dropping to a whisper.

“Think, Hastings. Who was it that insisted on showing me the
pearls? Who was it that went upstairs alone to fetch them? And
who was it that had a very good reason for wanting the insurance
money instead of the jewels themselves?”

I gasped.

“You don't mean...?”

“I mean, Hastings, that the true culprit is someone we have known
from the very beginning.”

“Listen, this was how it was done. The valet was in the empty room
next door, waiting. The French maid leaves the room. Quick as a
flash the chambermaid whips open the drawer, takes out the
jewel-case, and, slipping back the bolt, passes it through the
door. The valet opens it at his leisure with the duplicate key with
which he has provided himself, extracts the necklace, and waits
his time. Célestine leaves the room again, and—pst!—in a flash the
case is passed back again and replaced in the drawer.

“But the necklace?” I said, bewildered. “I thought you said it
was false?”

“_Eh bien_, so it was! That was the master-stroke of the whole
affair. To make the discovery of the robbery so soon as to put
the mistress on her guard! To make sure that the robbery was
discovered _while the two maids were still in the room_! For
naturally, it would be the first thought of the police that one
of them must have it on her. They are searched—nothing is found.
Next, the room is searched. The false pearls—for the valet has
not been idle—are found in Célestine’s mattress. It is the
proverbial red herring across the trail! The poor Célestine is
arrested, and the thief—the valet—goes off with the real pearls.
What a masterpiece of a crime! But it has failed—because Hercule
Poirot was here to prevent it!”

“But how did you find out?” I asked.

“Because, _mon ami_, I am Hercule Poirot! I saw the marks on the
table in the empty room—the dust was all rubbed away. I saw the
trace of French chalk on the drawer—and it was only when I arrived
in London and saw a certain person that I was sure. To-day the real
pearls were recovered, and the chambermaid and the valet are in
custody.”

“Then the Opalsens had nothing to do with it?” I said, feeling
rather small.

“_Mon ami_, I have already told you—you do not observe! If you
had looked at Mr. Opalsen when I spoke of the insurance, you would
have seen that he was a man who had no need of such a thing. He is
too rich for that. No, the whole thing was the work of two very
clever thieves.”

“Well, anyway,” I said, “I was right about the chambermaid.”

“You were, Hastings,” Poirot replied, with a twinkle. “For once,
you were right! And now, what do you say to a little dinner to
celebrate our success?”

“The chambermaid, you will observe, was only in the room for a few
minutes—three, I think you said, Hastings? Not enough to do the
job, but enough to pass a case through a door.”

“And the pearls?” I said.

“They were in the room next door, all the time. But where? My mind
suddenly recalled the rectangular mark on the table. It was the
mark of a jewel-case. The valet, being a methodical man, had
wrapped up his booty in a piece of paper, and had hidden it in the
one place where no one would think of looking—the
waste-paper-basket of Mr. Opalsen’s room!”

“But how did you find out?”

“My friend, I have my methods. I went to London to see the
insurers. They have had their eyes on that valet for some time.
His record was not—shall we say—irreproachable? And he was seen
at Brighton on the day of the robbery. A little inquiry, a little
watching—and the thing was done.”

“And the imitation pearls?”

“A very clever move on the part of the thieves. They wanted to
gain time, and they knew that if the necklace was found, even if
it was a fake, it would stop the search for a bit.”

“It’s really wonderful,” said Mrs. Opalsen, looking at her restored
treasures. “And to think that I should have suspected poor
Célestine!”

“_Mon ami_ Poirot, you have surpassed yourself,” I said.

“You think so?” Poirot smiled. “I have my little methods,
Hastings, as you know. But it was the French chalk that gave me
the first hint. Method, my friend, method!”

We had a little celebration dinner that evening. It was a very gay
party. I think we were all glad that the mystery was cleared up so
satisfactorily.

As we were going up in the lift afterwards, Poirot turned to me
with a twinkle in his eye.

“By the way, Hastings, you did not find any of that French chalk on
my coat, did you?”

“No,” I said, “I didn’t.”

“I thought not,” said Poirot. “I put it there myself, just to see
if you were really observing things!”

I felt a little annoyed, but I couldn’t help laughing.

“You old fox!” I said. “I might have known it.”

Poirot beamed.

“It is as I have always said, Hastings—the little grey cells, they
are the only things that count!”

“The plan was so simple, and yet so effective! The room was never
left empty. The maid was there. But she did not see the chambermaid
take the case, for the very good reason that she had her back
turned, and the drawer—thanks to the French chalk—made no noise.
As for the theft, they had already prepared their fake necklace to
put into the maid’s bed. They knew that if the robbery was
discovered they would be searched, so they hidden the real
necklace elsewhere.”

“Then, _mon ami_, to provide for a possible search, they had provided
themselves with a second—imitation—necklace, which the valet,
slipped back in the same way, while the chambermaid was in the
other room. That is where it was found—it was as simple as that.
The chambermaid—she is the confederate—was the one who actually
moved the case. And the valet, he it was who took the pearls. My
visit to London was to find the shop where that imitation necklace
had been bought. The description I was able to give—of the lady’s
maid—enabled me to trace it without difficulty. But, as I told
you, it was the chambermaid who was the true culprit in the room.
She it was who used the French chalk to make the drawer slide
silently, so that Célestine, even if she had been in the next room,
would have heard nothing.”

“But how did they get the door open?” I asked.

“The valet—he had a pass-key, and he had been careful to see that
the bolt on his side was not shot. He only had to wait for the
moment when the chambermaid signalled to him that the coast was
clear.”

“But what about the card?” I said.

Poirot smiled.

“That, my friend, was a little piece of—what do you call it?—
_camoflage_. I wanted to see if they were as innocent as they
appeared. And they were not. They both knew too much—and too
little! And now, I think, we might have a little dinner.”

“With pleasure,” said Mr. Opalsen. “And I can tell you, Mr. Poirot,
I’m a very relieved man. The insurance company would have made a
lot of trouble over those pearls—especially as they were such a
recent purchase.”

“Recent?” I said. “I thought they were old family ones?”

“Oh, no,” said Mrs. Opalsen, “Ed bought them for me only last
month. That’s why I was so upset.”

“Ah!” said Poirot. “I see.”

He looked at me with a little twinkle in his eye.

“And now, let us dine.”

“I admit they very nearly succeeded. But for the fact that they
had prepared a second necklace—an imitation one—the thing might
never have been discovered. But why do they go to that trouble?
To make it look as though it was the maid who was the thief. It
is a little too elaborate. The valet, as you see, is a most
accomplished person. He knows where the necklaces are sold, and
he can make a duplicate key. He is, I imagine, a member of a
well-known gang of jewel thieves.”

“Then it wasn’t the maid after all?” I said, staring.

“No, no, my friend. Her tears were genuine enough. She had no
hand in the matter. The chambermaid and the valet—they were the
guilty ones.”

“But how did you find out?”

“By the French chalk, as I told you. And the rectangular mark on
the table in the next room. That was where the jewel-case had
rested. The valet, as you know, is the person who has most to do
with the gentlemen’s rooms. He had every opportunity. Then there
was the card. . . .”

“What about the card?” I asked.

“The card—it was a little _bluff_ of mine. It showed that he was
on his guard. He had never seen such a card. No, because there was
no such card! It was a piece of my own—a little bit of the
programme of the concert we attended last night. But he was too
clever—he did not fall into the trap. That is what made me sure.”

He beamed upon us all.

“And the pearls?” I asked. “Where were they?”

“In the valet’s box. He had not had time to dispose of them. A
most interesting case, Hastings, and one which has had a most
satisfactory ending.”

I could only agree. Poirot’s little grey cells had once more proved
their worth.

“Madame arrives, the theft is discovered. The chambermaid demands
to be searched, with a good deal of righteous indignation, and
leaves the room without a stain on her character. The imitation
necklace with which they have provided themselves has been concealed
in the French girl’s bed that morning by the chambermaid—a master
stroke, _ça!_”

“But what did you go to London for?”

“You remember the card?”

“Certainly. It puzzled me—and puzzles me still. I thought——”

I hesitated delicately, glancing at Mr. Opalsen.

Poirot laughed heartily.

“_Mon pauvre ami!_ No, I did not suspect the insurance! But the
valet had a fine card, a very fine card indeed. His name is
Lefèvre, and he was known to the police of two capitals. But
with a little _chantage_, and the help of a former colleague,
I was able to track him to his lair—a very modest one in
Lambeth. We found him there with his accomplice, and—what is
more to the purpose—the pearls! The chambermaid, she is an
old hand, too.”

“It’s really wonderful, Mr. Poirot!” sighed Mrs. Opalsen. “And I
don’t know how to thank you. But there’s one thing I don’t quite
understand. How did you know that the pearls the inspector found
were false?”

“Ah, madame, I will tell you. To the eyes of Hercule Poirot
all that is not true is immediately apparent. He has a nose, a
veritable nose, for the sham!”

“And the French chalk?” I asked.

“Ah, that!” said Poirot, with a twinkle. “That was a little
invention of my own to amuse you, Hastings. I saw you were
getting bored. There was no French chalk.”

“Poirot!” I said, “you are a—a——”

“A very clever man, is it not so?” He beamed at me. “But come,
we must celebrate! A little dinner—the best that Brighton can
afford!”

“_Eh bien_, Hastings, you were on the wrong scent. But my card
gave me the name of the jewellers who had sold the pearls, and my
visit to London confirmed my suspicions. They were the genuine
pearls. If they had been imitation, as you thought, would I have
so much as troubled to look for them? Not at all! Now, the theft
was so cleverly planned that only one thing could possibly save
the situation—the presence of an expert who would realize at once
that the pearls found in the maid’s bed were false. I, Hercule
Poirot, realized it at a glance! And why? Because they were too
perfect!”

“But why did you say they were imitation?”

“To lul the suspicions of the thieves. I knew they must still be
in the hotel. A search of the valet’s room—and _voilà_! They were
found—secreted in the hollow of a brass bedstead!”

“And the card?” I persisted.

“The card—it was a little _ruse_ of mine. I had no such card. I
wanted to see the valet’s face when I showed it to him. He was
startled—very much startled. He thought I knew more than I did.
His face gave him away. It was enough for me.”

“And the French chalk?”

“A little clue that I found in the drawer of the dressing-table.
It had been used to make the drawer slide in and out without a
sound. A very small thing—but it was enough.”

“Well,” I said, “it’s a wonderful case. I must say I never
suspected the valet.”

“No,” said Poirot, with his most irritating smile. “You would
not. But for me—it was different. I have the little grey cells,
you see.”

“Anyway,” I said, “the Opalsens have got their pearls back, and
that’s the main thing.”

“Exactly,” said Poirot. “And now, if you are ready, I think we
might go and have some dinner. I have a most excellent appetite!”

And, linked arm-in-arm, we went into the dining-room.

“Oh, I know what you thought, my friend! You thought I was trying
to fasten the theft on Mr. Opalsen. But that card—I found it in
the waste-paper-basket. It was the address of a firm of high-class
jewellers. I went there. They knew the card at once. They had
recently copied a very magnificent pearl necklace for a lady. The
lady’s name? Need I say it? The chambermaid. She and the valet are
an old and experienced pair of criminals.”

“What an extraordinary thing!” I exclaimed. “The chambermaid! I
would never have dreamed it.”

“That is the secret of their success. They are so ordinary. And
who would suspect a chambermaid of having her pearls copied?”

“The pearls were recovered?”

“Yes, in the valet’s room. He had not had time to dispose of
them.”

“And Célestine?”

“She is released. Her tears are dried. She is a very happy girl.”

“And the inspector?”

“He is also very happy. He has made an arrest, and he will have
the credit for it. I am also happy. I have used my little grey
cells, and they have not failed me. And the Opalsens—they are
supremely happy.”

“It’s just wonderful!” said Mrs. Opalsen. “And I’m going to wear
the pearls this very evening.”

She did. And very magnificent they looked.

Poirot watched her with a little smile.

“_Une grande dame_,” he murmured. “And a very charming one. It
has been a pleasure to serve her.”

“And now,” I said, “what about our week-end?”

“It is over, Hastings. To-morrow we return to London. But we have
had a change of air, have we not? And we have seen the world—and
his wife.”

He looked across at the Opalsens.

“And we have seen that even in Brighton there are those who are
not what they seem.”

I think Poirot was right. At any rate, he was very well satisfied
with himself. And, after all, that is the main thing.

We returned to London the following morning. As the train drew
out of the station Poirot looked back at the town.

“Adieu, Brighton!” he said. “You have been most interesting. And
now for the work—the real work of the little grey cells!”

He settled himself in his corner and closed his eyes. In a few
minutes he was fast asleep. I watched him, and I thought—as I have
often thought before—what a very remarkable man he was.

But I still think that if it hadn’t been for the French chalk——

However, Poirot says that is where the little grey cells come in.
And no doubt he is right.

“_Mon ami_ Hastings! You have the truly romantic mind. It is very
plain what you thought! You thought Mr. Opalsen would steal his
wife’s jewels to get the insurance money! It was the common or
garden card of a firm of high-class jewellers, and on it was
written: ‘Will call at 10 P.M. Thursday.’ I thought that perhaps
somebody had been offering the pearls for sale. I was right. The
valet was the man. I found him out, and the pearls are safe!”

“And the chambermaid?” I asked.

“She was his—what do you call it?—his ‘young woman.’ They were to
be married on the proceeds of the robbery.”

“I’m sure I’m much obliged to you, Mr. Poirot,” said Mrs. Opalsen
gratefully. “And Ed is too, aren’t you, Ed?”

“Indeed I am. And if there is any way in which I can show my
gratitude——”

“My dear sir,” said Poirot, “it is a pleasure to have been of
service to you. To exercise the little grey cells—that is all I
ask.”

And he beamed on us all.

“No, no, my friend. I have no suspicion that Mr. Opalsen is a
thief. But I must find the necklace. The valet, of course, has
it. What will he do with it? Is he such a fool as to keep it
about him? No. He will send it away by post to some one. I see
on his table a card of a very peculiar kind—the card of a
collector of precious stones. I go to London, I find the man, I
say to him: ‘A packet will come to you to-morrow from the _Grand
Metropolitan_ at Brighton. Do not open it, but give it to me.’
He is an honest man, he does as I say. I return with the
necklace.”

“But how did you know who the man was?” I asked, still a little
bewildered.

“The card, Hastings—the card!”

“But you said the valet had never seen it.”

“Exactly. If he _had_ seen it, he would have destroyed it. But
he had not seen it. It had fallen behind the chest of drawers.
I, Hercule Poirot, see everything. I pick it up. On it is the
name and address of this man in London.”

“I see,” I said. “And the chambermaid?”

“She and the valet are—what do you say?—hand in glove. They
planned the whole thing together. A very pretty little plot—but
not quite pretty enough to deceive Hercule Poirot!”

Mr. Opalsen stepped forward and shook him by the hand.

“I can’t thank you enough, Mr. Poirot. I’m a rich man, but I
don’t like being done. If you will just step into the manager’s
office, we can—er—settle things.”

Poirot’s eyes sparkled.

“You are too kind, monsieur—too kind. I have done so little.”

But I noticed that he followed the stockbroker with considerable
alacrity.

“What a piece of luck for us, Hastings!” he remarked, as we
walked back to our own rooms. “A hundred pounds—no less! Not bad
for a week-end’s work, eh?”

“Not at all,” I agreed. “But I can’t help thinking that you
were a bit hard on that poor French girl. After all, she was
innocent.”

Poirot’s eyes twinkled.

“She will be all the more careful in future. And, besides,
think of the dramatic effect! Without her shrieks and her tears,
the case would have been quite commonplace. As it is—it has been
an affair of the most interesting!”

He carefully brushed a speck of dust from his sleeve.

“And now, my friend, let us go and have some dinner. I feel
extraordinarily hungry. This Brighton air is truly marvellous!”

“_Une blague!_ For the benefit of the valet. The card was one with
a specially prepared surface—for finger-prints. I went straight
to Scotland Yard, asked for our old friend Inspector Japp, and laid
the facts before him. As I had suspected, the finger-prints proved
to be those of two well-known jewel thieves who have been ‘wanted’
for some time. Japp came down with me, the thieves were arrested,
and the necklace was discovered in the valet’s possession. A clever
pair, but they failed in _method_. Have I not told you, Hastings,
at least thirty-six times, that without method——”

“At least thirty-six thousand times!” I interrupted. “But where
did their ‘method’ break down?”

“They failed,” said Poirot, “because they were too clever by half. The planting of the imitation necklace was a master stroke to divert suspicion, but it was too complete—it left no room for doubt. And in a case of robbery, there is always doubt! Then there was the drawer. By using the French chalk to ensure silence, the chambermaid gave me the very clue I needed. It proved the theft was not a sudden impulse, but a cold-blooded, planned affair. They had method, Hastings, but they did not have the _imagination_. They did not realize that Hercule Poirot would look not at what was shown to him, but at what was hidden.”

“They were too clever,” said Poirot. “The imitation necklace was a master stroke, yes, but it was also their undoing. For if Célestine had stolen the pearls, she would have hidden the _real_ pearls, not a paste replica. To find an imitation so quickly suggested it had been placed there to be found. And then, there was the drawer. It moved with a silence that was—how shall I say?—supernatural! The French chalk told me that the drawer had been prepared. And since only the chambermaid had the opportunity to prepare that drawer without being seen, the conclusion was inevitable. She and the valet were partners in crime, but they did not reckon with the little grey cells of Hercule Poirot!”

“In this, my friend: they provided the ‘clue’ of the imitation necklace too quickly. It was found too easily. And the chambermaid, she was too ready to be searched! It is a mistake often made by the criminal mind—to be too eager to prove an innocence that has not yet been questioned. But it was the French chalk that was their undoing. They used it to ensure the drawer would not creak and alert the maid, but in doing so, they left the signature of their premeditation. They had method, yes, but it was a method that did not take into account the eyes of Hercule Poirot!”

“Their ‘method’ broke down, my friend, because they attempted to be too clever. The planting of the imitation necklace was a mistake; it suggested a premeditation that a simple theft would not have required. And then, there was the little matter of the French chalk. To the police, it was nothing; to Hercule Poirot, it was everything. It indicated that the drawer had been prepared for a silent and rapid operation. But the most fatal flaw of the chambermaid was her own performance. By insisting so loudly on being searched, she hoped to clear herself forever; she forgot that to the eyes of Poirot, true innocence does not need to protest with such theatricality.”

“They were too clever, Hastings. They relied upon a framing of the poor Célestine that was a little too perfect. By placing the imitation necklace in her bed, they sought to close the case at once; but in doing so, they revealed that the crime was one of premeditation and required an accomplice. Furthermore, they forgot the dust! In the empty room next door, I saw a rectangular mark upon the table near the window. It was the exact size of the jewel-case. That told me that the case had rested there while the valet worked upon the lock with his duplicate key. Had they been truly methodical, they would have dusted the table! But no, they were focused only on the brilliance of their own scheme. They did not account for the eyes of Hercule Poirot, which see not only what is there, but what *should* not be there!”

“_Mon ami_, it is a good plan to take a place as chambermaid or
valet—but you must not shirk your work. They left an empty room
undusted; and therefore, when the man put down the jewel-case on
the little table near the communicating door, it left a square
mark——”

“I remember,” I cried.

“Before, I was undecided. Then—I _knew_!” There was a moment’s
silence.

“And I’ve got my pearls,” said Mrs. Opalsen as a sort of Greek
chorus.

“Well,” I said, “I’d better have some dinner.” Poirot accompanied
me.

“This ought to mean kudos for you,” I observed.

“Kudos?” Poirot smiled. “A little, perhaps. But more than kudos, Hastings. Mr. Opalsen has a very pretty taste in gratitude. For me, however, there is the supreme satisfaction of the mind. It was a neat little problem, and it has served to exercise the grey cells. But remember, my friend, that the smallest detail—a smudge of dust, a squeak of a drawer—is enough to betray the most cunning criminal to the eyes of Hercule Poirot. And now, let us dine. I have a great desire for a _sole à la normande_, and after that, perhaps, a little _crème de menthe_ to settle the stomach and stimulate the brain.”

“My friend,” said Poirot, “it is not the kudos that matters. It is the triumph of the little grey cells! And also,” he added with a twinkle, “I have the satisfaction of knowing that I have saved the reputation of a very pretty girl. Célestine will no longer weep; she will perhaps find a more honest suitor than a thief who hides pearls in mattresses! Come, Hastings, let us dine. The salt air of Brighton, it gives one an appetite that is truly formidable—even for an old man like Hercule Poirot!”

“The kudos, it is nothing,” said Poirot, with a grand gesture. “But to have once again proved the value of the little grey cells—that is everything! And now, Hastings, let us dine. The salt air of Brighton, it has given me a most formidable appetite. I think that even the most famous jewels in the world are not so important, at this moment, as a well-cooked omelette!”

“The kudos,” said Poirot, “it is for the little grey cells. But I will tell you, Hastings, I am a little disappointed. I had hoped to find a criminal of more... distinction. To use French chalk for a drawer—it is practical, yes—but where is the imagination? Where is the art? Still,” he added, his face brightening, “I have saved the jewels of Madame, and tomorrow, if the sun shines, we shall walk upon the promenade and you shall see that even in Brighton, the fame of Hercule Poirot is not unknown!”

“Kudos?” Poirot shrugged his shoulders. “I do not know. But I have a souvenir. See, Hastings!” He reached into his pocket and produced a small velvet case. Inside was a tie-pin of a single, perfect pearl. “The grateful Mrs. Opalsen, she insisted. It is a beautiful thing, is it not? And it will remind me that even when one goes to Brighton for a ‘change of air,’ the little grey cells must never be permitted to go on strike. It was a very pretty little problem, Hastings, very pretty indeed.” He sighed with profound satisfaction and turned his attention once more to the menu.

“_Pas du tout_,” replied Poirot tranquilly. “Japp and the local
inspector will divide the credit between them. But”—he tapped his
pocket—“I have a cheque here, from Mr. Opalsen, and, how say you,
my friend? This week-end has not gone according to plan. Shall we
return here next week-end—at my expense this time?”
